en.abandonar:
From French ~abandonner~, from the Old French phrase ~a bandon~ (“at one's discretion, under one's control”), from ~a~ (“to, at”) and ~bandon~ (“power, jurisdiction, permission”). ~bandon~ goes back to Late Latin ~bannum~ (“proclamation, ban”), a borrowing from Frankish *~ban~, from Proto-Germanic *~banną~ (“proclamation, command”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰeh₂-~ (“to speak”). Cognate with English ~abandon~ and, through the Germanic root, with English ~ban~ and ~banns~.

The phrase ~a bandon~ meant “under someone's control,” hence “left to another's will.” A medieval feudal formula, ~mettre à bandon~, meant to throw one's forest open — to let anyone freely graze or cut wood there — so “to place at everyone's disposal” slid into “to give up, relinquish, forsake.” Spanish borrowed the fully formed French verb rather than inheriting it directly. The same Germanic root of “proclamation” gave ~bando~ (“edict; faction”) and ~bandido~ (“outlaw,” one proclaimed against).
en.abordar:
Spanish ~abordar~ is formed from ~a-~ (“to, toward”) and ~bordo~ (“the side of a ship; on board”), plus the verbal ending. ~bordo~ comes from ~borde~ (“edge, border”), and that from Frankish *~bord~ (“plank, board, ship's side”), a Germanic word from Proto-Germanic *~burdą~ (“board, plank”). So this is a Germanic root that entered Romance through the Franks. It is cognate with English ~board~ and ~border~, German ~Bord~, and — as a nautical borrowing — with Italian ~abbordare~ and French ~aborder~.

The literal sense is nautical: to come up alongside a ship's ~bordo~ — its side or planking — hence to board a vessel, and by a natural extension to approach or accost a person. From there Spanish developed the figurative meaning that now dominates everyday speech: to ~abordar~ a subject, a problem, or a task is to take it on, to tackle it head-on. English preserves the same maritime image in “to board” a ship and in the adverb “aboard.” From the Germanic ~bord~ Spanish also keeps a nautical and edge-related family: ~bordo~, ~borde~, ~bordear~ (“to skirt”), ~abordaje~ (“a boarding”), and ~francobordo~ (“freeboard”).
en.abrir:
From Latin ~aperīre~ (“to open, uncover”), which reached Spanish through Vulgar Latin *~operīre~ and Old Spanish ~abrir~. The deeper origin is debated. By the standard account ~aperīre~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~apweriō~, analyzed as Proto-Indo-European *~h₂epó~ (“off, away”) plus *~h₂wer-~ (“to cover, shut”) — so “to un-cover” — which would make it a near-mirror of its opposite ~operīre~ (“to cover, close”). This decomposition is plausible but not certain, and other explanations have been proposed. Cognate Romance forms include Italian ~aprire~, Portuguese ~abrir~ and French ~ouvrir~.

Whatever its ultimate source, ~aperīre~ meant “to open” throughout its history, and Spanish ~abrir~ carries that unbroken. Its past participle is the irregular ~abierto~, and from the Latin verb and its relatives Spanish draws ~abertura~ and the learned ~apertura~ (“opening,” as of a chess game or a session), ~abridor~ (“opener”) and ~aperitivo~ (“aperitif” — literally something that “opens” the appetite before a meal). Through French, the same Latin verb gave English ~aperture~ and ~overt~ (from Old French ~ouvert~, “opened”), so an ~overt~ act is, etymologically, an opened one.
en.acabar:
Spanish ~acabar~ was formed within Romance from the noun ~cabo~ (“end, tip, extremity”), with the prefix ~a-~ and the verbal ending ~-ar~; the reconstructed Vulgar Latin form is *~accapāre~. ~cabo~ comes from Latin ~caput~ (“head”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kaput-~ (“head”). That root is cognate, by Grimm’s law (k → h), with English ~head~ and German ~Haupt~; from ~caput~ itself came English ~capital~, ~captain~, and ~chief~. French ~achever~ (“to complete”) and, borrowed from it, English ~achieve~ rest on the same image.

The metaphor is bodily: the ~cabo~ is the “head” or far tip of a thing, so to ~acabar~ is to carry something to its extremity — to finish it off. Spanish put the verb to hard work: ~acabar de~ + infinitive means “to have just” done something, while the phrase ~el acabóse~ names an utter end or a disaster. From ~caput~ the language also drew ~cabeza~ (“head,” via ~capitia~), ~cabecera~ (“headboard, head of a table”), ~cabo~ (the “cape” of a coast and the military “corporal”), ~capital~, and ~capitán~. One Latin word for “head,” then, tops off a Spanish verb for “to end” — and is quietly cognate with the English ~head~ you nod.
en.acceder:
From Latin ~accēdere~ (“to approach, go toward, be added”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~cēdere~ (“to go, move, yield”). The origin of ~cēdere~ is debated: it goes back to Proto-Italic *~kezdō~, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱyesdʰ-~ (“to drive away, go away”), though some instead build it from *~ḱe~ (“here”) plus *~sed-~ (“to sit”). It is cognate with French ~accéder~, Italian ~accedere~, and Portuguese ~aceder~, and with English ~accede~ and ~access~.

Since ~cēdere~ meant “to go” or “to yield,” ~accēdere~ was “to go toward” — and from approaching came both “to assent” and “to gain entry.” Spanish ~acceder~ still carries both: to accede to a request and to access a place. The computing sense “to access” is a modern loan from English. The root threw off a large family — ~ceder~, ~conceder~, ~proceder~, ~suceder~, ~preceder~, ~retroceder~ — plus the nouns ~acceso~ and ~proceso~, its close relatives.
en.aceptar:
From Latin ~acceptāre~ (“to receive willingly, accept”), a frequentative of ~accipere~ (“to receive, take to oneself”), which is ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~capere~ (“to take, seize”), from Proto-Italic *~kapjō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~kap-~ (“to grasp, seize”). English ~heave~ is a native cognate of that root; the verb itself came into English as ~accept~, into French as ~accepter~ and into Italian as ~accettare~.

A frequentative denotes repeated or intensive action, so ~acceptāre~ was, strictly, “to keep receiving” — and the willingness in “accepting” grew out of that habitual taking-toward-oneself. Spanish ~aceptar~ narrowed it to agreeing to receive: one ~acepta~ a gift, an offer, a fate. The prolific ~capere~ root fills the language — ~aceptación~, ~captar~, ~capaz~, ~cautivo~, ~concebir~, ~recibir~, ~percibir~ and ~excepto~ — everywhere the idea of taking or holding persists.
en.acercar:
A parasynthetic verb built from ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”), the adverb ~cerca~ (“near”), and the ending ~-ar~ — literally “to make near.” ~cerca~ comes from Latin ~circā~ (“around, round about”), an adverb bound to ~circum~ (“around”) and the noun ~circus~ (“ring, circle”). ~circus~ was most likely taken from, or shared with, Ancient Greek ~kríkos~ / ~kírkos~ (“ring”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)ker-~ (“to turn, to bend”); by one account English ~ring~ belongs to the same root.

The semantic hinge is neat: what lies “round about” a spot is precisely what lies “near” it, so Latin ~circā~ “around” slid into Spanish ~cerca~ “nearby,” and the causative ~acercar~ came to mean “to bring closer.” The same word ~cerca~, as a noun, also means a “fence” — that which rings a field — beside the verb ~cercar~ “to encircle, to besiege.” Other kin of the turning-root include ~círculo~, ~circo~, ~circular~, ~cerco~, and the learned dating word ~circa~ itself.
en.aclarar:
From ~a-~ plus the adjective ~claro~ (“clear, bright”), from Latin ~clārus~, which in Vulgar Latin already spawned a verb ~clārāre~ (“to make bright”). ~Clārus~ derives from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱelh₁-~ (“to shout, call out”), the very root behind Latin ~clāmāre~ (“to cry out”) and ~calāre~ (“to summon”) and Ancient Greek ~καλέω~ (“I call”). English took the descendants as the borrowings ~clear~, ~declare~ and ~clarion~.

Here is the surprise: ~clārus~ first described sound, not light. Its earliest sense was “clear-sounding, loud, ringing” — fitting a root that meant to shout — and only afterward did it slide to “bright” (of light), then “transparent” (of water), then “evident” (of an idea). Spanish ~aclarar~ inherited that whole fan of senses: you can ~aclarar~ a doubt, ~aclarar~ the rinse water, or watch the sky ~aclarar~ at dawn. The family is large — ~claridad~, ~clarear~, ~aclaración~, ~declarar~, ~clarín~ and the given name ~Clara~ — every one a ripple from an ancient act of calling aloud.
en.acompañar:
From the prefix ~a-~ on ~compañero~/~compaña~, the family goes back to Late Latin ~companio~ (accusative ~companiōnem~), “companion, mess-mate,” a compound of ~com-~ (“with”) and ~pānis~ (“bread”) — literally one who shares bread. This ~companio~ is generally taken as a calque of Proto-West Germanic *~gahlaibō~ (“mess-mate”), first recorded in the Lex Salica, while ~pānis~ itself is traced — with some caution — to Proto-Indo-European *~peh₂-~ (“to feed, protect”). Cognates: Italian ~accompagnare~, French ~accompagner~, English ~accompany~ and ~company~.

The heart of the word is a homely image: a ~companio~ is a “bread-fellow,” the person with whom you break bread. Spanish keeps that warmth in ~compañero~ and ~compañía~, and ~acompañar~ is simply to go alongside someone, to keep them company. The bread at its center, ~pānis~, lives on directly as Spanish ~pan~, and spreads through ~panadería~ (“bakery”) and ~empanada~ (something “breaded,” wrapped in dough).
en.acordar:
From Vulgar Latin *~accordāre~ (“to bring hearts together, agree”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~cor~, stem ~cord-~ (“heart”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱḗr~, *~ḱerd-~ (“heart”). That root is the direct ancestor of English ~heart~ and German ~Herz~, and the source of Ancient Greek ~καρδία~ (“heart”) and Latin's own ~cordiālis~. Italian has the parallel ~accordare~.

Classical Latin never had *~accordāre~; Vulgar Latin coined it on the model of ~concordāre~ (“to be of one heart”), and Spanish drew from it both ~acordar~ (“to agree, resolve”) and the noun ~acuerdo~ (“agreement, accord”). The heart here is no idle metaphor: to Romans and medieval Spaniards the ~cor~ was the seat of memory as much as feeling, which is why the same organ underlies ~recordar~ (“to remember,” literally to bring back to the heart) and ~acordarse~ (“to recall”). Around them gather ~corazón~, ~cordial~, ~concordar~, ~cordura~ (“good sense”) and ~misericordia~ — a whole life of the heart.
en.actualizar:
A modern coinage, ~actual~ plus the verb-forming suffix ~-izar~. Spanish ~actual~ comes from Late Latin ~āctuālis~ (“active, practical”), from ~āctus~ (“a doing, an act”), the participle of ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive, to lead”). Cognate with English ~act~, ~agent~, and ~actual~, and with French ~actualiser~.

Here a false friend hides in plain sight: Spanish ~actual~ does not mean English “actual” (real) — it means “current, present-day,” the time that is now being enacted. So ~actualizar~ means “to make current,” that is, to update — a nuance the software age made everyday. From the same ~agere~ Spanish keeps a large family: ~acto~ (“act”), ~acción~ (“action”), ~agente~ (“agent”), ~actuar~ (“to act”), ~agenda~ (“things to be done”), and even ~examen~ (“examination,” from ~exigere~, “to weigh out, drive out”).
en.actuar:
From Medieval Latin ~actuāre~ (“to put into action, to carry out”), formed on ~actus~ (“a doing, an act”), the past participle of ~agere~ (“to drive, to lead, to do”). ~agere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~agō~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive, to set in motion”), one of the most fertile roots in the whole language family — source also of Greek ~ágō~ and, in the north, of English ~act~, ~agent~, and ~agile~. Its Romance siblings are Italian ~attuare~ and Portuguese ~atuar~.

In Latin, ~agere~ meant to drive cattle, to conduct business, to plead a case, to spend time — an enormous fan of senses all radiating from “setting something in motion.” The derived ~actuāre~ meant to make actual, to realize; Spanish ~actuar~ kept that and added the theatrical sense of “to act, to perform” and the legal sense of a court's “proceeding.” The past participle ~actus~ seeded an astonishing crowd of Spanish words — ~acto~, ~acción~, ~actor~, ~actividad~, ~actual~ (which in Spanish means “present-day,” not “real”), ~agente~, ~ágil~, and even ~agitar~ and, more distantly, ~examen~ (through ~exigere~, “to drive out, to weigh”). Few Latin roots left so wide a footprint.
en.acudir:
The origin of ~acudir~ is debated, but the account favored by Corominas derives it from Old Spanish ~recudir~ (“to rebound, respond, pay back what is owed”), with the original prefix ~re-~ later reshaped to ~a-~. ~recudir~ comes from Latin ~recutere~ (“to strike back, cause to rebound”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back”) and ~quatere~ (“to shake, to strike”). ~quatere~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~kʷeh₁t-~ (“to shake”). Through ~quatere~ and its participle it is cognate with English ~percussion~, ~concussion~, ~discuss~, and ~rescue~.

The thread that ties the senses together is response: ~recudir~ meant “to rebound” and then “to respond to a call or pay what one owes,” and from “responding to a summons” came the modern ~acudir~ — “to come when called, to show up, to turn to someone for help.” One still ~acude a~ an appointment, a call, or a person in need. Its clearest surviving cousin is ~sacudir~ (“to shake”), from a sibling compound of ~quatere~; the learned line of the same root gave Spanish ~discutir~ (“to discuss”) and ~percutir~ (“to strike, percuss”). A verb of coming, then, that began life as a verb of shaking and rebounding.
en.acusar:
From Latin ~accūsāre~ (“to call to account, to accuse”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~causa~ (“cause, reason; lawsuit, legal case”). The literal sense is to call someone toward a causa — to summon them to answer a charge in court. Spanish ~acusar~ is a learned borrowing that preserves the Latin form. It is cognate with Italian ~accusare~, French ~accuser~, Portuguese ~acusar~, and English ~accuse~, and — through ~causa~ — with English ~cause~.

The origin of ~causa~ itself is uncertain within Latin, so the chain of ~acusar~ reaches back confidently only to that noun and no further — a reminder that even a common verb can have a firm middle and a hazy floor. From the courtroom sense the verb broadened: Spanish ~acusar~ means to accuse, but also to acknowledge (~acusar~ recibo, “to acknowledge receipt”) and, tellingly, to reveal or betray — a face may ~acusar~ fatigue, letting a hidden state show. From the same ~causa~ root come ~causar~, ~acusación~, ~excusar~ (from ~excūsāre~, “to free from a charge”), and ~recusar~.
en.adaptar:
Spanish ~adaptar~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~adaptāre~ (“to fit to”), from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~aptāre~ (“to fit, adjust”), a frequentative of ~apere~ (“to fasten, attach”); its participle ~aptus~ (“fitted, suitable”) is the form that survives. The root is Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ep-~ (“to grasp, take”). Cognates run through Italian ~adattare~, French ~adapter~, and Portuguese ~adaptar~, and through ~aptus~ to English ~adapt~, ~apt~, and ~aptitude~.

The simple verb ~apere~ was already so old in Rome that it survived mainly in grammarians’ notes; the living forms were the participle ~aptus~ and the frequentative ~aptāre~. A charming offshoot is ~attitude~: through Italian ~attitudine~ and Late Latin ~aptitūdo~, an “attitude” was first the fitting posture of a figure in a painting. Spanish keeps the family in ~apto~ (“apt, fit”), ~aptitud~ (“aptitude”), ~adaptación~ (“adaptation”), ~inepto~ (“inept,” “not fitted”), and ~adaptador~ (“adapter”) — the last now most often a plug between incompatible devices, still doing exactly what the root means: making one thing fit another.
en.adecuar:
Spanish ~adecuar~ was borrowed from Latin ~adaequāre~ (“to make equal, to level”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to”) and the verb ~aequāre~ (“to make even”), which was built on the adjective ~aequus~ (“equal, level, fair”). The further origin of ~aequus~ is uncertain, so the chain is secure only back to Latin. The Latin verb gave learned, late-borrowed forms across Romance rather than an inherited popular one, so beside ~adecuar~ stand the parallel loans French ~adéquat~ and English ~adequate~, all reflecting the past participle ~adaequātus~. The same ~aequus~ also yielded Spanish ~igual~ (“equal,” through Vulgar Latin) and the openly learned ~ecuación~ and ~ecuador~.

The core idea is “to make one thing match another,” to bring it to the same level; adapting comes from equalizing. That is why ~adecuar~ today means “to adapt, fit, suit,” as in fitting a text to its audience — one levels the register to the reader. A small surprise lives in the present tense: usage divides between the older ~adecuo~ (stress on the ~a~) and the analogical ~adecúo~ (stress on the ~u~), and the Real Academia now admits both. Kin of ~aequus~ crowd the vocabulary of fairness and measure — ~igualdad~, ~ecuánime~, ~equidad~, ~equinoccio~ (“equal night”), and ~adecuado~ (“adequate, suitable”) itself — every one of them still turning on the notion of two things brought level.
en.adelantar:
From ~adelante~ (“forward, ahead”), formed with the directional prefix ~a-~ on ~delante~ (“in front”), which comes from Latin ~dē~ (“from”) plus ~in ante~ (“in front”), where ~ante~ means “before,” from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ent-~ (“front, forehead”). The Latin ~ante~ is cognate with Greek ~antí~ (“against, opposite”) and Sanskrit ~ánti~ (“before, facing”), and, through the ~and-~ element it preserves, with English ~answer~.

Layer by layer the word piled up spatial prefixes: ~ante~ (“before”) became ~in ante~, then Old Spanish ~denante~ and ~delante~, then ~adelante~ (“forward”), and finally the verb ~adelantar~ — to put or move something forward. Hence its modern senses fan out from a single image of “forward”: to advance, to overtake on the road, to pay in advance, to run fast (of a clock). Kin in Spanish include ~delantero~, ~antes~, ~antaño~ and ~adelanto~.
en.admitir:
From Latin ~admittere~ (“to let in, allow to enter”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~mittere~ (“to send, let go, release”), from Proto-Indo-European *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, remove”), an extension of *~mey-~ (“to change”); its past participle ~admissus~ gives the Spanish noun ~admisión~. English carries the borrowings ~admit~, ~mission~, ~permit~ and ~message~.

The semantic path is neat: from “exchange,” the verb ~mittere~ moved to “give, let go” and finally “send,” while ~admittere~ layered on a sense of direction — to send toward and let across the threshold — hence “to admit, allow in,” and by a short moral step “to accept, concede as true.” Spanish keeps both senses in ~admitir~. From the same ~mittere~ comes a sprawling family: the plain verb ~meter~ (“to put in”), plus ~prometer~ (“to promise”), ~comprometer~, ~permitir~, ~remitir~, ~someter~ and the noun ~mensaje~ (“message”) — all, at bottom, acts of sending and letting go.
en.adoptar:
From Latin ~adoptāre~ (“to choose for oneself, to take by choice, to adopt”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + ~optāre~ (“to choose, to wish for”). The origin of ~optāre~ is uncertain; De Vaan links it to Proto-Italic *~opeje-~ (“to choose, to grab”) and a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to choose, to seize,” comparing Hittite ~ēpzi~ (“takes, seizes”) — but the reconstruction is debated. Cognate with Italian ~adottare~ and French ~adopter~, and with English ~adopt~, ~opt~, and ~option~.

In Roman law ~adoptāre~ was a precise term: the formal act by which a paterfamilias took an outsider — often an adult male — into his family as a legal heir, a practice so central that emperors chose their successors this way. The core verb ~optāre~ simply meant “to choose,” and the prefix ~ad-~ points the choosing toward oneself. Spanish carries both the legal sense (adopting a child) and a figurative one (to ~adoptar~ a measure, a posture, a custom). From the same ~optāre~ come Spanish ~optar~ (“to opt”), ~opción~ (“option”), ~optativo~ (“optional”), ~adoptivo~ (“adoptive”), and ~cooptar~ (“to co-opt”).
en.adquirir:
From Latin ~acquīrere~ (also ~adquīrere~, “to acquire, get”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~quaerere~ (“to seek, look for, ask”). The deep origin of ~quaerere~ is uncertain, and no secure Proto-Indo-European root is established for it. Spanish ~adquirir~ is a learned borrowing that kept the Latin ~-quir-~ stem visible; the same verb gave French ~acquérir~, Italian ~acquisire~, and English ~acquire~.

The Latin verb meant literally “to seek in addition,” to get something over and above what one already had, and that sense of gaining by effort survives in modern ~adquirir~. Its everyday sibling in Spanish is ~querer~, also from ~quaerere~: where the acquisitive prefix pulled one branch toward “getting,” the bare verb drifted from “seeking” to “wanting” and “loving.” From the same ~quaerere~ family Spanish also inherited ~cuestión~, ~requerir~, ~inquirir~, ~pesquisa~, ~exquisito~, and the noun ~adquisición~.
en.advertir:
From Latin ~advertere~ (“to turn toward, direct one’s attention to”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~vertere~ (“to turn”); Spanish shifted it into the -ir conjugation. ~vertere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~wertō~ and from the Proto-Indo-European root *~wert-~ (“to turn, rotate”), a highly productive root that surfaces across the family. Through Latin it gives Spanish and English a legion of “turn” words; through Germanic the same *~wert-~ yields English ~-ward~ (“turned toward,” as in toward, forward) and the verb ~worth~ in the archaic sense “to become.” Romance cognates of the verb itself include French ~avertir~ and Italian ~avvertire~, both, like Spanish ~advertir~, meaning “to warn, notify.”

The literal image behind ~advertir~ is turning: to “turn toward” something is to notice it, and to make another person turn toward it is to warn or point it out. Spanish holds both halves of that logic at once — ~advertir~ means “to notice, perceive” and “to warn, caution,” so context decides whether you have spotted the danger or flagged it for someone else. The English doublet ~advertise~ took the “make others turn toward” sense down the commercial road to mean “publicize.” From the same *~wert-~ Spanish is thick with descendants: ~verter~ (“to pour”), ~convertir~, ~invertir~, ~divertir~ (literally “to turn aside”), ~advertencia~ (“a warning”), ~verso~ and ~versión~, and the borrowed ~universo~ — the whole “turned into one.”
en.afectar:
From Latin ~affectāre~ (“to strive after, aim at”), the frequentative of ~afficere~ (“to influence, affect”), itself ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~facere~ (“to do, make”). ~facere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~fakiō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place, do”). Spanish took the learned ~afectar~ straight from written Latin, yet the very same ~affectāre~ also travelled the popular, spoken road and surfaced as the doublet ~afeitar~ (once “to adorn, to make up,” today simply “to shave”). Cognate with Italian ~affettare~, French ~affecter~, Portuguese ~afetar~, and English ~affect~.

The frequentative sense — to do something repeatedly or pointedly — is why ~afectar~ still splits two ways in Spanish: to affect or influence (« la sequía afectó la cosecha ») and to feign or put on airs (« afectar indiferencia »), the latter preserving the Latin idea of studiously aiming at an effect. The shared root *~dʰeh₁-~ is one of the most fertile in the language, and beyond ~facere~ it seeded ~hacer~, ~hecho~, ~fábrica~, and — through ~afficere~ — the nouns ~afecto~, ~afición~, and ~afectación~.
en.afirmar:
From Latin ~affirmāre~ (“to make firm, strengthen”), from ~ad-~ + ~firmāre~ (“to make firm”), from ~firmus~ (“firm, strong, steadfast”), from Proto-Italic *~fermos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰer-~ (“to hold, support”). Cognate with French ~affirmer~, Italian ~affermare~, Portuguese ~afirmar~ and English ~affirm~; through the root, with Sanskrit ~dharma~ (“that which upholds, law, duty”).

To affirm is literally “to make firm” — to hold a statement steady. Latin ~firmus~ gave Spanish a broad family: ~firme~, ~firma~ (a signature, what one holds to), ~firmar~ and ~confirmar~. The negative ~infirmus~ (“not firm, weak”) yielded ~enfermo~ (“sick”), so the sick person is, etymologically, one who has lost firmness. The PIE root *~dʰer-~ also underlies the Indian ~dharma~, the cosmic order that “holds” all things in place.
en.agradecer:
Spanish ~agradecer~ builds on Old Spanish ~gradecer~ (“to be thankful”) with the prefix ~a-~. The base descends from an inchoative Vulgar Latin *~grātēscere~, formed on Latin ~grātus~ (“pleasing, thankful”), from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷerH-~ (“to praise, welcome”). The adjective ~grātus~ also gave the noun ~grātia~ (“favor, thanks”), whence Spanish ~gracia~, English ~grace~, and — via ~ad grātum~, “to one’s liking” — English ~agree~.

The ~-ēscere~ ending marked an inchoative, “to come to find pleasing,” which in Spanish settled into the everyday “to thank.” Its most useful quirk is that ~agradecer~ takes the thing as object — one thanks a favor, ~agradezco tu ayuda~ — where English needs a preposition. The same root spread widely: ~gratitud~ (“gratitude”), ~agradable~ (“pleasant”), ~grato~ (“agreeable”), ~gratis~ and ~gratuito~ (“free of charge”), and ~congratular~ (“to congratulate,” literally “to rejoice together”).
en.agregar:
From Latin ~aggregāre~ (“to add to a flock, gather together, join”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~gregāre~ (“to herd, gather into a flock”), the verb of ~grex~ (genitive ~gregis~, “flock, herd”). The noun goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~ger-~ (“to gather, come together”), which also gave Greek ~ageírō~ (“I gather”) and ~agorá~ (the gathering place, the marketplace). Through the Latin ~grex~ branch, ~agregar~ is cognate with a cluster of English words — ~gregarious~, ~congregate~, ~aggregate~, and ~segregate~. Italian ~aggregare~ and Portuguese ~agregar~ match it directly.

The whole family is about the flock. To ~agregar~ is to add one more to the group — the plainest modern sense, “to add.” Spanish keeps the herd-image alive in ~grey~ (“flock; congregation of the faithful”), ~congregar~ (“to congregate”), ~segregar~ (“to separate from the flock”), and ~disgregar~ (“to scatter, break up”). The most vivid relative is English ~egregious~: Latin ~egregius~ meant “out of the flock” (~ex~ + ~grex~) and so “outstanding, distinguished” — a compliment in Latin that soured in English into ‘outstandingly bad.’ Spanish preferred the neutral path: an ~agregado~ is simply something added, or an embassy’s attaché.
en.ajustar:
Formed within Romance from the prefix ~a-~ and ~justo~ (“just, exact, right”), from Latin ~iūstus~, itself from ~iūs~ (“law, right”), a noun of debated Indo-European origin. The Late or Vulgar Latin verb is reconstructed as *~adiūstāre~ (“to make right, fit exactly”). Cognate with Italian ~aggiustare~, French ~ajuster~, and Portuguese ~ajustar~; English ~adjust~ was borrowed through Old French from the same verb.

The thread of meaning runs through “right, exact”: to ~ajustar~ is to bring a thing into just proportion — to fit two parts so they meet exactly, to tighten a screw, to settle an account, to agree on a price. From the same ~justo~ Spanish built a broad family: ~ajuste~ (“adjustment, settlement”), ~ajustado~ (“tight, close-fitting”), ~reajustar~ (“to readjust”), and, sharing the deeper root, ~justicia~ (“justice”), ~justo~ (“fair; exact”), and ~ajusticiar~ (“to execute a condemned person,” literally to do justice upon). The financial ~ajuste de cuentas~ (“settling of accounts”) preserves the original sense of making two sides balance exactly.
en.alcanzar:
The origin is debated, but the favored account traces ~alcanzar~ to a Vulgar Latin *~incalciāre~ (“to tread on someone's heels, to pursue”), a verb built on Latin ~calx~ (“heel”). Old Spanish had ~alcanzar~ beside a more transparent ~encalzar~, and the shift of the prefix to ~al-~ is itself uncertain — it may reflect the influence of Latin ~ad~, of the Spanish contraction ~al~, or, by one hypothesis, of the Arabic article ~al-~. Whatever reshaped the head, the Romance kin agree on the body: Portuguese ~alcançar~, Galician ~alcanzar~, and Catalan ~encalçar~ all point back to the same heel-chasing verb.

The image behind the word is vivid: to ~alcanzar~ was first to chase so close that you trod on the runner's ~calx~, his heel — and then, naturally, to catch him, to reach him, to attain your goal. Spanish kept the whole arc of that metaphor, from physical overtaking (« alcanzar la meta ») to abstract achievement (« alcanzar un acuerdo ») to sheer sufficiency (« el dinero no alcanza »). From the same Latin ~calx~ come ~calzar~ (“to put on footwear”), ~calcetín~ (“sock”), ~coz~ (“a kick”), and ~recalcar~ (“to stress, to press down on”).
en.alejar:
A Spanish formation from the prefix ~a-~ and the adverb ~lejos~ (“far”), with the verbal ending ~-ar~. ~Lejos~ descends from Latin ~laxius~ (“more loosely, more widely apart”), the comparative adverb of ~laxus~ (“loose, slack, wide”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sleg-~ (“to be slack, to be languid”). Through that root ~laxus~ is cognate with English ~slack~ and ~lax~, and within Spanish with ~laxo~, ~relajar~ and ~dejar~.

The image hidden in ~lejos~ is spatial slackness: Latin ~laxius~ meant “more loosely, more spread out,” so to be far away was, literally, to be more loosely spaced — and ~alejar~ is to make something take up that slack distance, to move it away. From the same “loosen” idea Spanish also built ~dejar~ (“to let go, to leave”), from Latin ~laxāre~ (“to loosen, to release”), so that letting go and being far apart are quietly the same gesture. Nearby in the family stand ~lejano~, ~lejanía~, ~alejamiento~, ~relajar~, ~laxo~ and ~laxante~ — a cluster all turning on the idea of looseness and release.
en.amar:
From Latin ~amāre~ (“to love”), inherited directly and preserved across Romance: Italian ~amare~, Portuguese ~amar~, Catalan ~amar~, and Old French ~amer~ (surviving in modern ~aimer~). Beyond Latin the origin is genuinely uncertain. One traditional view treats ~amāre~ as a nursery or affectionate word, alongside ~amita~ (“aunt”) and ~amīcus~ (“friend”), from a Lallwort root *~am-~ of the babbling type also seen in “mama.” A different proposal, favored by de Vaan, connects it to a Proto-Indo-European *~h₂emh₃-~ (“to seize, take hold of”), so that “to love” would have grown from “to take by the hand.” The sources disagree; treat the deep root as debated.

Whatever its ultimate source, ~amāre~ named the warmest and most voluntary kind of love, distinct from the desire of Latin ~cupere~; Latin ~amor~ passed intact into Spanish ~amor~. Spanish kept ~amar~ as the elevated, literary verb for love — one ~ama~ God, a country, or a beloved in poetry — while everyday affection is carried by ~querer~ (“to want, to love”). From the same stem flow a large and tender family: ~amor~, ~amante~ (“lover”), ~amado~ (“beloved”), ~amistad~ (“friendship,” through ~amīcus~), ~amable~ (“kind”), ~amigo~, ~enamorar~ (“to make someone fall in love”) and ~desamor~ (“lovelessness”). French ~amateur~ — one who does a thing for love of it — reached Spanish and English from this same root.
en.ampliar:
From Latin ~ampliāre~ (“to widen, enlarge”), a verb built on the adjective ~amplus~ (“large, spacious, ample”). Where ~amplus~ itself comes from is uncertain. De Vaan sets out the leading proposal — a derivation from Proto-Italic *~amlo-~ (“seizable, graspable”), tied to a noun ~ampla~ (“handle, grip; opportunity”) and ultimately to a Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂emh₃-~ (“to take hold of”), the same root proposed behind ~amāre~ (“to love”) — but he flags weaknesses in it, so the origin is best treated as unresolved rather than settled. Spanish took ~ampliar~ from Latin as a learned word; its everyday cousin ~amplio~ (“wide, roomy”) descends from the same ~amplus~, as do French ~ample~ and English ~ample~.

The meaning has stayed remarkably close to home: ~ampliar~ is simply “to make ~amplio~,” to widen, extend, or enlarge — a room, a business, a photograph, a body of rights. Spanish uses it where English splits the job among “expand,” “extend,” “enlarge,” and “broaden.” The photographic sense gave the noun ~ampliación~ (“an enlargement,” both the act and the enlarged print). The adjective ~amplio~ carries the spatial idea into everyday speech, and the adverb ~ampliamente~ means “widely, amply, at length.” If De Vaan’s tentative link to *~h₂emh₃-~ (“to take hold of”) is right, there is a quiet irony in it: a word now all about opening things up would share its deepest root with ~amāre~, “to grasp” having drifted toward both embracing and enlarging.
en.analizar:
From ~análisis~ (“analysis”), a verb back-formed (via French ~analyser~) from the noun, which came through Latin ~analysis~ from Ancient Greek ~análusis~ (“a dissolving, a loosening-up”). That word joins ~aná-~ (“up, throughout”) to ~lúsis~ (“a loosening”), a noun of ~lúō~ (“to loosen, release, dissolve”), from Proto-Indo-European *~lewh₁-~ (“to cut off, separate, free”). English ~loose~ and ~-less~ are native cognates of that root.

The Greek image is chemical before it is logical: to analyse is to dissolve a whole into its parts, to loosen the knot. Spanish ~analizar~ carries that from laboratory to reasoning — one ~analiza~ a compound or an argument alike. From the same ~lúō~ root, borrowed through Greek, Spanish holds a technical family in which the “loosening” is still visible: ~diálisis~ (a dissolving-apart), ~parálisis~ (a loosening beside, i.e. disablement), ~catálisis~ and ~electrólisis~. The relatives ~análisis~, ~analista~ and ~analítico~ complete the set.
en.andar:
The origin is debated. Spanish ~andar~, like Italian ~andare~ and French ~aller~ (all meaning “to go”), descends from Vulgar Latin, but no single source is agreed. The most widely favored account derives it from Latin ~ambulāre~ (“to walk, travel about”): Corominas proposes that ~ambulāre~ was reduced in casual speech to *~amlāre~ and then to *~andāre~. A competing account starts instead from a Vulgar Latin *~ambitāre~ (a frequentative of ~ambīre~, “to go around”), which some hold explains the Spanish, Portuguese, and Italian forms better than ~ambulāre~ does.

Whatever the exact etymon, the deep sense is “to go about, walk around,” and Spanish ~andar~ kept a wide range: to walk, to function (a clock ~anda~ or not), and to be in a state (~andar~ cansado, “to go about tired”). If ~ambulāre~ is the source, ~andar~ shares its root with the borrowings ~ambulancia~, ~ambulante~, ~deambular~, and ~preámbulo~, and with English ~amble~ and ~ambulance~ — though, given the dispute, that kinship holds only under the ~ambulāre~ hypothesis. From ~andar~ itself Spanish built ~andén~ (“platform”) and ~andanza~ (“fortune, adventure”).
en.animar:
From Latin ~animāre~ (“to give life to, enliven”), a verb formed on ~anima~ (“breath, air, soul, life”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂enh₁-~ (“to breathe, blow”). Italian ~animare~, French ~animer~ and Portuguese ~animar~ share the same descent, and through the root ~anima~ is cognate with Ancient Greek ~ἄνεμος~ (“wind”) and Sanskrit ~ánila~ (“wind, air”). The learned English ~animate~ and the everyday ~animal~ (originally “a breathing being”) come from the same Latin family.

The metaphor was already alive in Latin: to ~animāre~ someone was literally to breathe life or spirit into them, and Spanish kept that thread — to ~animar~ a friend is to put ~ánimo~ (“spirit, courage”) back into them. The reflexive ~animarse~ means to cheer up or to work up the nerve to do something. From ~anima~ Spanish inherited a remarkable pair of doublets: the learned ~ánima~ (“soul in purgatory”) and the popular, everyday ~alma~ (“soul”), whose ~l~ arose from the same Latin word by regular sound change. The root fanned out into ~ánimo~, ~animoso~, ~unánime~ (“of one mind”), ~magnánimo~ (“great-souled”), ~desanimar~ (“to dishearten”) and ~reanimar~ (“to revive”).
en.anunciar:
From Latin ~annuntiāre~ (“to announce, report, bring word”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~nuntiāre~ (“to report, make known”), the verb of the noun ~nuntius~ (“messenger; message, news”). The deeper origin of ~nuntius~ is disputed. An old and appealing account contracted it from *~noventios~ and tied it to ~novus~ (“new”), making the messenger a bringer of news; de Vaan rejects that derivation on formal grounds and tentatively prefers a Proto-Indo-European root *~newH-~ (“to shout, cry out”), which would make ~nuntius~ literally “the one who calls out.” Either way, the Spanish verb ~anunciar~ comes down from ~annuntiāre~ through regular sound change.

Whatever its ultimate root, ~nuntius~ was the ordinary Roman word for the bearer of a message, and its verb ~nuntiāre~ spawned a whole prefixed set that Spanish inherited almost intact: ~anunciar~ (“to announce,” to bring word toward someone), ~denunciar~ (“to denounce,” to report against), ~pronunciar~ (“to pronounce, declare forth”), and ~renunciar~ (“to renounce,” to report back that one gives something up). The noun lives on as ~anuncio~ (“announcement, advertisement”) and, in the Church, as ~nuncio~ (“nuncio,” the pope’s ambassador — still, faithfully, a messenger). English ~announce~, ~denounce~, ~pronounce~, and ~renounce~ mirror the Spanish set step for step.
en.aparecer:
From Latin ~appārēscere~, an inchoative (“to begin to appear”) built on ~appārēre~ (“to appear, to become visible”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~pārēre~ (“to come forth, to be visible”). The ultimate Proto-Indo-European source of ~pārēre~ is uncertain, with more than one reconstruction proposed. Cognate with French ~apparaître~, Italian ~apparire~, and English ~appear~ and ~apparent~.

Latin ~pārēre~ had a second, everyday meaning — “to obey,” to present oneself when summoned — and it seeded a nicely paired set of Spanish verbs. From the plain inchoative ~pārēscere~ came ~parecer~ (“to seem, to appear to be”), while the prefixed ~appārēscere~ gave ~aparecer~ (“to appear, to show up”): to seem is to be merely visible; to appear is to arrive into sight. The family also includes ~aparición~ (“appearance, apparition”), ~aparente~ (“apparent”), and the formal ~comparecer~ (“to appear in court”) — where the old sense of presenting oneself on command still lingers.
en.aplicar:
From Latin ~applicāre~ (“to attach to, to bring toward, to fold onto”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”). ~plicāre~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to fold”), an enlargement of *~pel-~ (“to fold”). It is cognate with Latin ~plectere~, Ancient Greek ~plékō~ (“I plait”), and, through Germanic, English ~fold~ and ~ply~. The compound survives in Italian ~applicare~, French ~appliquer~, and Portuguese ~aplicar~.

The literal image is of folding one thing onto another; from “laying on” came the figurative “to devote oneself to” and “to put into practice.” The humble root hides a surprise: ~plicāre~ also meant to fold up a ship's sails on nearing the coast, and Vulgar Latin turned that “coming to shore” into a general verb of arrival — the direct source of Spanish ~llegar~ (“to arrive”) and Portuguese ~chegar~. Relatives of the fold-root abound in Spanish: ~plegar~, ~pliegue~, ~plegaria~, ~explicar~, ~complicar~, ~replicar~, and ~emplear~ (from ~implicāre~).
en.aportar:
Two originally distinct verbs fell together in ~aportar~. One is nautical: ~aportar~ (“to reach port”), from Latin ~portus~ (“harbor”). The other is the modern everyday sense, “to contribute,” from ~apportāre~ — ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~portāre~ (“to carry”) — literally to carry something toward someone. But the two are cousins, not strangers: ~portus~ (“harbor”), ~porta~ (“gate, passage”), and ~portāre~ (“to carry”) all descend from Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to cross over, pass through, bring across”). Through the Germanic branch of that root run English ~ford~ and ~fare~; through Latin come English ~port~ and ~portable~.

The shared image is movement across a threshold — a harbor, a gate, a load carried over. From the ‘carry’ sense Spanish built a broad family: ~portar~ (“to carry, bear”), ~aportación~ (“contribution”), ~transportar~, ~importar~, and ~exportar~. From the ‘harbor’ sense come ~puerto~ (“port”) and, by regular diphthongization, ~puerta~ (“door”). A quiet gem is ~oportuno~ (“opportune”): Latin ~opportūnus~ meant ‘(a wind) driving toward the harbor,’ hence favorable — so an ~oportuno~ moment is one that, like a good wind, carries you safely in. To ~aportar~ today, whatever the harbor, is still to bring your share across.
en.apoyar:
Spanish ~apoyar~ was probably borrowed from Italian ~appoggiare~ and reshaped around the native ~poyo~ (“a stone bench”); it is first attested in 1496. The Italian verb goes back to Vulgar Latin *~appodiāre~, a compound of ~ad-~ (“onto”) and ~podium~ (“raised platform, support”), which Latin itself had taken from Ancient Greek ~pódion~ (“little base”), the diminutive of ~poús~ (“foot”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ped-~ (“foot”). Literally, then, to ~apoyar~ is “to set something on a footing.” It is cognate with French ~appuyer~ and Portuguese ~apoiar~, and — through the foot-root — with English ~foot~ and ~pew~, the last of these having reached English from that same ~podium~ by way of Old French.

The picture behind the verb is bodily: to ~apoyar~ is to lean one thing against another so that it will not fall — to give it something to rest on. From that physical leaning Spanish widened the meaning to “to back, endorse, second,” so that today one may ~apoyar~ a friend, a motion, or a candidate. The Greek “foot” at the root is still visible in the noun ~poyo~ (“stone seat built against a wall”), a homely doublet of the learned ~podio~. Other relatives include ~apoyo~ (“support”) and the musical ~apoyatura~ (“appoggiatura, a leaning grace note”), which Spanish and Italian both built on the same idea of leaning. And the same Indo-European *~ped-~ (“foot”) underlies a whole crowd of words, from Spanish ~pie~ and ~peatón~ to English ~pedal~.
en.apreciar:
From Late Latin ~appretiāre~ (“to value, set a price on”), from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~pretium~ (“price, value, worth”), from Proto-Indo-European *~preti-~, from *~per-~ (“forward, against, in exchange”), with a core notion of equivalence or recompense. Cognate with Italian ~apprezzare~, French ~apprécier~, and Portuguese ~apreciar~. English ~appreciate~ comes from the same Late Latin verb; and from ~pretium~, by various routes, English also has ~price~, ~precious~, ~prize~, and ~appraise~.

The starting point is commercial — ~appretiāre~ meant to appraise, to fix a price — and Spanish ~apreciar~ still holds both a measuring sense (“to appraise, gauge, perceive a difference”) and an affective one (“to value, esteem, be fond of”): we appraise a jewel and cherish a friend with the same verb. Its opposite is built transparently as ~despreciar~ (“to despise,” literally to price down). The family includes ~precio~ (“price”), ~aprecio~ (“esteem”), ~apreciación~ (“appreciation, assessment”), ~apreciable~ (“appreciable, considerable”), ~precioso~ (“precious, lovely”), and ~preciar~ (“to prize”), with the reflexive ~preciarse de~ meaning “to pride oneself on.”
en.aprender:
From Latin ~apprehendere~ (“to seize, grasp”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + ~prehendere~ (“to grasp, take hold of”), itself ~prae-~ (“before”) plus a ~-hendere~ from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵʰend-~ (“to seize, take”). Cognate with French ~apprendre~, Italian ~apprendere~ and Portuguese ~aprender~; through the same root, with Ancient Greek ~khandánō~ (“to hold, contain”) and — via Germanic — English ~get~.

The mental leap “to seize with the mind” happened already in Latin: ~apprehendere~ moved from grabbing physically to grasping an idea, and by Old French ~aprendre~ that figurative sense was the only one left. So to learn is, etymologically, to “get hold of” knowledge. The learned doublet ~aprehender~ preserves the literal “seize, arrest” meaning. From the same root: ~aprendiz~, ~aprendizaje~, ~comprender~, ~emprender~, ~sorprender~ and ~prender~.
en.aprobar:
From Latin ~approbāre~ (“to approve, to sanction”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~probāre~ (“to test, to try, to find good”), itself from the adjective ~probus~ (“good, upright, honest”). Through Proto-Italic, ~probus~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European, joining ~pro-~ (“forth, in front”) with the root *~bʰuH-~ (“to be, to grow”) — roughly “growing well, standing straight.” Its Romance kin include Italian ~approvare~, French ~approuver~, and Portuguese ~aprovar~, and through the same Latin stock it matches English ~approve~, ~prove~, and ~probe~.

In Latin ~probāre~ first meant “to test the quality of” a thing, and only by extension “to judge it good.” That double sense survives in Spanish ~probar~, which still means both “to taste, to try” and “to prove.” The prefixed ~aprobar~ narrowed to the favorable verdict — to pass a student, to ratify a law. The same family seeded ~prueba~ (“proof, test”), ~probable~, ~comprobar~ (“to verify”), ~probeta~ (“test tube”), and ~aprobación~. English keeps the fork too: to ~probe~ is to put to the test, while to ~approve~ is to bless the result — the two halves of one Latin idea, trying a thing and finding it worthy.
en.aprovechar:
From ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “toward”) plus the noun ~provecho~ (“benefit, profit”) and the verbal suffix ~-ar~. ~Provecho~ descends from Latin ~prōfectus~ (“progress, profit”), the past participle of ~prōficere~ (“to advance, make headway”), itself ~pro-~ (“forward”) plus ~facere~ (“to make, do”). The Latin cluster ~-ct-~ regularly palatalized to ~-ch-~ and the ~f~ voiced to ~v~, so ~prōfectus~ became ~provecho~. Cognate with English ~profit~ and French ~profit~.

The verb ~aprovechar~ means literally to “put to profit,” to turn a thing or a moment to good account, and the reflexive ~aprovecharse~ took on the pointed sense of taking advantage of someone. The toast ¡Buen ~provecho~! at table — “may it do you good” — preserves the older, wider meaning of ~provecho~ as benefit rather than mere money. From the same ~facere~ Spanish drew a huge family, among them ~hacer~, ~afición~, ~perfecto~, and ~aprovechamiento~.
en.apuntar:
From ~a-~ plus ~punto~ (“point, dot”), which descends from Latin ~punctum~ (“a prick, a puncture, a point”), the neuter past participle of ~pungere~ (“to prick, to pierce”). ~pungere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~pewǵ-~ (“to prick, to punch”). It is cognate with Italian ~appuntare~ and French ~pointer~, and — through ~pungere~ and its participle — with English ~point~, ~puncture~, ~pungent~, and ~poignant~, all of them sharp in one way or another.

The core idea is making a point or mark, and ~apuntar~ fanned out from it into a startling spread of senses: to aim a weapon (to bring it to a point on a target), to point at something, to jot down (to set a point of ink on paper), and — in the theatre — to prompt an actor, which is why a prompter is an ~apuntador~. From the same ~punctum~ Spanish also drew ~punto~ (“point”), ~punta~ (“tip”), ~puntual~ (“punctual”), ~puntería~ (“aim”), ~apunte~ (“note”), and ~puntuar~ (“to punctuate”). The tiny prick of ~pungere~ thus points, notes, aims, and punctuates all at once.
en.armar:
From Latin ~armāre~ (“to arm, equip with weapons”), a denominal verb from ~arma~ (“weapons, tools, equipment”). ~arma~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂er-~ (“to fit together, join”), via a form *~h₂(e)rmos~ (“that which is fitted”) — so weapons were, literally, the things fitted together, the gear. The root is richly attested: cognate with Ancient Greek ~ararískō~ (“to fit together”) and Sanskrit ~áram~ (“fittingly”). Within Latin it also produced ~ars~ (“skill, art”) and ~artus~ (“joint, limb”). The Romance verbs run parallel: Italian ~armare~, French ~armer~, Portuguese ~armar~.

The core image never left: to ~armar~ is to fit pieces together, and Spanish keeps that concrete sense vividly — one can ~armar~ a bookshelf, a tent, or an argument, not only an army. From the sense of fitting and joining, the vocabulary of skill and order also grew: the same root underlies ~arte~ (“art”), ~artículo~ (“article; joint”), ~armonía~ (Greek for “a fitting-together”) and ~arma~ itself. Colloquial idiom pushed the “assemble” sense toward chaos, too: ~armar~ un lío or ~armar~ un escándalo is to kick up a fuss — to assemble a mess. From ~armāre~ come directly ~armario~ (“wardrobe,” a place to store gear), ~armada~ (“fleet”) and ~armadura~ (“armor”).
en.asegurar:
From ~a-~ plus ~seguro~ plus the verbal ending ~-ar~ — literally “to make secure.” ~seguro~ comes from Latin ~sēcūrus~ (“free from care, safe”), a compound of ~sē-~ (“without”) and ~cūra~ (“care, concern”). Cognate with French ~assurer~ and ~sûr~, and with English ~secure~ and ~sure~ — the latter two a famous doublet, ~secure~ borrowed straight from Latin and ~sure~ worn down through Old French.

So to assure or ensure is, at root, to remove someone’s cares. The Latin ~sēcūrus~ described a mind at peace, untroubled; from that inner calm the word drifted toward outward safety and reliability. Spanish keeps both threads in ~seguro~, which is at once “safe,” “sure,” and (as a noun) “insurance” — the contract that buys freedom from worry. Relatives include ~seguridad~ (“security”) and, from the same ~cūra~, the verb ~curar~ (“to cure, to care for”) and the noun ~cura~ (“cure,” and also “priest,” the one charged with the care of souls).
en.asignar:
From Latin ~assignāre~ (“to mark out, allot, assign”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~signāre~ (“to mark”), from ~signum~ (“sign, mark, standard”). The deeper root is disputed: ~signum~ is traced either to Proto-Indo-European *~sek-~ (“to cut,” a mark cut in) or to *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow,” the standard a legion follows), and the sources do not settle which. From ~assignāre~ come Italian ~assegnare~, Portuguese ~assinar~, and French ~assigner~; from ~signum~ itself, English ~sign~.

To assign was originally to mark something out and set it apart for a purpose — a plot of land, a duty, a share. Spanish shows the usual split between a popular and a learned line from ~signum~: the inherited ~seña~ and ~señal~ beside the bookish ~signo~, ~signar~, and ~designar~. A charming descendant is ~asignatura~ — a school “subject,” literally something “assigned” to be studied — and ~insignia~, ~consigna~, and ~diseñar~ (“to design,” to mark out a plan) belong to the same clan. Whether the root first meant a cut or a thing-to-follow may stay unresolved, but either way ~asignar~ has always been about marking one thing off for another.
en.asistir:
From Latin ~assistere~ (“to stand by, take one’s place beside”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~sistere~ (“to cause to stand, to take a stand, to halt”). ~sistere~ is a reduplicated form built on ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”) — the same root behind ~estar~. It gave Italian ~assistere~, French ~assister~, and English ~assist~; and through ~sistere~ it is cognate with English ~exist~, ~insist~, ~resist~, ~consist~, and ~persist~.

To “stand beside” someone is to be there both for support and as a witness, and ~asistir~ split along exactly that line. In Spanish (as in French ~assister~) it chiefly means “to attend, to be present”: one ~asiste a~ a class or a concert. But it also keeps the “stand-by-to-help” sense in ~asistir~ (“to assist”) and in ~asistencia~ (“assistance; attendance”) and ~asistente~ (“assistant”). English ~assist~, by contrast, narrowed to helping alone — a tidy false-friend trap. The ~sistere~ family stands tall across Spanish: ~existir~, ~insistir~, ~resistir~, ~consistir~, ~persistir~, ~desistir~, and ~subsistir~, every one of them, at root, a way of standing.
en.asociar:
From Latin ~associāre~ (“to join to, unite with”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward,” assimilated to ~as-~) and ~sociāre~ (“to join, ally”), the verb built on ~socius~ (“companion, ally, partner”). ~socius~ meant literally “a follower” and descends from Proto-Indo-European *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”) — the same root that gave Latin ~sequī~ (“to follow”). The cognate web is wide: through ~sequī~ English took (by borrowing) ~sequence~, ~sequel~, ~second~ (“the following one”) and ~pursue~. The learned Romance descendants of the compound include Italian ~associare~, French ~associer~ and Portuguese ~associar~.

The logic is transparent: companions are those who follow together, and to associate is to make someone a ~socius~, a fellow-goer. From ~socius~ Spanish keeps ~socio~ (“partner, member”), ~social~, ~sociedad~ (“society”), ~asociación~ (“association”) and ~asociado~ (“associate”). The deeper root *~sekʷ-~, through ~sequī~ and its participle ~secūtus~, fanned out enormously: ~seguir~ (“to follow”), ~seguido~, ~secuencia~ (“sequence”), ~consecuencia~ (“consequence”), ~perseguir~ (“to pursue”), ~ejecutar~ (“to execute, follow through”) and even ~segundo~ (“second,” the following one). To associate ideas, then, is to let one “follow” another — companionship written into cognition itself.
en.asumir:
From Latin ~assūmere~ (“to take up, adopt, claim”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~sūmere~ (“to take up”), itself ~sub-~ (“up from below”) plus ~emere~ (“to take, buy”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁em-~ (“to take, distribute”). It is cognate with French ~assumer~, Italian ~assumere~, and Portuguese ~assumir~, and with the Latin-derived English ~assume~; through ~emere~ it is also kin to English ~example~ and ~exempt~.

In Latin ~emere~ first meant “to take” and only later specialized to “to buy” — a shift from grasping a thing to grasping it by purchase. Its compound ~sūmere~ kept the “take up” sense, and ~asumir~ today means to take something on: a duty, a role, a cost. The ~sūmere~ line gave Spanish ~consumir~, ~presumir~, and ~resumir~, while the older ~emere~ surfaces in ~ejemplo~ (from ~exemplum~, “a sample taken out”), ~redimir~, and ~eximir~. What unites them all is the plain, physical act of taking.
en.atacar:
From Italian ~attaccare~ (“to attach, to join,” and in ~attaccare battaglia~, “to join battle”), taken into Spanish in the sixteenth century as a military term. The Italian verb is generally linked to a Germanic word for a stake or post — Gothic *~stakka~, also the source of Spanish ~estaca~ — the idea being to fasten one thing to another; but the details of that descent are disputed. From the same Italian source come French ~attaquer~ and, as doublets, English ~attach~ and ~attack~.

The journey from a fence post to open warfare runs through the idea of fastening: to ~attaccare~ was to fix things together, and ~attaccare battaglia~ was to “knit” two armies into combat. Spanish borrowed only the martial sense, so ~atacar~ came to mean purely “to assault,” while the older “fasten” meaning stayed abroad in English ~attach~. If the stake origin holds, the native Spanish cousin is ~estaca~, and with it ~destacar~ (originally “to detach a body of troops,” now “to stand out”) and ~estacada~. It is a striking case of one Germanic post branching, through Italian, into fastening, detaching and attacking.
en.atender:
From Latin ~attendere~ (“to stretch toward, direct one’s mind to”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~tendere~ (“to stretch”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Cognate with Italian ~attendere~ and — with a telling shift of sense — French ~attendre~ (“to wait”) and Portuguese ~atender~; through ~tendere~ it is kin to English ~tend~ and ~tension~.

The Romans pictured attention as a physical reaching: to ~atender~ was to stretch the mind toward something. Spanish kept the engaged senses — to heed, to look after, to serve — so that in a shop a clerk ~atiende~ a customer, a false friend for English speakers who expect it to mean simply to be present. The same ~tendere~ left a homely trace: Spanish ~tienda~ (“shop,” earlier “tent”) began as a stretched-out awning of cloth. Related descendants include ~atención~ (“attention”), ~tender~ (“to spread, hang out”), ~extender~ (“to extend”), and ~tenso~ (“tense”).
en.aumentar:
From Latin ~augmentāre~ (“to increase”), from ~augmentum~ (“growth, increase”), from ~augēre~ (“to increase, enlarge”), from Proto-Italic *~augeō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ewg-~ (“to grow, increase”). Cognate with Italian ~aumentare~, French ~augmenter~, Portuguese ~aumentar~ and English ~augment~; through the root, with English ~eke~ and — via Germanic — ~wax~ (“to grow”).

The PIE root *~h₂ewg-~ was extraordinarily productive in Latin. Beyond ~aumentar~ it gave ~aumento~ and ~auge~ (“peak, height”); through ~auctor~ (“originator, one who makes grow”) came Spanish ~autor~; through ~augustus~ (“consecrated, majestic”), the month ~agosto~ and the name ~Augusto~; and through ~auxilium~ (“help, reinforcement”), ~auxilio~. Even the diviner’s ~augurio~ may belong to this family. To increase is, at bottom, to make something grow.
en.autorizar:
From Medieval Latin ~auctorizāre~ (“to give authority to”), from Latin ~auctor~ (“originator, promoter, author”), an agent-noun of ~augēre~ (“to increase, to make grow”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ewg-~ (“to increase”). The growth-root is prolific: cognate with English ~augment~, ~auction~ (Latin ~auctiō~, “an increasing” of bids), and ~august~, and — through Germanic — with the archaic English ~eke~ (“to add to, to increase”).

An ~auctor~ was one who caused a thing to grow — who originated, backed, or vouched for it — so to ~autorizar~ is to lend one's authority to an act and let it stand. At the center of the Spanish family sit ~autor~ (“author”) and ~autoridad~ (“authority”), joined by ~aumentar~ (“to increase”), ~auge~ (“peak, boom,” a high point of growth), and ~augusto~ (“august, majestic”), the imperial epithet of ~Augusto~ (Augustus) that also named a month.
en.avanzar:
Spanish ~avanzar~ (“to advance”) goes back to Vulgar Latin *~abantiāre~, a verb built on Late Latin ~abante~ (“forward, in front”), itself the univerbation of ~ab~ (“from”) and ~ante~ (“before”). The ~ante~ half rests on Proto-Indo-European *~h₂énti~ (“in front, before”). It is cognate with French ~avancer~, Italian ~avanzare~ and Catalan ~avançar~ — and, through Old French, with English ~advance~. That English ~d~ is a historical mistake: scribes wrongly read the ~av-~ as if it held the prefix ~ad-~ and inserted a ~d~ that never belonged there. The war-word English ~vanguard~ (from French ~avant-garde~, “fore-guard”) comes of the same ~abante~.

The etymology is a picture of forward motion: to ~avanzar~ is to move “from the front,” to push the front line onward. In Spanish the verb serves every kind of progress — an army, a project, an argument, a clock all ~avanzan~. It kept, too, a quieter commercial sense of “to advance” money, to pay ahead. Its Spanish family marches in the same direction: ~avance~ (“advance, progress; a film trailer”), ~avanzado~ (“advanced”), ~avanzada~ (“outpost, vanguard”) and ~avanzadilla~ (“advance party”). And the ~ante~ at its heart is everywhere in Spanish — in ~antes~, ~anterior~, ~antaño~ and ~delante~ — the little Indo-European word for “in front” still doing its work.
en.ayudar:
From Latin ~adiūtāre~ (“to help, assist”), the frequentative of ~adiuvāre~, itself ~ad-~ (“toward”) plus ~iuvāre~ (“to help, please”), a verb of uncertain deeper origin. Old Spanish had ~aiudar~ before settling on ~ayudar~. It is cognate with Italian ~aiutare~, Portuguese ~ajudar~ and French ~aider~, and — borrowed through Old French — with English ~aid~ and the learned ~adjutant~.

The frequentative ~adiūtāre~ conveyed repeated or earnest helping, and it is this intensive form, not plain ~iuvāre~, that the Romance languages inherited. Because ~iuvāre~ has no secure Proto-Indo-European pedigree, prudence forbids attaching it to a root here. Within Latin it kept lively company: it was linked to ~iūcundus~ (“pleasant, agreeable”), the source of English ~jocund~. In Spanish the same stem gives ~ayuda~ (“help, aid”), ~ayudante~ (“assistant”) and the learned ~coadyuvar~ (“to contribute, cooperate”), which preserves the ~-iuv-~ that popular ~ayudar~ wore away.
en.añadir:
Spanish ~añadir~ comes, through Old Spanish ~eñadir~ (also ~añader~), from a Vulgar Latin *~innaddere~ or *~inaddere~ — Latin ~addere~ (“to add, put to”) reinforced with the prefix ~in-~. The doubled ~nn~ of the reconstructed form is what Spanish needed to yield the ~ñ~. ~addere~ is itself ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~dare~ (“to give”): literally “to give to, put to.” ~dare~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~ (“to give”), one of the most widespread roots there is — source of Latin ~dōnum~ (“gift”) and Spanish ~dar~, Greek ~dídōmi~ (“I give”), and, via Latin, English ~date~, ~donate~, and ~add~ — the last from ~addere~ itself, the very verb that ~añadir~ elaborates.

The quiet lesson of ~añadir~ is redundancy: Latin ~addere~ already meant “to add” (its ~ad-~ = “to”), yet Vulgar Latin piled a second directional prefix, ~in-~, on top — a doubling-up of “to it” that is exactly what adding feels like. The word’s ~ñ~ is a fossil of the assimilated ~in-~ + ~n~ cluster. Spanish also inherited ~addere~ by the learned road as ~aditar~ (“to add, annotate”) and the nouns ~adición~ (“addition,” including the arithmetic operation) and ~aditivo~ (“additive”). From the broader *~deh₃-~ root come ~dar~, ~dado~ (“die; given”), ~dádiva~ (“gift”), ~donar~, ~perdonar~, and ~dosis~ (from Greek ~dósis~, “a giving”).
en.bajar:
From Vulgar Latin *~bassiāre~ (“to lower”), from Late Latin ~bassus~ (“low, short, thick”). Old Spanish had ~baxar~, later reshaped to ~bajar~ as its old sh-sound hardened into the jota. Cognate with French ~baisser~ and Italian ~abbassare~; the same parent adjective surfaces in English ~base~ (“low, mean”) and the musical ~bass~ (“low in pitch”).

The engaging part is the disputed source of ~bassus~ itself. Classical Latin used the word only rarely, mainly as a personal name, and its origin is genuinely uncertain; the sources hedge. By competing accounts it was borrowed from Oscan, or from a Celtic word, or connected to Greek ~bathýs~ (“deep”) — none settled, so the adjective is best labeled “of uncertain origin.” Whatever its root, ~bassus~ flourished in Spanish, yielding ~bajo~ (“low; under”), ~bajada~ (“descent”), ~rebajar~ (“to lower, reduce”), ~abajo~ (“below”), and ~bajón~ (“slump”).
en.basar:
From the noun ~base~ (“base, foundation”) plus the verbal ending ~-ar~; ~basar~ is a denominal verb, coined rather than inherited. ~base~ comes from Latin ~basis~ (“base, pedestal”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~βάσις~ (“a step, a stepping, base”), a noun built on the verb ~βαίνω~ (“to go, to step”). That verb descends from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to go, come”) — the same root that, on the Germanic side, produced English ~come~. Romance preserved the Latin noun broadly: Italian ~base~, French ~base~, Portuguese ~base~.

Because ~basar~ was formed on the noun, its story is really the story of ~base~, which moved from the concrete “pedestal, that on which a thing stands” to the abstract “foundation, grounds”; the reflexive ~basarse~ means “to rest on, be grounded in.” A pleasant surprise: the modest Greek ~βαίνω~ (“to step”) also hides inside ~diabetes~ (Greek for “a passing through”) and ~acróbata~ (one who “walks” on the heights). Spanish relatives of ~base~ include ~básico~, ~basamento~, and the chemistry term ~base~.
en.beneficiar:
~beneficiar~ is built on ~beneficio~ (“benefit”), from Latin ~beneficium~ (“a kindness, favor, service”), a compound of ~bene~ (“well”) and ~-ficium~, from ~facere~ (“to do, make”) — literally “a well-doing.” The adverb ~bene~ belongs to ~bonus~ (“good”), from Old Latin ~duenos~, of debated further origin; ~facere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, do”), the root of English ~do~ and German ~tun~. Romance kept the verb: French ~bénéficier~, Italian ~beneficiare~, Portuguese ~beneficiar~.

In Latin a ~beneficium~ ranged from a personal good turn to an official grant of land or office — the feudal “benefice” that let a churchman live off an endowment. Spanish ~beneficiar~ thus spans “to benefit, do good to” and the technical “to work, process” (to ~beneficiar~ ore or a hide is to render it useful). The reflexive ~beneficiarse~ is “to profit from.” Kin include ~benéfico~, ~beneficencia~, ~benefactor~, and — from ~bene~ alone — ~bendecir~ and ~benévolo~.
en.brindar:
Unlike its Latinate neighbors, ~brindar~ is a Germanic import. It derives from the noun ~brindis~ (“a toast”), which Spanish borrowed in the sixteenth century from the German toasting phrase ~bring dir’s~ — a running-together of ~(ich) bring dir’s~, “I bring it to you.” The verb behind it is German ~bringen~ (“to bring”), cognate with English ~bring~, both from Proto-Germanic *~bringaną~. The little words matter too: ~dir~ is “to you” (dative, cognate with English ~thee~) and the clitic ~’s~ is ~es~ (“it”). Italian ~brindare~ and Portuguese ~brindar~ borrowed the same festive word from Spanish.

The story behind the word is vivid and, unusually, well documented: when the Landsknechte — German mercenaries in the service of Charles V — sacked Rome in 1527, they are said to have raised their cups crying ~bring dir’s~, offering the drink to a companion. Spanish soldiers carried the custom and the cry home, and by the early 1600s ~brindar~ and ~brindis~ were common enough that Covarrubias recorded them in his 1611 Tesoro de la lengua castellana. The meaning then broadened gracefully: from “to drink someone’s health” to “to offer, to provide” in general — today one can ~brindar~ apoyo (“offer support”) or ~brindar~ una oportunidad (“provide an opportunity”), a generosity still audible in that original “I bring it to you.”
en.buscar:
Inherited from Old Spanish ~buscar~, but of genuinely uncertain origin — Corominas and the DLE alike label it « de origen incierto ». Several hypotheses compete, none settled. By one account it is tied to ~bosque~ (“forest”), the earliest sense being to beat the woods for game; by another it descends from a Celtic *~boudi~ (“gain, victory”), compared with Old Irish ~búaid~ and Welsh ~budd~. It shares its mystery with cognate Portuguese ~buscar~ and Italian ~buscare~ (“to scrounge, wangle”).

Whatever its source, ~buscar~ had by the medieval period already generalized to “to look for, seek,” and it remains one of the plainest, most frequent verbs in the language. The hunting-in-the-woods story is memorable but rests on the unproven ~bosque~ link, so it is best told as one guess among several rather than as fact. The verb is productive in its own right: it yields ~búsqueda~ and ~busca~ (“search”), ~buscador~ (“search engine; seeker”), ~rebuscar~ (“to search thoroughly”), and the old noun ~buscón~ (“petty crook”), immortalized in Quevedo's picaresque novel ~El Buscón~.
en.caber:
From Old Spanish ~caber~, from Latin ~capere~ (“to take, seize, hold, contain”), from Proto-Italic *~kapiō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~kap-~ (“to grasp, seize”). Cognate with Portuguese ~caber~ and — through the same Latin verb — with the borrowings ~capaz~ and ~captura~; English has ~capture~ and ~capable~ from ~capere~, and, from the same PIE root, the native ~heave~.

The meaning shifted from grasping to spatial room: Latin ~capere~ meant “to take” or “to hold, contain,” and Spanish narrowed the “contain” side to “to fit, have room for” — a box ~cabe~ on the shelf, five people ~caben~ in the car. The irregular present ~quepo~ (“I fit”) preserves Latin ~capiō~ under metathesis, and the preterite ~cupe~ reflects a Vulgar Latin perfect *~capuī~. From ~capere~ Spanish also drew ~capaz~, ~cabida~ (“capacity”), ~caudal~, and the shared-root ~recibir~ and ~concebir~.
en.caer:
From Latin ~cadere~ (“to fall”), from Proto-Italic *~kadō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱad-~ (“to fall”). The intervocalic ~-d-~ dropped away, giving Old Spanish ~caer~. Cognate with Italian ~cadere~, Portuguese ~cair~ and the now-archaic French ~choir~.

Latin’s ~cāsus~ (“a falling”), the past participle of ~cadere~, became a metaphor for whatever “befalls,” hence Spanish ~caso~ (“case, chance”) and ~casualidad~ (“coincidence”), and grammatical “case.” The setting sun falls: ~ocaso~ (“sunset, decline”) and ~occidente~ (“the West”) come from ~occidere~ (“to fall down, to set”). English borrowed the same verb widely — ~cadence~, ~accident~, ~occasion~, ~decay~ and ~cascade~. Other Spanish descendants: ~caída~, ~decaer~, ~recaer~ and ~cadencia~.
en.calcular:
From Latin ~calculāre~ (“to compute, reckon”), from ~calculus~ (“a pebble”), the diminutive of ~calx~ (genitive ~calcis~, “limestone, small stone”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~khálix~ (“small pebble, gravel”). The ultimate origin is unknown — Beekes finds no convincing etymology for the Greek word. Cognate with Italian ~calcolare~, French ~calculer~ and Portuguese ~calcular~.

The homely detail is that a ~calculus~ was a counting-pebble: Romans “placed pebbles” (~ponere calculōs~) on a reckoning board to add and subtract, so to ~calcular~ is, at root, to push stones around. From ~calx~ English also drew ~chalk~ and ~calcium~, and the medical ~calculus~ is still a “little stone” in the body. Spanish keeps ~cálculo~, ~calculadora~ and ~recalcular~.
en.calificar:
~calificar~ comes from Medieval Latin ~quālificāre~ (“to endow with a quality”), a compound of Latin ~quālis~ (“of what kind”) and ~facere~ (“to make, do”) — literally “to make of a certain kind.” ~quālis~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European interrogative-relative stem *~kʷo-~ (source also of ~qué~ and ~cuál~), while ~facere~ goes back to *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place, do”), the root behind English ~do~ and ~deed~ and German ~tun~. The same coinage spread as Italian ~qualificare~, French ~qualifier~, and English ~qualify~.

The scholastic Latin verb meant “to attribute a quality to,” a technical sense still alive in “to qualify” a statement with reservations. Spanish specialized it toward judgment and assessment: a teacher ~califica~ (“grades”) an exam and gives it a ~calificación~ (“grade, rating”). The neutral “assign a quality” lingers when we ~calificar~ a remark as rude or brilliant. Kin from the ~facere~ half include ~fácil~, ~hacer~, ~facción~, and countless ~-ificar~ verbs; from the ~quālis~ half come ~cualidad~ and ~cualitativo~.
en.cambiar:
From Late Latin ~cambiāre~ (“to exchange, barter”), a term of Gaulish (Celtic) origin, traced to a Gaulish ~cambion~ and a Celtic *~kambos~ (“curved, crooked”), reflecting Proto-Indo-European *~(s)kamb-~ (“to bend, curve”). It is cognate with Italian ~cambiare~, Portuguese ~cambiar~ and French ~changer~, and — through Old French — with English ~change~.

The verb began as commercial jargon: ~cambiāre~ first surfaces in Apuleius, and the noun ~cambium~ (“exchange”) appears only later, in medieval Latin banking. The tie to the Celtic root is engaging but wants care: by one account the sense moved from the physical “to bend, turn” of *~kambos~ to the abstract “to give one thing and turn it into another,” yet this semantic bridge is a proposal, not a documented step. What is secure is the family the verb seeded in Spanish: ~cambio~ (“change, small coin”), ~intercambiar~, ~recambio~ (“spare part”) and, borrowed back through Catalan and Occitan, ~canje~ (“exchange, swap”).
en.caminar:
From ~camino~ (“road, path”) plus the verbal suffix ~-ar~; ~camino~ descends through Old Spanish from Vulgar Latin ~camminus~, a word Latin borrowed from Gaulish (Celtic), ultimately from Proto-Celtic *~kanxsman-~ (“step, pace”), an action-noun built on *~kengeti~ (“to step”). Being Celtic rather than Latin, it is cognate not with a Latin verb but with Welsh ~cam~ (“step”). The Romance family kept it everywhere: French ~chemin~ and ~cheminer~, Italian ~cammino~ and ~camminare~, Portuguese ~caminho~ and ~caminhar~.

The Celtic loan spread precisely because road-building and road-travel were where Gaulish vocabulary left its deepest mark on Latin; ~camminus~ eventually displaced native Latin words for “road” across much of the West. The verb ~caminar~ simply means “to walk” or “to travel a road,” and Spanish elaborated the family richly: ~caminante~ (“traveler, wayfarer”), ~caminata~ (“a long walk, hike”), ~encaminar~ (“to set on the right path, direct”), and the pilgrim’s ~Camino~ de Santiago. The English ~camino~, now used for that pilgrimage route, is a direct borrowing of the Spanish noun.
en.cantar:
From Latin ~cantāre~ (“to sing”), the frequentative of ~canere~ (“to sing”), from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂n-~ (“to sing”). It passed unchanged in shape to Portuguese ~cantar~ and Italian ~cantare~, and became French ~chanter~; through the same root it is cognate with English ~chant~ and ~accent~, and even with English ~hen~ (originally “the singing bird”) and German ~Hahn~ (“rooster”).

~Cantāre~ began as an intensive of ~canere~ — not just to sing but to sing repeatedly — and it so thoroughly displaced the plain verb that every Romance language sings with the frequentative. The root *~keh₂n-~ radiated widely in Spanish: ~canto~, ~cántico~, ~cantante~, ~encantar~ (“to enchant,” literally to sing a spell over someone) and, borrowed back from French, ~chantaje~ (“blackmail”).
en.caracterizar:
Spanish ~caracterizar~ is formed from ~carácter~ plus the verb-forming suffix ~-izar~. ~carácter~ comes from Latin ~character~, a borrowing from Ancient Greek ~kharaktḗr~ (“an engraving tool; the mark it stamps; a distinctive imprint”), from the verb ~kharássō~ (“to scratch, to engrave, to sharpen”). The Greek noun first named the stamp on a coin or the brand cut into a surface, then the distinctive mark it left, and finally a person's stamped-in nature. Spanish ~caracterizar~ is a learned formation. It is cognate with Italian ~caratterizzare~, French ~caractériser~, Portuguese ~caracterizar~, and English ~characterize~.

The metaphor buried in ~caracterizar~ is the engraver's: to characterize something is, at root, to press a distinguishing mark into it, to say what stamp it bears. Spanish uses it in two live senses — to describe the defining traits of a thing (“what characterizes this region”) and, in the theatre, to make oneself up and dress for a role, to ~caracterizar~ a character on stage. The Greek ~kharássō~ (“to engrave”) sits behind the whole family: Spanish ~carácter~, ~característica~, ~caracterización~, and the typographic sense of ~carácter~ as a written sign — the “characters” of an alphabet, still literally little marks stamped onto a page.
en.cargar:
From Vulgar Latin *~carricāre~ (“to load a wagon”), a verb built on Latin ~carrus~ (“wheeled vehicle, wagon”). ~carrus~ was itself borrowed from Gaulish ~carros~, a Celtic word, and traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱers-~ (“to run”), the same root behind Latin ~currere~ (“to run”). In its passage to Spanish the double consonant softened, the ~-i-~ dropped, and the second ~c~ voiced to ~g~, giving ~cargar~, already attested in the twelfth-century Poem of the Cid. It is cognate with Italian ~caricare~, French ~charger~, Portuguese ~carregar~, and English ~charge~ and ~cargo~.

The image at the root is concrete: to pile a load onto a ~carrus~, a Gaulish cart — so ~cargar~ began as a teamster's word for loading a wagon and then generalized to loading of every kind: a ship, a rifle, a battery, a debt, an emotional weight. English shows how far the ~carrus~ family traveled — “car,” “carriage,” “career,” “cargo,” and “charge” in its electrical sense all descend from the same Celtic-Latin cart. In Spanish the family is large: ~carga~, ~carro~, ~cargo~, ~cargamento~, ~descargar~, ~encargar~, ~acarrear~, and ~ferrocarril~.
en.casar:
Spanish did not inherit its everyday verb for marrying from Latin's marriage vocabulary; it built one at home. ~casar~ comes from the noun ~casa~ (“house”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-ar~ — literally “to set up house” or “to become a member of the household.” The noun descends from Latin ~casa~ (“hut, cottage, cabin”), a humble word of uncertain further origin. The same household-based verb arose across Ibero-Romance: Portuguese ~casar~ and Catalan ~casar~ likewise mean “to marry.”

Where Latin framed marriage with ~mātrimōnium~ and stately legal phrases, Iberian Romance reframed it as founding a house — a domestic fact as much as a rite. That image survives in the reflexive ~casarse~ (“to get married”) and in ~casamiento~ (“wedding”), and echoes in ~casero~ (“homely; landlord”) and the diminutive ~casilla~ (“box on a form, cubbyhole”). Beware a look-alike: the legal ~casar~ (“to quash a judgment”) is a wholly separate verb, from Latin ~cassāre~ (“to annul”), from ~cassus~ (“empty, void”); the two merely fell together in spelling. From the same ~casa~ also come ~caserío~ (“hamlet”) and, borrowed worldwide, ~casino~.
en.causar:
From Latin ~causāre~ (“to cause, to give as a reason”), a verb built on the noun ~causa~ (“cause, reason, legal case”). It is cognate with Italian ~causare~, French ~causer~ and Portuguese ~causar~, and with English ~cause~, taken through Old French. The ancestry of ~causa~ beyond Latin is genuinely uncertain: it goes back to Old Latin ~caussa~, but no secure Proto-Indo-European source is agreed, and some scholars have proposed a non-Indo-European — possibly Etruscan — origin.

In Roman usage ~causa~ leaned heavily toward the courtroom — a “case, suit, legal matter” — and Spanish still keeps that legal sense alongside the ordinary one, so a ~causa~ can be either a cause or a criminal case. The noun's most startling descendant, though, is utterly ordinary: in Vulgar Latin ~causa~ (“matter, affair”) weakened all the way to “thing,” giving Spanish ~cosa~, French ~chose~ and Italian ~cosa~. From the same Latin stem come ~acusar~, ~excusar~, ~recusar~ and ~causante~.
en.celebrar:
From Latin ~celebrāre~ (“to frequent, throng, honor, solemnize”), from ~celeber~ (“much-frequented, crowded, populous; famous”). Cognate with Italian ~celebrare~, French ~célébrer~, Portuguese ~celebrar~ and English ~celebrate~. The deeper origin of ~celeber~ is uncertain; it has been linked to ~celer~ (“swift”), but that connection is unproven and the sources leave the root undetermined, so it is best treated as disputed.

The core image is a crowd: a ~celeber~ place was one thronged with people, and ~celebrāre~ first meant “to fill, to frequent in numbers,” then “to honor with a gathering,” and finally “to solemnize.” A festival is still, etymologically, a well-attended event. The same family gave Spanish ~célebre~ (“famous”), ~celebridad~ and ~celebración~. The oft-repeated claim that ~celeber~ comes from ~celer~ “swift” is appealing but not established — by most accounts the origin remains unknown.
en.centrar:
From Spanish ~centro~ (“center”), from Latin ~centrum~ (“center of a circle; the fixed point of a compass”), itself a borrowing of Ancient Greek ~κέντρον~ (~kéntron~, “sharp point, goad, the stationary leg of a compass”), from the verb ~κεντέω~ (~kentéō~, “to prick, goad”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱent-~ (“to prick”). Cognate with Italian ~centrare~, French ~centrer~ and Portuguese ~centrar~; English ~center~ descends from the same Greek word.

The Greek noun first named the sharp point of a goad and then the fixed pivot around which a compass sweeps a circle — the geometric sense Latin took over.
