From that idea of a central point Spanish built the verb ~centrar~, “to place at the center,” whose senses branched into balancing, aligning and, reflexively, focusing: ~centrarse en~ means “to concentrate on.” The same root seeded a broad family in Spanish, among them ~centro~, ~céntrico~, ~concentrar~, ~excéntrico~ and ~centímetro~.
en.cerrar:
Spanish ~cerrar~ comes from Late Latin ~serāre~ (“to bolt, lock, close”), a verb derived from the noun ~sera~ (“a bolt, bar, or lock for a door”). The classical form ~serāre~ appears already in Varro and Tibullus (~serāre forēs~, “to bolt the doors”). Two changes reshaped it in the mouths of speakers. First, the ~-r-~ doubled to ~-rr-~ through confusion with ~serra~ (“saw”) and ~serrāre~ (“to saw”) — an entirely different word — so a Vulgar Latin *~serrāre~ arose, still living as Italian ~serrare~, French ~serrer~ (“to tighten, squeeze”), and Portuguese ~cerrar~. English ~serried~ (as in “serried ranks”) is borrowed from the French. Second, the initial ~s-~ became ~c-~ in Castilian — a shift Corominas attributes to the pull of the near-synonym ~cercar~ (“to enclose”).

So the word’s history hides a small comedy of errors: a verb for locking a door got tangled with the unrelated verb for sawing wood, borrowing its double ~r~, and then swapped its opening consonant under the influence of a synonym. The s-to-c shift is Corominas’s proposal, not a certainty, and is best held as the favored account rather than settled fact. Meaning stayed stable — to shut, close, seal — and Spanish grew a rich brood: ~cerradura~ (“lock”), ~cerrojo~ (“bolt”), ~cierre~ (“closure, zipper”), ~encerrar~ (“to lock up, enclose”), ~cerrado~ (“closed; dense; unintelligible”), and ~cerca~ (“fence,” and the adverb “near”). Beware the false friend: Spanish ~cerrar~ (“to close”) and ~serrar~ (“to saw,” from that same ~serra~) are separate verbs that merely sound alike.
en.citar:
From Latin ~citāre~ (“to summon, call forth, set in motion”), a frequentative of ~ciēre~ (“to move, rouse, stir”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱey-~ (“to set in motion”). Cognate with French ~citer~, Italian ~citare~, and — as learned borrowings — English ~cite~ and ~excite~.

The frequentative ~citāre~ meant to summon repeatedly or insistently, and that legal-sounding “call before a court” underlies the modern “quote an authority.” It also explains a happy Spanish ambiguity: ~cita~ means at once a “quotation,” an “appointment,” and a “romantic date” — all of them a calling-together at an agreed time. Kin from the same root abound: ~incitar~ (“to incite”), ~excitar~ (“to excite”), ~recitar~ (“to recite”), ~solicitar~ (“to request”), and vividly ~resucitar~ (“to resuscitate”), literally to stir back to life.
en.clasificar:
A learned compound coined from Latin ~classis~ (“a division, class, fleet”) plus the combining form ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”) — literally “to make into classes.” ~Classis~ came from Proto-Italic *~klāssis~, from Proto-Indo-European *~kelh₁-~ (“to call, shout out”), and so is kin to Latin ~calāre~ (“to call”), ~clāmāre~ (“to shout”) and ~clārus~ (“clear”), and to Ancient Greek ~kaléō~ (“I call”). Cognate formations include Italian ~classificare~, French ~classifier~ and Portuguese ~classificar~.

The startling turn is that a ~classis~ began as a military summons: by De Vaan's account the sense ran from a “calling out” of citizens to arms, to the ~classis~ or body of soldiers so called, to the property classes into which Servius Tullius sorted Roman citizens, and finally to any “class” or category. ~Clasificar~ therefore means to sort things into ranks first drawn up by a herald's cry. Related Spanish words are ~clase~, ~clásico~ and ~clasificación~.
en.cobrar:
From Old Spanish ~cobrar~, an aphetic (head-clipped) form of ~recobrar~ (“to recover, get back”), from Latin ~recuperāre~ (“to regain, recover”), related to ~recipere~ (“to take back, receive”). Some scholars instead posit a Vulgar Latin *~cuperāre~, a back-formation drawn out of ~recuperāre~, which would make ~cobrar~ old rather than merely clipped — the point is debated. Whatever the route, Latin ~recuperāre~ also survives as the learned Spanish doublet ~recuperar~, and gave Italian ~ricoverare~, French ~recouvrer~ and English ~recover~ and ~recuperate~.

The starting sense was “to get back what was lost,” and Spanish ~recobrar~ and ~recuperar~ still carry it. The clipped ~cobrar~, though, drifted toward money: its dominant modern meaning is “to charge, to collect payment, to get paid.” It keeps older senses too — a hunter ~cobra~ (retrieves) downed game, and a feeling can ~cobrar fuerza~, “gather strength.” The family includes ~cobro~ (“collection, charge”), ~cobranza~, ~cobrador~, ~recobrar~ and ~recuperar~.
en.coger:
From Old Spanish ~coger~ (first attested around 1140), from Latin ~colligere~ (“to gather, collect”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~legere~ (“to gather, pick, read”). ~legere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, collect”), the root that also gave Ancient Greek ~légō~ (“to gather, to say”) and hence ~lógos~. Sister forms of ~colligere~ include Italian ~cogliere~, French ~cueillir~, Portuguese ~colher~, and Catalan ~collir~.

The journey from “to gather up” to plain “to grasp, take, catch” was gradual, and Spanish generalized ~coger~ into one of its handiest everyday verbs — coger el autobús, coger un objeto, coger fruta. But the meaning kept drifting regionally: across much of the Americas (Argentina, Mexico, and beyond) ~coger~ acquired a vulgar sexual sense, so speakers there favor ~agarrar~ or ~tomar~ for the neutral idea. From the same ~legere~ root Spanish also holds ~colegir~ (“to infer,” to gather a conclusion), ~recoger~, ~escoger~, ~coleccionar~, and the learned ~colección~ — a whole cluster around the image of gathering things together.
en.coincidir:
From Medieval Latin ~coincidere~ (“to fall together, occupy the same place”), a learned compound of ~co-~ (“together”) and ~incidere~ (“to fall upon, into”), itself ~in-~ (“on, into”) plus ~cadere~ (“to fall”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱad-~ (“to fall”). English carries the borrowings ~coincide~, ~incident~, ~accident~ and ~cadence~.

Unlike the inherited verbs, ~coincidir~ was assembled by scholars — first for geometry, where two figures “coincide” by falling exactly onto each other — and only later widened to the everyday “to agree, to happen at once.” The parent ~cadere~ left Spanish an enormous progeny: the plain ~caer~ (“to fall”), ~caso~ (“case,” a “falling-out” of events), ~casualidad~ (“chance”), ~decaer~, ~ocaso~ (“sunset, decline”), ~incidente~, ~accidente~ and even ~cadáver~ — the Latin ~cadāver~, literally “the fallen one.” To coincide, then, is for two things to fall onto the very same point.
en.colaborar:
From Latin ~collaborare~ (“to labor together”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together, with”) and ~laborare~ (“to work, to toil”), which derives from the noun ~labor~ (“work, effort, hardship”). Spanish took it as a learned borrowing rather than by unbroken oral descent. It is cognate with English ~collaborate~, Italian ~collaborare~, French ~collaborer~, and Portuguese ~colaborar~, all reflecting the same late-Latin formation.

In classical Latin ~laborare~ carried a note of toil and hardship, not just activity; the prefix ~com-~ added the sense of shared effort toward a common end. That cooperative meaning stayed remarkably stable, though the twentieth century gave ~colaborar~ a darker political shading in the sense of aiding an occupying enemy. From the same root Spanish keeps ~labor~, ~laborable~, ~laboratorio~, ~laborioso~ and ~elaborar~, all turning on the old idea of work.
en.colocar:
From Latin ~collocāre~ (“to place together, to arrange, to set in order”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together, with”) and ~locāre~ (“to place”), from ~locus~ (“place”). ~locāre~ and ~locus~ go back, through Old Latin ~stlocus~, to an uncertain earlier form, but the family is unmistakable in Romance: Italian ~collocare~, Portuguese ~colocar~, and — by inheritance rather than borrowing — French ~coucher~ (“to lay down, to put to bed”) and English ~locate~ and ~couch~ all spring from the same Latin verb.

Spanish inherited ~collocāre~ twice over. The popular, orally transmitted line — its pretonic vowel lost and its consonants worn smooth — yielded ~colgar~ (“to hang”), while a later learned borrowing taken straight from the books gave ~colocar~ (“to place, to position”). The two form an etymological doublet: a single Latin word that entered Spanish by two different roads. From ~locus~ the language also draws ~local~, ~localizar~, and ~lugar~ (the fully popularized reflex of ~locālis~). And from the French ~coucher~ branch came the borrowed ~colcha~ (“bedspread”) and ~colchón~ (“mattress”) — so that a sleeper's mattress and the tidy verb ~colocar~ are, at a great distance, the very same word.
en.combinar:
From Late Latin ~combīnāre~ (“to join two by two”), from ~com-~ (“together”) plus ~bīnī~ (“two at a time, in pairs”), a distributive of ~bis~ (“twice”) that traces back to ~duo~ (“two”) and ultimately to Proto-Indo-European *~dwóh₁~ (“two”). English borrowed the same verb as ~combine~, and the ~bīnī~ element survives in ~binary~.

The word's whole logic is pairing: to combine is to set things two by two until they hold together. Late Latin coined ~combīnāre~ precisely to name that yoking of pairs, and Spanish kept the sense intact in ~combinación~ (“combination”), which can mean a chemical union, a subway connection, or a woman's slip. The numeral core shows up wherever “two-ness” is at stake — in ~binario~, ~combinado~ and the mathematics of ~combinatoria~. Far older, that same *~dwóh₁~ underlies Spanish ~dos~, ~doble~ and ~dúo~, making combine and its cousins a distant echo of the plain word for two.
en.comentar:
From Latin ~commentārī~ (“to consider thoroughly, study, discuss”), a deponent verb linked to ~comminīscī~ (“to devise, contrive, think up”), formed with ~com-~ (“together, thoroughly”) on the root of ~meminī~ (“to remember”) and ~mēns~ (“mind”), from Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to think”). ~Comentar~ therefore shares its deepest root with ~mencionar~. It is cognate with Italian ~commentare~, French ~commenter~, Portuguese ~comentar~ and English ~comment~, and — through *~men-~ — with English ~mind~ and ~mental~.

The literal sense is “to have thoroughly in mind” — to turn something over in thought — and from that came the ideas of studying a text and remarking on it. The Latin noun ~commentārius~ meant a notebook or memorandum, a set of things thought over; Julius Caesar titled his war memoirs ~Commentāriī~, and the English “commentary” descends straight from it. Modern Spanish keeps the reflective streak: to ~comentar~ is to offer one's considered remark, and the ~comentario~ can range from a scholarly gloss to a passing aside. Related through *~men-~ are ~mente~, ~memoria~, ~mencionar~ and ~mentar~.
en.comenzar:
From Vulgar Latin *~cominitiāre~, a compound of intensive ~com-~ and ~initiāre~ (“to begin, initiate”), the verb of ~initium~ (“a beginning”). ~initium~ comes from ~inīre~ (“to go in, enter”), from ~in-~ (“in”) plus ~īre~ (“to go”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”). Cognate with French ~commencer~, Italian ~cominciare~, Portuguese ~começar~, and Catalan ~començar~; English ~commence~ was borrowed from the Old French form.

The literal core is quietly logical: to begin is to “go into” a thing — ~inīre~ — and ~initium~ named the threshold, the point of entry. Late Latin stacked an intensifying ~com-~ onto ~initiāre~ to make the everyday “start,” and that doubled form, not classical ~incipere~, is what the western Romance languages inherited. Spanish paired the popular ~comenzar~ with the noun ~comienzo~, while borrowing the learned doublets ~iniciar~ and ~inicio~ straight from ~initium~. The same PIE *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”) also underlies ~ir~ itself and words such as ~éxito~ (“exit” of effort → “success”) and ~tránsito~.
en.comer:
From Latin ~comedere~ (“to eat up, to consume”), an intensive compound of ~com-~ (here a strengthening prefix) and ~edere~ (“to eat”). ~edere~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁ed-~ (“to eat”), one of the oldest words humans can reconstruct — the same root that gave English ~eat~ and ~edible~, German ~essen~, and, through the image of “the biter,” even the ~tooth~ (from *~h₃dónts~, “the eating one”). Portuguese shares the choice exactly: ~comer~.

Here Spanish went its own way. Classical Latin's plain ~edere~ (“to eat”) was short and riddled with irregular forms, so it faded; where French, Italian, and Romanian reached instead for ~mandūcāre~ (“to chew, to munch” — originally a slangy, comic word, and the source of French ~manger~ and Italian ~mangiare~), Spanish and Portuguese kept the older, more dignified ~comedere~, worn down to ~comer~. So a Spaniard still “eats” with a verb Cicero would recognize, while a Frenchman “chews.” From the same root Spanish holds ~comida~ (“food, meal”), ~comestible~ (“edible”), and ~comilón~ (“big eater, glutton”).
en.cometer:
From Latin ~committere~ (“to bring together, join; to entrust; to commit”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~mittere~ (“to send, let go, release”). ~mittere~ most likely goes back to Proto-Italic *~meitō~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, remove”), itself an extension of *~mey-~ (“to change, exchange”) — the same root that gives Latin ~mūtāre~ (“to change”) and ~commūnis~ (“common”), and, through Germanic, English ~mad~ (“insane,” originally “changed for the worse”). Spanish inherited ~cometer~ in a somewhat worn shape (Old Spanish also had ~cometre~), while keeping many learned relatives. Romance cognates of the compound include French ~commettre~ and Italian ~commettere~.

The semantic path is memorable. ~committere~ first meant “to join, bring together” — Romans used it for “to join battle,” to commit troops to the fight — and from “to put together, engage in” it slid to “to bring about, perpetrate.” Spanish ~cometer~ inherited that darker end: one “commits” an error, a crime, or a sin. The noun ~cometido~ means “a task, assignment” — what one has been entrusted with. Around it stand a crowd of ~mittere~-derived words: ~comisión~ and ~comité~ (both, through French, from the same ~committere~), ~comprometer~ (“to compromise, commit”) and ~compromiso~ (“commitment, obligation”). English ~commit~, ~committee~, and ~commission~ are the same verb’s English harvest.
en.comparar:
From Latin ~comparāre~ (“to couple, match, place side by side”), a verb built on ~compar~ (“equal, a match”), itself ~com-~ (“together”) plus ~par~ (“equal, a pair”). The comparison sense thus rests on the idea of setting equals together. Cognate with Italian ~comparare~, French ~comparer~, and Portuguese ~comparar~, and with English ~compare~ and ~pair~.

Latin ~comparāre~ carried a broad range — to pair, to furnish, to procure — and Spanish drew two different verbs from it. The ordinary inherited outcome was ~comprar~ (“to buy,” from the sense “to procure, get together”), while ~comparar~ (“to compare”) was reborrowed later as a learned form closer to the Latin spelling; the two are doublets from one source. From the same root ~par~ Spanish keeps ~pareja~ (“couple, partner”) and ~impar~ (“odd, unequal”), and the family branches into ~comparación~ and ~comparativo~.
en.compartir:
A prefixed compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~partir~ (“to divide, to split”), which comes from Latin ~partīre~ (also deponent ~partīrī~, “to divide, to share out”), from the noun ~pars~, ~partis~ (“part, portion”). ~pars~ descends from Proto-Italic *~partis~; its deeper Proto-Indo-European root is disputed, usually tied to *~per-~ in a sense of apportioning and to the root behind Latin ~pariō~ (“to bring forth”), but no single reconstruction has won out. Compare Italian ~compartire~ and Portuguese ~compartir~, alongside English ~part~ and ~portion~.

Latin ~partīre~ meant to cut a whole into shares; Spanish kept that (“to divide”) but also, through the idea of separating oneself from a place, developed the everyday ~partir~ “to set off, to depart” — the same journey French ~partir~ (“to leave”) completed. Prefixed with ~com-~, the verb means to divide something in common, and so “to share.” The teeming ~pars~ family in Spanish includes ~parte~, ~partido~, ~partícula~, ~partida~, ~repartir~, ~impartir~, and ~apartar~.
en.completar:
From Latin ~complētus~ (“filled up, complete”), the past participle of ~complēre~ (“to fill up, finish”), a compound of ~com-~ (intensive “thoroughly”) and ~plēre~ (“to fill”). ~plēre~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill; full”), one of the great word-families of the language. Through Latin it gives ~plēnus~ (“full”) and ~plēbs~ (“the multitude”); through Germanic the very same *~pleh₁-~ yields English ~full~ (“full”) and ~fill~ (“to fill”); and it also stands behind English ~plenty~ (“abundance”) and ~plus~. Romance built a fresh verb on the participle: Spanish ~completar~, Italian ~completare~, and — reborrowed through French — English ~complete~ all rest on ~complētus~ rather than directly on the old verb ~complēre~.

The image is of filling: to complete something is to fill it up until nothing is missing — hence ~completar~ “to complete, finish, fill in.” Spanish preserves a beautiful doublet here. Alongside the learned ~completar~ (from the participle), the very same verb ~complēre~ came down by unbroken popular speech as ~cumplir~ — “to fulfill, carry out, keep (a promise); to turn (a given age); to come due.” Learned and inherited, ~completar~ and ~cumplir~ are two Spanish reflexes of one Latin verb, worn to different shapes by different histories. The wider family fills a page: ~completo~ (“complete, full”), ~complemento~, ~cumplido~ (“courteous; a compliment”), ~cumplimiento~, and — straight from ~plēnus~ — the everyday ~lleno~ (“full”), plus ~llenar~ (“to fill”).
en.complicar:
From Latin ~complicāre~ (“to fold together, roll up”), from ~com-~ (“together”) plus ~plicāre~ (“to fold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to fold, to plait”). Cognate with Italian ~complicare~, French ~compliquer~, and Portuguese ~complicar~, and with English ~complicate~; through the same root it is kin to English ~ply~ and ~pleat~ and to German ~flechten~ (“to braid”).

The image is concrete: to complicate a thing was to fold it over on itself until its parts no longer lay flat and separable — the opposite of ~explicar~ (“to explain,” literally “to unfold”). Spanish preserves the whole folding family from ~plicāre~: ~plegar~ (“to fold”), ~desplegar~ (“to unfold, deploy”), ~aplicar~ (“to apply, fold onto”), and the adjective ~complejo~ (“complex, folded-together”). Even ~emplear~ (“to employ”) belongs here, through Latin ~implicāre~ (“to enfold, involve”).
en.componer:
From Latin ~compōnere~ (“to put together, arrange”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~pōnere~ (“to put, place, set down”). ~pōnere~ itself was ~po-~ (a reduced form of *~apo~, “off, away”) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, leave, allow”), so its literal image was “to set down and leave.” ~compōnere~ gave Italian ~comporre~, Portuguese ~compor~, and — reinforced by French — English ~compose~ and ~component~.

In Spanish ~componer~ kept “to compose” and “to put together,” but also became the everyday word for “to fix, to mend” — to put the broken pieces back in order — and the reflexive ~componérselas~ means “to manage, to get by.” A tidy false friend lurks here: the ~-pose~ of English ~compose~, ~propose~, and ~impose~ does not in fact descend from ~pōnere~ but from Latin ~pausāre~ (“to rest, pause”) by way of French ~poser~ — the two families simply merged in meaning. From ~pōnere~ Spanish drew a great crowd of verbs: ~poner~, ~disponer~, ~exponer~, ~imponer~, ~proponer~, and ~suponer~, plus ~componente~, ~compuesto~, and ~composición~.
en.comprar:
Spanish ~comprar~ descends from Latin ~comparāre~ (“to procure, prepare, get”), through a Vulgar Latin variant *~comperāre~. This ~comparāre~ is ~com-~ (“together, wholly”) plus ~parāre~ (“to prepare, procure, furnish”), which goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to grant, allot”) — the root also behind Latin ~pariō~ (“to bring forth”) and Sanskrit ~pṛṇā́ti~ (“he grants”). The Romance family is unanimous: Portuguese and Catalan ~comprar~, Italian ~comprare~, Romanian ~cumpăra~.

Here lies a genuine trap. Latin had two verbs spelled ~comparāre~: one from ~parāre~ (“to procure”), which became ~comprar~ (“to buy”); the other from ~pār~ (“equal”), meaning “to pair, to match, to compare,” which Spanish later re-borrowed intact as ~comparar~ (“to compare”). The everyday “buy” and the bookish “compare” are thus look-alikes from different Latin bases, not one word split in two. From ~parāre~ Spanish also draws ~preparar~, ~reparar~, ~separar~, ~parar~ (“to stop”), ~aparato~, and the agent noun ~comprador~ (“buyer”); the plain noun ~compra~ (“purchase”) rounds out the set.
en.comprender:
From Latin ~comprehendere~ (also ~comprendere~), “to grasp, seize, take in together”, a compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~prehendere~ (“to seize, grasp”). ~prehendere~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʰed-~ (“to seize, take”), which — surprisingly — makes it cognate with English ~get~ and with Ancient Greek ~χανδάνω~ (khandánō, “to hold, contain”).

The metaphor is the familiar one that turns holding into knowing: to seize a thing bodily became to “grasp” it mentally, and Spanish ~comprender~ means “to understand” as well as “to comprise”. The verb ~prehendere~ was extraordinarily fertile in Spanish: ~prender~ (“to seize, to catch fire”), ~aprender~ (“to learn”, literally to grasp), ~emprender~ and ~sorprender~, plus ~preso~ and ~prisión~ from the same root. English harvested ~comprehend~, ~apprehend~, ~comprehensive~ and, through Old French, ~prison~ — all ways of taking hold, like the humble cognate ~get~.
en.comprobar:
From Latin ~comprobāre~ (“to approve fully, to confirm, to prove”), from ~com-~ (“together, thoroughly”) + ~probāre~ (“to test, to prove, to approve”), from ~probus~ (“good, upright, honest”). ~probus~ derives from Proto-Indo-European *~pro-~ (“forward”) + *~bʰuH-~ (“to be, to grow”) — literally “growing well, turning out well.” Cognate with Italian ~comprovare~ and Portuguese ~comprovar~, and — through ~probāre~ — with English ~prove~, ~probe~, and ~approve~.

At the root sits ~probus~, “good” in the deep sense of “growing forward, turning out well” — the same *~bʰuH-~ (“to be, to grow”) that underlies English ~be~ and the Spanish preterite ~fui~ (“I was”). To ~probāre~ was to test whether a thing was truly ~probus~, genuinely sound; the ~com-~ prefix adds thoroughness, so ~comprobar~ means to “check right through,” to verify. The family is large and thoroughly everyday: ~probar~ (“to try, to taste, to prove”), ~prueba~ (“proof, test”), ~aprobar~ (“to approve, to pass an exam”), ~probable~ (“probable,” literally “provable”), and ~probeta~ (“test tube”).
en.comprometer:
From Latin ~compromittere~ (“to make a mutual promise, to submit to arbitration”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~promittere~ (“to promise”), which is itself ~pro-~ (“forth”) plus ~mittere~ (“to send, to let go”). Spanish ~comprometer~ thus rests on the image of sending forth a word together. It is cognate with English ~commit~ and ~compromise~, Italian ~compromettere~ and Portuguese ~comprometer~.

In Roman law ~compromittere~ meant that two parties jointly promised to abide by an arbiter’s ruling, and that double edge survives: ~comprometer~ can mean to commit or pledge oneself, but also to compromise in the sense of endangering or implicating — to leave someone exposed. The reflexive ~comprometerse~ is the ordinary verb for getting engaged to marry. From ~mittere~ Spanish draws a huge family, among them ~meter~, ~prometer~, ~someter~, ~admitir~, ~misión~ and ~mensaje~.
en.comunicar:
From Latin ~commūnicāre~ (“to share, make common, impart”), from ~commūnis~ (“common, shared”). ~commūnis~ goes back through Old Latin ~commoinis~ to Proto-Italic *~kommoinis~ and Proto-Indo-European *~ḱom-moy-ni-s~, built on the root *~mey-~ (“to change, exchange”) — the same element seen in Latin ~mūnus~ (“duty, service, gift”). Cognate with French ~communiquer~, Italian ~comunicare~ and English ~communicate~; and, through ~commūnis~, with English ~common~ and, via ~mūnus~, ~immune~ and ~municipal~.

Etymologically, to communicate is to “make common” — to put something into the shared pool, which is why the word covers passing on news, connecting rooms and receiving Communion alike. The ancient root *~mey-~ carried the idea of reciprocal exchange: a ~mūnus~ was a service or gift given with the expectation of return, and one who owed no such service was ~immūnis~, “exempt.” From this stock Spanish keeps ~común~, ~comunidad~, ~comunión~, ~municipio~, ~inmune~ and ~remunerar~, all circling the notion of shared obligation.
en.conceder:
From Latin ~concēdere~ (“to yield, give way, grant”), from ~con-~ (intensive here) and ~cēdere~ (“to go, withdraw, yield”). The deeper origin of ~cēdere~ is disputed: by one account it comes from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱe-~ (“here”) plus *~sed-~ (“to sit”) — “to sit down, then go” — while another connects it to a root *~ḱyesd-~ (“to drive away”); the sources do not settle the question. Cognate with Italian ~concedere~, French ~concéder~, and Portuguese ~conceder~; English ~concede~ comes from the same Latin verb, and English ~cede~ from ~cēdere~ itself.

The image is spatial: ~concēdere~ is to step aside, to give ground — and from yielding physical space came the sense of yielding a point, then granting a favor or a right. Spanish ~conceder~ still means “to grant, concede, award,” whether a prize, a loan, or an argument. The noun ~concesión~ covers both a concession in debate and a commercial franchise. ~cēdere~ seeded one of Spanish’s most productive verb families through its prefixed compounds: ~ceder~ (“to yield”), ~acceder~ (“to agree; to access”), ~exceder~ (“to exceed”), ~preceder~ (“to precede”), ~proceder~ (“to proceed”), and ~suceder~ (“to happen; to succeed”), plus their nouns in ~-cesión~ and ~-ceso~.
en.concentrar:
A modern compound of ~con-~ (“together”) + ~centrar~ (“to centre”), from Latin ~centrum~ (“centre, fixed point of a compass”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~kéntron~ (“a sharp point, goad, the still point of a drawn circle”), from ~kentéō~ (“I prick, goad”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱent-~ (“to prick, jab”). Cognate formations include Italian ~concentrare~, French ~concentrer~ and Portuguese ~concentrar~.

The Greek ~kéntron~ was first the spike a compass leg stood on, then the centre that spike marked; to ~concentrar~ is to gather things toward one such point. The pricking sense of *~ḱent-~ still shows through the medical ~-centesis~ of a puncture (as in amniocentesis). Spanish relatives include ~centro~, ~céntrico~, ~concentración~ and ~excéntrico~.
en.concluir:
From Latin ~conclūdere~ (“to shut up, close, conclude”), a compound of ~con-~ (“together, thoroughly”) and ~claudere~ (“to close, shut”). ~claudere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~klaudō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~kleh₂u-~ (“hook, peg, key” — the fastening that shuts a door). Cognates of the root include Ancient Greek ~kleís~ (“key, bolt”) and, in Germanic, Old High German ~sliozan~ (“to close, lock,” ancestor of German ~schließen~). Latin ~clāvis~ (“key”) belongs here too. The learned Romance descendants include Italian ~concludere~, French ~conclure~ and Portuguese ~concluir~.

The metaphor is architectural: to conclude is to “close” something up completely — a speech, a deal, a proof. Old Spanish drew the verb from the learned Latin form, keeping the sense of bringing to a close and inferring as a final step. The image of the key and the bolt runs through the whole family: the same root *~kleh₂u-~ gave Spanish ~llave~ (“key,” from ~clāvis~) and its learned doublet ~clave~ (“key, code, clef”), along with ~concluir~’s siblings ~incluir~ (“to shut in”), ~excluir~ (“to shut out”) and ~clausura~ (“closure, cloister”). Even ~claustro~ (“cloister”) and ~esclusa~ (“lock, sluice”) belong to this shut-and-fasten kin.
en.condenar:
From Latin ~condemnāre~ (“to condemn, sentence”), from intensive ~con-~ and ~damnāre~ (“to harm, condemn”), from ~damnum~ (“damage, loss, penalty”). It is cognate with Italian ~condannare~ and French ~condamner~, and, through ~damnāre~, with English ~condemn~, ~damn~ and ~damage~. The deeper origin of ~damnum~ is disputed: by one account it goes back to Proto-Italic *~dapnom~ and a Proto-Indo-European root *~deh₂p-~ (“to apportion, share in a sacrifice”), tied to Latin ~daps~ (“sacrificial feast”) — but this is uncertain and not universally accepted.

Latin ~damnāre~ was a courtroom word — to declare someone liable to a penalty — and ~con-~ intensified it; the moral and religious sense of “condemn” grew from the legal one. In Spanish ~damnum~ also descended by the popular route to ~daño~ (“harm”), giving ~dañar~; the learned line yields ~condena~, ~condenación~, ~indemne~ and ~indemnizar~.
en.conducir:
From Latin ~condūcere~ (“to lead together, bring together”), a compound of ~con-~ (“together”) and ~dūcere~ (“to lead, draw”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ (“to lead, draw”). Cognate with Italian ~condurre~, French ~conduire~, and Portuguese ~conduzir~; through the same verb ~dūcere~ Spanish also has ~ducto~ and ~duque~, and English has ~conduct~, ~duke~, and — natively — ~tow~ and ~tug~.

In Latin ~condūcere~ meant “to lead or draw together,” and in commercial usage “to hire, contract for.” Spanish kept the core sense of guiding and leading — one ~conduce~ an army, a negotiation, or electricity — and in the automotive age extended it to “to drive” a vehicle, the driver being the one who leads the machine. The same root *~dewk-~ seeded a broad family: ~producir~, ~reducir~, ~traducir~, ~inducir~, ~educar~, and the nouns ~conducta~ (“conduct, behavior”) and ~conductor~ (“driver; conductor”).
en.conectar:
Spanish ~conectar~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~conectere~ (also spelled ~connectere~, “to bind together”), from ~con-~ (“together”) and ~nectere~ (“to bind, tie”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ned-~ (“to bind, tie”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~connect~, ~annex~, and ~nexus~, with Latin ~nodus~ (“knot”) — source of Spanish ~nudo~ — and with Old English ~net~.

Because it entered Spanish through scholarly and, later, technical channels, ~conectar~ never underwent the sound changes of an inherited word; it kept its Latin shape almost intact. Its spread is modern: the everyday senses of joining wires, machines and, eventually, people and computers grew with electricity and telecommunications, reinforced by English ~connect~. From the same ~nectere~ Spanish also holds ~nexo~ (“link”), ~conexión~ (“connection”), ~anexar~ (“to annex”), and ~desconectar~ (“to disconnect”). The Latin past participle ~nexus~ still names, in many languages, the point where strands are tied together.
en.confiar:
From ~con-~ (“with, thoroughly”) + ~fiar~, the latter from Vulgar Latin *~fīdāre~, a reshaping of Latin ~fīdere~ (“to trust”). This goes back to Proto-Italic *~feiðō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~bʰeydʰ-~ (“to trust, confide”). Cognate with Italian ~confidare~, French ~confier~ and Portuguese ~confiar~, and — through the same root — with English ~faith~, ~fidelity~ and ~confide~, and with Ancient Greek ~peíthō~ (“I persuade”).

The Latin noun ~fidēs~ meant “trust, good faith,” and to ~confiar~ is to place that faith together with another. The same root gave Spanish a wide field of reliance: ~fe~, ~fiar~ (“to trust; to sell on credit”), ~fiel~, ~confianza~, ~fidelidad~ and ~desafiar~, literally “to un-trust” someone and so challenge them.
en.confirmar:
From Latin ~confirmāre~ (“to make firm, strengthen”), a compound of the intensive prefix ~con-~ and ~firmāre~ (“to make firm, secure”), itself from the adjective ~firmus~ (“firm, steadfast”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰer-~ (“to hold, support”). Cognate with Italian ~confermare~, French ~confirmer~, and Portuguese ~confirmar~, and — through ~firmus~ — with English ~firm~.

The path from “make solid” to “verify” ran through the idea of settling something so firmly that it can no longer be shaken: to ~confirmar~ a fact is to make it firm against doubt, and to confirm an appointment is to fix it in place. Medieval Latin also gave the verb an ecclesiastical career, in the sacrament of confirmation that “strengthens” the baptized. The same ~firmus~ seeded a rich Spanish family: ~firme~ (“steady”), ~firmar~ (“to sign,” literally to give a document firmness), ~firma~ (“signature; business firm”), ~afirmar~ (“to affirm”), and even ~enfermo~ (“sick”), literally “not firm,” from ~infirmus~.
en.conformar:
From Latin ~conformāre~ (“to shape, fashion, form symmetrically”), a compound of ~con-~ (“together, thoroughly”) and ~formāre~ (“to form, shape”), from ~forma~ (“form, shape, figure”). Cognate with Italian ~conformare~, French ~conformer~, and Portuguese ~conformar~; English borrowed the same verb as ~conform~.

~conformar~ meant “to give shape to,” and from “to shape together” came “to make things agree, bring into accord,” whence the modern reflexive ~conformarse~ (“to make do, resign oneself, be content with”). The base ~forma~ is of uncertain origin: it has long been linked to Greek ~morphḗ~ (“form, shape”), supposedly by a transposition of consonants, but that account is problematic and disputed, so the resemblance is best treated as unproven. Whatever its source, ~forma~ seeded ~formar~, ~fórmula~, ~informar~, ~transformar~, ~deforme~, and ~uniforme~.
en.conocer:
From Old Spanish ~conoçer~, from Vulgar Latin *~cōnōscere~, a reshaping of Latin ~cognōscere~ (“to get to know, recognize”), from ~com-~ (“together, thoroughly”) plus ~gnōscere~/~nōscere~ (“to know”), from Proto-Italic *~gnōskō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know, recognize”). Cognate with Italian ~conoscere~, French ~connaître~, and Portuguese ~conhecer~; through the same root Spanish is kin to English ~know~ and ~cognition~, to Latin-derived ~recognize~ and ~notice~, and to Greek ~gnosis~.

Latin ~cognōscere~ was itself built on ~nōscere~, the simple verb “to know,” with the intensive prefix ~com-~ adding the nuance of coming to know something fully or by acquaintance — which is why Spanish ~conocer~ leans toward knowing a person or place, while ~saber~ covers knowing a fact. The verb’s ~-cer~ ending preserves the Latin inchoative ~-scere~, marking a knowledge that is entered into, a process of becoming acquainted. The same PIE root *~ǵneh₃-~ seeded an enormous Spanish family: ~conocimiento~, ~reconocer~, ~desconocido~, and — through the parallel Latin ~nōscere~/~nōtus~ — ~noticia~, ~nota~, ~notar~, and ~noble~ (“knowable, well-known”).
en.conseguir:
From Latin ~consequī~ (“to follow after, to pursue, to attain”), from intensive ~com-~ plus ~sequī~ (“to follow”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”). It is a learned or semi-learned relative of the inherited ~seguir~ (directly from ~sequī~). Through the same root come Italian ~conseguire~, English ~sequence~, ~consequence~, ~second~, and ~pursue~, and — from the Greek branch — ~hépomai~ (“to follow”).

The logic of “to obtain” is a small chase: ~consequī~ meant to follow something all the way through until you reach it, so “to attain” is simply “to follow to the end.” Spanish keeps that hunting sense sharp in ~perseguir~ (“to pursue, persecute”) and ~conseguir~ (“to get, to manage to”), where the prize is whatever you have chased down. From the same *~sekʷ-~ Spanish also has ~seguir~, ~consecuencia~ (“that which follows”), ~consecutivo~, ~secuencia~, and ~séquito~ (“retinue,” the followers of a great person) — a whole vocabulary built on the simple act of coming after.
en.conservar:
From Latin ~cōnservāre~ (“to keep safe, preserve”), from ~con-~ (here intensive) plus ~servāre~ (“to watch over, guard, keep”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ser-~ (“to protect, watch over”), a root also attested in Avestan ~haraiti~ (“heeds, protects”). English holds the learned borrowings ~conserve~, ~preserve~, ~observe~ and ~reserve~.

A crucial distinction hides here: Latin had two similar verbs, ~servāre~ (“to guard, keep”) and ~servīre~ (“to serve,” from ~servus~, “slave”), and only the first is the parent of ~conservar~. To conserve is thus to guard-and-keep, not to serve. Spanish built a rich family on the guarding verb: ~conserva~ (“preserve, canned food”), ~conservación~, ~conservador~ (“conservative; curator”), and, from the prefixed relatives, ~observar~, ~preservar~ and ~reservar~. When you keep fruit as ~conserva~ in a jar, you are doing exactly what a Roman ~servāre~ named — standing guard over something so that time cannot take it.
en.considerar:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~cōnsīderāre~ (“to look at closely, examine, weigh”), cognate with Italian ~considerare~, French ~considérer~, Portuguese ~considerar~, and English ~consider~. The word is traditionally parsed as ~con-~ (an intensifying prefix) plus a stem tied to ~sīdus~ (stem ~sīder-~, “star, constellation”) — but this is only a proposal: the sources hedge it as « perhaps » from ~sīdus~, and ~sīdus~ itself is of uncertain origin.

By that appealing hypothesis, ~cōnsīderāre~ was once an augur's or astronomer's term meaning “to observe the stars attentively,” paired with ~dēsīderāre~ (“to cease watching the stars,” hence “to long for, miss”), the source of Spanish ~desear~ and English ~desire~. It is a lovely story — attention to the heavens becoming careful thought — but because the ~sīdus~ link is unproven, it should be offered as a guess, not a fact. What is secure is the classical sense already present in Latin: to examine, to weigh in the mind. From ~cōnsīderāre~ Spanish drew ~consideración~ (“consideration”), ~considerable~, ~considerado~ (“considerate”), and ~desconsiderado~ (“inconsiderate”).
en.consistir:
From Latin ~consistere~ (“to stand firm, take a stand, be composed of”), a compound of ~con-~ (“together”) and ~sistere~ (“to cause to stand, come to a stop”), a reduplicated form built on ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Cognate with Italian ~consistere~, French ~consister~, and Portuguese ~consistir~; English borrowed the same verb as ~consist~.

Latin ~sistere~ was the causative-reduplicated partner of ~stāre~: where ~stāre~ meant simply “to stand,” ~sistere~ meant “to make stand” or “to come to a stand.” Prefixed with ~con-~, ~consistere~ meant “to stand firm together,” and from “to hold together” came the abstract “to be made up of,” the ordinary modern meaning — a thing ~consiste en~ its parts. The reduplicated ~sistere~ underlies a whole Spanish set: ~existir~, ~insistir~, ~resistir~, ~persistir~, ~desistir~, and ~asistir~; the plain ~stāre~ gave ~estar~ itself, sharing the deep root *~steh₂-~.
en.constar:
~constar~ continues Latin ~constāre~ (“to stand together, stand firm, be settled, cost”), a compound of ~con-~ (“together, with”) and ~stāre~ (“to stand”). ~stāre~ comes from Proto-Italic *~stāō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”) — the same root behind ~estar~, English ~stand~ and ~stay~, and German ~stehen~. From ~constāre~ come English ~constant~ and ~cost~, Italian ~costare~, and French ~coûter~ (both “to cost”), showing how “to stand firm at a price” slid into “to cost.”

Spanish took the abstract branches. To ~constar~ de is “to consist of, be composed of” (things that stand together make a whole); and ~constar~ alone is “to be on record, be evident” — ~me consta~ means “I know it for a fact,” and something ~consta~ en acta (“is entered in the minutes”). The idea is of a fact that stands firm and established. Kin include ~constante~, ~constancia~ (“perseverance; written proof”), ~costar~ (“to cost,” the popular doublet), and ~costo~ or ~coste~.
en.constituir:
From Latin ~constituere~ (“to set up, establish, arrange”), a compound of ~con-~ (“together, thoroughly”) and ~statuere~ (“to set up, cause to stand”), itself from ~status~ (“a standing, condition”), from ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). The same root stands behind English ~stand~ and ~stay~; the verb itself was borrowed into English as ~constitute~ and lives on in Italian ~costituire~ and French ~constituer~.

The literal image is architectural: to ~constituere~ was to make the parts of a thing stand together, and so to found or compose it. Spanish ~constituir~ kept exactly that: a set of members ~constituye~ a body, a law ~constituye~ an offense. From ~statuere~ and ~status~ Spanish drew a whole legal-institutional vocabulary — ~constitución~, ~estatuto~, ~instituir~, ~restituir~, ~sustituir~ and ~destituir~ — all built on the notion of causing something to stand in place.
en.construir:
Spanish ~construir~ comes from Latin ~cōnstruere~ (“to heap up, build, construct”), a compound of the prefix ~con-~ (“together”) and ~struere~ (“to pile up, arrange, build”). ~struere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~strew-~ (“to spread, strew”), the same root that, in the Germanic line, gave English ~strew~ and ~straw~ (originally “that which is strewn”). The Latin verb seeded a large family: ~īnstruere~ (“to build in, equip, teach”), ~dēstruere~ (“to un-build, destroy”), and the noun ~strūctūra~. English took ~construct~, ~structure~, ~instrument~, and ~destroy~ from these; Italian has ~costruire~, French ~construire~, and Portuguese ~construir~.

The image at the root is spreading things out in layers — laying courses one over another — so ~construere~ literally piled materials together into a structure. Spanish inherited the verb with an irregular twist: the ~-uir~ conjugation inserts a ~-y-~ before an ending that begins with a strong vowel (~construyo~, ~construyó~, ~construyendo~), a pattern shared by ~huir~ and ~destruir~. Beyond building, ~construir~ serves grammar (~construir una frase~, “to construct a sentence”) and geometry. From the same root Spanish keeps ~estructura~, ~construcción~, ~instruir~, ~instrumento~, ~destruir~, and ~industria~ — the last, by one account, from ~indu-~ (“within”) plus a ~struere~ element, though that derivation is debated.
en.consultar:
From Latin ~consultāre~ (“to deliberate, take counsel repeatedly”), the frequentative of ~consulere~ (“to take counsel, consult”). Cognate with Italian ~consultare~, French ~consulter~ and English ~consult~ and ~counsel~. The origin of ~consulere~ is debated: de Vaan takes it as the primary verb (not derived from ~consul~) — probably ~com-~ (“together”) plus a root meaning “gather,” so “to call the Senate together.”

However ~consul~ and ~consulere~ are ultimately related, the shared image is people brought together to deliberate. From ~consilium~ (“counsel, deliberation”) Spanish drew ~consejo~ (“advice, council”) and ~consejero~; from the verb come ~consulta~, ~consultor~ and ~consultorio~, and the ancient title ~cónsul~. To consult, then, is to gather minds — whether around a doctor, a lawyer, or a book.
en.consumir:
From Latin ~consūmere~ (“to use up, to take up completely”), from ~con-~ (intensive) plus ~sūmere~ (“to take”), which is itself ~sub-~ plus ~emere~ (“to take, to buy”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁em-~ (“to take, to distribute”). Cognate with Italian ~consumare~, French ~consumer~ and Portuguese ~consumir~; through ~emere~ it is related to English ~exempt~, ~redeem~ and ~example~.

Latin ~consūmere~ pointed at using a thing up to nothing — burning it, wearing it out, eating it away — and Spanish still uses ~consumir~ both for spending goods and for the slow ravages of grief or fire. A famous trap sits next door: ~consumir~ is constantly confused with ~consumar~ (“to accomplish, to consummate”), yet the two are unrelated — ~consumar~ descends from ~consummāre~, from ~summa~ (“sum, total”), and only looks like its neighbor. From the same ~emere~ and ~sūmere~ family Spanish also drew ~asumir~, ~presumir~, ~resumir~, ~redimir~, ~ejemplo~ and ~exento~.
en.contar:
From Latin ~computāre~ (“to reckon, to calculate”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~putāre~ (“to reckon, to think; originally to prune, to clean up”). Through Vulgar Latin the word wore down to Old Spanish ~contar~. Its Romance kin are Italian ~contare~ and Portuguese ~contar~; French split it into two spellings, ~compter~ (“to count”) and ~conter~ (“to tell”). English ~count~ came through Old French, while the undamaged Latin form re-entered as the learned doublet ~compute~.

The double life of the verb is the memorable part: ~contar~ means both “to count” and “to tell, to narrate,” exactly as English pairs ~count~ with ~recount~ and French pairs ~compter~ with ~conter~ — to enumerate and to recount are the same act of running through items in order. Spanish keeps both alive in ~cuenta~ (“a bill, an account”) and ~cuento~ (“a tale, a story”). Other kin include ~contador~ (“accountant; meter”), ~contable~, ~descontar~ (“to discount”), and the learned ~cómputo~ (“computation”) and ~computadora~ (“computer”).
en.contemplar:
From Latin ~contemplārī~ (“to gaze at attentively, to observe”), from ~con-~ (here intensive) plus ~templum~ — in the language of augury, the region of sky or ground that a priest marked out to watch for omens. Spanish inherited it as a learned word, alongside Italian ~contemplare~, French ~contempler~, and Portuguese ~contemplar~, and it is the source of English ~contemplate~. By one traditional account ~templum~ is linked to Greek ~témenos~ (“a precinct cut off and set apart”), from a root meaning “to cut,” though the deeper origin is debated.

The augur who “contemplated” quite literally fixed his gaze on that consecrated ~templum~ and watched the birds pass across it; from that ritual attentiveness the sense widened to any absorbed, careful looking, and then to unhurried mental consideration. Modern Spanish keeps both directions at once — one can ~contemplar~ a landscape with the eyes and ~contemplar~ a plan with the mind. From the same ~templum~ Spanish also draws ~templo~ (“temple,” the marked-off holy building) and the learned pair ~contemplación~ and ~contemplativo~.
en.contener:
From Latin ~continēre~ (“to hold together, contain, keep in”), a compound of ~con-~ (“together”) and ~tenēre~ (“to hold”). ~Tenēre~ comes from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”), the sense of holding growing out of keeping something taut. Spanish ~contener~ was reshaped on the inherited ~tener~ (“to have, hold”), and is cognate with Italian ~contenere~, French ~contenir~, Portuguese ~conter~ and English ~contain~. Through *~ten-~ it is also kin to English ~tenant~, ~tenor~ and ~tension~.

The metaphor inside *~ten-~ is worth pausing on: to “hold” is to keep something stretched taut in the hand, and Latin ~tenēre~ carried that grip into dozens of compounds. ~Continēre~ meant both to enclose (a vessel contains water) and to hold oneself in check — which is why ~contener~ still means both “to contain” and “to hold back, restrain,” and ~contenerse~ is “to restrain oneself.” The ~tenēre~ family is one of Spanish's largest: ~tener~, ~mantener~, ~sostener~, ~retener~, ~obtener~, ~detener~ and ~entretener~, plus nouns like ~contenido~ (“content”) and ~continente~ (“container; continent”).
en.contestar:
From Latin ~contestārī~ (“to call to witness”), from ~con-~ (“together”) and ~testārī~ (“to bear witness”), a verb built on ~testis~ (“witness”). Strikingly, ~testis~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~tri-sth₂-~, literally “the third one standing” — the impartial third party who stands by at a dispute — from *~tréyes~ (“three”) and *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). It is cognate with Italian ~contestare~ and French ~contester~, and, through ~testis~, with English ~contest~, ~testify~ and ~testament~.

In Roman law ~litem contestārī~ meant to open a suit by both parties calling their witnesses; from that “joining of issue” the verb drifted, in Spanish, toward the give-and-take of a reply — first “to answer a charge,” then simply “to answer.” French ~contester~ instead kept the combative sense, “to dispute,” which English ~contest~ inherited. Same-root Spanish words include ~testigo~, ~testimonio~, ~atestiguar~ and ~protestar~.
en.continuar:
From Latin ~continuāre~ (“to join, to make continuous”), from the adjective ~continuus~ (“uninterrupted, hanging together”), from ~continēre~ (“to hold together”), which is ~con-~ (“together”) + ~tenēre~ (“to hold”). ~tenēre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~tenēō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch, to draw”). The stretching sense links it, across the family, to Ancient Greek ~teínō~ (“I stretch”) and Sanskrit ~tanóti~ (“he stretches”). Cognate Romance verbs include Italian ~continuare~, French ~continuer~, and Portuguese ~continuar~.

The metaphor hidden in ~continuar~ is textile: something ~continuus~ is a thread held together without a break, so to continue is literally to keep the thread taut and unbroken. That same *~ten-~ runs through a remarkable range of Spanish words — ~tener~, ~tenso~, ~tienda~ (a “tent,” a stretched cloth, and by extension a “shop”), ~tono~, ~contener~, and ~mantener~. Curiously, the “stretch” root even reaches ~tenue~ (“thin, faint”), a thing stretched until it is fine.
en.contratar:
From Latin ~contractāre~ (“to handle, deal with repeatedly”), a frequentative of ~contrahere~ (“to draw together, enter into”), built from ~con-~ (“together”) and ~trahere~ (“to draw, drag, pull”). The deeper origin of ~trahere~ is genuinely disputed — it answers to no inherited Proto-Indo-European root cleanly, and de Vaan proposes instead a non-Indo-European substrate word borrowed into both Italic and Celtic. English borrowed its relatives as ~contract~, ~treat~ and ~treaty~.

The commercial sense grew straight from the image of drawing parties together: ~contrahere~ meant to conclude a deal or contract, and its frequentative ~contractāre~ — “to keep handling, to deal with” — yielded modern ~contratar~, “to hire, to engage by agreement.” Spanish preserves an unusually vivid witness to ~trahere~: the everyday verb ~traer~ (“to bring”) descends from it directly, still literally “drawing” something toward you. Around it cluster ~tratar~ (“to treat, deal with”), ~trato~, ~tratado~ (“treaty”), ~contrato~, ~contrata~ and ~atraer~ (“to attract”) — a whole vocabulary of pulling, handling and coming to terms.
en.contribuir:
Spanish ~contribuir~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~contribuere~ (“to bring together, to pay jointly”), from ~con-~ (“together”) and ~tribuere~ (“to allot, assign, grant”). The verb ~tribuere~ was formed on the noun ~tribus~, the Roman “tribe” or citizen division: to ~tribuere~ was, at root, to distribute something among the tribes. Cognates through ~tribuere~ include English ~contribute~, ~attribute~, ~distribute~, and ~tribute~, and Italian ~contribuire~.

The origin of ~tribus~ itself is debated. It is often linked to ~trēs~ (“three”) and taken to name the three founding tribes of early Rome — the Ramnes, Tities and Luceres — with a second element sometimes tied to *~bʰuH-~ (“to be”); but the sources caution that no sense of “three” actually survives in ~tribuere~, and the tripartite story may be later rationalization, so it should be given as a hypothesis rather than fact. What is solid is the accounting sense: to “assign a share.” From it Spanish holds ~contribución~ (“contribution, tax”), ~tributo~ (“tribute”), ~atribuir~ (“to attribute”), ~distribuir~ (“to distribute”), and ~retribuir~ (“to remunerate”).
en.controlar:
A late arrival from French ~contrôler~, from the noun ~contrôle~, a contracted form of Middle French ~contre-rôle~ (“counter-roll”). This joined ~contre-~ (“against”, from Latin ~contra~) to ~rôle~, “a roll of parchment”, from Latin ~rotulus~, the diminutive of ~rota~ (“wheel”). ~rota~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root *~Hret-~ (“to run, roll”), cognate with German ~Rad~ (“wheel”) and Sanskrit ~ratha~ (“chariot”).

A ~contre-rôle~ was a duplicate register kept alongside the original so that one could be checked against the other — to “control” an account was to audit it against its counter-roll, and the official in charge was the ~controller~ (later respelled ~comptroller~). Spanish ~controlar~ thus carries the double sense of “to check, verify” and “to command”. The wheel at the root turns up everywhere: Spanish ~control~ and ~rueda~, and English ~roll~, ~rotate~ and — from the very same ~rôle~, once the roll bearing an actor's lines — the word ~role~.
en.convencer:
~convencer~ descends from Latin ~convincere~, a compound of the intensive prefix ~con-~ and ~vincere~ (“to conquer, overcome, win”). ~vincere~ arose from a nasal-infixed Proto-Italic *~winkō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~weyk-~ (“to overcome, fight”); the ~-n-~ inside ~vincere~ is that infix. The root's cousins include Gothic ~weihan~ (“to fight”) and, through Latin, English ~victor~, ~convince~, and ~evince~; Italian ~vincere~ still plainly means “to win.”

In Latin ~convincere~ meant “to overcome decisively,” especially “to refute someone conclusively” in court — winning the argument, not the war. Spanish softened the courtroom edge: to ~convencer~ is to win someone over by reasoning, and the reflexive ~convencerse~ is “to become convinced.” The martial metaphor is intact: persuasion as a small, bloodless conquest of another's judgment. From the same ~vincere~ come ~vencer~ (“to defeat”), ~invencible~, ~vencedor~, and ~convincente~ (“convincing”), while the ~con-~ plus participle pairing gave the noun ~convicción~.
en.convertir:
Spanish ~convertir~ derives from Latin ~convertere~ (“to turn around, transform”), from the prefix ~con-~ and ~vertere~ (“to turn”). ~vertere~ rests on Proto-Indo-European *~wert-~ (“to turn, rotate”), a root richly attested across the family: Sanskrit ~vártate~ (“it turns”), German ~werden~ (“to become”) and the English suffix ~-ward~ (as in “toward,” a turning in some direction) all descend from it.

To convert is, at heart, to turn something into something else — a religious “conversion” is a turning of the soul, and ~convertir~ keeps that pivot of transformation. Spanish inherited ~vertere~ directly as ~verter~ (“to pour, spill”), and built a wide prefixed family: ~invertir~ (“to invert; to invest”), ~advertir~ (“to warn, to notice”), ~divertir~ (“to divert; to amuse”) and ~revertir~ (“to revert”), alongside the nouns ~verso~ (“verse,” a line that turns) and ~versión~.
en.convocar:
From Latin ~convocāre~ (“to call together, to assemble”), from ~con-~ (“together”) and ~vocāre~ (“to call”), a verb derived from ~vōx~ (“voice”). All of this rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~wekʷ-~ (“to speak, to utter”). Spanish ~convocar~ is a learned borrowing that kept the Latin form closely. It is cognate with Italian ~convocare~, French ~convoquer~, Portuguese ~convocar~, and English ~convoke~, and — through the same root — with English ~voice~ and ~vociferous~.

The picture behind ~convocāre~ is vivid and literal: to use the voice to call people into one place. Spanish keeps that civic, formal flavor — a government convenes (~convoca~) elections, a university convenes a competitive examination, a leader convenes a meeting — so the verb lives largely in the language of institutions and public summons. From the same ~vōx~ / *~wekʷ-~ root Spanish inherited and borrowed a broad family: ~voz~, ~vocal~, ~vocación~, ~vocabulario~, ~convocatoria~, ~invocar~, ~provocar~, and ~abogado~ (through ~advocātus~, “one called to aid”).
en.corregir:
From Latin ~corrigere~ (“to make straight, set right, reform”), a compound of the intensive ~com-~ and ~regere~ (“to guide, to rule, to keep straight”). ~regere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, to make right”), one of the most productive roots in the family — source of Sanskrit ~rā́jati~ (“directs, rules”), Latin ~rēx~ (“king”), and English ~right~ and ~regent~. Sisters of ~corrigere~ include Italian ~correggere~, Portuguese ~corrigir~, and French ~corriger~.

The metaphor is bodily: to correct is to take something crooked and make it straight again. That physical sense survives in ~recto~ (“straight”) and ~regla~ (“ruler, rule”), both from the same *~h₃reǵ-~, and in the wider Spanish clan ~regir~, ~dirigir~, ~erigir~, ~régimen~, ~regular~, ~rey~, and ~reino~. English inherited the split too: a straightedge that traces lines and a monarch are, at root, the same idea — the one who keeps the line straight. From ~corrigere~’s own participle ~corrēctus~ came ~correcto~ and, by way of French, English “correct.”
en.correr:
From Latin ~currere~ (“to run”), from Proto-Italic *~korzō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱers-~ (“to run”). It is cognate with Italian ~correre~, French ~courir~ and Portuguese ~correr~, and the same root, in the sense “vehicle”, surfaces in Welsh ~car~ (“car”) and in Latin ~currus~ (“chariot”).

Latin ~currere~ meant simply “to run”, and Spanish ~correr~ still does — of people, water, time and rumours alike. The verb spun off a busy family: ~corriente~ (“current, stream”), ~correo~ (“mail”, once carried by a courier who literally ran), ~corredor~ (“runner; corridor”), ~corrida~ (“bullfight; a run”) and ~recorrer~ (“to travel over”). Through Latin ~currere~ and its chariot-noun ~currus~, English inherited a whole fleet of learned words, among them ~current~, ~course~, ~courier~ and ~corridor~.
en.corresponder:
A compound of the prefix ~con-~ (here assimilated to ~cor-~, “together, mutually”) and ~responder~ (“to answer”), which descends from Latin ~respondēre~ (“to answer, reply”), itself ~re-~ (“back”) plus ~spondēre~ (“to pledge, promise solemnly”), from Proto-Indo-European *~spend-~ (“to make an offering, perform a rite, engage oneself by a vow”). The root’s ritual charge survives in Greek ~spéndō~ (“to pour a libation”) and ~spondḗ~ (“libation, solemn treaty”), and in English ~sponsor~ and ~spouse~ — a spouse being literally one who has been pledged. From the Latin participle ~sponsus~/~sponsa~ (“betrothed”) Spanish drew ~esposo~ and ~esposa~.

To ~respondēre~ was originally to answer for something by pledging in return — a promise given back — so the idea of matched, reciprocal obligation sat inside the word from the start. Adding ~con-~ (“mutually”) sharpened exactly that: to ~corresponder~ is for two things to answer to each other, whether letters, feelings, or duties. Spanish returns often to this root — ~responder~, ~respuesta~ (“answer”), ~responsable~ (“responsible,” one who must answer), ~correspondencia~ (“correspondence”), and, through the marriage sense, ~esposo~ and ~esposa~, spouses bound by a mutual vow. English responsibility and correspondence travel the same route from a Roman word for a sacred, binding promise.
en.cortar:
From Latin ~curtāre~ (“to shorten”), a verb built on the adjective ~curtus~ (“short, cut off, mutilated”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)ker-~ (“to cut”). Portuguese ~cortar~ is its exact twin, and French keeps the adjective as ~court~ (“short”), from which English borrowed ~curt~. Through the same PIE root ~cortar~ is cognate with English ~short~, ~shear~, and ~shard~, all carrying the root’s core idea of cutting or being cut down.

Latin already had a plain verb for cutting, but Vulgar Latin preferred the vivid ~curtāre~, “to make short,” and it is this that Spanish inherited as the everyday word for “to cut.” The adjective ~corto~ (“short”) comes straight from ~curtus~, and the noun ~corte~ names both a cut and the edge that makes it. The family is large: ~cortante~ (“cutting, sharp”), ~recortar~ (“to trim, cut out”), ~acortar~ (“to shorten”), ~cortadura~ and ~cortacésped~ (“lawnmower,” literally a grass-cutter). The homograph ~corte~ meaning “royal court,” however, belongs to a different Latin word, ~cohors~, and is unrelated.
en.costar:
From Latin ~constāre~ (“to stand together, stand firm, be settled, cost”), a compound of ~con-~ (“together”) and ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Cognate with Italian ~costare~, French ~coûter~ (Old French ~coster~), and Portuguese ~custar~; English borrowed the French descendant as ~cost~.

The commercial sense grew from the idea of a fixed, settled price: Latin ~constāre~ meant “to stand together, be established,” and in accounting the phrase ~constat~ (“it stands at, it amounts to”) fixed what a thing was worth. From “to be settled at a price” came simply “to cost.” The learned doublet ~constar~ survives beside inherited ~costar~ with the older meaning “to be on record, be evident.” The same root *~steh₂-~ underlies ~estar~, ~costa~ (“cost”), and ~coste~/~costo~.
en.crear:
From Latin ~creāre~ (“to create, produce, bring forth”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱer-~ (“to grow, become bigger”). The same root produced Latin ~crēscere~ (“to grow”) and the grain-goddess ~Cerēs~, whose name gave us ~cereal~. Cognate Romance descendants include Italian ~creare~, Portuguese ~criar~ and French ~créer~; English ~create~ is a learned borrowing of the Latin participle ~creātus~.

The Latin verb tied creating to growing and bringing forth, and Spanish kept both threads: ~crear~ means “to create,” while its inherited doublet ~criar~ means “to raise, rear, breed” — to make something grow. From the same root Spanish draws ~creación~, ~creador~, ~criatura~ (“creature”) and ~criadero~ (“breeding ground”), and, through ~crēscere~, the growth family ~crecer~, ~creciente~ and ~incremento~. English shares the harvest: ~create~ and ~creature~, but also ~crescent~ (a “growing” moon), ~increase~ and even ~recruit~ — originally a fresh “growth” of new soldiers.
en.crecer:
Spanish ~crecer~ was inherited from Latin ~crēscere~ (“to grow, arise, increase”), the inchoative of an older stem: Proto-Italic *~krēskō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱreh₁-~ (“to grow, become bigger”). The ~-sc-~ that runs through the Latin is exactly the inchoative marker, “to begin to grow,” so the verb carries the idea of growth-in-progress in its very shape. The same root fed Latin ~creāre~ (“to bring forth, create”) and the goddess ~Cerēs~. It is cognate with Italian ~crescere~, French ~croître~ and Portuguese ~crescer~; through Latin borrowings it is also kin to English ~crescent~, ~increase~ and ~recruit~.

A pleasing image hides in the family. The waxing moon is the ~crescent~ moon — the “growing” one — because ~crēscere~ named its nightly increase; and a ~recruit~ is, etymologically, fresh growth, a re-growing of the ranks, from ~recrūta~ “new increase.” The Roman goddess ~Cerēs~, who made the crops grow, gave her name to ~cereal~. In Spanish the verb's own brood is plain and useful: ~creciente~ (“growing; crescent; flood-tide”), ~crecimiento~ (“growth”), ~crecida~ (“river flood”), ~decrecer~ (“to decrease”) and ~acrecentar~ (“to increase, augment”) — all of them still measuring how much a thing has grown.
en.creer:
From Old Spanish ~creer~ (also ~creder~), from Latin ~crēdere~ (“to believe, trust, entrust”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱred-dʰeh₁-~ (“to place one’s heart”), a compound of *~ḱḗr~ (“heart”) and *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place”). Cognate with Italian ~credere~, French ~croire~, and Portuguese ~crer~; through the same Latin verb English gained ~creed~, ~credo~, ~credit~, and ~credible~. The first element is the same *~ḱḗr~ that gave Latin ~cor~ and English ~heart~ and ~cardiac~.

The etymology is unusually vivid: to believe was, literally, to “put your heart” into something — the same gesture of trust that lets ~crēdere~ mean both “believe” and, in commerce, “lend on trust,” the source of ~credit~. Latin ~crēdere~ took the dative of the person trusted, and Spanish still says ~creer a alguien~ (“to believe someone”) beside ~creer en~ (“to believe in”). The heart-root *~ḱḗr~ hides inside a surprising crowd of Spanish words: ~creencia~, ~crédito~, ~credo~, ~increíble~, ~credencial~, and ~credibilidad~, while its “heart” sense survives directly in ~cordial~, ~acordar~, and ~recordar~ (“to remember,” literally to bring back through the heart).
en.criticar:
From Latin ~criticus~ (“critic”), from Ancient Greek ~kritikós~ (“able to judge, discerning”), from ~krínein~ (“to separate, sift, decide”), from Proto-Indo-European *~krei-~ (“to sieve, distinguish”). It is cognate with Italian ~criticare~ and French ~critiquer~, and, through the same Greek verb, with English ~critic~, ~crisis~ and ~criterion~; the Latin branch of the root gave ~cernere~ (“to sift”), cognate with English ~discern~ and ~certain~.

The root idea is a sieve: to ~krínein~ was to shake grain through a screen and so to separate, and from separating came judging and deciding. ~Criticar~ entered Spanish late and learnedly, straight from the Greek-Latin technical vocabulary rather than by unbroken popular descent. From the same source Spanish holds ~crítica~, ~crítico~, ~criterio~ and ~crisis~, and, from the Latin twin ~cernere~, such words as ~discernir~ and ~certero~.
en.cruzar:
From ~cruz~ (“cross”), from Latin ~crux~ (accusative ~crucem~), whose ultimate origin is genuinely uncertain and disputed. One old proposal ties it to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)ker-~ (“to turn, to bend”), another to a root *~krewk-~ (“heap, hill; spine”), but each meets phonetic and semantic difficulties, and many scholars suspect ~crux~ is instead a loan from a lost substrate language. What is secure is the Latin word's Romance spread: Italian ~croce~ and Portuguese ~cruz~, and cognate English ~cross~ and ~crucial~.

From the shape of the ~crux~ Spanish drew the verb ~cruzar~ — to lay one thing across another, or to pass from one side to the other. Travelers ~cruzan~ a river; to ~cruzarse~ with someone is to pass them going the opposite way. The religious charge of the cross runs through ~cruzada~ (“crusade,” whose warriors “took the cross”), while the plain geometry runs through ~crucero~, ~encrucijada~ (“crossroads”), ~crucigrama~ (“crossword”), and ~crucifijo~.
en.cubrir:
From Latin ~cooperīre~ (“to cover completely”), from ~co-~ (an intensive ~con-~) plus ~operīre~ (“to cover, close”), which linguists analyze as a prefix related to ~ob-~ plus a Proto-Indo-European root *~wer-~ (“to cover, shut”). Cognate with French ~couvrir~, Italian ~coprire~, Portuguese ~cobrir~, and — through Old French — English ~cover~.

A nice twist: Latin paired ~operīre~ (“to close, cover”) with ~aperīre~ (“to open”), built on the same “cover” root with opposite prefixes — and ~aperīre~ is the source of Spanish ~abrir~ (“to open”). So ~cubrir~ and ~abrir~ are, at the Latin level, two sides of one coin. From ~cooperīre~ Spanish also drew ~cubierta~ (“cover, deck”), ~cobertura~ (“coverage”), ~encubrir~ (“to conceal”), ~descubrir~ (“to discover, uncover”), and the bedtime ~cobija~ (“blanket”).
en.cuidar:
From Old Spanish ~cuidar~ (also ~coidar~, “to think”), from Latin ~cōgitāre~ (“to think, ponder, consider”), a compound of ~co-~ (from ~cum~, “together”) and ~agitāre~ (“to set in motion, turn over”), the frequentative of ~agere~ (“to drive, do”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive”). Cognate with Portuguese ~cuidar~ and Old French ~cuidier~ (“to think”); English inherited the same Latin verb in ~cogitate~.

The whole history is a metaphor of the mind in motion: Latin ~cōgitāre~ literally set thoughts “moving together.” Old Spanish ~cuidar~ still meant “to think, believe, suppose,” but as one thinks anxiously about a person or thing the sense drifted to “to take care of, look after,” the ordinary modern meaning — to ~cuidar~ someone is to keep them in mind. The older “think” sense survives fossilized in ~cuidado~ (“care; caution; watch out!”) and in ~descuidar~ (“to neglect”). From the same root ~agere~ Spanish also has ~agitar~, ~agente~, and ~acto~.
en.cumplir:
From Latin ~complēre~ (“to fill up, complete, fulfill”), from ~com-~ (intensive) plus ~plēre~ (“to fill”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”). Medieval Spanish had ~complir~ before ~cumplir~ prevailed. It is cognate with Portuguese ~cumprir~ and, through the same Latin verb, with English ~complete~, ~comply~ and ~compliment~; the bare root surfaces in English ~full~ and ~fill~.

The sense ran from “to fill up” to “to fulfill, discharge, carry out (a duty).” Two byways are memorable. First, the phrase ~cumplir años~ (“to complete years”) produced ~cumpleaños~ (“birthday”). Second, the courtesy sense of ~complēre~ passed through Italian ~complimento~ to give both Spanish ~cumplido~ and, back in English, ~comply~ and ~compliment~ — once, to ~comply~ was simply to be gracious. From the same root Spanish keeps the popular ~lleno~ (“full,” from ~plēnus~) beside the learned ~pleno~, along with ~completo~ and ~complemento~.
en.dar:
Spanish ~dar~ descends straight from Latin ~dare~ (“to give”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deh₃-~ (“to give”) — one of the most stable meanings in the whole family. The same root shines through Latin ~dōnum~ (“gift”), Greek ~dídōmi~ (“I give”), and Sanskrit ~dádāti~. Italian ~dare~ and Portuguese ~dar~ kept the plain verb, but French abandoned it for ~donner~ (from ~dōnāre~, “to make a gift”), leaving Spanish among the languages that still simply “give” with ~dare~.

For so short a verb, ~dar~ carries an enormous idiomatic load in Spanish, while its root branches out into a whole family of giving. The language has ~dádiva~ (“gift”), ~don~ (“gift, talent”) and ~donar~ (“to donate”), and, through the Latin participle, ~dado~ (“given; a die”) and ~dato~ (“fact, datum”). Even English ~date~ and ~data~, borrowed from the same Latin participle ~datum~ (“given”), belong to this quietly generous root.
en.deber:
Spanish ~deber~ comes from Latin ~dēbēre~ (“to owe”), which began as a contraction of ~dē-~ (“from, away”) plus ~habēre~ (“to have”): to owe was “to have something from someone else,” held but not truly one's own. So ~deber~ is, at root, a compound of ~haber~. Its Romance siblings share it: French ~devoir~, Italian ~dovere~, Portuguese ~dever~. English ~debt~ and ~due~ come from the same Latin verb, borrowed through French, so they are cousins rather than natives.

From “owe,” ~deber~ grew a second, modal life: to owe an action is to be obliged to do it, so ~deber~ came to mean “must, ought” — ~debo irme~ (“I must go”). The noun ~deber~ means “duty,” and ~deberes~ are a schoolchild's “homework,” obligations owed. The financial thread survives in ~débito~ (“debit”), ~deuda~ (“debt”), and ~debido~ (“due, owed”) — the whole family circling the idea of something held that must be given back.
en.decidir:
From Latin ~dēcīdere~ (“to cut off, to determine”), from ~dē-~ (“off, away”) plus ~caedere~ (“to cut, to strike down”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kh₂eyd-~ (“to strike, to cut”). Cognate with French ~décider~, Italian ~decidere~, and English ~decide~ and ~decision~.

The metaphor is a blade: to decide is to cut off deliberation, severing every alternative but the chosen one — the mental equivalent of slicing through a knot. ~caedere~ was a violent, physical verb, and it left a bloody trail across Latin: it is the ~-cide~ of ~homicida~ (“murderer”) and ~suicidio~, literally acts of cutting down. Gentler siblings survive in Spanish too: from ~praecīdere~ (“to cut in front”) came ~preciso~ and ~precisar~ (“precise,” cut to exact measure), and from ~concīdere~ came ~conciso~ (“concise,” cut short). Every ~decisión~, then, is a small cut.
en.decir:
Spanish ~decir~ comes, through Old Spanish ~dezir~, from Latin ~dīcere~ (“to say, to tell”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, to point out”) — saying imagined first as pointing something out. That root of showing gave, on the Germanic side, English ~teach~ and ~token~, and in Greek ~deíknymi~ (“I show”). The Romance reflexes stayed close: Italian ~dire~, French ~dire~, Portuguese ~dizer~.

The step from “point out” to “speak” is the whole story of the word, and the pointing sense lingers in its relatives. Spanish keeps the past participle ~dicho~ (“said; a saying”) and builds ~contradecir~ (“to contradict”) and ~bendecir~ (“to bless,” literally “to say well”). From the same root come ~dictar~ (“to dictate”) and ~dictado~, the legal ~edicto~ (“edict”), and ~índice~ (“index, forefinger”) — the very finger that points.
en.declarar:
From Latin ~dēclārāre~ (“to make clear, reveal, announce”), formed from an intensive ~dē-~ and ~clārāre~ (“to make clear, brighten”), a verb from the adjective ~clārus~ (“clear, bright, loud”). ~Clārus~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~kelh₁-~ (“to shout, call out”), by way of *~kl̥h₁rós~ (“loud”). Spanish ~declarar~ is cognate with Italian ~dichiarare~, French ~déclarer~, Portuguese ~declarar~ and English ~declare~ and ~clear~; through *~kelh₁-~ it is kin to Latin ~clāmāre~ (“to shout”) and even to German ~hell~ (“bright”).

Here is the memorable twist: ~clārus~ began as a word for sound, “loud, ringing,” and only later crossed over to light and sight, “bright, clear” — the ancient mind treating the spreading of a shout and the spreading of light as one image. ~Dēclārāre~ rode that shift, moving from making a thing audibly plain to making it visibly clear, and finally to the modern “to declare,” to state openly. From ~clārus~ Spanish drew ~claro~ (“clear”), ~aclarar~ (“to clarify”), ~clarear~, ~claridad~ and ~clarín~ (“bugle”); and from the same root *~kelh₁-~, through ~clāmāre~, came ~clamar~ and the everyday ~llamar~ (“to call”).
en.dedicar:
From Latin ~dedicāre~ (“to consecrate, to dedicate, to proclaim”), from ~de-~ (“completely, down”) + ~dicāre~ (“to proclaim solemnly, to consecrate”). ~dicāre~ is a first-conjugation relative of ~dīcere~ (“to say”), and both go back to Proto-Indo-European *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, to point out”). That root surfaces in Ancient Greek ~deíknumi~ (“I show”), German ~zeigen~ (“to show”), and English ~teach~ and ~token~. Spanish took the learned ~dedicar~ from Latin. Cognate with Italian ~dedicare~, French ~dédier~, and Portuguese ~dedicar~.

The root idea is pointing: to ~dicāre~ was to point something out with words, to proclaim it — and to ~dedicāre~ was to point it out entirely, to set it apart by solemn declaration, as a temple was dedicated to a god. Modern ~dedicar~ keeps that sense of setting time or effort apart for a purpose. The pointing root *~deyḱ-~ is astonishingly productive in Spanish: ~decir~, ~índice~ (“the pointing finger”), ~dedo~ (“finger”), ~juez~ and ~juzgar~ (“to point out the law,” ~ius~ + ~dicere~), ~predecir~, and ~dictar~.
en.defender:
From Latin ~dēfendere~ (“to ward off, protect”), from ~dē-~ (“away, off”) and a bound root ~-fendere~ (“to strike, push”), from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷʰen-~ (“to strike, kill”). The same root gave ~offendere~ (“to strike against”). Cognate with Italian ~difendere~, French ~défendre~, and — as borrowings — English ~defend~, ~fend~, and ~offend~.

Curiously, ~-fendere~ never stood on its own in Latin: no simple verb “to strike” is attested, only the compounds ~dēfendere~ (to strike the enemy away) and ~offendere~ (to strike against — hence to give offense). French pushed ~défendre~ in a legal direction, so it means both to defend and to forbid, while Spanish ~defender~ held to protection. Descendants in Spanish include ~defensa~ (“defense”), ~defensor~ (“defender”), ~ofender~ (“to offend”), and ~ofensa~ (“offense”).
en.definir:
From Latin ~dēfīnīre~ (“to set bounds to, limit, define”), formed from the prefix ~dē-~ (“off, completely”) and ~fīnīre~ (“to limit, bring to an end”), itself built on the noun ~fīnis~ (“boundary, border, end”). The deeper origin of ~fīnis~ is uncertain: one proposal links it to ~fīgere~ (“to fix, fasten, drive in”), as if a boundary were a stake fixed in the ground, but that connection is disputed and far from secure. Spanish ~definir~ is a learned borrowing, cognate with Italian ~definire~, French ~définir~ and Portuguese ~definir~; and because ~fīnīre~ passed through Old French, English ~finish~ belongs to the same family.

In Latin ~dēfīnīre~ meant to mark out the limits of a thing, whether a field or an idea; from drawing those edges came the abstract sense of saying precisely what something is — the modern “to define.” The noun ~fīnis~ was extraordinarily productive in Spanish, yielding the everyday ~fin~ (“end”), together with ~final~, ~finalizar~, ~confín~, ~finito~, ~infinito~ and, of course, ~definición~. The legal ~finiquito~ (“final settlement”) and the verb ~afinar~ (“to tune, refine”) descend from the same source, all preserving the core idea of bringing something to its edge or its end.
en.dejar:
From Old Spanish ~dexar~ (also ~lexar~), from Latin ~laxāre~ (“to loosen, slacken, let go”), the denominative verb of ~laxus~ (“loose, slack”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)leg-~ (“to be slack”). Cognate with Portuguese ~deixar~, French ~laisser~, and Italian ~lasciare~, all of which kept the original ~l-~; through the same Latin verb English acquired ~relax~, ~release~, and ~lease~, and through the same PIE root the native English ~slack~.

Latin ~laxāre~ first meant to slacken a rope or relax the limbs; in Ibero-Romance the sense drifted to “let go,” then “leave behind, allow.” The startling feature of the Spanish form is its initial ~d-~: by one commonly cited account, the expected ~l-~ shifted to ~d-~ under the pull of ~dar~ (“to give”), a neighbor in both meaning and grammar — a swap that sets ~dejar~ apart from its ~l-~-keeping cousins. First documented around 1140, it later spread from “leave” into “stop” and “let.” The same Latin verb seeded the learned Spanish ~laxo~, ~laxante~, and ~relajar~ (a bookish doublet of ~dejar~), plus ~dejadez~ (“lassitude, neglect”).
en.demostrar:
Spanish ~demostrar~ comes from Latin ~dēmōnstrāre~ (“to point out, indicate, prove”), a compound of ~dē-~ (“fully, from”) and ~mōnstrāre~ (“to show, point out”). ~mōnstrāre~ is a denominal verb from ~mōnstrum~ — originally “a divine omen, a portent” — which in turn derives from ~monēre~ (“to warn, advise, remind”). ~monēre~ reflects Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to think”), the vast root behind Latin ~mēns~ (“mind”) and English ~mind~, ~mental~, and ~mean~. English took ~demonstrate~, ~monster~, ~monstrance~, and ~monitor~ from this branch. Italian ~dimostrare~, French ~montrer~ / ~démontrer~, and Portuguese ~demonstrar~ are the Romance parallels of ~demostrar~.

The buried surprise is ~mōnstrum~: a monster was first not a beast but a sign — something shown by the gods as a warning, from ~monēre~ (“to warn”). A ~mōnstrum~ was a portent that pointed to something, and ~mōnstrāre~ meant to point it out; ~dēmōnstrāre~ intensified this into showing thoroughly, and thence proving. Spanish split the inheritance: popular ~mostrar~ evolved by regular sound change, while learned ~demostrar~ was reborrowed closer to the Latin. From the same ~monēre~ / *~men-~ family Spanish keeps ~mostrar~, ~muestra~ (“sample, sign”), ~monstruo~, ~amonestar~ (“to admonish”), ~mente~, and ~mención~.
en.denominar:
From Latin ~dēnōmināre~ (“to name, designate”), formed from ~de-~ (here intensive) and ~nōmināre~ (“to name”), from ~nōmen~ (“name”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁nómn̥~ (“name”). It is cognate with French ~dénommer~, Italian ~denominare~, and Portuguese ~denominar~, and with the Latin-derived English ~denominate~. Straight from *~h₁nómn̥~ come English ~name~, German ~Name~, and Greek ~ónoma~.

Latin ~nōmen~ left Spanish two lines: the patrimonial ~nombre~ (“name”) and the learned ~nominar~ and ~denominar~ (“to name, designate”). A quiet gem sits in arithmetic: the ~denominador~ of a fraction is literally what “names” its parts — in three-fifths, the fifths are the name and the count.
