The same family gave ~nómina~ (“payroll,” once simply a list of names), ~nomenclatura~, ~denominación~ (as in the wine label ~denominación de origen~), ~renombre~ (“renown”), and the grammatical ~pronombre~ (“pronoun”).
en.denunciar:
From Latin ~dēnūntiāre~ (“to announce officially, give notice, proclaim, threaten”), from ~dē-~ (“down, fully”) plus ~nūntiāre~ (“to announce”), a verb built on ~nūntius~ (“messenger, message”). The origin of ~nūntius~ is uncertain: it is usually traced to Proto-Indo-European *~newH-~ (“to shout, cry”), with possible cognates in Sanskrit ~návate~ (“cries, sounds”) and Old Irish ~núall~ (“a loud cry”), while an older derivation from ~novus~ (“new”) is now rejected. Cognate with Italian ~denunciare~, French ~dénoncer~ and Portuguese ~denunciar~, and with English ~denounce~.

In Latin the word was formal and legal — to serve official notice, lodge a public declaration, even proclaim war. Spanish ~denunciar~ preserved that accusatory edge: to report a crime to the authorities or to condemn a wrong in public, a sense the noun ~denuncia~ carries in everyday legal Spanish. The ~nūntius~ family branched widely: ~anunciar~ (“to announce”), ~pronunciar~ (“to pronounce”), ~renunciar~ (“to renounce”) and ~nuncio~, the papal envoy who is, etymologically, simply a “messenger.”
en.depender:
From Latin ~dependēre~ (“to hang from, to hang down”), a compound of ~dē-~ (“down from”) and ~pendēre~ (“to hang, to be suspended”). ~pendēre~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to pull, to stretch, to spin”). The verb is thoroughly Romance — Italian ~dipendere~, French ~dépendre~, Portuguese ~depender~ — and through the same Latin root it matches English ~depend~, ~pendant~, ~pending~, and ~suspend~.

The metaphor is beautifully literal: to ~depender~ is to “hang from” something, exactly as a ~pendiente~ (“earring, pendant”) hangs from an ear. What hangs from a support is held up by it and cannot stand alone — so “hanging from” became “being contingent upon,” relying on. The same ~pendēre~ family gave Spanish ~pender~, ~pendiente~, ~suspender~, ~depender~, and ~independiente~. And here is the surprise: the frequentative ~pēnsāre~ (“to weigh carefully”), from the same root, split into two Spanish verbs — ~pesar~ (“to weigh”) and ~pensar~ (“to think”) — because to weigh an idea in the mind is to think it over. So ~depender~, ~pesar~, and ~pensar~ all hang, in the end, from the same thread.
en.derivar:
From Latin ~dērīvāre~ (“to lead or draw off [water]”), from ~dē-~ (“from, away”) + ~rīvus~ (“brook, stream, channel”). ~rīvus~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reyH-~ (“to flow”). Cognate with Italian ~derivare~ and French ~dériver~, and — through ~rīvus~ — with English ~derive~ and ~rival~.

The literal image is hydraulic: to ~derivar~ water is to lead it away from its main channel into a side one — exactly what an irrigation engineer does. From that physical sense grew the abstract one still dominant today: one thing “flows from” another, so a word, a right, or a conclusion is ~derivado~ (“derived”) from its source. The most charming relative is ~rival~: in Latin a ~rīvālis~ was literally someone who shared the same ~rīvus~ — a neighbor drawing water from the same stream — and since people who share a water source tend to quarrel over it, the word came to mean “competitor.” Spanish kept the whole watery family: ~río~ (“river,” straight from ~rīvus~), ~riachuelo~ (“little stream”), ~derivación~ (“derivation”), and ~deriva~ (“drift,” as in a boat going adrift).
en.desaparecer:
From ~des-~ (a privative prefix, from Latin ~dis-~, “apart, reversal”) prefixed to ~aparecer~ (“to appear”), which comes from Latin ~appārēscere~, an inchoative (“to begin to be visible”) built on ~appārēre~ (“to appear, come into view”), from ~ad-~ (“to”) plus ~pārēre~ (“to come forth, be visible, obey”). The further origin of ~pārēre~ is uncertain. Cognate with Italian ~apparire~ (and ~sparire~), French ~apparaître~ (and ~disparaître~) and Portuguese ~desaparecer~, and with English ~appear~ and ~apparent~.

The ~-ēscere~ inflection is telling: ~aparecer~ is not merely “to be visible” but “to come into visibility,” an entering; ~des-~ then reverses the motion into “to pass out of sight, vanish.” The same ~pārēre~ underlies ~parecer~ (“to seem, to appear-to-be”) — appearing and seeming from one Latin verb — and feeds a wide family: ~aparición~ (“apparition”), ~aparente~ (“apparent”), ~transparente~ (“transparent”) and ~comparecer~ (“to appear in court”).
en.desarrollar:
A Spanish formation from ~des-~ (a prefix of reversal) and ~arrollar~ (“to roll up”), which is ~a-~ plus ~rollo~ (“a roll, scroll”). ~rollo~ descends from Latin ~rotulus~ (“little wheel, roll”), the diminutive of ~rota~ (“wheel”), from Proto-Indo-European *~Hret-~ (“to run, to roll”). The wheel-root has far-flung cognates: German ~Rad~ (“wheel”), Sanskrit ~rátha~ (“chariot”), and Old Irish ~roth~ (“wheel”); ~rotulus~ itself gave English ~roll~ and ~role~ through French ~rôle~.

The image is vivid and exact: to develop is literally to un-roll — ~des-~ + ~arrollar~ — as one opens a rolled scroll to reveal what is written inside. Growth, in this metaphor, is a scroll unspooling. English ~develop~ carries the very same picture by a different route (Old French ~desveloper~, “to unwrap”), so the two languages independently imagine progress as undoing a wrapping. From the same wheel-root Spanish keeps ~rollo~, ~arrollar~, ~rueda~ (“wheel,” straight from ~rota~), ~rótula~ (“kneecap”), and the borrowed ~rotación~ and ~control~ (via the roll-counter of French ~contre-rôle~).
en.descargar:
A compound of the prefix ~des-~ (“un-, reversal,” from Latin ~dis-~) and ~cargar~ (“to load”), from Vulgar Latin ~carricāre~ (“to load a wagon”), a verb built on Latin ~carrus~ (“wheeled wagon, cart”). ~Carrus~ was a Gaulish loan, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱers-~ (“to run”). Cognate with French ~charger~, Italian ~caricare~ and Portuguese ~carregar~; through ~carrus~ it is related to English ~charge~, ~cargo~ and ~car~.

At bottom ~descargar~ means to take the load off a cart — to ~cargar~ was to pile goods onto a ~carrus~, and ~des-~ reverses it. From that concrete image the word fanned out: to unload a ship, to fire (“discharge”) a weapon, to vent one's anger, to relieve an electric ~carga~ — and, in our century, to ~descargar~ a file from the internet, so that the newest sense of the word still rides on a Roman ox-cart. The family is large in Spanish: ~carga~, ~cargo~, ~cargamento~, ~carguero~, ~descarga~, ~recargar~, ~sobrecargar~ and ~encargar~, this last meaning “to entrust,” literally to load a task onto someone.
en.desconocer:
A Spanish formation: ~des-~ (a negating and reversing prefix, from Latin ~dis-~) prefixed to ~conocer~ (“to know”). ~Conocer~ descends through Old Spanish ~conoscer~ from Latin ~cognoscere~ (“to get to know”), a compound of ~com-~ (intensive) and ~gnoscere~ / ~noscere~ (“to know”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~know~ and ~can~, and with the heirs of ~cognoscere~: Italian ~conoscere~ and French ~connaître~.

The prefix ~des-~ negates, so ~desconocer~ literally means “to not know,” but Spanish sharpened it into two everyday senses: to be unaware of or unacquainted with something, and, more pointedly, to refuse to recognize — to disown a signature, a debt, or a person one no longer acknowledges. The PIE root *~ǵneh₃-~ is one of the most fertile in the language, behind ~conocer~, ~conocimiento~, ~reconocer~, ~noticia~ and the learned ~cognición~.
en.describir:
From Latin ~dēscrībere~ (“to write down, copy off, sketch, describe”), a compound of the prefix ~dē-~ (“down, off”) and ~scrībere~ (“to write”). ~scrībere~ originally meant “to scratch, incise” — writing was cutting marks into a surface — and descends from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)kreybʰ-~ (“to scratch, tear, cut”), an extension of *~(s)ker-~ (“to cut”). A striking cognate survives in Ancient Greek ~skáriphos~ (“a scratching, outline, sketch”). Note the false friend: German ~schreiben~ (“to write”) looks cognate but was actually borrowed from the Latin verb, and English ~write~ comes from a different root entirely. The learned Romance descendants include Italian ~descrivere~, French ~décrire~ and Portuguese ~descrever~.

The metaphor of scratching stayed alive across the whole family. To describe is, etymologically, to “write down” the shape of a thing — to sketch it in words. From ~scrībere~ Spanish inherited ~escribir~ (“to write”) and built a dense thicket of compounds — ~describir~, ~inscribir~, ~prescribir~, ~suscribir~, ~transcribir~ — plus nouns like ~escritura~ (“writing, deed”), ~escritor~ (“writer”) and ~escritorio~ (“desk”). From the past participle ~scrīptus~ came ~escrito~ (“written; a writing”) and ~inscripción~ (“inscription”). English drew a matching crop of borrowings from the same Latin verb — ~scribe~, ~script~, ~scripture~, ~describe~ — all still carrying, faintly, the old sense of a stylus scoring a line.
en.descubrir:
From ~des-~ (a reversative prefix, from Latin ~dis-~) plus ~cubrir~ (“to cover”), which comes from Latin ~cooperīre~ (“to cover completely”), a compound of ~co-~ (intensive) and ~operīre~ (“to cover, close”). ~Operīre~ derives from Proto-Italic *~opweriō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂wer-~ (“to cover, shut”). The formation matches Old French ~descovrir~, whence English ~discover~; compare Italian ~scoprire~ and Portuguese ~descobrir~.

The morphology is beautifully transparent: to ~descubrir~ is literally to un-cover, to take the lid off — and Spanish uses it both for physically uncovering and for the mental act of discovery, exactly as English ~discover~ pairs with ~cover~. Columbus’s ~descubrimiento~ of America is the same word as lifting a cloth. From the ~cubrir~ family come ~cubierta~, ~cobertura~, ~encubrir~ and ~recubrir~, while the reversative ~des-~ productively negates hundreds of Spanish verbs.
en.desear:
From Latin ~dēsīderāre~ (“to long for, miss, feel the want of”), traditionally analyzed as ~dē-~ + ~sīdus~ (stem ~sīder-~, “star, constellation”), and inherited by Old Spanish as ~desear~. Cognate with Italian ~desiderare~ and Portuguese ~desejar~, and — through the noun ~dēsīderium~ — with English ~desire~ (via Old French).

The star etymology is the classic account, pairing ~dēsīderāre~ with ~cōnsīderāre~ (“to observe the stars closely”): to desire would be to note a star’s absence, to long for what is no longer in sight. But this is disputed — some scholars reject the ~sīdus~ connection outright and derive the verb from a root meaning “stretch, survey,” so the celestial story, charming as it is, should be taken as one proposal, not settled fact. Secure descendants include ~deseo~, ~deseable~ and ~desiderátum~; from ~sīdus~ itself come ~sideral~ and ~considerar~.
en.destacar:
A comparatively late loan: Spanish took ~destacar~ from French ~détacher~ (“to detach”), from Old French ~destachier~, the negative counterpart of ~atachier~ (“to attach”). French itself leaned on Italian ~staccare~ / ~distaccare~ (“to separate”), the antonym of ~attaccare~ (“to attach, join battle”). At the base lies a Germanic (Frankish) *~stakka~ (“stake, post”), the same source that gave Spanish ~estaca~ (“stake”). It entered Spanish dictionaries around 1705, cognate with English ~detach~.

The oldest sense was military: to ~destacar~ was to detach a body of troops from the main force. From “separate a part from the whole” grew the figurative “stand out, be conspicuous” — that which is set apart draws the eye. The very pair survives elsewhere in Spanish: ~atacar~ (“to attack”), taken from the ~attaccare~ side of the same Italian opposition, once meant “to join, engage.” Modern relatives include ~destacamento~ (“military detachment”), ~destacado~ (“prominent, outstanding”) and the shared ~estaca~.
en.destinar:
From Latin ~dēstināre~ (“to make fast, fix, determine, resolve”), a compound of the intensive prefix ~dē-~ and a verbal stem *~stanāre~ built on ~stāre~ (“to stand”). That stem descends from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand, stand firm”) — the very root behind Spanish ~estar~. So to “destine” something was, at root, to make it stand fixed. The root’s cognates are everywhere: English ~stand~ and ~stay~, German ~stehen~, Greek ~hístēmi~ (“to make stand”). The learned Romance descendants include Italian ~destinare~, French ~destiner~ and Portuguese ~destinar~.

The image is of fixing something firmly in place — and from there the meaning slid toward fixing a purpose or endpoint. To ~destinar~ is to set something aside for a fixed use or send it toward a fixed goal; the past participle gave the noun ~destino~ (“destination; destiny, fate” — the fixed end toward which one stands bound). The same root *~steh₂-~ seeded an enormous Spanish family: ~estar~, ~estación~, ~estable~, ~estatua~, ~constante~, ~obstinado~ (“obstinate,” standing firm against) and ~destino~ itself. Curiously, ~obstinarse~ (“to be obstinate”) shares the exact ~-stinare~ stem — to stand fixed, but in stubbornness rather than fate.
en.destruir:
From Latin ~dēstruere~ (“to tear down, demolish”), from ~dē-~ (“down, un-”) and ~struere~ (“to pile up, build”), from Proto-Indo-European *~strew-~ (“to spread, strew”). Through Old Spanish ~destruir~ it is cognate with Italian ~distruggere~ and French ~détruire~, and — via the same ~struere~ — with English ~structure~, ~construct~ and, borrowed through Old French ~destruire~, ~destroy~.

Where ~struere~ meant to build by heaping things up, the prefix ~dē-~ reversed it: to unbuild, to pull a pile apart. The PIE root *~strew-~ (“to spread”) also underlies English ~strew~ and ~street~ (a “strewn,” paved way). In Spanish the same family gives ~construir~, ~instruir~, ~estructura~ and ~destrucción~.
en.detallar:
A borrowing from French ~détailler~ (“to cut up, sell at retail”), formed from ~dé-~ plus ~tailler~ (“to cut”), from Vulgar Latin *~tāliāre~ (“to cut, split”), from Latin ~tālea~ (“a cutting, rod, twig”). Spanish took the noun ~detalle~ from French ~détail~ at the same time. The French verb ~tailler~ also gave English ~tailor~ (one who cuts cloth) and ~entail~, while ~detail~ itself entered English from the same French source; Italian has the parallel ~dettagliare~.

The image at the root is concrete: ~tālea~ was a twig or slip cut for grafting, so “to detail” is literally to reduce a whole into small cut pieces — the retailer’s sense of selling in fractions and the descriptive sense of itemizing point by point are the same metaphor. Modern ~detallar~ means “to specify, itemize,” and ~detalle~ ranges from “a detail” to “a thoughtful gesture.” A ~detallista~ is both a retailer and a person attentive to little things. The native Spanish reflex of *~tāliāre~ survives separately as ~tajar~ (“to slice”) and the noun ~tajo~ (“a cut, gash”), the popular doublet of the learned, French-clothed ~detallar~.
en.detectar:
From Latin ~dētēctus~, the past participle of ~dētegere~ (“to uncover, lay bare”), formed from ~dē-~ (“off, away”) plus ~tegere~ (“to cover”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)teg-~ (“to cover”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~thatch~ and ~toga~ (a garment that “covers”), and with Portuguese ~detectar~ and French ~détecter~, the shared learned borrowing the Romance languages took from the same Latin stem.

To detect was, at heart, to un-cover — to strip away whatever conceals. Latin ~tegere~ founded a broad family: the roofing tile ~tēgula~ descended to Spanish ~teja~ and, with it, ~tejado~ and ~techo~ (“roof”), the very things that cover a house. The learned prefixed verbs surface in ~proteger~ (“to protect,” literally to cover in front of) and in the anatomical ~tegumento~ (“integument, covering skin”). ~Detectar~ itself entered Spanish late, as a technical term, keeping the crisp Latin logic that to detect a thing is to pull the cover off it.
en.detener:
From ~de-~ (“away, down”) joined to ~tener~, which comes from Latin ~tenēre~ (“to hold, keep”); the Latin verb rests on Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”), holding being understood as keeping something taut. It is cognate with Italian ~tenere~, French ~tenir~ and Portuguese ~ter~, and — through the same root — with English ~tenant~, ~tenure~ and ~contain~.

Latin ~dētinēre~ meant “to hold back, keep back,” and Spanish ~detener~ inherited exactly that: to stop something in its course, and by a natural step to arrest — which is why a person taken into custody is a ~detenido~. The reflexive ~detenerse~ softened to “to pause, to linger over.” The “hold” family is one of Spanish's densest — ~tener~, ~contener~, ~mantener~, ~obtener~, ~sostener~ and ~retener~ — while the underlying “stretch” sense surfaces in relatives like ~tenso~ and ~tienda~, a “tent” of stretched cloth.
en.determinar:
Spanish ~determinar~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dētermināre~ (“to set bounds, mark off”), a compound of ~dē-~ (here intensive) and ~termināre~ (“to limit”), a verb on the noun ~terminus~ (“boundary, limit”). ~terminus~ descends from Proto-Italic *~termnos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~térmn̥~ (“boundary marker”), cognate with Ancient Greek ~τέρμα~ (térma, “goal, turning-post”) and ~τέρμων~ (térmōn, “border”). English took the same Latin word as ~determine~; ~term~ and ~terminal~ share the root.

The metaphor at the heart of the verb is spatial: to ~determinar~ is to draw a line around something, and by fixing its edges to fix what it is — hence the senses “to establish,” “to decide,” and “to cause.” The boundary was no small matter to the Romans: ~Terminus~ was a god, the deity of boundary stones, whose markers were sacred and whose festival, the ~Terminalia~, was kept each February. From the same root Spanish inherited ~término~ (“term, end”), ~terminar~ (“to finish”), ~terminal~, ~exterminar~, ~interminable~, and ~determinación~. To determine something, then, is to give it a ~terminus~ — an end that defines its beginning.
en.devolver:
From Latin ~dēvolvere~ (“to roll down, roll off”), a compound of ~dē-~ (“down, away, back”) and ~volvere~ (“to roll, turn, wind”). ~volvere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~welwō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~welH-~ (“to turn, to wind, to roll”) — the same root behind English ~wallow~ and Ancient Greek ~helíssō~ (“to turn round”) and ~hélix~. From ~dēvolvere~ descend Spanish ~devolver~ and Portuguese ~devolver~; from plain ~volvere~, Italian ~volgere~.

Latin ~dēvolvere~ was purely physical — to send something rolling downhill — but Spanish spun the “back” sense of ~dē-~ into the abstract idea of returning, giving back, sending back. A wonderful relative is ~volumen~: a Roman ~volūmen~ was a papyrus scroll, a thing literally rolled up, and only later did it come to mean a book’s bulk or a “volume” of sound. The ~volvere~ family is large in Spanish — ~volver~, ~revolver~, ~envolver~, ~volcar~, ~voluble~, ~revuelta~ — and even the pistol name ~revólver~ came into Spanish from English, where it was coined, at bottom, from the same rolling root.
en.dictar:
~dictar~ comes from Latin ~dictāre~ (“to say over and over, dictate, compose”), the frequentative of ~dīcere~ (“to say, tell”). ~dīcere~ derives from Proto-Italic *~deikō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, point out”) — the same root, with meaning shifted from showing to saying, that gave Ancient Greek ~deíknumi~ (“I show”), English ~teach~ and ~token~, and German ~zeigen~ (“to show”). From ~dictāre~ directly come Italian ~dettare~, French ~dicter~, and English ~dictate~.

The frequentative force of ~dictāre~ — “to say again and again” — fits both senses Spanish keeps: to ~dictar~ a letter (speaking so another writes it down) and to ~dictar~ a law or sentence (pronouncing it with authority). A ~dictador~ was originally a Roman magistrate granted emergency power to “pronounce”; only later did the word darken. The same ~dīcere~ underlies a huge family: ~decir~, ~dicho~, ~contradecir~, ~predecir~, ~dictamen~, ~diccionario~, and ~índice~.
en.dirigir:
Spanish ~dirigir~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dīrigere~ (“to set straight, guide, direct”), a compound of ~dis-~ (“apart, asunder”) and ~regere~ (“to keep straight, rule, guide”). ~regere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, direct, rule”), one of the most productive of all roots, cognate with Latin ~rēx~ (“king”), Sanskrit ~rājan~ (“king”), German ~recht~ (“right”), and English ~right~ itself. French ~diriger~ and Italian ~dirigere~ are the Romance parallels.

The literal image is a straight line: to ~dirigir~ is to make something go straight toward a target — hence “to aim,” “to guide,” “to address (a letter),” and “to conduct or manage” an orchestra, a company, a film. Its popularly inherited cousin ~aderezar~ (“to season, to garnish, to set right”), worn smooth by ordinary transmission from the same Latin stock, stands beside the bookish, near-intact ~dirigir~. From ~regere~ and its root Spanish drew a rich harvest: ~regir~ (“to govern”), ~dirección~, ~director~, ~corregir~ (“to correct,” literally “to set right again”), ~erigir~, ~recto~ (“straight”), ~regla~ (“rule”), ~región~, and — presiding over them all — ~rey~ (“king”).
en.diseñar:
A Renaissance borrowing from Italian ~disegnare~ (“to draw, to design”), which itself continues Latin ~dēsignāre~ (“to mark out, trace, designate”), a compound of ~dē-~ (“out, down”) and ~signāre~ (“to mark”), from the noun ~signum~ (“sign, mark”). It is cognate with French ~dessiner~ and English ~design~, and — from the same Latin verb by a learned path — with Spanish's own ~designar~.

Here lies a neat doublet. Latin ~dēsignāre~ reached Spanish twice: once directly from Latin as the learned ~designar~ (“to appoint, designate”), and once through Italian, where ~disegnare~ had narrowed to the artist's act of “drawing, laying out a design” — that borrowing became ~diseñar~, with the noun ~diseño~. So a single Latin verb split into “to designate” and “to design.” The base ~signum~ radiates through Spanish in ~signo~, ~señal~, ~seña~, ~insignia~ and even ~enseñar~ (“to teach”), literally to “mark out” something for a learner.
en.disfrutar:
Spanish ~disfrutar~ was formed within Spanish itself from the prefix ~dis-~ and ~fruto~ (“fruit, produce”), with the verbal ending ~-ar~. ~fruto~ comes from Latin ~frūctus~ (“fruit, produce, profit”), the past participle of the deponent verb ~fruī~ (“to enjoy, have the use of”). That verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰruHg-~ (“to make use of, enjoy”). The root surfaces widely: Latin ~frūx~ (“crop, fruit”) gave ~frūgālis~, source of English ~frugal~; and through the Germanic branch it yielded English ~brook~ (the verb “to tolerate, put up with,” originally “to make use of, enjoy”) and German ~brauchen~ (“to need, use”). French ~fruit~ and Portuguese ~fruto~ / ~desfrutar~ are close Romance kin.

The metaphor is agricultural: to ~disfrutar~ something was first to draw the fruits or profit from it — to reap the yield of an estate — and only afterward to enjoy it in the modern sense of taking pleasure. Old legal Spanish kept the concrete meaning of usufruct, the right to gather another’s produce, and the doublet ~usufructo~ still names it in law. Today ~disfrutar de la vida~ (“to enjoy life”) has fully abstracted the harvest into pleasure. From the same ~fruto~ family Spanish holds ~fruta~, ~fructífero~ (“fruitful”), ~usufructo~, and ~frugal~; the learned ~fruición~ (“keen enjoyment”) comes straight from ~fruī~’s participle ~fruitus~.
en.disminuir:
From Latin ~dēminuere~ (“to lessen, to make smaller”), from ~dē-~ (here intensive, “completely”) and ~minuere~ (“to make small, to diminish”), a verb from ~minus~ (“less”). All of this rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~mey-~ (“small, few”). The Spanish form was reshaped under the influence of the prefix ~dis-~, giving ~disminuir~; it is attested from the early fifteenth century. It is cognate with Italian ~diminuire~, French ~diminuer~, Portuguese ~diminuir~, and English ~diminish~, and — through ~minus~ — with English ~minus~, ~minor~, and ~minute~.

The root *~mey-~ is the great Indo-European word for smallness, and the Latin verb ~minuere~ meant to make something less — to chip away at a quantity. Spanish ~disminuir~ carries exactly that: to reduce, to lessen, to make or grow smaller in number, size, or intensity. A curious point of morphology is the prefix swap — Latin's ~dē-~ was replaced by ~dis-~ in the Spanish outcome — so the standard word today wears a prefix its Latin ancestor did not. From the same ~minus~ / *~mey-~ family Spanish drew a crowd of words: ~menos~, ~menor~, ~mínimo~, ~minuto~, ~menudo~, ~menguar~, ~ministro~, and ~disminución~.
en.disponer:
Spanish ~disponer~ continues Latin ~dispōnere~ (“to arrange, set in order, distribute”), a compound of ~dis-~ (“apart, in different directions”) and ~pōnere~ (“to place, put”). ~pōnere~ is itself contracted from an older ~po-~ (a by-form of the prefix meaning “away”) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, leave”), so its literal weight is “to set down, put in place.” The Romance cognates are exact — Italian ~disporre~, French ~disposer~, Portuguese ~dispor~ — and English ~dispose~ arrived through Old French.

The prefix ~dis-~ paints the picture: to ~disponer~ is to place things about, each in its own spot — hence “to arrange” and, from having things arranged and ready, “to have at one’s disposal.” The reflexive ~disponerse a~ means to get ready to do something. ~pōnere~ is one of the great Latin verb-factories, and Spanish reflects it everywhere: ~poner~ (“to put”), ~componer~, ~exponer~, ~proponer~, ~suponer~, ~posición~, ~puesto~, and the derived noun ~disposición~ (“arrangement, disposal, willingness”). The adjective ~disponible~ (“available”) carries the same idea — something set out and ready to hand.
en.distribuir:
From Latin ~distribuere~ (“to divide, deal out”), from ~dis-~ (“apart, individually”) + ~tribuere~ (“to allot, assign”), itself from ~tribus~ (“tribe, division of the people”). The origin of ~tribus~ is uncertain: it is often connected to ~trēs~ (“three”), as if an original threefold partition of the Roman people, but the derivation is disputed. Cognate with Italian ~distribuire~, French ~distribuer~ and Portuguese ~distribuir~.

To ~tribuere~ was to allot something “to the tribes,” so distribution began as an act of civic division. English took the whole cluster from the same ~tribuere~: ~tribute~ (what is paid out), ~attribute~, ~contribute~ and ~distribute~. Spanish keeps ~tribu~, ~tributo~, ~atribuir~, ~contribuir~ and ~retribuir~.
en.divertir:
From Latin ~dīvertere~ (“to turn aside, go separate ways”), from ~dī-~ (a form of ~dis-~, “apart”) plus ~vertere~ (“to turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *~wert-~ (“to turn, rotate”). Cognate with Italian ~divertire~, French ~divertir~, Portuguese ~divertir~, and English ~divert~ and ~diversion~; the root also gives English ~-ward~ and German ~werden~ (“to become”).

English and Spanish took the same “turning aside” in different directions. English ~divert~ stayed close to the literal — to turn something off its course. Spanish ~divertir~ turned inward and pleasant: to turn the mind aside from its cares, hence “to amuse, entertain.” From the shared ~vertere~ Spanish keeps a great wheeling family: ~verter~ (“to pour”), ~verso~ (“verse,” a turning of the line), ~versión~, ~convertir~, ~adverso~, ~universo~ (“turned into one”), and ~aniversario~ (“a turning of the year”).
en.dividir:
From Latin ~dīvidere~ (“to force apart, to divide”), from ~dis-~ (“apart”) and a distinct verbal root *~-videre~ (“to separate”) — not, despite appearances, the ~vidēre~ that means “to see.” The separating root goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₁weydʰ-~ (“to divide”), the very root that also produced Latin ~vidua~ and thus, through Germanic, English ~widow~ — a person “separated” from a spouse. Cognates include English ~divide~ and French ~diviser~.

The image beneath ~dīvidere~ is forcible separation, and Spanish keeps that edge in ~dividir~. Its most philosophical descendant is ~individuo~ (“individual”), from Latin ~indīviduus~ (“undivided, indivisible”) — the individual being, literally, that which cannot be split further. From the same source come ~división~, ~dividendo~, ~divisor~, and ~divisa~ (a “device” or emblem, and later a “currency”), all turning on the idea of a whole parcelled into shares.
en.dormir:
From Latin ~dormīre~ (“to sleep”), from Proto-Italic *~dormiō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~drem-~ (“to sleep”). The Romance sisters kept it almost untouched: Italian ~dormire~, French ~dormir~, Portuguese ~dormir~. Outside Latin the root surfaces in Ancient Greek ~darthánō~ (“to sleep”), Sanskrit ~drāti~ (“he sleeps”), and Old Church Slavonic ~drěmati~ (“to doze”).

Latin already had the frequentative ~dormītāre~ (“to be drowsy, keep nodding off”), and from ~dormīre~ Spanish grew a rich bedtime vocabulary: ~dormitorio~ (“bedroom, dormitory”), ~durmiente~ (“sleeping” — as in ~La Bella Durmiente~, “Sleeping Beauty”), ~adormecer~ (“to lull to sleep, numb”), and ~dormitar~ (“to doze”). Notice the stem-vowel play Spanish keeps from the Latin conjugation: the ~o~ of ~dormir~ becomes ~ue~ when stressed (“duermo”) and ~u~ elsewhere (“durmió”), a living trace of how the verb was accented.
en.dudar:
From Old Spanish ~dubdar~, from Latin ~dubitāre~ (“to waver, to hesitate, to doubt”), a frequentative tied to ~dubius~ (“wavering, doubtful”), which goes back to ~duo~ (“two”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dwóh₁~ (“two”). To doubt is to be “of two minds.” Cognate with Italian ~dubitare~, French ~douter~ and Portuguese ~duvidar~; through ~duo~ it is kin to Spanish ~dos~ and to English ~two~, and English ~doubt~ is itself a borrowing of the same Latin verb by way of French.

At the heart of ~dudar~ lies the number two: to doubt is to hover between two possibilities, unable to come down on either side. Old Spanish still wrote the Latin ~b~ as ~dubdar~, which the language later smoothed away — just as ~dubda~ became ~duda~ and ~cibdad~ became ~ciudad~. English kept the opposite habit: the silent ~b~ in ~doubt~ was put back by Renaissance scholars to advertise its descent from ~dubitāre~, a fossil of the very letter Spanish threw out. From ~dubius~ Spanish also has ~duda~, ~dudoso~, ~indudable~ and the learned ~dubitativo~, and from ~duo~, the numeral ~dos~ and ~doble~.
en.durar:
From Latin ~dūrāre~ (“to last, harden”), from ~dūrus~ (“hard”), and from Proto-Italic *~dūros~. The deeper root is debated: by one account ~dūrus~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~dweh₂-~ (“long, far”) — making it kin to Ancient Greek ~dērós~ (“long-lasting”) and Sanskrit ~dūrá~ (“distant”) — while another derives it from *~deru-~ (“firm, solid”), the source of English ~tree~ and ~true~. Cognate with Italian ~durare~, French ~durer~ and Portuguese ~durar~.

Latin ~dūrāre~ meant both “to harden” and “to hold out, last,” and Spanish kept the durative sense while physical hardness stayed with the adjective ~duro~. English borrowed the same family as ~durable~, ~during~ (originally “while something lasts”) and ~endure~. From the same Latin stock Spanish also draws ~duración~, ~durante~, ~endurecer~ and ~perdurar~.
en.echar:
From Latin ~iactāre~ (“to throw repeatedly, to toss about”), the frequentative of ~iacere~ (“to throw, to cast”). The root reaches back to the Proto-Indo-European *~(H)yeh₁-~ (“to throw, to let go”). ~iactāre~ also produced Italian ~gettare~ and French ~jeter~, and through French it seeded English ~jet~, ~jetsam~, and ~jettison~; the participial stem ~-ject-~ of ~iacere~ underlies English ~eject~, ~inject~, ~project~, and ~reject~.

Few Spanish verbs travel further from their spelling: ~iactāre~ lost its ~j~-sound and its ~-ct-~ cluster to become ~echar~, one of the language’s most protean verbs — to throw, pour, put, emit, sprout, or dismiss. It anchors countless idioms: ~echar de menos~ (“to miss”), ~echar a correr~ (“to break into a run”), ~echar una mano~ (“to lend a hand”). The learned ~-ject-~ stem re-entered Spanish in ~sujeto~, ~objeto~, ~proyecto~, ~inyectar~, and ~trayecto~. And the stative twin of ~iacere~ — Latin ~iacēre~ (“to lie down”) — gave Spanish ~yacer~, so that the verb for throwing and the verb for lying at rest are, in the end, cousins.
en.efectuar:
From Medieval Latin ~effectuāre~ (“to bring about, to carry out”), built on Latin ~effectus~, participle of ~efficere~ (“to accomplish, to bring to pass”), from ~ex-~ (“out, thoroughly”) + ~facere~ (“to do, to make”). ~facere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to place, to set”). Cognate with Italian ~effettuare~ and French ~effectuer~, and — through ~facere~ — with English ~effect~, ~effectuate~, and ~fact~.

The chain packs the meaning tightly: ~ex-~ (“out”) intensifies ~facere~ (“to make”), so ~efficere~ is to “make something come out” — to accomplish it fully — and its result-noun ~effectus~ is the “thing brought out,” the effect. ~efectuar~ therefore means to carry a plan through to its result, a shade more formal than hacer. The root *~dʰeh₁-~ is one of the most productive in Indo-European, underlying not only the huge Latin ~facere~ family but Greek ~títhēmi~ (“I place”) and English ~do~ and ~deed~. Spanish descendants of ~facere~ are everywhere: ~hacer~ (“to do, to make”), ~hecho~ (“fact, deed”), ~efecto~ (“effect”), ~eficaz~ (“effective”), ~defecto~, ~perfecto~, and ~fábrica~ (“factory”).
en.ejecutar:
From Latin ~exsequī~ / ~exsequor~ (“to follow out, carry through, pursue to the end”), from ~ex-~ (“out, thoroughly”) plus ~sequī~ (“to follow”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”). Spanish ~ejecutar~ was formed on the participial stem ~exsecūtus~ (later ~exēcūtus~). The root ~sequī~ is one of the most prolific in the Romance languages, giving Spanish ~seguir~, Italian ~seguire~ and French ~suivre~; through it English gained ~sequence~, ~consequence~, ~prosecute~ and ~execute~ itself, and Ancient Greek ~ἕπομαι~ (~hépomai~, “to follow”) shows the same root outside Latin.

The evolution runs from “to follow through” to “to accomplish, carry out,” and Spanish ~ejecutar~ inherited the full spread: to execute a plan, to perform a piece of music (~ejecutar una sonata~), to run a computer program, and — chillingly — to put a condemned person to death. That grim sense arose because a sentence, once pronounced, was “followed out” upon the body of the offender. From the same participle come ~ejecución~, ~ejecutivo~ (“executive”) and ~ejecutor~; from the wider ~sequī~ family Spanish has ~seguir~, ~conseguir~ (“to obtain”), ~perseguir~ (“to pursue”), ~consecuencia~, ~secuencia~ and ~obsequio~ (“a gift,” originally a following-after in attendance).
en.ejercer:
From Latin ~exercēre~ (“to keep busy, train, drill, carry on”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~arcēre~ (“to keep off, shut in, confine”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂erk-~ (“to hold, contain, guard”) — the same root that gave Latin ~arca~ (“chest, box”). Cognate with Italian ~esercitare~, French ~exercer~ and Portuguese ~exercer~; English ~exercise~ was borrowed from the same verb through Old French.

The literal image is of driving animals or workers out of their enclosure to set them to work — hence “to keep busy, keep in motion, train.” In military Latin it meant to drill troops, and the past participle gave ~exercitus~, “a trained force,” the direct source of Spanish ~ejército~ (“army”). Spanish ~ejercer~ narrowed toward “to practice (a profession), exert (a right or authority),” while ~ejercitar~ kept the sense of training and physical exercise. From the same family come ~ejercicio~, ~ejercitar~ and ~ejército~.
en.elaborar:
From Latin ~ēlabōrāre~ (“to work out, produce by effort”), formed from ~ex-~ (“out, thoroughly”) and ~labōrāre~ (“to labor, toil”), from the noun ~labor~ (“labor, hardship”). It is cognate with French ~élaborer~, Italian ~elaborare~, and Portuguese ~elaborar~, and with the Latin-derived English ~elaborate~ and ~laborious~.

The origin of ~labor~ itself is uncertain: it has been proposed that it is related to ~labāre~ (“to totter, slip”), from the image of a body swaying under a heavy burden, but this is not established. The prefix ~ex-~ lent an intensive “thoroughly” force, so ~ēlabōrāre~ meant to work something out fully — hence the modern “to elaborate, produce.” The verb ~labōrāre~ left two Spanish descendants: the patrimonial ~labrar~ (“to till, work the land”) and the learned ~laborar~. The same family gave ~laboratorio~, ~colaborar~, ~laborioso~, and ~laborable~, all circling the ancient Roman sense of sustained, hard work.
en.elegir:
From Latin ~ēligere~ (“to pick out, to choose”), from ~ex-~ (“out of”) + ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick, to read”). ~legere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~legō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, to collect”). The same root gave Ancient Greek ~légō~ (“I gather, I say”), the ancestor of ~-logy~ and ~logic~. Old Spanish inherited the verb as ~esleer~/~eslecher~ before the learned ~elegir~ reshaped it on the Latin model. Cognate with Italian ~eleggere~, French ~élire~, and Portuguese ~eleger~.

~legere~ began concretely — to gather up, as one gathers olives or firewood — and then specialized in two directions: to gather written signs with the eye (“to read”) and to gather out the best (“to choose,” with ~ex-~). Spanish ~elegir~ keeps only the choosing sense, and its past participle ~electo~ gave the political ~elección~ and ~electorado~. The gathering root *~leǵ-~ also seeded ~leer~ (“to read”), ~colegio~, ~coleccionar~, ~legión~, and ~inteligente~ (“one who chooses between,” ~inter-~ + ~legere~).
en.elevar:
From Latin ~elevāre~ (“to lift up, raise”), from ~ex-~ (“out, up”) and ~levāre~ (“to lighten, to raise”), a verb built on the adjective ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”); the root reaches back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“lightweight”). It is cognate with Italian ~elevare~ and French ~élever~, and — through the same root — with English ~elevate~, ~lever~ and even ~light~ itself.

The striking fact is that Latin ~levāre~ left Spanish two verbs at once. ~Elevar~ is the learned borrowing, taken from books with its ~-l-~ intact and its “raise, lift” sense; but the same verb, inherited by mouth through the centuries, became the wholly ordinary ~llevar~, its ~l-~ palatalised to ~ll-~ and its meaning drifted from “to lift” to “to carry, to take.” The two are twins from one source. Around them cluster ~elevación~, ~elevador~, ~relieve~ and, straight from ~levis~, the adjectives ~leve~ and ~liviano~ and the verb ~aliviar~ (“to lighten, relieve”).
en.eliminar:
From Latin ~ēlimināre~ (“to turn out of doors, expel, banish”), formed from ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~līmen~ (“threshold, doorway”). The word thus literally meant to put someone out across the threshold — to show them the door. It is cognate with French ~éliminer~, Italian ~eliminare~, and Portuguese ~eliminar~, and with the Latin-derived English ~eliminate~.

From that concrete image of a doorway the sense broadened to “remove, get rid of, do away with.” The noun ~līmen~ (“threshold”) stands beside ~līmes~ (“boundary, path”), source of Spanish ~límite~; whether the two are the same word is itself debated, so the link is best left open. The prefix ~prae-~ (“before”) joined ~līmen~ in ~preliminar~, literally something standing “before the threshold” of a matter. In modern Spanish the verb gave the everyday ~eliminación~ and, from sport and competitions, ~eliminatoria~ (“qualifying round”).
en.emitir:
Spanish ~emitir~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~ēmittere~ (“to send out, let go”), from ~ē-~ / ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~mittere~ (“to send, release”). French ~émettre~, Italian ~emettere~, and Portuguese ~emitir~ share the source; from ~mittere~’s participle ~missus~ English drew ~emit~, ~mission~, ~missile~, and ~transmit~.

The origin of ~mittere~ is genuinely uncertain, and scholars have offered rival Indo-European roots — among them *~smeit-~ (“to throw,” losing its ~s-~) and *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, remove”) — so any single etymon should be presented as a proposal, not settled fact. Its own Latin sense drifted from “let go” to “send,” and Spanish spread it through a large prefixed family: ~meter~ (its own inherited, everyday reflex, “to put in”), ~emisión~ (“emission, broadcast”), ~emisor~ (“transmitter”), ~admitir~, ~permitir~, ~transmitir~, and ~prometer~ (“to promise,” literally “to send forth”). In modern use ~emitir~ ranges from emitting light to broadcasting a program to issuing an opinion.
en.empezar:
Spanish ~empezar~ is a compound of the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”) and the noun ~pieza~ (“piece”) — some accounts reconstruct an intervening Vulgar Latin *~impettiāre~, though that form is only proposed, not attested. What is clear is the ~pieza~ at its core, and ~pieza~ is not Latin: it comes from Late Latin ~pettia~, borrowed from Gaulish *~pettyā~, from Proto-Celtic *~kʷezdis~. So one of Spanish's common verbs for “to begin” has a Celtic heart. Its Romance kin through ~pieza~ include French ~pièce~, Italian ~pezza~ and Portuguese ~peça~.

The image behind ~empezar~ is concrete and homely: to begin something is to break into it — to break off the first ~pieza~, to broach a whole. You start a loaf or a task by taking the first piece of it. From the same Celtic-derived ~pieza~ Spanish built ~despiezar~ (“to dismantle, to break into pieces”) and the noun ~empiece~ (“a beginning”), while ~pieza~ itself ranges from a coin to a room to a musical or theatrical piece. It is a small monument to the Gaulish substrate embedded in everyday Castilian.
en.emplear:
From Old French ~empleiier~, a variant of ~emploiier~ (whence modern French ~employer~), from Latin ~implicāre~ (“to enfold, involve, entangle”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in”) and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~plek-~ (“to plait, weave”). Cognate with English ~employ~, Italian ~impiegare~ and Portuguese ~empregar~; and, as a learned twin of the very same Latin verb that entered Spanish directly, ~implicar~.

Latin ~implicāre~ literally meant to fold one thing into another, and from “to involve, engage” its Old French descendant slid toward “to put to use, occupy.” Spanish took it in that practical sense of setting things — and hands — to work, so ~emplear~ covers both « usar » and « dar trabajo a ». The bookish doublet ~implicar~ kept the abstract Latin idea of “to involve, imply,” a neat case of one etymon yielding two Spanish verbs. From the same root *~plek-~ come ~empleo~, ~aplicar~, ~explicar~, ~plegar~ and ~pliegue~, plus the everyday ~empleado~ (“employee”).
en.encantar:
From Latin ~incantāre~ (“to sing over, to chant a spell upon”), a compound of ~in-~ (“on, upon”) and ~cantāre~ (“to sing”), which is the frequentative of ~canere~ (“to sing”). The root is the Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂n-~ (“to sing”). ~incantāre~ gave Italian ~incantare~, Portuguese ~encantar~, and — through Old French ~enchanter~ — English ~enchant~ and ~incantation~. From the related Latin ~carmen~ (“song, spell,” itself from ~canere~) English even draws ~charm~.

The magic here was literally sung: to ~incantāre~ was to chant a spell over someone, and Spanish ~encantar~ still means both “to bewitch” and, softened, “to delight, to charm.” The past participle ~encantado~ (“enchanted”) became the everyday courtesy for “pleased to meet you” — a small linguistic spell cast at every introduction. The noun ~encanto~ is a “charm” and ~encantador~ means “charming” (or “a sorcerer”). Alongside these stand the plain musical descendants of ~cantāre~: ~cantar~ (“to sing”), ~canto~ (“song”), ~canción~ (“song”), and ~cantante~ (“singer”). To enchant, in the end, was only ever to sing — and to sing well enough that someone fell under the spell.
en.encargar:
From ~en-~ plus ~cargar~ (“to load”), from Late Latin ~carricāre~ (“to load a wagon”), a verb built on Latin ~carrus~ (“wheeled cart, wagon”). ~carrus~ was itself borrowed from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *~karros~, and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱers-~ (“to run”) — a cart being, in essence, “the running thing.” Through ~carricāre~ it is cognate with Italian ~caricare~, French ~charger~, and Portuguese ~carregar~; and, by way of Old French, with English ~charge~ and ~cargo~, while ~carrus~ itself lies behind English ~car~.

The literal image was “to load a cart,” and ~cargar~ kept that sense of loading, carrying, and burdening. The prefixed ~encargar~ shifted figuratively from “to load a burden onto someone” to “to entrust, commission, or order.” The same family crowds modern Spanish: ~carga~ (“load”), ~cargo~ (“post, charge”), ~descargar~ (“to unload, download”), ~recargar~ (“to recharge”), ~sobrecargar~ (“to overload”), and the noun ~encargo~ (“an order, an errand”). It is a fittingly busy brood for a root that, at its Indo-European base *~ḱers-~, meant only “to run.”
en.encontrar:
From Vulgar Latin *~incontrāre~ (“to meet, to come up against”), a verb built from Latin ~in-~ (“in, upon”) plus ~contrā~ (“against, facing”), itself from ~cum~ / ~com-~ (“with”). Old Spanish inherited it as ~encontrar~. Its Romance relatives include Italian ~incontrare~, Portuguese ~encontrar~, and French ~encontrer~ (surviving today mainly in ~rencontrer~, “to meet”); English borrowed the same formation as ~encounter~ and, more plainly, ~counter~.

The literal core is confrontational — to come face to face, even against one another — but Spanish softened the edge: ~encontrar~ is now the neutral, everyday verb both for meeting a person and for finding a thing (« no encuentro las llaves »). The reflexive ~encontrarse~ adds “to be located” and “to feel” (« me encuentro bien »). From the same stem come the noun ~encuentro~ (“a meeting, a match”), the blunt ~encontronazo~ (“a collision, a run-in”), and, through the shared ~contrā~, a whole regiment of words — ~contra~, ~contrario~, ~encontrado~ (“opposing, conflicting”), and ~contrariar~.
en.enfrentar:
From ~en-~ (“in, into”) plus ~frente~ (“forehead; front”) and the verbal ending ~-ar~ — a verb built directly on the noun. ~frente~ descends from Latin ~frontem~, accusative of ~frons~ (“forehead, brow, front”), whose ultimate origin is uncertain; De Vaan finds “no plausible etymology”. The Latin noun lives on in Italian ~fronte~, French ~front~ and Portuguese ~frente~, and English ~front~ is its doublet, borrowed through Old French.

In Latin ~frons~ named the forehead and, by an easy metaphor, the foremost part of anything, including an army's front line — the sense that powers military ~frente~. Spanish keeps both meanings and even sorts them by gender: ~la frente~ is the forehead, ~el frente~ the front. To ~enfrentar~ is literally to set foreheads or fronts against each other, hence “to confront, to face”. From the same root grew ~frontera~ (“frontier”), ~afrontar~, ~confrontar~ and ~frontal~, while English gained ~frontier~ and ~confront~ along the way.
en.enseñar:
From Vulgar Latin *~insignāre~ (“to mark, point out”), a reshaping of Latin ~insignīre~ (“to distinguish, mark”), from ~in-~ (“on, upon”) plus ~signum~ (“sign, mark”). ~signum~ is itself of uncertain deeper origin, traced by different scholars either to Proto-Indo-European *~sek-~ (“to cut”) or to *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”). Cognate with French ~enseigner~, Italian ~insegnare~ and Portuguese ~ensinar~; and, by way of ~signum~, with English ~sign~.

The road from “to mark” to “to teach” runs through “to point out, show”: teaching is marking knowledge onto a mind, and tellingly ~enseñar~ still means both “to teach” and “to show” — « me enseñó la casa » may be a lesson or a tour. From ~signum~ Spanish drew a large family: ~seña~, ~señal~, ~señalar~, ~diseñar~ (“to design,” literally to mark out), ~insignia~ and ~signo~ itself. And because that root is contested, the tempting gloss “to cut a mark” has to stay a maybe: the sign may be something cut — or something that lets one follow.
en.entender:
From Latin ~intendere~ (“to stretch toward, direct, aim at”), formed from ~in-~ (“toward”) and ~tendere~ (“to stretch”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch, extend”). It is cognate with Italian ~intendere~, Portuguese ~entender~ and French ~entendre~, and — through the same Latin verb — with English ~intend~; the bare root shows up in English ~tend~ and ~thin~.

The Latin phrase ~intendere animum~ meant “to direct the mind toward” something; that mental aiming narrowed from “pay attention” to “grasp, understand.” A neat contrast: French ~entendre~ took the same verb and settled on “to hear” instead. The root *~ten-~ is remarkably fertile in Spanish: besides ~atender~ (“to attend to”) and ~intención~, it yields ~tensión~, the Greek-derived ~tono~, and — unexpectedly — ~tienda~ (“shop; tent”), originally a “stretched” awning under which goods were sold.
en.entrar:
Spanish ~entrar~ comes, through Old Spanish ~entrar~, from Latin ~intrāre~ (“to go in, enter”), a verb built on ~intrā~ (“within, inside”). ~intrā~ is the feminine ablative of an adjective going back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₁énteros~ (“inner”), a comparative formed from *~h₁én~ (“in”) with the contrastive suffix *~-teros~. The word thus meant, quite literally, to move into the more-inner space. English ~enter~ (borrowed through Old French ~entrer~) and Italian ~entrare~ are close relatives, as are Portuguese and Catalan ~entrar~.

The Latin sense was concrete and spatial, and Spanish ~entrar~ keeps that physical core — to enter a room, a country, a stage — while branching into countless idioms: ~entrar en razón~ (“to see reason”), ~entrar en calor~ (“to warm up”), the new year that ~entra~. From the same ~intrā~/~inter~ stock Spanish holds ~entrada~ (“entrance, ticket”), ~entrante~ (“incoming; starter course”), and ~adentro~; the sister preposition ~inter~ underlies ~interior~, ~íntimo~, and ~entre~ (“between”) itself. The comparative shape of *~h₁énteros~ — “more inward” — reminds us that Latin often located actions not just in space but along a scale of depth.
en.entregar:
From Latin ~integrāre~ (“to make whole, renew, restore”), a verb built on the adjective ~integer~ (“whole, untouched, intact”), which is itself ~in-~ (“not”) plus the root of ~tangere~ (“to touch”) — literally “untouched.” The Proto-Indo-European root is *~teh₂g-~ (“to touch, handle”). ~Entregar~ is a semi-learned descendant that underwent metathesis (~integrāre~ → ~entregar~); its fully learned doublet is ~integrar~ (“to integrate”). The pair is cognate with Portuguese ~entregar~, Italian ~integrare~ and English ~integrate~ and ~integer~.

The semantic path is unexpected. Latin ~integrāre~ meant to make something whole again, to restore it; Old Spanish ~entregar~ first meant to give back or restore what was owed, and from “to hand back” it slid to the general “to hand over, deliver” it means today. So the modern act of delivering a parcel hides an older idea of restoring something to wholeness. From the same ~tangere~ Spanish also has ~tangible~, ~tañer~ (“to play an instrument, to ring”), ~contacto~ and ~intacto~ (“untouched”), while ~integer~ lives on in ~íntegro~ (“whole, upright”) and ~entrega~ (“delivery, devotion”).
en.enviar:
Spanish ~enviar~ comes from Old Spanish ~enviar~, from Late Latin ~inviāre~ (“to send on a journey, dispatch”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in, on”) and ~via~ (“way, road”). To ~inviāre~ was literally to put someone or something ~in viam~ — “on the road.” ~via~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~weǵʰ-~ (“to go, transport in a vehicle”), one of the great roots of the family: it gave Latin ~vehere~ (“to carry”) and English ~way~, ~weigh~, ~wain~, and ~wagon~, plus the borrowings ~via~, ~vehicle~, and ~voyage~. French ~envoyer~ is the exact cognate — and English ~envoy~ (“a messenger”) is simply its past participle ~envoyé~ borrowed whole.

The metaphor is transparent and durable: sending is still, etymologically, a matter of setting something on its way. From ordinary dispatch Spanish extended ~enviar~ to letters, messengers, goods, and now email and messages (~enviar un correo~, “to send an email”). A quirk of stress splits its present tense — the accent falls on the ~i~ in ~envío~ and ~envías~ but not in ~enviamos~ — a hiatus Spanish marks with a written accent. The verb’s own nouns are ~envío~ (“shipment, dispatch”) and ~enviado~ (“envoy, correspondent”). From the same ~via~ Spanish also keeps ~vía~, ~viaje~, ~enviar~’s cousin ~desviar~ (“to divert”), ~obvio~ (“obvious,” literally “in the way”), and ~trivial~ (from ~trivium~, “a place where three roads meet”).
en.escribir:
Spanish ~escribir~ descends from Latin ~scrībere~ (“to write”), whose original sense was “to scratch, to incise.” It goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)kreybʰ-~ (“to scratch, to cut”), an extension of *~(s)ker-~ (“to cut,” also behind English ~shear~). Its native cognate is Greek ~skáriphos~ (“a scratching, an outline”). Tellingly, Germanic had no inherited verb for writing and simply borrowed this one from Latin — so German ~schreiben~ and Old English ~shrive~ are early loans, not true cognates. Romance kin include Italian ~scrivere~ and French ~écrire~.

The etymology preserves the physical act: to write was to gouge marks into wax, clay or stone with a stylus long before it meant putting ink to paper. From ~scrībere~ Spanish inherited a large family: ~escritura~ (“writing; Scripture; a legal deed”), ~escritor~ (“writer”), the participle ~escrito~ (“written; a document”), and the prefixed verbs ~describir~ (“to describe”) and ~inscribir~ (“to inscribe”), plus ~manuscrito~ (“manuscript,” literally hand-written).
en.escuchar:
From Old Spanish ~ascuchar~ (also ~escuchar~), from Vulgar Latin *~ascultāre~, a metathesis of Latin ~auscultāre~ (“to listen, give ear to”). The verb was built on the stem of ~auris~ (“ear,” from *~aus-~) plus a second element from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱlew-~ (“to hear”); by another account the second piece is *~ḱel-~ (“to incline”), itself linked to *~ḱlew-~. Romance kept the word everywhere: French ~écouter~, Italian ~ascoltare~, Portuguese ~escutar~.

The sound history is memorable: Latin ~auscultāre~ shed its heavy cluster through metathesis to Vulgar Latin *~ascultāre~, and the initial ~au-~ opened to ~e-~, yielding ~escuchar~. Centuries later the medical verb ~auscultar~ (“to listen to the chest”) was borrowed afresh straight from Latin, so Spanish keeps a doublet: everyday ~escuchar~ beside learned ~auscultar~, both literally “to lend an ear.” Many speakers preserve an aspectual contrast between ~oír~ (“to hear,” passive) and ~escuchar~ (“to listen,” attentive). From the same “ear” root come ~auricular~ and, of course, ~auscultar~.
en.especializar:
A modern, learned coinage: the adjective ~especial~ (“special, particular”) plus the productive verb-forming suffix ~-izar~ (ultimately from Greek ~-ίζειν~ via Latin ~-izāre~). ~especial~ descends from Latin ~speciālis~ (“of a particular kind”), from ~speciēs~ (“appearance, kind”), from ~specere~ (“to look at”), from Proto-Indo-European *~speḱ-~ (“to observe”). The Spanish verb was shaped in the 1800s under the pull of French ~spécialiser~.

Unlike verbs inherited by word of mouth over centuries, ~especializar~ was assembled from Latin parts by scholars in the modern age. The learned ~speciēs~ even has a popular twin: worn down through everyday speech, the same Latin word also became ~especia~ (“spice”). The root *~speḱ-~, “to look,” is among the most productive in the language: from it Spanish has ~especie~, ~especial~, ~espejo~ (“mirror,” from ~speculum~), ~espía~, ~espectáculo~ and ~aspecto~, while English, from the same Latin stock, has ~special~, ~species~, ~spy~ and ~spectacle~. To specialize, then, is to look ever more closely at one narrow ~especie~ of thing.
en.esperar:
From Old Spanish ~esperar~, from Latin ~spērāre~ (“to hope”), a verb built on the noun ~spēs~ (“hope”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~speh₁-~ (“to thrive, prosper”). Cognate with Italian ~sperare~, French ~espérer~, and Portuguese ~esperar~, and — through the same Latin stem — with English ~prosper~, ~desperate~, and ~despair~, this last from ~dēspērāre~ (“to lose hope”).

As with ~estar~ and ~escuela~, Spanish grew a prothetic ~e-~ before the awkward ~sp-~ cluster, turning ~spērāre~ into ~esperar~. More striking is a semantic merger unusual among the big Romance languages: ~esperar~ carries both “to hope” and “to wait, expect,” so the same verb that voices optimism also names the patience it demands — context and prepositions do the sorting, as in ~esperar a~ someone (wait) versus ~esperar que~ something happen (hope). The root flowered into ~esperanza~ (“hope”), ~espera~ (“a wait”), and the darker ~desesperar~ and ~desesperado~ (“to despair”; “desperate”), alongside ~inesperado~ (“unexpected”).
en.establecer:
From Old Spanish ~establecer~, from Latin ~stabilīre~ (“to make firm, to establish”), a verb from the adjective ~stabilis~ (“steady, firm”), from ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Cognate with French ~établir~, Italian ~stabilire~, and Portuguese ~estabelecer~; English ~establish~ was borrowed through Old French ~establir~, and its unetymological -sh reflects the Old French stressed stem.

Spanish reshaped the inherited verb with the inchoative suffix ~-ecer~ (from Latin ~-ēscere~, “to become”), the same ending seen in ~crecer~ and ~conocer~ — so ~establecer~ literally colors “to make firm” with a sense of coming-to-stand. The e- at the front is the familiar Spanish prop-vowel that Latin ~st-~ always acquires (compare ~estar~, ~escuela~). All of this rests on the great PIE root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”), one of the most productive in the language: from it Spanish also has ~estable~, ~estabilidad~, ~establecimiento~, ~estado~, and ~estar~ itself.
en.estar:
From Latin ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Italic *~stāō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Cognate with Italian ~stare~ and Portuguese ~estar~, and — through the same root — with English ~stand~ and ~stay~ and French ~ester~, an Old French verb now surviving only as a legal term.

Spanish inherited two verbs from Latin's copula system and split the work of “to be” between them: ~ser~ (from ~esse~, reinforced by ~sedēre~, “to sit”) carries permanent, essential being, while ~estar~ (from ~stāre~, “to stand”) carries location, state, and condition — literally, how something “stands” at a given moment. That is why someone ~es~ tall but ~está~ tired. The past participle ~estado~ (“been; state”) gave the noun ~estado~ (“state, condition,” and by extension the political “State”). The same PIE root *~steh₂-~ seeded a vast family of Spanish words, among them ~estación~, ~estable~, ~estatua~, ~constante~, ~restar~, and ~estatuto~.
en.estimar:
Spanish ~estimar~ comes from Latin ~aestimāre~ (older ~aestumāre~, “to value, to appraise, to reckon”), taken in as a learned word; Old Spanish also had the worn popular form ~asmar~ (“to reckon, judge”), long since obsolete. French ~estimer~, Italian ~stimare~, and Portuguese ~estimar~ share the source, and through French ~estimer~ English gained both ~esteem~ and ~estimate~.

The deep origin of ~aestimāre~ is disputed. It has traditionally been analyzed as ~aes~ (“copper, bronze,” hence money) plus a second element meaning “to cut,” yielding roughly *~ais-temos~, “one who cuts (i.e. mints) copper” — an appealing image of the money-valuer. But the connection is far from secure; de Vaan judges it “not very credible,” so it is best flagged as a proposal, not a fact. What is certain is the semantic core “to set a value on,” which in Spanish branched into both “to calculate” (~estimación~) and “to hold dear” (~estima~; ~estimado~, “dear” in a letter’s salutation).
en.estudiar:
Spanish ~estudiar~ comes from Latin ~studiāre~ (also read as a denominal from ~studium~, “zeal, application, study”), which belongs to the verb ~studeō~ (“to be eager, to apply oneself”). That verb goes back to Proto-Italic *~studēō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~(s)tewd-~ (“to push, thrust”), an extension of *~(s)tew-~ (“to push, hit”) — so its Latin sibling is ~tundō~ (“to beat, strike”). It is cognate with Italian ~studiare~, French ~étudier~ and Portuguese ~estudar~, and, as a borrowing from Old French, with English ~study~; through the deeper root it even touches English ~stub~ (“to strike, knock”).

The surprise is in that root: to study was once, at bottom, to push hard. Latin ~studeō~ meant an eager, driving zeal — a shoving of oneself toward a goal — and ~studium~ named that ardor before it ever named schoolwork. Only in late and medieval Latin did the “zeal” narrow to intellectual application, “to study.” The old heat still flickers in English ~studious~ and in Spanish ~estudioso~. The family the verb heads in Spanish is large and familiar: ~estudio~ (“study, studio”), ~estudiante~ (“student”), ~estudiantil~ (“student-related”), and ~estudioso~ (“studious; a scholar”) — every one of them descended from a word that first meant sheer eager pushing.
en.evaluar:
A relatively late borrowing (19th century) from French ~évaluer~ (“to evaluate, assess”), from Old French ~evaluer~, built on ~value~ (“value, worth”) — the feminine past participle of ~valoir~ (“to be worth”) — with the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~). The root is Latin ~valēre~ (“to be strong, be well, be worth”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂welh₁-~ (“to be strong”). Through that root ~valēre~ is cognate with English ~value~, ~valiant~, ~valid~ and ~wield~, with German ~walten~ (“to rule, govern”), and with the Romance kin Italian ~valutare~ and Portuguese ~avaliar~.

Where the native Spanish ~valorar~ and ~valuar~ descend straight from ~valēre~, ~evaluar~ arrived dressed in French clothes and at first meant to reckon a numerical value; it broadened to today's “to assess, judge the worth of.” The Latin ~valēre~ was above all about strength and health — a Roman closed a letter with ~valē~ (“be strong, farewell”) — and that vigor still shines through the family: ~valer~ (“to be worth”), ~valor~ (“value; courage”), ~valiente~ (“brave”), ~válido~, ~valía~, ~valioso~ (“valuable”), ~equivaler~ (“to be equivalent”), ~prevalecer~ (“to prevail”) and ~convalecer~ (“to convalesce,” to regain one's strength). Even the parting ~vale~ (“okay,” originally “be well”) belongs here.
en.evitar:
Spanish ~evitar~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~ēvītāre~ (“to shun, avoid”), a compound of ~ē-~/~ex-~ (“out, away”) and ~vītāre~ (“to avoid, evade”). The origin of ~vītāre~ is genuinely uncertain, and the sources disagree: by one account (De Vaan) it rests on an unattested *~vītus~ (“avoiding”), linked to Proto-Indo-European *~weyh₁-~ (“to chase, pursue”); others connect it instead to *~weyk-~ (“to yield”), or to the root of ~dīvidō~ (“to divide”). None of these is settled. Its Romance kin are straightforward: French ~éviter~, Italian ~evitare~, Portuguese ~evitar~.

Whatever its deep root, ~vītāre~ already meant in Latin “to keep clear of,” and the prefix ~ē-~ (“away”) reinforces the sense of drawing back from something — so ~evitar~ has meant “to avoid, prevent, spare” throughout its Spanish life. Because the verb entered Spanish as a learned Latinism rather than by the slow mouth-worn route of inheritance, it kept its Latin shape almost unchanged, and its Spanish family is correspondingly small and transparent: chiefly the adjectives ~evitable~ (“avoidable”) and its negation ~inevitable~ (“unavoidable”), with the adverb ~inevitablemente~. The lesson of ~evitar~ is a quieter one: not every common verb comes with a tidy prehistory, and an honest etymology sometimes ends in a shrug.
en.exigir:
From Latin ~exigere~ (“to drive out, demand, exact, weigh precisely”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~agere~ (“to drive, lead, do”). ~agere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive”), making it cognate with Ancient Greek ~ἄγω~ (ágō, “I lead”) and Sanskrit ~ajati~ (“drives”). The Latin verb descends in parallel as Italian ~esigere~, French ~exiger~ and Portuguese ~exigir~.

The core image is forceful: to ~exigere~ was to drive a debt out of someone, to exact what was owed, and Spanish ~exigir~ keeps that insistence in “to demand, to require”. A quieter branch meant “to weigh out exactly”, which is why the past participle ~exactus~ yielded ~exacto~ (“exact”), and why Latin ~examen~ (“the tongue of a balance”) gave both “swarm” and, through “a weighing”, English ~exam~. Spanish adds ~exigente~ and ~exigencia~, while ~agere~ underlies ~acto~, ~agente~ and ~ágil~; English took ~exact~, ~exigent~, ~act~ and ~agent~ from the same stock.
en.existir:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~exsistere~ (also ~existere~, “to step forth, emerge, come into being”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out, forth”) and ~sistere~ (“to stand, take a stand”), a reduplicated form of ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Cognate with Italian ~esistere~, French ~exister~, and Portuguese ~existir~, and — through ~sistere~ and ~stāre~ — with English ~exist~, ~insist~, ~resist~, and ~consist~, and with Spanish ~estar~.

The image hidden in ~existir~ is startlingly physical: to exist is to “stand forth,” to step out of the background into visibility. Latin ~exsistere~ first meant to emerge or come into view, and only from there did it settle into the abstract “to be.” Because it is a bookish, late-arriving word — not a battered popular inheritance — it kept its Latin shape almost intact. It supplies philosophy's most famous first person, Descartes' ~existo~ in “pienso, luego ~existo~” (“I think, therefore I am”). From it Spanish built ~existencia~ (“existence”), ~existente~, ~existencial~ and ~existencialismo~, plus ~inexistente~ (“nonexistent”) and ~coexistir~ (“to coexist”).
en.experimentar:
From Latin ~experīmentum~ (“a trial, test, proof”), the noun of ~experīrī~ (“to try, to put to the test”), which joins the prefix ~ex-~ to an old verb ~perīrī~ (“to attempt, to go through”). The deeper root is debated: it is traditionally linked to a Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to try, to risk, to traverse”), the family that also underlies Latin ~perīculum~ (“trial, danger”) and ~perītus~ (“experienced, skilled”) and, through Greek, English ~empirical~.

Spanish ~experimentar~ carries both branches of the meaning: “to experiment” (to test) and “to experience, to undergo” (to live through). The same Latin verb gave the pair ~experiencia~ (“experience”) and ~experimento~ (“experiment”), and the ~perīculum~ branch surfaces vividly in ~peligro~ (“danger”) — for to test and to risk were, to the Roman mind, close kin — alongside ~experto~ (“expert”) and ~pericia~ (“skill, expertise”).
en.explicar:
Spanish ~explicar~ comes from Latin ~explicāre~ (“to unfold, unroll, unravel”), from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”). ~plicāre~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to fold”). Through that root it is cognate with Greek ~plékō~ (“I plait, weave”) and German ~flechten~ (“to braid”). To explain, then, was to unfold something rolled up — to spread a folded scroll open so it could be read.

The root ~plicāre~ was extraordinarily productive. Prefixed, it gave ~aplicar~ (“to apply”), ~implicar~ (“to implicate”), ~complicar~ (“to complicate”) and ~replicar~ (“to reply”); inherited by regular sound change it became ~plegar~ (“to fold”). Its most surprising Spanish descendant is ~llegar~ (“to arrive”): from Latin ~applicāre~ (~ad-~ + ~plicāre~), which in the peninsula's seafaring usage meant to bring a ship to shore — so “to fold in to land” became simply “to arrive.” Also here: ~pliegue~ (“fold, crease”).
en.exponer:
From Latin ~exponere~ (“to set forth, put out, display”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~ponere~ (“to put, place”). ~ponere~ is traditionally parsed as ~po-~ (“away”) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, leave”), though its deeper Proto-Indo-European ancestry is uncertain. Spanish ~exponer~ shares its Latin source with Italian ~esporre~ and Portuguese ~expor~.

The literal sense “to place out” ran in two directions: one displays an object and one sets forth an argument, and Spanish ~exponer~ still means both “to exhibit” and “to expound”, while reflexively ~exponerse~ is “to expose oneself” to danger. The derived noun ~exposición~ likewise covers an art “exhibition” and a reasoned “exposition”. The verb ~ponere~ seeded an enormous Spanish family — ~poner~, ~componer~, ~proponer~, ~imponer~ and the noun ~posición~ — and reached English in the learned derivatives ~expose~ and ~exponent~.
en.expresar:
From Late Latin ~expressāre~, a frequentative of ~exprimere~ (“to press out, squeeze out”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~premere~ (“to press”), whose past participle is ~expressus~. ~premere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~premō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~pres-~ (“to press”), an extension of *~per-~ (“to strike, press”). Cognates: French ~exprimer~, Italian ~esprimere~, English ~express~; and through ~premere~, English ~press~ and ~print~.

The metaphor is physical: ~exprimere~ meant to squeeze the juice from a fruit, and from “pressing out” juice came the figurative “pressing out” of words and feelings — to express. Spanish still holds both halves as a doublet: concrete ~exprimir~ (“to squeeze a lemon”) beside abstract ~expresar~ (“to put into words”). An ~expreso~ train, and espresso coffee, are likewise “pressed,” quick. From ~premere~ Spanish also drew ~prensa~ (“press, the press”), ~imprimir~ (“to print”), ~comprimir~, and ~oprimir~.
en.extender:
From Latin ~extendere~ (“to stretch out, spread”), from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~tendere~ (“to stretch”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Cognate with French ~étendre~, Italian ~estendere~ and English ~extend~; and, through ~tendere~, with English ~tend~ and ~tent~.

~tendere~ literally meant to pull something taut, and that image of stretching runs through the whole clan: to extend is to draw a thing out across space, time or scope. A charming relative is Spanish ~tienda~, meaning both “tent” and “shop” — a tent being cloth stretched over poles, and a market stall much the same. From the participle ~tēnsus~ come ~tensión~ and ~tenso~. The far-reaching root *~ten-~ also yields Spanish ~tender~, ~atender~, ~extensión~, ~tono~ and ~contento~, and, in English, ~tend~, ~tense~ and even ~thin~ (what is stretched grows thin).
en.fabricar:
From Latin ~fabricāre~ (“to build, construct, forge”), from ~fabrica~ (“workshop, craft, construction”), from ~faber~ (“craftsman, smith”). The deeper origin of ~faber~ is uncertain; it is often traced to a Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeHbʰ-~ (“to fit together, be fitting”), but the reconstruction is not secure. Cognate with Italian ~fabbricare~, French ~fabriquer~, and Portuguese ~fabricar~. English ~fabricate~ and ~fabric~ come from the same Latin family, and English ~forge~ descends, through Old French ~forge~, from ~fabrica~ itself.

Latin ~fabrica~ took two roads into Spanish. As a learned borrowing it gave ~fábrica~ (“factory”), while its inherited, sound-worn descendant became ~fragua~ (“forge, smithy”) — the same word, one in Latin dress and the other showing the full erosion of popular speech, a classic doublet. From ~fragua~ comes the verb ~fraguar~, “to forge,” and figuratively “to hatch or concoct a plan.” The learned line gives ~fabricar~ (“to manufacture, make up”), ~fabricante~ (“manufacturer”), ~fabricación~ (“manufacture”), and ~fabril~ (“industrial, of factories”). Because ~fabricar~ can also mean “to fabricate” in the sense of inventing — a lie, an excuse — it carries, like its English cousin, a shadow of falsehood alongside honest making.
en.facilitar:
From the adjective ~fácil~ (“easy”) with a verb-forming suffix, ~fácil~ itself from Latin ~facilis~ (“easy, feasible”), which meant literally “do-able” — from ~facere~ (“to do, to make”) plus the ending ~-ilis~. ~Facere~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to set, put, do”). Spanish ~facilitar~ is cognate with Italian ~facilitare~, French ~faciliter~ and Portuguese ~facilitar~, and with English ~facilitate~ and ~facile~.

Because ~facilis~ was built as “(a thing) that can be done,” its Spanish descendant ~facilitar~ means precisely “to make do-able,” to smooth the way. Its antonym preserves the same logic in reverse: ~difícil~ is ~dis-~ plus ~facilis~, “not do-able.” The parent ~facere~ is one of the great root-verbs of Spanish, surviving above all as the everyday ~hacer~ — its Latin ~f-~ softened to ~h-~ — and branching into ~fábrica~, ~facultad~ and ~facilidad~, among many others.
en.faltar:
From Vulgar Latin *~fallitare~, a frequentative of Latin ~fallere~ (“to deceive, to trip, to fail”). The origin of ~fallere~ is uncertain, but it is often traced to a Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)gʷʰh₂el-~ (“to stumble”); on that account it is cognate with Ancient Greek ~σφάλλω~ (sphállō, “to bring down, trip up”). The same Latin verb reached English, through Old French, in ~fail~, ~fault~ and ~false~.

The semantic drift is neat: from “to deceive” to “to disappoint or come up short” and finally to “to be missing”. Spanish ~faltar~ is now the ordinary verb for something's absence — ~falta~ un ingrediente, “an ingredient is missing” — and its noun ~falta~ means “lack”, “fault”, even a sporting “foul”. The root threw off a wide family: ~falla~, ~fallar~, ~falso~ and, most strikingly, ~fallecer~ (“to die”), which began as “to fail, to expire”. English ~fallacy~ belongs here too, another child of deceiving ~fallere~.
en.favorecer:
~favorecer~ is a Spanish formation from the noun ~favor~ (“favor, goodwill”) plus the inchoative suffix ~-ecer~ (from Latin ~-ēscere~), meaning roughly “to come to favor.” The noun continues Latin ~favor~ (“goodwill, approval”), a derivative of the verb ~favēre~ (“to be well-disposed, be favorable”). The Romance sisters built the verb the same way: Italian ~favorire~, French ~favoriser~, and Portuguese ~favorecer~; English ~favor~ itself is a borrowing from the same Latin stock through Old French.

The deep origin of ~favēre~ is genuinely disputed. By one account it goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰeh₂-~ (“to shine”) or *~bʰuH-~ (“to be, become”); by another, to *~gʷʰew-~ (“to worship, heed”), which would make it a distant cognate of Old Church Slavonic ~gověti~ (“to fast, revere”). The sources hedge, so the most striking link is best left open. What is clear is the semantic arc: from a god's or a crowd's ~favor~ at the games, to social approval, to the modern “to favor, help along.” From the same family come ~favorable~, ~favorito~ (“favorite,” via Italian), ~desfavorecer~, and ~favorecedor~ (“flattering,” of clothes).
en.fijar:
Spanish ~fijar~ derives from the adjective ~fijo~ (“fixed”), earlier ~fixo~, from Latin ~fixus~, the past participle of ~fīgere~ (“to fasten, drive in, pierce”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeygʷ-~ (“to stick, set up”). Cognates include Italian ~fissare~, French ~fixer~, and Portuguese ~fixar~; English took ~fix~ and ~fixate~ from the same participle, and ~crucifix~ preserves ~fīgere~ literally as “fastened to a cross.”

Because ~fijar~ was reshaped from the participle rather than inherited whole, Spanish shows a telling split: the learned ~fijo~ (“fixed”) stands beside an older, popular descendant ~hito~ (“landmark, milestone”), where Latin ~f-~ became silent ~h-~ — a boundary-post is literally a “fixed” thing. From ~fīgere~ the language also draws ~fijación~ (“fixation”), ~fijeza~ (“fixity”), ~prefijo~ and ~sufijo~ (things “fastened” before and after), and ~crucifijo~ (“crucifix”). Note the distinct root of ~fingir~ and ~figura~, from ~fingere~ (“to shape”), easy to confuse but etymologically separate.
en.finalizar:
From Spanish ~final~ (“final”), from Latin ~fīnālis~ (“of the end or boundary”), from ~fīnis~ (“boundary, limit, end”). The deeper origin of ~fīnis~ is uncertain; it has traditionally been traced to an earlier *~fīg-sn-is~, a derivative of ~fīgere~ (“to fix, drive in, fasten”), on the idea that a boundary was originally a marker driven into the ground — though this account remains a proposal rather than settled fact. Cognate with Italian ~finalizzare~, French ~finaliser~ and Portuguese ~finalizar~, and with English ~finalize~.

The verb itself is a modern formation, ~final~ plus the suffix ~-izar~, meaning “to bring to a close.” If the ~fīgere~ hypothesis holds, the notion of an “end” began with a stake fixed into the earth to mark where one field stopped and another began — a vivid image, but one to be offered cautiously. From ~fīnis~ Spanish drew a large family: ~fin~, ~final~, ~definir~, ~confín~ (“far border”), ~finiquito~ (“settlement, final receipt”) and the literary ~finar~ (“to pass away”).
en.firmar:
From Latin ~firmāre~ (“to make firm, strengthen, confirm”), from the adjective ~firmus~ (“firm, strong, stable”), from Proto-Italic *~fermos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~dʰer-mo-s~ (“holding”), from the root *~dʰer-~ (“to hold, support”). It is cognate with Italian ~firmare~ and Portuguese ~firmar~, and — with a striking shift — with French ~fermer~ (“to close”). It is kin to English ~firm~, ~confirm~, and ~affirm~, and, far afield, to Sanskrit ~dhárma~, “that which upholds.”

The path to “sign” runs through the law: to ~firmar~ a document was first to make it firm, to confirm and ratify it, and from ratifying an act came the act of subscribing one's name to it. French, meanwhile, took ~firmāre~ toward “to shut firmly,” yielding ~fermer~, “to close.” The Spanish family keeps the core sense of steadiness: ~firme~, ~firmeza~, ~confirmar~, ~afirmar~, the ~firmamento~ (the “firm” vault of heaven), and ~firma~, the signature itself.
en.formar:
From Latin ~formāre~ (“to shape, to fashion”), from ~forma~ (“form, shape, mold”). The deeper origin of ~forma~ is genuinely disputed: one long-standing account connects it to Ancient Greek ~morphḗ~ (“shape”) by metathesis, the swapping of sounds, but scholars object that Latin shows no trace of an intermediate stage and that the required sound changes are irregular. Others reconstruct a native Proto-Indo-European source instead. Cognate with French ~former~, Italian ~formare~, and English ~form~ and ~format~.

Whatever its ultimate root, ~forma~ was one of Latin’s most productive nouns, covering shape, beauty, and pattern alike. Spanish multiplied it into ~formación~, ~fórmula~ (a diminutive, “a little form”), ~informar~ (“to give form to,” to shape into knowledge), ~transformar~, and ~uniforme~ (“of one form”). A charming survival is ~horma~, the shoemaker’s or hatmaker’s last — the wooden mold that shapes a shoe. ~horma~ is the popular, inherited descendant of ~forma~, while ~forma~ itself is the learned borrowing: a doublet in which the down-to-earth mold and the abstract idea of “form” are the same Latin word taking two roads into Spanish.
en.funcionar:
~funcionar~ is a denominal verb built on the noun ~función~, from Latin ~functiō~ (accusative ~functiōnem~), “a performing, execution,” from the deponent verb ~fungī~ (“to perform, discharge, carry out”), past participle ~functus~. This goes back to Proto-Italic *~fungōr~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰewg-~ (“to enjoy, make use of”), the present stem carrying a nasal infix. English borrowed ~function~; French has ~fonctionner~, Italian ~funzionare~.

In Latin ~fungī~ meant “to carry out a duty,” and ~función~ named the carrying-out itself; only in the modern age did Romance coin ~funcionar~ for machines and systems that “do their job” — which is why in Spanish an engine ~funciona~. A striking cousin: ~dēfungī~ meant “to finish, be done with,” so the one who has discharged life is the ~difunto~ (“deceased”), and death is a ~defunción~.
