From the “use up” sense comes ~fungible~ (goods consumed in use); everyday kin include the ~funcionario~, the civil servant who performs an office.
en.fundar:
From Latin ~fundāre~ (“to lay a base, to found”), a verb built on ~fundus~ (“bottom, ground, landed estate”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰudʰmn̥~ (“bottom”). It is cognate with Italian ~fondare~, French ~fonder~ and Portuguese ~fundar~; the underlying noun ~fundus~ is kin, through that root, to English ~bottom~ and German ~Boden~.

Latin ~fundāre~ meant to give a thing its ~fundus~ — its bottom — hence to establish a city, a house, or an institution on solid ground, the sense Spanish still carries. The same noun descended into Spanish twice: as the learned ~fundar~ and ~fundamento~, and as the popular ~hondo~ (“deep”), by the regular change of initial ~f-~ to ~h-~. So a firm foundation and a deep place turn out to be relatives — what is well ~fundado~ rests on the bottom of things. From the family also come ~fondo~, ~profundo~ and ~ahondar~, and, through Latin, English ~found~, ~fund~ and ~profound~.
en.ganar:
The origin of ~ganar~ is debated. Corominas argues it descends, with Portuguese ~ganhar~, from a Gothic *~ganan~ (“to covet, desire eagerly”), akin to Old Norse ~gana~ (“to gape, yearn”) — a Germanic family whose primitive sense was “to open the mouth.” Its meaning was then crossed with a separate Romance family from Frankish *~waidanjan~ (“to forage, harvest, gain”): Italian ~guadagnare~, French ~gagner~ and Catalan ~guanyar~. Corominas stresses that ~ganar~ is phonetically incompatible with ~guadagnare~, so it is not simply the same word — the tidy “all from *~waidanjan~” story is exactly what he rejects.

The “desire” origin ties the verb to Spanish ~ganas~ (“urge, desire,” as in ~tener ganas~), from the very same root — a satisfying link, though it rests on the debated Gothic etymology and should be flagged as such. The senses “to gain, earn, win” all grew from there. Modern kin include ~ganancia~ (“profit”), ~ganador~ (“winner”) and, strikingly, ~ganado~ (“livestock”) — literally “what has been gained,” a reminder of an age when wealth was counted in cattle.
en.garantizar:
From ~garante~ (“guarantor”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-izar~. ~garante~ was borrowed from French ~garant~ (“warrantor, defender”), of Germanic origin: from Frankish *~werēnt~, the present participle of a verb *~werjan~ (“to warrant, to vouch for”), tracing to the Proto-Germanic root *~war-~ (“to watch, to guard, to be aware”). The same Frankish word entered English by another door: kept with its Germanic w-, it became ~warrant~ and ~warranty~, while the Central-French gu- form gave ~guarantee~ — so ~garantizar~ and ~guarantee~ are, letter for letter across the w/gu alternation, the same word.

The Germanic idea behind the word is protection. A ~garante~ was originally the one who stood surety — who vouched for another and would answer for him — and Old French already used ~garant~ in this sense in the Chanson de Roland around 1080. From this Germanic stock Spanish built a whole legal and commercial family: ~garantía~ (“guarantee, warranty”), ~garante~, ~garantizar~, and ~garantizado~, all of them galicismos layered over older native vocabulary. English keeps the twin senses in its own doublet — a ~warrant~ authorizes and vouches, while a ~guarantee~ promises and secures — two faces of the single Frankish notion of standing good for something.
en.generar:
From Latin ~generāre~ (“to beget, to produce”), from ~genus~ (“birth, origin, kind”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to give birth, to beget”), one of the most fertile roots in the whole language family. Cognate with Ancient Greek ~génos~ (“race, kind”), with English ~genus~ and ~generate~, and — through Germanic — with English ~kin~ and ~kind~.

At its heart the word is about birth: to generate is to bring forth offspring, and only later, by extension, to produce anything at all — heat, electricity, income, ideas. The Latin ~genus~ meant a family or stock, which is why so much vocabulary of both kinship and classification springs from it. Spanish descendants include ~género~ (“gender, genre”), ~generación~, ~gente~ (“people,” from Latin ~gens~), ~genio~ and ~ingenio~ (the inborn talent one is “born with”), and ~degenerar~ — and, more surprisingly, ~nacer~ itself, from Latin ~nāscī~ (“to be born”), a cousin from the very same root.
en.gestionar:
A modern Spanish verb, formed from the noun ~gestión~ (“management”) plus ~-ar~. ~Gestión~ comes from Latin ~gestiō~ (“a carrying out, administration”), from ~gestus~, the past participle of ~gerere~ (“to carry, to conduct, to manage”). The deeper root of ~gerere~ is uncertain — De Vaan connects it hesitantly to ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”), but the reconstruction is not secure. Through ~gerere~ and ~gestus~ the word is cognate with English ~gesture~, ~digest~ and ~register~, and with French ~gérer~ and Italian ~gestire~.

Latin ~gerere~ meant, very physically, to carry or bear — to carry on war, to carry an office, to carry oneself — and its noun ~gestiō~ was the carrying-out of a task. Spanish inherited the abstract sense: to ~gestionar~ is to carry a matter through the necessary steps, to administer it. The same “carrying” underlies some surprising relatives: ~gesto~ (a “bearing” of the body), ~gestación~ (the carrying of a child), and ~congestión~ (a carrying-together, a piling up). All belong to the wide ~gerere~ family that also gave ~gestión~, ~gerente~, ~sugerir~, ~digerir~ and ~registro~ — a lexicon of bearing, doing and managing.
en.grabar:
~grabar~ is one of Spanish's Germanic imports: it was borrowed from French ~graver~ (“to engrave”), which comes from Frankish *~graban~, from Proto-Germanic *~grabaną~ (“to dig”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʰrebʰ-~ (“to dig, scratch, scrape”). Its Germanic cousins stay homely: English ~grave~ (“a dug pit”) and ~grub~, German ~graben~ (“to dig”), and Dutch ~graven~. The engraver's art is, at root, a kind of controlled digging into metal or stone.

From cutting lines into a plate, ~grabar~ generalized to “to engrave, carve,” then leapt to modern technology: to ~grabar~ is now “to record” sound or video — the groove of a phonograph record being, fittingly, an incised line. Figuratively an image can ~grabarse~ (“become etched”) in the memory. Kin include ~grabado~ (“engraving, print”), ~grabación~ (“a recording”), and ~grabadora~ (“recorder”). Beware the near-twin ~gravar~ (“to tax, burden”), a separate word from Latin ~gravāre~ (“to weigh down”) — same sound, unrelated root.
en.guardar:
From Old Spanish ~guardar~, from a West Germanic verb *~wardōn~ (“to watch, keep guard”) taken into Hispano-Romance, from Proto-Germanic *~wardōn~, from Proto-Indo-European *~wer-~ (“to perceive, watch out for, heed”). Germanic initial ~w-~ was regularly reshaped as ~gu-~ in Romance. Cognate with Italian ~guardare~, French ~garder~ (and ~regarder~) and Portuguese ~guardar~. English inherited the same root twice: natively as ~ward~ (with ~warden~ and ~reward~) and, borrowed through French, as ~guard~ and ~guardian~ — a ~w-~/~gu-~ doublet of one Germanic word.

The oldest sense was “to keep watch, guard,” and Spanish widened it toward “to keep, store, put away safely,” and “to observe” a rule — ~guardar silencio~ is “to keep silent,” ~guardar las formas~ “to observe the proprieties.” The doublet is the memorable part: ~ward~ and ~guard~ are the very same Germanic word, one native to English, the other looped back in through French centuries later. From the root Spanish built ~guarda~, ~guardia~, ~guardián~, ~guardarropa~ (“wardrobe”), ~aguardar~ (“to wait for”) and ~resguardar~ (“to shelter”).
en.gustar:
Spanish ~gustar~ goes back to Latin ~gustāre~ (“to taste, sample, enjoy”). Curiously, the inherited Old Spanish form was ~gostar~; modern ~gustar~ is a later reborrowing closer to the Latin, whereas Portuguese kept the inherited ~gostar~. The Latin noun ~gustus~ (“a tasting, a flavor”) comes from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵews-~ (“to taste; to choose”). Through that root ~gustar~ is cognate with English ~choose~ and with the archaic English ~gust~ (“relish, keen enjoyment”).

The remarkable Spanish development is grammatical: ~gustar~ came to mean “to be pleasing to,” so the thing tasted becomes the subject and the taster an indirect object — hence ~me gusta~ literally says “it is pleasing to me,” not “I like it.” This “to like” sense is peculiar to Ibero-Romance; the older “to taste” survives in ~degustar~ (“to taste, sample”). From the same root come ~gusto~ (“taste, pleasure”), ~gustoso~ (“tasty; glad to”) and ~disgusto~ (“displeasure, upset”).
en.haber:
Spanish ~haber~, through Old Spanish ~aver~, descends from Latin ~habēre~ (“to have, hold”), from Proto-Italic *~habēō~, and — the root is generally traced this way, though debated — from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰh₁bʰ-~ (“to grab, take, hold”). Its Romance siblings all preserve the sense of holding or possessing: French ~avoir~, Italian ~avere~, Portuguese ~haver~, and Romanian ~avea~. English ~have~ looks and sounds like an obvious cousin, but it is a false friend: it belongs to the Germanic family and, as we will see, springs from an entirely different root, so the resemblance is pure coincidence.

Where French and Italian kept ~avoir~ and ~avere~ as the everyday verb of possession, Spanish demoted ~haber~ to a near-pure auxiliary and handed ownership to ~tener~ (from Latin ~tenēre~, “to hold”). Two roles remained: the auxiliary of the compound tenses (~he cantado~, “I have sung”) and the impersonal existential ~hay~, ~había~, ~habrá~ (“there is, there are”). The old possessive sense survives only fossilized, in the noun ~haber~ / ~haberes~ (“assets, wages”) and set phrases like ~habérselas con~. The form ~hay~ deserves its own note: it is medieval ~ha~ plus the locative clitic ~y~ (from Latin ~ibī~, “there”), exactly parallel to French ~il y a~ and Catalan ~hi ha~ — literally “it has there,” hence “there is.” From the same Latin verb Spanish also draws a learned family: ~hábito~, ~habitar~, ~exhibir~, ~prohibir~, and — via ~dēbēre~, that is ~dē-~ plus ~habēre~ — the verb ~deber~.

German ~haben~ completes the trap. It comes not from the root behind ~habēre~ but from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp”) — the very root that in Latin produced ~capiō~ (“I seize”), and through it Spanish ~captar~, ~cautivo~, and ~aceptar~. So the two great “have” verbs of Western Europe are not related at all; they were pulled into the same shape by a ~Sprachbund~, the long convergence of neighboring languages, until each ended up an auxiliary: Spanish ~he comido~ mirrors German ~ich habe gegessen~. There is a final twist. Old Spanish did once share the European auxiliary split, taking “be” for verbs of motion and change — ~es nacido~ (“is born”), ~so venido~ (“is come”) — but it later leveled the system, generalizing ~haber~ to every compound tense (~ha muerto~, not older ~es muerto~). So modern Spanish, unlike French and German, no longer keeps the ~ser~/~haber~ division it once had. English quietly did the same: it once formed the perfect of verbs of motion and change with ~be~ — ~I am come~, ~he is risen~ — before ~have~ took over there too.
en.hablar:
From Old Spanish ~fablar~, from Latin ~fābulārī~ (“to chat, converse”), a verb built on ~fābula~ (“story, talk”), itself from ~fārī~ (“to speak”) and the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰeh₂-~ (“to speak”). Cognate with Portuguese ~falar~ and Italian ~favellare~, and — through the same root — with Latin ~fāma~ (whence English ~fame~) and the learned English doublet ~fable~, borrowed straight from ~fābula~.

The Latin ~f~ of ~fablar~ weakened to an aspirated ~h~ in early Castilian and then fell silent, so medieval ~fablar~ became modern ~hablar~ while the letter lingered on, mute — one of the sound-changes that most sharply distinguishes Spanish from its Romance siblings. The meaning drifted too: where classical Latin used ~fābulārī~ for idle chatting, Spanish promoted it to the ordinary word for “to speak,” displacing ~loquī~. From ~fābula~ Spanish also drew the learned ~fábula~ (“fable”) and ~fabuloso~, while ~hablar~ itself seeded ~habla~ (“speech”), ~hablador~ (“chatterbox”), ~hablante~ (“speaker”), and ~hablilla~ (“rumor”).
en.hacer:
Spanish ~hacer~ comes, through Old Spanish ~fazer~, from Latin ~facere~ (“to do, to make”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, set, place”). The same root gave the English verb ~do~ and German ~tun~, so ~hacer~ and ~do~ are true cousins under the skin. Its Romance siblings kept the Latin ~f-~: Italian ~fare~, French ~faire~, Portuguese ~fazer~. Spanish alone let that ~f-~ drift to a silent ~h-~, the regular change that turned ~facere~ into ~hacer~.

Latin ~facere~ was the great all-purpose verb of doing and making, and its progeny is enormous. Spanish keeps the past participle ~hecho~ (“done; fact”), and builds ~deshacer~ (“to undo”), ~satisfacer~ (“to satisfy,” literally “to make enough”), and ~hacienda~ (“estate, treasury”). Learned borrowings that skipped the ~f-~-to-~h-~ shift preserve the older look: ~factor~, ~efecto~ (“effect”), and ~factible~ (“feasible”) — a whole workshop of words for making.
en.hallar:
From Old Spanish ~fallar~ (“to find”), from Latin ~afflāre~ (“to blow toward, breathe on”), from ~ad-~ (“toward”) plus ~flāre~ (“to blow”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰleh₁-~ (“to blow”). The initial ~f-~ became ~h-~ in the regular Castilian shift (as ~facere~ → ~hacer~), and the ~h~ fell silent. Portuguese ~achar~ and Romanian ~afla~ (both “to find”) descend from the very same ~afflāre~.

How does “to blow toward” become “to find”? The sources agree on the etymon but debate the path; Corominas favors applying to the Latin verb the sense of a hound catching a scent — the dog winds its game and so comes upon it. That hunting image, though the preferred account, is not certain, and other Romanists proposed “to reach with one’s breath, and thus to touch.” The ~h~ of ~hallar~ itself likely arose by a metathesis of the internal ~-f-~. Spanish keeps the noun ~hallazgo~ (“a find, discovery”) beside everyday ~hallar~ (“to find, to come upon”).
en.identificar:
From Medieval Latin ~identificāre~ (“to make identical”), a compound of ~identitās~ (“sameness, identity”) and ~-ficāre~, the combining form of ~facere~ (“to make, to do”). ~identitās~ was itself a late, learned coinage from ~idem~ (“the same”). The word spread through the Romance languages as a scholarly borrowing rather than by inheritance: Italian ~identificare~, French ~identifier~, Portuguese ~identificar~, and English ~identify~ all arrived by the same learned route in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

Because ~identificar~ is a bookish, relatively modern formation, its story belongs to philosophy and law rather than to folk speech. ~idem~, “the very same,” carried the Latin idea of exact sameness, and ~-ficāre~ carried “to make,” so the verb means literally “to make one and the same” — to establish that a person and a name denote a single thing. From ~idem~ Spanish also keeps ~ídem~ (the ditto word), ~identidad~, and ~idéntico~; from ~facere~ descends a whole crowd of ~-ficar~ verbs such as ~verificar~, ~clasificar~, and ~modificar~. The reflexive ~identificarse~ (“to identify oneself” — to show one's papers, or to feel kinship with someone) is a later extension, its bureaucratic and emotional senses growing up side by side.
en.imaginar:
From Latin ~imāgināri~ (“to picture to oneself, imagine, fancy”), a verb formed on ~imāgō~ (“image, likeness, copy; also phantom, apparition”). ~imāgō~ was built on the stem of ~imitārī~ (“to imitate, copy”), and the pair is usually traced to Proto-Indo-European *~aim-~ (“to copy”), the root also behind Latin ~aemulus~ (“rival, emulous”). Cognate with Italian ~immaginare~, French ~imaginer~ and Portuguese ~imaginar~, and with English ~imagine~.

Before it meant a mental picture, ~imāgō~ named a very physical thing: the wax death-masks of ancestors that Roman families kept and paraded at funerals — an ~imāgō~ was a likeness of the dead, and the word also meant a ghost. From “likeness” it moved inward to “the image formed in the mind,” which is what ~imaginar~ carries today. The same family gave Spanish ~imagen~, ~imaginación~, ~imaginario~, ~imitar~ (“to imitate”) and ~émulo~ (“emulator, rival”).
en.impedir:
From Latin ~impedīre~ (“to hinder, obstruct”), literally “to shackle the feet,” from ~in-~ (“in, on”) and ~pēs~, ~pedis~ (“foot”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pṓds~ (“foot”). Cognate with Italian ~impedire~ and English ~impede~; and, through ~pēs~, with English ~foot~, ~pedal~ and ~pedestrian~ and Spanish ~pie~.

The image is wonderfully concrete: to impede someone is to snare their feet, as with a fetter — and Latin had the exact opposite, ~expedīre~, “to free the feet,” which yields Spanish ~expedito~ (“unobstructed”) and English ~expedite~. Popular Latin also coined ~impedicāre~, “to entangle,” which travelled a separate road into French ~empêcher~ (“to prevent”). From the “foot” root Spanish keeps ~pie~, ~pedal~, ~peatón~, ~expedir~ and ~impedimento~, while the same Proto-Indo-European *~pṓds~ surfaces across the family, from Greek ~poús~ to German ~Fuß~.
en.implementar:
From ~implemento~ (“implement, tool”), and, more directly, borrowed in the twentieth century from English ~implement~ (verb, “to carry out”). The ultimate source is Late Latin ~implēmentum~ (“a filling-up”), from Latin ~implēre~ (“to fill, fulfil”), from ~in-~ (intensive) and ~plēre~ (“to fill”), from the same Proto-Indo-European root *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”) that underlies ~lleno~. It is cognate with English ~complete~ and ~supply~ and, through the root, with Spanish ~pleno~ and ~lleno~.

Curiously, Castilian never really took up the Latinism ~implemento~ on its own; the noun and the verb ~implementar~ came in from English, where ~implement~ had specialized from “a thing that fills a need, a tool” to “to put into effect.” Prescriptivists long flagged ~implementar~ as an ill-formed anglicism, but the DLE now records it. Its fill-root cousins in Spanish include ~lleno~, ~llenar~, ~pleno~, ~plenitud~ and ~completar~.
en.implicar:
From Latin ~implicāre~ (“to fold in, entangle, involve”), from ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, fold”). Cognate with — and in several cases borrowed as — English ~imply~, ~employ~, and ~implicate~, and French ~impliquer~.

The image is physical: to ~implicar~ is to fold something in so that it becomes entangled with something else — hence “to involve” and, of a statement, “to imply.” A quiet surprise is that Spanish ~emplear~ (“to employ, use”) is a doublet: the same ~plicāre~ reached it by a worn popular road through Old French, whereas the learned form was lifted straight from Latin. The fold-family is large: ~aplicar~ (“to apply”), ~explicar~ (“to explain,” to unfold), ~complicar~ (“to complicate”), ~plegar~ (“to fold”), and ~replicar~ (“to reply”).
en.imponer:
From Latin ~impōnere~ (“to set upon, lay on”), a compound of ~in-~ (“on, upon”) and ~pōnere~ (“to put, place”). ~Pōnere~ was itself a contraction of the particle ~po-~ and ~sinere~ (“to let, set down”). Spanish ~imponer~ is cognate with Italian ~imporre~ and Portuguese ~impor~; French ~imposer~ and English ~impose~ belong to the family too, though both were reshaped on the participle stem ~positus~ rather than the infinitive.

The literal “place upon” quickly turned figurative: to ~imponer~ is to lay a tax, a rule, or a penalty on someone, and reflexively ~imponerse~ is to assert oneself or prevail. The participle ~impositus~ gave the popular ~impuesto~, which in Spanish is not only “imposed” but the everyday noun “tax.” The parent ~pōnere~ founded one of Spanish's largest verb families — ~poner~, ~componer~, ~disponer~, ~exponer~, ~proponer~ — each pairing a learned noun in ~-posición~ with a popular participle in ~-puesto~, as in ~composición~ beside ~compuesto~.
en.importar:
From Latin ~importāre~ (“to bring in, carry in”), a compound of the prefix ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~portāre~ (“to carry, bear”). ~portāre~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to cross over, pass through, bring across”), the same root that gave Latin ~porta~ (“gate”) and ~portus~ (“harbor”). The cognate branches are many: through Germanic the root surfaces in English ~ford~ and ~ferry~, and through Greek in ~póros~ (“passage, ford”). Within Romance the compound yields Italian ~importare~, French ~importer~ and Portuguese ~importar~.

The verb’s two modern senses both flow from “carrying in.” Commercially, to ~importar~ is to carry goods into a country — the plain, literal meaning. But Spanish ~importar~ also means “to matter, to be of concern.” The bridge is the notion of what a thing “brings in” or “carries” as its weight or value: what is entered into an account is its ~importe~ (“sum, amount”), and what carries weight is ~importante~ (“important”). From the same Latin ~portāre~ Spanish also built ~transportar~, ~exportar~, ~deporte~ (“sport,” originally “to carry oneself off, amuse”) and ~puerto~ (“port”).
en.impulsar:
From ~impulso~ (“impulse”) + ~-ar~, on Latin ~impulsus~, the participle of ~impellere~ (“to drive against, to push forward”), from ~in-~ (“in, upon”) + ~pellere~ (“to push, to drive, to beat”). ~pellere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~pelh₂-~ (“to drive, to thrust”). Cognate with French ~impulser~ and Portuguese ~impulsar~, and — through ~pellere~ — with English ~impel~, ~impulse~, and ~pulse~.

The root sense is a forceful push, and the ~in-~ prefix aims it forward: to ~impulsar~ is to drive something ahead — a boat, a reform, a career. The participle ~pulsus~ (“driven, struck”) spawned a whole cluster about pushing and throbbing. ~pellere~ was remarkably fertile in Latin compounds, each surviving in Spanish: ~expulsar~ (“to expel,” drive out), ~repeler~ (“to repel,” drive back), ~compeler~ (“to compel,” drive together), ~propulsar~ (“to propel”), and ~pulsar~ (“to press, to pulse”). The plain noun ~pulso~ means both “pulse” and “steadiness of hand,” while everyday ~empujar~ (“to push”) reached Spanish from the same ~impellere~ through Vulgar Latin ~impulsāre~.
en.incluir:
A semi-learned borrowing from Latin ~inclūdere~ (“to shut in, enclose”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in”) and ~claudere~ (“to close, shut”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kleh₂u-~ (“hook, peg; to close”). Cognate with Italian ~includere~, French ~inclure~, and Portuguese ~incluir~, and — through ~claudere~ — with English ~include~, ~conclude~, ~exclude~, and ~close~, plus Latin ~clāvis~ (“key,” whence Spanish ~llave~ and ~clave~).

That ~incluir~ is only semi-learned shows in its shape: a fully popular descent would have battered the word far more, but scholars and scribes reintroduced it close to the Latin, keeping the combining form ~-clūdere~ (with the ~au~ of ~claudere~ raised to ~ū~). The literal image is spatial — to shut something inside — from which the modern “to contain, comprise, include” follows directly. The same ~claudere~ radiates through Spanish ~concluir~, ~excluir~, and ~recluir~, and ~inclūdere~ itself yields ~inclusión~, the adverb ~incluso~ (“even, including”), and ~inclusivo~ (“inclusive”).
en.incorporar:
From Latin ~incorporāre~ (“to form into a body, embody”), from ~in-~ (“into”) plus ~corpus~ (stem ~corpor-~, “body”) plus the verbal suffix ~-āre~. ~Corpus~ descends from Proto-Italic *~korpos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~krep-~ (“body, form”). Cognate with French ~incorporer~ and English ~incorporate~; the root itself is shared with English ~midriff~, from Old English ~hrif~ (“belly”).

The literal sense is “to put into a body,” to make separate things into one mass — it is the verb for folding egg whites into a batter, and the reason a company is “incorporated” into one legal body. Spanish ~incorporarse~ also means to sit or stand up, to bring the body upright. From ~corpus~ Spanish inherited ~cuerpo~ (“body”), ~corporal~, ~corpóreo~, ~corporación~, ~corpiño~ (“bodice”), and — by a French detour — ~corsé~ (“corset”).
en.incrementar:
From Latin ~incrementum~ (“growth, increase”), the noun of ~incrēscere~ (“to grow in, swell”), from ~in-~ plus ~crēscere~ (“to grow”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱreh₁-~ (“to grow, nourish”). Spanish ~incrementar~ is a fairly modern verb coined from the noun ~incremento~. Cognate with English ~increment~ and ~increase~, and, through the same root, with ~crescent~, ~create~, and ~recruit~ (originally “a fresh growth of troops”).

The Latin ~crēscere~ was an inchoative — a verb of beginning, “to start to grow” — and it seeded a wide Spanish family: ~crecer~ (“to grow”), ~creciente~ (“growing, crescent”), ~crear~ and ~criar~ (both “to create, raise,” doublets from ~creāre~), and ~concreto~ (“concrete,” literally “grown together”). Beside the everyday ~crecer~, ~incrementar~ keeps a more measured, quantitative ring — one ~incrementa~ a figure, a rate, a dose.
en.indicar:
From Latin ~indicāre~ (“to point out, show, declare”), from ~in-~ (“toward”) and ~dicāre~ (“to proclaim, dedicate”), a cousin of ~dīcere~ (“to say”); all go back to Proto-Indo-European *~deik-~ (“to show, point out”). It is cognate with Italian ~indicare~, Portuguese ~indicar~ and French ~indiquer~, and with English ~indicate~ and ~index~; through Germanic the same root gives English ~teach~ and ~token~.

Where ~dicāre~ was “to proclaim aloud,” ~indicāre~ was “to point a finger at,” and the finger is not incidental: the ~índice~ (“index finger”) is literally the pointer, and an ~índice~ in a book points you to its contents. From *~deik-~ Spanish gathers a wide family — ~indicio~ (“clue”), ~indicador~ (“indicator”), ~dedicar~ (“to dedicate,” from ~dēdicāre~) and ~predicar~ (“to preach,” from ~praedicāre~) — while Latin ~digitus~ (“finger”), from the same root, underlies ~dígito~ and English ~digit~.
en.informar:
From Latin ~informāre~ (“to give shape to, to form, to describe, to instruct”), a compound of ~in-~ (“into”) and ~formāre~ (“to form, to shape”), from the noun ~forma~ (“form, shape, figure”). The origin of ~forma~ is genuinely uncertain: it has long been proposed to derive from Ancient Greek ~morphḗ~ (“shape, form”) by metathesis, perhaps mediated by Etruscan, but the account is disputed and remains unproven, so the deeper source is best left open. The verb carried into Italian ~informare~, French ~informer~, and English ~inform~.

The literal sense is “to put into form,” and the abstract senses grew straight out of it: to shape the mind (“to instruct”), to shape an account (“to describe, to report”), and at last “to inform.” The very word “information” is, at root, a shaping of the mind. A charming doublet hides in the family: Spanish ~forma~ and ~horma~ (a shoemaker's “last” or mold) are the same Latin ~forma~ — one learned, one popularly inherited with ~f~ turned to ~h~. Alongside them stand ~formar~, ~fórmula~, ~formal~, ~transformar~, ~reformar~, and ~uniforme~.
en.ingresar:
From Latin ~ingressus~, participle of ~ingredī~ (“to step in, to enter”), from ~in-~ (“into”) + ~gradī~ (“to step, to walk”). ~gradī~ derives from ~gradus~ (“a step, a pace”) and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰredʰ-~ (“to walk, to stride”). Cognate with Portuguese ~ingressar~, and — through ~gradī~ — with English ~ingress~, ~progress~, ~grade~, and ~gradual~.

The image is a footstep: ~gradus~ was literally “a step,” and to ~ingredī~ was to “step into.” Spanish ~ingresar~ kept that spatial core — to enter — but specialized it in ways English splits across several words: one ~ingresa~ (is admitted) into a university or hospital, ~ingresa~ (deposits) money into a bank account, and ~ingresos~ are “income,” the money that steps in. The old ~gradus~ “step” also became a rung on a ladder of rank or measurement, giving ~grado~ (“degree”) and ~grada~ (“tier of seats”). From the same root Spanish drew a whole march of words: ~progresar~ (“to progress”), ~regresar~ (“to return”), ~agredir~ (“to attack,” literally to step toward), ~transgredir~ (“to transgress”), and ~gradual~.
en.iniciar:
From Latin ~initiāre~ (“to begin, to initiate into”), from ~initium~ (“a beginning, an entrance”), from ~inīre~ (“to go in, to enter”), which is ~in-~ (“into”) + ~īre~ (“to go”). ~īre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~eō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”), a root shared with Sanskrit ~éti~ (“he goes”) and Ancient Greek ~eîmi~ (“I will go”). Spanish borrowed the learned ~iniciar~ from Latin. Cognate with Italian ~iniziare~, French ~initier~, and Portuguese ~iniciar~.

In Rome ~initiāre~ carried a solemn charge beyond “to begin”: it meant to admit someone into the ~initium~ — the entrance, the threshold — of the mystery religions, to initiate them into secret rites. Spanish ~iniciar~ preserves both the everyday “to start” and this ceremonial “to initiate.” The going-root *~h₁ey-~ is faint in Spanish because ~īre~ was largely replaced, but it still shows in ~ir~ (whose forms mix three Latin verbs), ~inicio~, ~iniciativa~, ~éxito~ (“a going-out,” hence “success”), and ~tránsito~.
en.insistir:
From Latin ~īnsistere~ (“to stand on, set foot on; persist”), from ~in-~ (“on, upon”) and ~sistere~ (“to cause to stand, take a stand”), a reduplicated form built on ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). It is cognate with Italian ~insistere~ and French ~insister~, and — through ~sistere~ — with English ~insist~, ~assist~ and ~resist~.

To insist was, at root, to plant your feet on a spot and not move — ~in-~ (“on”) plus “to stand.” The metaphor is still legible: someone who insists takes a stand and holds it. The prolific root *~steh₂-~ gave Spanish a whole regiment of ~-sistir~ verbs — ~asistir~, ~resistir~, ~consistir~, ~persistir~, ~desistir~ and ~existir~ — alongside ~estar~ itself.
en.instalar:
From French ~installer~, borrowed from Medieval Latin ~installare~, a compound of Latin ~in-~ (“in”) and ~stallum~ (“stall, seat”). ~stallum~ was itself taken from a Germanic word for a standing-place or stable, Frankish *~stall~, from Proto-Germanic *~stallaz~, traceable to the Proto-Indo-European root *~stel-~ (“to put, stand”). The Germanic noun surfaces directly in English ~stall~ and German ~Stall~ (“stable”).

The medieval verb was strikingly concrete: to ~installare~ a canon or official was to seat him in his ~stallum~ — the assigned stall or choir seat that marked his office. From “to place someone in his seat” the meaning widened to “to set anything in its proper place”, and modern Spanish ~instalar~ ranges from installing a person in a post to installing plumbing or software. Spanish keeps the family in ~instalación~ and ~instalador~, while the same Germanic root gave English ~stall~, ~stallion~ and ~forestall~.
en.integrar:
From Latin ~integrāre~ (“to make whole, to renew”), from the adjective ~integer~ (“whole, untouched, intact”), from Proto-Italic *~n̥tagros~ (“untouched”): the negative prefix ~in-~ (“not”) joined to the root of ~tangere~ (“to touch”), from Proto-Indo-European *~teh₂g-~ (“to touch”). Something ~integer~ was, literally, un-touched. English borrowed the same Latin adjective as ~integer~ and ~entire~, and the root surfaces again in the borrowed ~tangent~ and ~tact~; the Italian ~integrare~ and French ~intégrer~ descend from the same verb.

Latin ~integrāre~ meant “to make whole again, to renew, to restore,” and that sense of completing and unifying carried into Spanish ~integrar~ (“to integrate, to make up, to compose”). The idea of the untouched-and-therefore-whole also gave Spanish a pair of doublets from the same ~integer~: the learned ~íntegro~ (“upright, complete”) and the inherited ~entero~ (“entire, whole”). From the “touch” root came a wide family — ~integridad~, ~integración~, and, through ~tangere~, the words ~tacto~, ~contacto~, ~intacto~, ~tangente~ and ~contagio~.
en.intentar:
From Latin ~intentāre~ (“to stretch toward, to aim at”), a frequentative of ~intendere~ (“to direct, to focus one's attention”), formed from ~in-~ (“toward”) plus ~tendere~ (“to stretch”). ~tendere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~tendō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~tend-~, a d-extension of the root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Through that root it is cognate with Ancient Greek ~teínō~, Sanskrit ~tanóti~, and English ~thin~, ~tend~, and ~tense~. Italian ~intentare~ and Portuguese ~intentar~ preserve the same compound.

The frequentative suffix once painted a repeated, insistent stretching-toward, and from that intensified aiming the sense narrowed to “to attempt, to try.” Spanish also kept a legal and rhetorical use, where ~intentar~ una demanda means “to bring a suit.” The prolific root *~ten-~ seeded a wide family in Spanish, among them ~tender~, ~tienda~ (a “tent,” and hence a “shop”), ~tensión~, ~intención~, ~atender~, ~extender~, and ~contender~.
en.interesar:
From ~interés~ (“interest”), a noun Spanish took from Latin ~interest~ (“it matters, it concerns”), the third-person form of the verb ~interesse~ (“to be between, to be present at, to concern”). That verb joins ~inter-~ (“between, among”) to ~esse~ (“to be”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁es-~ (“to be”), the same root behind Spanish ~ser~ and ~es~. Spanish ~interesar~ is cognate with Italian ~interessare~, French ~intéresser~ and English ~interest~, all descending from that Latin idiom for something that “lies between” the parties and therefore concerns them.

The semantic journey is a small lesson in economics and psychology alike. What “is between” people was, in Roman law, what mattered to them — a stake, a share, a concern. From that came the financial ~interés~ (the “concern” a lender holds in a loan, hence the money it earns) and, in parallel, the mental ~interés~, the attention we give to what concerns us. The reflexive ~interesarse~ (“to take an interest”) captures the second sense, while ~interesado~ can mean both “interested” and, less flatteringly, “self-interested.” Kin through ~esse~ include ~esencia~, ~ausente~, ~presente~ and ~interesante~ itself.
en.interpretar:
From Latin ~interpretārī~ (“to explain, translate, understand”), a deponent verb from the noun ~interpres~ (genitive ~interpretis~, “a go-between, negotiator, translator”). The first element is clearly ~inter-~ (“between”); the second element, ~-pres~, is of debated origin. One account links it to ~pretium~ (“price, value”), as though the interpreter were a broker who set a price between two parties; de Vaan and others reject a direct tie to ~pretium~ and connect ~-pres~ instead to a root meaning “to speak out, make known,” comparing Ancient Greek ~φράζω~ (~phrázō~, “to point out, declare”). The safest statement is that the second half is uncertain. Romance cognates include Italian ~interpretare~, French ~interpréter~ and Portuguese ~interpretar~.

In Rome the ~interpres~ stood between two sides who could not understand each other — a translator of tongues, but also a mediator of meaning, and even an interpreter of omens who explained the will of the gods. Spanish ~interpretar~ carries all three: to translate speech, to make sense of a text or a dream, and — via the stage — to perform a role or a piece of music, since an actor or musician “interprets” the work. From the same noun come ~intérprete~ (“interpreter, performer”), ~interpretación~ and ~interpretativo~. The contested link to ~pretium~ is worth flagging precisely because it is the most memorable story — an interpreter as the one who prices the exchange between strangers — yet it is not securely established, so enjoy it as a possibility, not a fact.
en.intervenir:
From Latin ~intervenīre~ (“to come between”), a compound of ~inter-~ (“between”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”), from Proto-Italic *~gʷenjō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to go”). It is cognate with Italian ~intervenire~, French ~intervenir~ and Portuguese ~intervir~; through ~venīre~ it is also kin to Spanish ~venir~ and, more distantly, to English ~come~, which descends from that same Indo-European verb.

In Latin ~intervenīre~ was largely literal — to come in the middle of something, to interrupt, to fall between events — and from there it grew the senses of coming to someone's aid and stepping into an affair. Spanish preserved both readings: an army ~interviene~, and so does a surgeon or a mediator. The learned prefix ~inter-~ marks “betweenness” throughout the language, while ~venīre~ seeded a large family, among them ~venir~, ~convenir~, ~avenida~, ~porvenir~, ~aventura~ and ~convento~. The last two are a small surprise: an ~aventura~ is etymologically a thing “about to come” (from ~adventūra~), and a ~convento~ a “coming together” (from ~conventus~).
en.introducir:
From Latin ~intrōdūcere~ (“to lead in, bring in”), from ~intrō~ (“inward, within”) and ~dūcere~ (“to lead, draw”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ (“to lead, draw”). The Spanish form was refashioned on ~-ducir~ (like ~conducir~ and ~producir~), the learned outcome of ~-dūcere~. Cognate with French ~introduire~, Italian ~introdurre~ and English ~introduce~; and, through ~dūcere~, with English ~duke~, ~duct~ and ~educate~ and German ~ziehen~.

To introduce is etymologically to “lead something inward” — hence both “to insert, put in” and the social “to bring a person in” by presentation. ~dūcere~ was a leader among Latin verbs for compounding, and Spanish inherited a whole column of its offspring in ~-ducir~: ~conducir~, ~producir~, ~reducir~, ~traducir~, ~seducir~ and ~aducir~, plus nouns like ~conducto~, ~producto~ and ~duque~ (“duke,” literally “leader”). The root *~dewk-~ even surfaces in English ~tow~ and ~team~, distant Germanic cousins of the Latin verb that Spanish borrowed so freely.
en.invertir:
From Latin ~invertere~ (“to turn upside down, reverse”), from ~in-~ plus ~vertere~ (“to turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *~wert-~ (“to turn”) — the same root as ~divertir~. Cognate with Italian ~invertire~, Portuguese ~inverter~, and English ~invert~ and ~inverse~.

Spanish ~invertir~ carries two meanings that look unrelated: “to invert, reverse” and “to invest money.” The first is straightforward from ~invertere~ (“to turn over”). The second is disputed: the favored account holds that the financial sense is not native but a semantic loan — the “put money to work” meaning is first recorded in English around 1610 in the East India trade and probably borrows a special use of Italian ~investire~ (literally “to clothe,” from Latin ~investīre~), which also gave Spanish ~investir~ (“to invest with an office”); the two look-alikes then converged on ~invertir~. So the “reverse” sense descends cleanly from ~vertere~, while the money sense likely rode in from elsewhere. From ~vertere~ Spanish also keeps ~verter~, ~inverso~, and ~convertir~.
en.investigar:
From Latin ~investīgāre~ (“to track down, search into”), from ~in-~ (“in, into”) plus ~vestīgāre~ (“to follow a trail”), from ~vestīgium~ (“footprint, track, trace”). Cognate with Italian ~investigare~, Portuguese ~investigar~, and English ~investigate~ and ~vestige~. The origin of ~vestīgium~ itself is uncertain — perhaps from ~verrō~ (“to sweep”), perhaps ~vē-~ plus a root *~steygʰ-~ (“to stride, walk”); the sources disagree.

The picture behind the word is the hunter or tracker reading the ground: to investigate was to go step by step along the ~vestīgia~, the footprints, until the quarry was found. That physical trailing hardened into the modern sense of methodical inquiry — scientific, criminal, journalistic. Spanish keeps the concrete noun ~vestigio~ (“vestige, trace, relic”) beside the abstract family ~investigación~ (“research, investigation”) and ~investigador~ (“researcher, investigator”), all still carrying, faintly, the shape of a footprint in soft earth.
en.invitar:
From Latin ~invītāre~ (“to invite, summon, entertain, treat”). Spanish in fact inherited this verb twice: the patrimonial form is ~convidar~ (from Vulgar Latin *~convītāre~, a remodeling of the classical verb), while ~invitar~ is a later learned borrowing — a cultismo — taken directly from ~invītāre~, so the two are doublets that split the labor of inviting. In the other Romance languages the learned form gives Italian ~invitare~, French ~inviter~ and Portuguese ~invitar~; English borrowed ~invite~ from the same Latin stock by way of French.

The deeper root is genuinely debated. Some etymologists connect ~invītāre~ with ~invocāre~ (“to call upon”), treating it as a frequentative of calling someone over; de Vaan instead derives it from a Proto-Indo-European *~weyh₁-~ (“to pursue, chase after”), so that to invite would be, at root, to “go after” a guest. An older account linked it to ~velle~ (“to want”). Because the sources hedge, none of these can be stated as settled fact. What is clear is the warmth the word kept: Latin ~invītāre~ meant not only to summon but to host graciously — which is why modern Spanish ~invitar~ commonly means to pay for another’s meal or drink. From the same family Spanish keeps ~convidar~, ~convite~ (“banquet, feast”) and the adjective ~invitado~ (“guest”).
en.involucrar:
~involucrar~ derives from the Latin noun ~involūcrum~ (“wrapper, covering, envelope”), itself from ~involvere~ (“to roll up, wrap up”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in”) and ~volvere~ (“to roll, turn”). ~volvere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~welwō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~welH-~ (“to turn, wind, roll”). Through that root ~volvere~ is kin to English ~involve~, ~revolve~, and ~volume~ (originally a rolled scroll), to Ancient Greek ~elýō~ (“I roll”), and, via Germanic, to English ~wallow~.

The image is physical: to ~involucrar~ someone is literally to “wrap them up” in a matter, to roll them into it. Spanish long used it for physically enveloping, then for entangling a person in an affair — the sense that now dominates, alongside the reflexive ~involucrarse~ (“to get involved”). The same ~volvere~ seeded a broad family: ~volver~ (“to return”), ~revolver~, ~envolver~ (“to wrap”), ~volumen~, ~revólver~ (the borrowed English name of the rotating pistol), and ~voluble~.
en.ir:
Spanish ~ir~ is, like ~ser~, a patchwork of several Latin verbs. Its infinitive and future come from Latin ~īre~ (“to go”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”), a root also visible in Greek ~eîmi~ (“I go”) and Sanskrit ~éti~. But the present tense (~voy~, ~vas~, ~va~, ~van~) comes instead from a different Latin verb, ~vādere~ (“to walk, advance”), and the preterite (~fui~, ~fue~) is borrowed wholesale from ~esse~, the perfect ~fuī~ that ~ser~ also uses.

So a single tiny verb draws on three sources — ~īre~ for the infinitive, ~vādere~ for the present, ~fuī~ for the past — one of the most thoroughly suppletive verbs in the language. The shared preterite is the memorable twist: ~fui~ means both “I went” and “I was,” the two verbs indistinguishable in that tense, context alone deciding. The ~vādere~ strand seeded further Spanish words — ~invadir~ (“to invade,” to go in), ~evadir~ (“to evade,” to go out), and ~vadear~ (“to ford”) — while ~īre~ itself left little behind but this one indispensable verb.
en.jugar:
From Latin ~iocāre~, a Vulgar-Latin variant of ~iocārī~ (“to jest, to play”), from ~iocus~ (“joke, jest”), from Proto-Indo-European *~yek-~ (“to speak”). Cognate with Italian ~giocare~, French ~jouer~, and Portuguese ~jogar~, and — through the same ~iocus~ — with English ~joke~ and ~juggle~ (the latter from Latin ~ioculārī~).

The surprise is that play began as talk. ~iocus~ was originally a spoken jest — the PIE root *~yek-~ means “to speak” — so the earliest “play” was word-play, banter, a joke. Only later did Spanish broaden ~jugar~ to cover games, sport, and gambling of every kind, leaving the verbal sense to ~bromear~. The old root still shows in ~jocoso~ (“humorous, jocular”), which kept close to the original joking. Everyday relatives include ~juego~ (“game, play”), ~jugador~ (“player”), and ~juguete~ (“toy”) — the whole vocabulary of fun grown from a single spoken quip.
en.justificar:
From Late Latin ~iūstificāre~ (“to do justice, to make righteous”), joining ~iūstus~ (“just, lawful”) to ~-ficāre~, the combining form of ~facere~ (“to make, to do”). ~iūstus~ in turn derives from ~iūs~ (“law, right, that which binds”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂yew-~ (“law, rule”). Through ~iūs~ it is cognate with English ~just~, ~justice~, and ~jury~.

In Roman thought ~iūs~ named binding right, often with a sacral tinge, and ~iūstus~ was what conformed to it; ~justificar~ thus began as “to make just” before it acquired its everyday sense of “to give reasons for.” (English borrowed it for the press, too: to ~justify~ a line of type is to make its edges straight and even.) The ~iūs~ family is large in Spanish: ~justo~, ~justicia~, ~juez~ (from ~iūdex~, “one who declares the law”), ~jurar~ (“to swear”), and ~injuria~ (“insult, wrong” — literally “that which runs against right”).
en.lanzar:
From Old Spanish ~lançar~, from Late Latin ~lanceāre~ (“to wield or hurl a lance”), from Latin ~lancea~ (“lance, light spear”). The origin of ~lancea~ itself is disputed: the Roman writer Varro reported it as a foreign, Hispanic word, so it is often traced to a Celtic or Iberian source — but the details are uncertain and no reconstruction is secure. Cognate with Italian ~lanciare~, French ~lancer~, and — borrowed through Old French — English ~lance~ and ~launch~.

The semantic path is neat: from a specific act, “to thrust with a lance,” Latin ~lanceāre~ broadened to any forceful throwing, and Spanish ~lanzar~ now covers hurling a ball, launching a rocket, or bringing a product to market. English ~launch~ took the very same journey through French. From ~lancea~ Spanish keeps the noun ~lanza~ (“lance”), ~lance~ (“incident, cast”), ~lanzamiento~ (“throw, launch”), and ~lanzadera~ (“shuttle”).
en.leer:
From Latin ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick out, to choose, to read”), from Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to collect, to gather”). Cognate with Italian ~leggere~, French ~lire~, and Portuguese ~ler~; the Greek branch, ~légō~ (“I gather, I say”), yielded ~lógos~ and the whole ~-logy~ family. Through Latin the same root gives English ~lecture~, ~legible~, ~legend~, ~collect~, and ~elect~.

The oldest sense was physical — ~legere~ meant to gather up or pick out, as one gathers firewood or picks grapes. “To read” is a metaphor grown from it: the eye gathers the scattered letters and picks out the words, one by one. Greek made the parallel leap from “gathering” to “speaking,” which is how a word for collecting became ~lógos~, “word, reason.” Spanish narrowed ~leer~ to reading alone but keeps the gathering sense in ~elegir~ (“to choose”) and ~colegir~ (“to infer, to gather”), plus the reading cluster ~lección~, ~lectura~, ~legible~, and ~leyenda~ (“legend,” literally “things to be read”).
en.levantar:
From Vulgar Latin *~levantāre~, built on ~levāns~ (stem ~levant-~), the present participle of Latin ~levāre~ (“to raise, lift, lighten”), from ~levis~ (“light in weight”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light, nimble”). It is cognate with Portuguese ~levantar~ and, through ~levāre~, with French ~lever~ and Italian ~levare~; through ~levis~ it is kin to English ~light~ (not heavy) and even ~lung~, the “light” organ that floats.

The base ~levāre~ meant both “to make lighter” and “to raise up,” and the frequentative ending gave ~levantar~ its brisk sense of lifting and getting up. Two descendants preserve a vivid picture: ~Levante~, the East, is the quarter where the sun “raises itself,” and ~levadura~ (“leaven, yeast”) is what makes dough rise. The wider family includes ~elevar~, ~aliviar~ (“to lighten, relieve”), ~leve~, ~liviano~, and ~levantamiento~ (“uprising”) — all turning on the double idea of lightness and rising.
en.liberar:
From Latin ~līberāre~ (“to set free, release”), from the adjective ~līber~ (“free”). ~līber~ goes back, through Old Latin ~loeber~ and Proto-Italic *~louðeros~, to Proto-Indo-European *~h₁léwdʰeros~ (“belonging to the people,” hence “free”), from the root *~h₁lewdʰ-~ (“to grow, to rise; people”). The kinship is striking: the same root gave Ancient Greek ~eleútheros~ (“free”), German ~Leute~ (“people”), and Russian ~ljúdi~ (“people”). Beside Spanish stand Italian ~liberare~ and Portuguese ~libertar~/~liberar~.

The etymology carries a whole social theory: to be ~līber~ was to belong to the people, the tribe, the free community — the opposite of the outsider or the slave, who was mere property. Freedom was membership, and German ~Leute~ still preserves that older “people” sense of the root. Spanish grew a large free-family — ~libre~, ~librar~, ~libertad~, ~liberal~, ~liberto~ (“freedman”), and ~libertino~ — while English borrowed ~liberty~ and ~liberate~ from the same Latin ~līber~. One caution: the noun ~libro~ (“book”) is no relative — it comes from a homonymous ~liber~, the inner tree-bark once written on.
en.limitar:
From Latin ~limitare~ (“to mark off, set bounds”), formed from ~limes~ (genitive ~limitis~), “a boundary, a cross-path between fields, a frontier”. ~limes~ is usually derived from ~limus~ (“sidelong, transverse”) and set beside ~limen~ (“threshold”), though the exact relationship among these words is debated. It descends in Italian ~limitare~, French ~limiter~ and Portuguese ~limitar~.

The Roman ~limes~ began as the balk or path running crosswise between plots, then hardened into something grander: the fortified ~limes~ that marked the edge of the empire, from the German frontier to Hadrian's Wall. To ~limitare~ was to trace such a boundary, and Spanish ~limitar~ still means both “to set a limit” and “to border on” a neighbour. The family includes ~límite~, ~limítrofe~ (“bordering”) and ~limitación~, and English drew ~limit~ and ~limitation~ straight from the same Latin, while the neighbouring ~limen~ surfaces in English ~liminal~.
en.llamar:
From Old Spanish ~clamar~, from Latin ~clāmāre~ (“to cry out, shout”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kelh₁-~ (“to call, shout”). Cognate with Italian ~chiamare~, French ~clamer~, and Portuguese ~chamar~, and — through the same root — with Latin ~calāre~ (“to call out”) and the English borrowings ~claim~ and ~clamor~.

The initial Latin cluster ~cl-~ palatalized to the Spanish ~ll-~ (the same shift that turned ~clāvem~ into ~llave~ and ~plēnum~ into ~lleno~), so ~clāmāre~ yielded popular ~llamar~ while a learned ~clamar~ (“to clamor, cry out”) was later re-borrowed alongside it. The sense softened from the urgency of shouting to the everyday acts of calling, summoning, and — reflexively, in ~llamarse~ — being named: one no longer cries out a name but simply ~se llama~ it. The root also gave Spanish ~clamor~, ~reclamar~ (“to claim, demand”), and ~exclamar~, plus the derivatives ~llamada~ (“call”), ~llamamiento~ (“summons”), and ~llamativo~ (“eye-catching”).
en.llegar:
From Old Spanish ~llegar~, from Latin ~plicāre~ (“to fold”) — or, by a competing account, from its compound ~applicāre~ (“to bring to, to land a ship”), the initial ~a-~ later lost. Either way the ~pl-~ hardened into Spanish ~ll-~. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to fold”). Portuguese ~chegar~ came the same way; the folding sense stayed put in the learned doublet ~plegar~ and in Italian ~piegare~ and French ~plier~; English ~ply~ and ~apply~ are relatives.

How “to fold” became “to arrive” is debated. The usual explanation is nautical — a ship reaching harbor folds its sails, or is brought folded up against the shore — fitting for the seafaring peninsula, though it remains a proposal rather than a proven fact. Strikingly, the very same Latin verb went the opposite way in Romanian ~pleca~ (“to leave, to depart”), by one account from folding up a tent to move on — so a single root yielded both “arrive” and “leave.” Spanish derivatives include ~llegada~ (“arrival”) and the doublet family of ~plegar~, ~aplicar~, ~replicar~, and ~complicar~.
en.llenar:
From ~lleno~ (“full”), from Latin ~plēnus~ (“full”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”); the Latin initial ~pl-~ regularly became Spanish ~ll-~. It is cognate with Italian ~pieno~, French ~plein~ and Portuguese ~cheio~, and, through the same root, with English ~full~ and ~plenty~ and German ~voll~.

The adjective ~plēnus~ gave the adjective ~lleno~, from which Spanish coined the verb ~llenar~, “to make full.” Beside the inherited ~ll-~ line, Spanish also borrowed the Latin ~pl-~ form learnedly, so the family runs double: popular ~lleno~, ~llenar~, ~rellenar~ alongside cultured ~pleno~, ~plenitud~ and ~pleamar~ (“high tide”). English ~fill~ itself is built on ~full~, from the very same PIE root *~pleh₁-~.
en.llevar:
From Old Spanish ~levar~, from Latin ~levāre~ (“to raise, to lift”), from the adjective ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light in weight”) — the same root that gave English its native ~light~. The Romance siblings are Italian ~levare~, French ~lever~, and Portuguese ~levar~; English also took the learned ~lever~, ~elevate~, ~alleviate~, and ~relieve~ from the same Latin stock.

The path from “to lift” to Spanish ~llevar~ (“to carry, to take, to wear”) runs through the natural chain of lifting a load, then bearing it, then bearing it away. Spanish split the work with a cousin: ~llevar~ carries something from here to there, while ~traer~ brings it toward the speaker. The plainer sense of “to raise” stayed with the doublet ~levantar~ (“to lift, to raise”), and the family also yields ~leve~ (“light, slight”), ~elevar~, ~aliviar~ (“to relieve”), ~relevar~ (“to relieve, to relay”), and ~sublevar~ (“to incite to revolt”).
en.lograr:
From Latin ~lucrārī~ (“to gain, to profit”), a deponent verb from the noun ~lucrum~ (“gain, profit, wealth”), from Proto-Indo-European *~leh₂w-~ (“to seize, to gain”). The same root surfaces in Germanic as Proto-Germanic *~launą~ (“reward”), giving German ~Lohn~ (“wage”) and Old English ~lēan~ (“reward”), and in Greek ~apolaúō~ (“to enjoy”). Within Romance, Spanish ~lograr~ stands beside the learned borrowing ~lucro~ and its Portuguese and Italian relatives.

The meaning traveled a satisfying road. Latin ~lucrārī~ was mercantile — to turn a profit — and Old Spanish ~lograr~ first meant “to enjoy or possess” something, to have the benefit of it. From “enjoying the gain” the verb slid to “obtaining the desired thing” and finally to today’s “to achieve, to manage to.” The word’s history is thus its own small success story: from raw profit, through enjoyment, to accomplishment. Alongside the popular ~lograr~ Spanish keeps the doublet ~logro~ (“achievement,” and formerly “usury, interest”), plus the learned ~lucro~ and ~lucrativo~, which stayed close to the original money-making sense.
en.luchar:
From Latin ~luctari~ (“to wrestle, to struggle”), attested since Plautus, from Proto-Indo-European *~lewg-~ (“to bend, to twist”). The Latin cluster ~-ct-~ palatalized to Spanish ~-ch-~, the same change that turned ~lacte~ into ~leche~ and ~pectus~ into ~pecho~. It is cognate with Italian ~lottare~, French ~lutter~ and Portuguese ~lutar~, and — through the deponent compound ~reluctari~ — with English ~reluctant~ (literally “struggling back”).

The image behind the root is a body twisting against an opponent, and ~luchar~ began as literal wrestling before broadening to any fight or striving — against an enemy, an illness, or oneself. By the traditional account the same *~lewg-~ root also yielded Latin ~luxus~ (“dislocated; excess”), whence Spanish ~lujo~ (“luxury”) and ~lujuria~ (“lust”) — the twist of a joint and the twist of indulgence sharing one ancestor. Closer to home the root gives ~lucha~, ~luchador~ and ~luchadora~.
en.mandar:
From Latin ~mandāre~ (“to entrust, to order”), a compound traditionally explained as ~manus~ (“hand”) + ~dāre~ (“to give”) — literally “to place in someone's hand.” ~dāre~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Cognate with Italian ~mandare~ (“to send”), French ~mander~, and Portuguese ~mandar~, and — through the compound — with English ~mandate~, ~command~, and ~demand~.

The literal picture — putting a task into someone's hand — explains the whole semantic spread. To hand someone a charge is to “entrust” it (the sense in English ~mandate~), and to entrust with authority shades into “to order,” which is why ~mandar~ means “to command.” But Spanish also took a second path: to put something in a messenger's hand is to “send” it, so ~mandar~ means “to send” as well — ~mandar una carta~ is to send a letter, ~mandar a alguien~ can be to order someone about. Few Spanish verbs carry so wide a range on one root. Related descendants include ~mando~ (“command, control”), ~mandato~ (“mandate”), ~mandamiento~ (“commandment”), ~comandar~ (“to command [troops]”), ~demandar~ (“to demand, to sue”), and ~encomendar~ (“to entrust”).
en.manejar:
From Italian ~maneggiare~ (“to handle, to manage, especially to handle a horse”), a denominative ultimately built on Latin ~manus~ (“hand”). Spanish borrowed it in the sixteenth century. The word is traditionally parsed as ~manus~ plus ~agere~ (“to drive by hand”), but that account is disputed: Corominas rejects it, treating ~maneggiare~ instead as a reinforced formation from ~mano~ / ~manus~, parallel to Italian ~maniglia~ (“handle”). Through the same Italian verb, Spanish ~manejar~ is cognate with English ~manage~ and French ~manège~ (“riding school”).

Its first home in Spanish was the riding school: to ~manejar~ a horse was to work it through its paces by hand and rein. From there it widened to handling tools, money, ideas and people — and in much of Latin America ~manejar~ became the ordinary verb for driving a car, where peninsular Spanish prefers ~conducir~. The Latin ~manus~ seeded a broad family, among them ~mano~, ~manejo~, ~manija~, ~maniobra~, ~manual~ and ~manuscrito~.
en.manifestar:
From Latin ~manifestare~ (“to make plain, reveal”), derived from the adjective ~manifestus~ (“caught in the act, flagrant, evident, palpable”). Its first element is clearly ~manus~ (“hand”); the second is disputed — it may descend from a Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰers-~ (“to be bold”), itself from *~dʰer-~ (“to hold”), but the analysis is uncertain and no confident sense can be assigned. Latin passed the verb to Italian ~manifestare~, French ~manifester~ and Portuguese ~manifestar~.

Whatever its build, ~manifestus~ evoked something so palpable it could almost be taken in the hand — a wrongdoer “caught red-handed”, a fact plain to all. Spanish ~manifestar~ accordingly means “to show, reveal, declare”, and reflexively ~manifestarse~ is “to demonstrate”, to make one's views public in the street. Hence the noun ~manifestación~ (“demonstration, manifestation”) and ~manifiesto~ (“manifesto”). The transparent first element ~manus~ anchors a huge Spanish family — ~mano~, ~manejar~, ~manual~ and ~mantener~ — and English borrowed the verb's own offspring in ~manifest~ and ~manifesto~.
en.mantener:
From Latin ~manū~ ~tenēre~, literally “to hold in the hand,” a phrase of ~manus~ (“hand”) and ~tenēre~ (“to hold, keep”) that fused into Vulgar Latin ~manutenēre~. The second element, shared with ~tener~, goes back to Proto-Italic *~tenēō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch, extend”); the first, ~manus~, comes from Proto-Italic *~manus~ and *~man-~ (“hand”). Cognate Romance descendants include Italian ~mantenere~, Portuguese ~manter~ and French ~maintenir~; English ~maintain~ is the same compound, borrowed through Old French ~maintenir~.

The image is concrete: to “hold in the hand” became to keep, support, sustain and maintain — the range Spanish ~mantener~ still spans, from ~mantener~ una promesa to ~mantener~ a la familia. Its ~tenēre~ half anchors a huge family — ~tener~, ~contener~, ~detener~, ~obtener~, ~sostener~ and ~retener~ — while ~manus~ gives ~mano~, ~manejar~, ~manual~ and ~maniobra~ (“maneuver,” from ~manū~ ~operāre~, “to work by hand”). Through the root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”) ~mantener~ is even distantly kin to ~tender~, ~tienda~ (a stretched tent-shop) and English ~tenant~ and ~tension~.
en.marcar:
Spanish ~marcar~ (“to mark”) has a debated immediate history: it is either a native formation from the noun ~marca~ (“mark, boundary”) plus the verb-ending ~-ar~, or a loan from Italian ~marcare~ (“to put a mark on”). Either way the deeper source is Germanic. The noun ~marca~ goes back, through Medieval Latin ~marca~, to Proto-Germanic *~markō~ (“boundary, borderland, region”), which entered Ibero-Romance from a Germanic tongue — Gothic or Frankish. So the root idea is not a scribble but a border. It is cognate with Italian ~marca~, German ~Mark~ and English ~mark~ and ~march~ (“borderland”).

The semantic path runs from the land inward. A ~marca~ was first a frontier district — the borderlands a ruler had to guard — which is exactly why medieval marches gave us titles like “marquis” (Spanish ~marqués~), the lord set over a ~marca~. From “boundary” the noun narrowed to the “mark” one sets to claim or delimit, and the verb ~marcar~ to the act of making such a mark — on cattle, on a page, on a scoreboard. Its Spanish kin spread across that whole span: ~marco~ (“frame”), ~marcador~ (“marker; scoreboard”), ~comarca~ (“district,” literally land within borders), ~demarcar~ (“to demarcate”) and ~marcapasos~ (“pacemaker”).
en.matar:
From Old Spanish ~matar~ (“to fell, subdue, kill”), a word shared by the Hispanic Romance languages whose ultimate origin is genuinely uncertain. The account favored by Corominas derives it from a Vulgar Latin *~mattāre~, from Latin ~mattus~ (“stunned, addled, sottish”) — the sense moving from “to daze, stun, fell” to “to kill.” ~mattus~ is itself of obscure origin; Corominas weighs, without endorsing, a link to Ancient Greek ~μάταιος~ (~mátaios~, “vain, foolish”), a connection that cannot be documented. By this account ~matar~ is related to Italian ~matto~ (“mad, crazy”) and French ~mat~ (“defeated,” as in checkmate); Portuguese also has ~matar~.

If the ~mattus~ etymology holds, the everyday Spanish verb for “to kill” is a cousin of the Italian word for “crazy” — a striking pairing, but one resting on a disputed root, so worth stating as hypothesis rather than fact. In Spanish the meaning settled firmly on killing and its figures: to ~matar~ time, thirst, or a light. From it grew a plain, grim family — ~matanza~ (“slaughter”), ~matador~ (“killer,” and the bullfighter who delivers the final blow) and ~rematar~ (“to finish off, to top off”).
en.medir:
From Old Galician-Portuguese ~medir~, from Latin ~metiri~ (“to measure”), a deponent verb, from Proto-Indo-European *~meh₁-~ (“to measure”). The Latin ~-t-~ between vowels voiced and then vanished, giving ~metiri~ → ~medir~. It is cognate with Portuguese ~medir~ and, through the same root, with English ~measure~ (via Latin ~mensura~) and with Greek ~métron~ (“measure”).

The PIE root carried the idea of marking off a due amount, and one striking branch measured time: by the traditional account *~meh₁-~ also produced the word for the moon as the great measurer of the months, seen in English ~moon~ and ~month~. In Spanish the verb stayed close to its plain sense — to determine a size or extent — while spawning ~medida~, ~medición~, ~medidor~, ~mensura~, ~dimensión~ and ~inmenso~ (literally “unmeasurable”).
en.mejorar:
Spanish ~mejorar~ comes from Late Latin ~meliōrāre~ (“to make better”), a verb built on the Latin comparative ~melior~ (“better”). ~melior~ is generally traced to Proto-Indo-European *~mel-~ (“strong, great”), the same root credited with Latin ~multus~ (“much”) and Ancient Greek ~μάλα~ (mála, “very”). Its Romance reflexes are everywhere: the adjective survives as Spanish ~mejor~, Portuguese ~melhor~, French ~meilleur~, and Italian ~migliore~, and the verb as Portuguese ~melhorar~ and Italian ~migliorare~. English ~ameliorate~ borrowed the Latin verb through French.

There is a small surprise in ~mejor~: it serves as the comparative of ~bueno~ (“good”) yet shares no root with it. Latin ~bonus~ lacked a comparative of its own and borrowed ~melior~ from an unrelated word — the pattern called suppletion, the same quirk behind English “good/better.” So ~mejorar~ means, transparently, to make or become better. From the root Spanish keeps ~mejor~, ~mejora~ (“improvement”), ~mejoría~ (“recovery”), and ~mejoramiento~; through the cognate ~multus~ come ~mucho~, ~muy~, ~multitud~, and ~múltiple~.
en.mencionar:
From ~mención~ (“mention”), a learned noun taken from Latin ~mentiō~ (stem ~mentiōn-~, “a calling to mind, a naming”), which grows from the same root as ~meminī~ (“to remember”) and ~mēns~ (“mind”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to think”). The verb ~mencionar~ is cognate with French ~mentionner~, Italian ~menzionare~ and English ~mention~; through the shared root *~men-~ it is also kin to English ~mind~ and ~mental~.

Latin ~mentiō~ literally named the act of bringing something back to mind, and Spanish kept that thread: to ~mencionar~ is to summon a thing into speech, to call it to notice. Older and more colloquial is the inherited doublet ~mentar~ (“to name, to bring up”), alive in the blunt phrase ~mentar~ la madre. From the same root *~men-~ Spanish drew a broad cognitive vocabulary — ~mente~ (“mind”), ~mental~, ~memoria~, ~comentar~ (“to comment”) and ~mentor~ — and, by one account, even ~mentir~ (“to lie”), as though a falsehood were merely something thought up; but that last link is debated.
en.merecer:
From Latin ~merēscere~ (“to earn, deserve”), an inchoative form of ~merēre~ / ~mereō~ (“to earn, deserve, serve for pay”), traditionally traced to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)mer-~ (“to allot, assign, get a share”). Old Spanish had ~merecer~ already in the earliest texts. Cognate Romance forms include Portuguese ~merecer~ and Italian ~meritare~ (from the participle ~meritum~), while French kept the noun in ~mérite~. Through the participle ~meritum~ (“that which is earned”) English received the borrowings ~merit~ and ~meritorious~. The same PIE root surfaces in Ancient Greek ~μέρος~ (~méros~, “part, share”) and ~μοῖρα~ (~moîra~, “portion, fate”).

The semantic path is striking: from “to receive one's share” the verb slid to “to earn by service,” especially a soldier's pay (~stipendia merēre~ meant to serve a military campaign), and finally to “to be worthy of.” That is why the same root binds the ideas of a share, a wage, and desert. Modern Spanish ~merecer~ carries the moral weight — ~merecer la pena~ (“to be worth the trouble”) is an everyday phrase — and yields ~merecido~ (“deserved,” or as a noun “just deserts”), ~merecedor~ (“deserving”), ~mérito~, ~meritorio~ and ~emérito~ (“emeritus,” one who has earned release from duty). The Greek ~μοῖρα~, personified as the Fates, shows how deeply the notion of an allotted share ran.
en.meter:
From Old Spanish ~meter~, from Latin ~mittere~ (“to send, let go, release”). The deeper origin is uncertain; by one account ~mittere~ traces to Proto-Italic *~meitō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, remove”), an extension of the root *~mey-~ (“to change”). It is cognate with Portuguese ~meter~, Italian ~mettere~, and French ~mettre~.

In Latin ~mittere~ meant “to send,” but already in Vulgar Latin the sense drifted toward “to put, place, insert,” which is what Spanish ~meter~ means today — you ~meter~ a key into a lock or a hand into a pocket. The learned family stayed closer to the original “send”: ~admitir~, ~remitir~, ~prometer~, and ~someter~ all preserve the Latin verb. From its participle ~missus~ came a cluster of everyday nouns: ~misión~ (“a sending”), ~mensaje~ (“message”), and ~remesa~ (“remittance, shipment”). Even ~misa~ (“Mass”) belongs here, from ~missa~ in the dismissal formula that once closed the service. English ~mission~ and ~message~ are cousins from the same Latin verb.
en.mirar:
From Latin ~mīrārī~ (“to wonder at, to marvel”), a deponent verb formed on the adjective ~mīrus~ (“wonderful, astonishing”). ~mīrus~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~smeiros~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)mey-~ (“to smile, to be glad”) — so, remarkably, ~mirar~ is a blood relative of English ~smile~ and of Sanskrit ~sméra~ (“smiling”). Italian ~mirare~, French ~mirer~, and Portuguese ~mirar~ share the inheritance.

Here the surprise is a loss: Latin ~mīrārī~ was charged with astonishment, but everyday Spanish ~mirar~ drained the wonder away until it meant simply “to look at, to watch.” The amazement did not vanish, though — it took refuge in the learned offspring ~admirar~, ~milagro~ (from ~mīrāculum~), and ~maravilla~ (from ~mīrābilia~, “wonders”). English drew from the same well for ~admire~, ~miracle~, ~marvel~, and — through Vulgar Latin's “to look at” — ~mirror~, the glass you gaze into. Spanish adds ~mirada~, ~mirador~, and ~mira~.
en.modificar:
From Latin ~modificāre~ (“to limit, measure off, regulate”), a compound of ~modus~ (“measure, bound, manner”) and the combining form ~-ficāre~ (from ~facere~, “to make, do”) — literally “to make to measure.” ~modus~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~med-~ (“to measure, take appropriate measures”), while ~facere~ goes back to *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place, set”). Cognates of *~med-~ include Latin ~moderārī~ (“to keep within measure”), ~medērī~ (“to heal”), and Ancient Greek ~mḗdomai~ (“to be mindful of, plan”). The Romance verbs align: Italian ~modificare~, French ~modifier~, Portuguese ~modificar~.

The word literally means “to make within measure,” and it kept the sense of adjusting something to fit — trimming, qualifying, tempering rather than remaking. That measuring instinct fans out across Spanish: from ~modus~ come ~modo~ (“manner, mode”), ~molde~ (“mold”), ~moderar~ (“to moderate”), ~cómodo~ (“comfortable, fitting”), ~modelo~ (“model”) and ~módulo~ (“module”). The “healing” side of the root *~med-~ — measured, prudent care — surfaces in ~médico~ (“doctor”), ~medicina~ (“medicine”) and ~remedio~ (“remedy”). And from ~facere~, the second half, Spanish keeps a vast crop of ~-ficar~ verbs (~verificar~, ~clarificar~, ~justificar~) all meaning “to make thus.”
en.montar:
From Vulgar Latin *~montāre~ (“to climb a mountain”), a verb built on Latin ~mōns~ (genitive ~montis~, “mountain”), from Proto-Italic *~monts~, from Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to project, jut out”) — the same root that yielded Latin ~ēminēre~ (“to stand out”) and ~prōminēre~ (“to project”). Cognate with Italian ~montare~, French ~monter~ and Portuguese ~montar~, and the source of English ~mount~ and ~amount~.

The image is a hill: to ~montar~ was first “to go up,” and from climbing a slope the verb spread to mounting a horse, then to assembling or “setting up” anything — a machine, a company, a play. English ~amount~ took the same path through Old French ~amonter~, “to go up (in total).” From ~mōns~ Spanish also keeps ~monte~, ~montaña~, ~montón~ and ~montura~.
en.morir:
From Vulgar Latin *~morīre~, a regularization of Classical Latin ~morī~ (“to die,” a deponent verb), from Proto-Indo-European *~mer-~ (“to die”). Cognate with Italian ~morire~, French ~mourir~ and Portuguese ~morrer~; through the root, with Sanskrit ~mṛtyú~ (“death”), Ancient Greek ~brotós~ (“mortal”) and — via Germanic — English ~murder~.

Classical ~morī~ was deponent (passive in form, active in meaning); Vulgar Latin recast it as an ordinary verb *~morīre~, the ancestor of every Romance form. From the participle ~mortuus~ and the noun ~mors~ (stem ~mort-~) came Spanish ~muerte~, ~muerto~, ~mortal~, ~moribundo~ and ~amortiguar~. A vivid relic survives in English ~mortgage~ — literally a “dead pledge” — while at the opposite pole Greek ~ambrosía~ (“the immortals’ food,” ~a-~ “not” + a form of *~mer-~) grows from the very same root.
en.mostrar:
From Latin ~mōnstrāre~ (“to show, point out”), a verb from the noun ~mōnstrum~ (“portent, omen, marvel”), itself derived from ~monēre~ (“to warn, remind, advise”), from Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to think”). Cognate with Italian ~mostrare~, French ~montrer~, and Portuguese ~mostrar~; through the same Latin family come English ~muster~ (borrowed via Old French), ~monster~, and ~demonstrate~.

The chain hides a striking image: a ~mōnstrum~ was originally a divine sign — something shown by the gods to warn mortals — so “to show” and “to warn” were once the same gesture. Latin drained the ominous charge, leaving ~mōnstrāre~ as the neutral “to point out,” while the noun kept the dread and became English ~monster~. Old Spanish ~mostrar~ inherited the plain sense of displaying and indicating. From the same root Spanish keeps ~muestra~ (“sample, sign”), ~demostrar~ (“to prove”), ~amonestar~ (“to admonish,” preserving the older warning sense), and the noun ~monstruo~, which carries the ancient shiver the verb long ago shed.
en.mover:
From Latin ~movēre~ (“to move, set in motion”), from Proto-Italic *~moweō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~mewh₁-~ (“to move, push away”). It is cognate with Italian ~muovere~, French ~mouvoir~ and Portuguese ~mover~, and — through the same root — with English ~move~, borrowed through Anglo-Norman, and ~motion~.

The core sense “to change position” stayed remarkably stable from Latin into Spanish, yet the verb grew figurative branches: one can ~mover~ a chess piece or ~mover~ an audience to tears. The Latin participle ~mōtus~ supplied a second, learned stem that seeded a broad family — ~movimiento~, ~móvil~, ~motor~, ~motivo~ and ~emoción~ (literally “a moving-out” of feeling) — beside the prefixed inheritances ~remover~, ~conmover~ and ~promover~. From the same source flow the everyday ~automóvil~ and ~mueble~ (“a piece of furniture,” that is, a movable good, opposed to ~inmueble~, “real estate”).
en.nacer:
From Old Spanish ~nascer~, from Vulgar Latin *~nāscere~ (a reshaping of the deponent), from Latin ~nāscī~ (“to be born”), earlier ~gnāscī~, from Proto-Italic *~gnāskōr~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to beget, give birth”). The initial ~gn-~ regularly simplified to ~n-~. Cognates run through Romance — Italian ~nascere~, French ~naître~, Portuguese ~nascer~ — and, through the root, Latin ~genus~ and ~gignō~ (“to beget”) and inherited English ~kin~.

The ~-sc-~ of ~nāscī~ is an inchoative suffix marking an action just beginning, so the verb frames birth as a coming-into-being in progress. From the same root *~ǵenh₁-~ Spanish drew a vast family: think of ~Navidad~, which descends from Latin ~nātīvitās~ (“birth” — the Nativity), and of ~nación~ (a people “born” together), ~naturaleza~, ~género~, and ~gente~. To be reborn is ~renacer~, the verb behind the very idea of a Renaissance.
en.necesitar:
From Latin ~necessitās~ (accusative ~necessitātem~, “necessity, unavoidability”), an abstract noun built on ~necesse~ (“necessary, inevitable”). ~necesse~ is commonly analyzed as ~ne-~ (“not”) plus ~cessus~, the past participle of ~cēdere~ (“to yield, give way”) — so its literal sense is that from which there is no yielding, though the exact formation is debated. Spanish built the verb ~necesitar~ on the inherited noun ~necesidad~ (from ~necessitātem~). It is cognate with Italian ~necessitare~, and shares its root family with French ~nécessité~, Portuguese ~necessidade~, and English ~necessity~ and ~necessary~, all drawn from the same Latin source.

In classical Latin the idea lived mostly in the impersonal phrase ~necesse est~ (“it is necessary”), so need entered Romance first as a state of affairs rather than an action; Spanish only later shaped it into a plain transitive verb. If the ~ne-~ + ~cēdere~ etymology holds, “to need” is at bottom “to have no room to give way” — necessity as a door that will not open. From the same family Spanish keeps the noun ~necesidad~, the adjective ~necesario~, and the adverb ~necesariamente~, a tidy cluster all pointing back to what cannot be avoided.
en.negar:
From Latin ~negāre~ (“to say no, to deny, to refuse”). The first element is the ancient Proto-Indo-European negator *~ne~ (“not”), the same “no” that runs through half the languages of Europe; the second element is less certain, often connected to a root meaning “to say,” so that ~negāre~ would be, literally, “to say-not.” It gave Italian ~negare~, Portuguese ~negar~, and French ~nier~, and — through Latin ~dēnegāre~ and ~negāre~ — English ~deny~, ~negate~, and ~renege~.

The sense has held remarkably steady: ~negāre~ meant “to deny,” and so does ~negar~ two thousand years later. Its most delightful descendant hides its “no” in plain sight — Latin ~negōtium~ (“business”) is literally ~nec~ (“not”) plus ~ōtium~ (“leisure, rest”): business is the negation of leisure. From it came Spanish ~negocio~ (“business”) and English ~negotiate~. The rest of the family is more transparent: ~negativo~ (“negative”), ~negación~ (“denial”), ~denegar~ (“to refuse”), ~renegar~ (“to renounce”), ~renegado~ (“renegade”), and ~abnegación~ (“self-denial”), each carrying that primordial *~ne~ at its heart.
en.nombrar:
From Latin ~nōmināre~ (“to name, to call by name”), a verb built on ~nōmen~ (“name”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁nómn̥~ (“name”). The root is one of the best preserved in the family: it is cognate with English ~name~, German ~Name~, Ancient Greek ~ὄνομα~ (“name”), and Sanskrit ~nā́man~, as well as the Latin-derived English ~nominate~ and ~noun~.

Where Latin ~nōmināre~ meant simply “to utter the name of,” Spanish ~nombrar~ widened toward “to appoint” — to name someone to an office — a sense already latent in Roman administrative usage. The noun ~nombre~ descends directly from ~nōmen~. From the same root Spanish gathered a rich family: ~nómina~ (originally a “list of names,” now a payroll), ~nominar~, ~denominar~, ~renombre~ (“renown”), ~pronombre~, and ~nomenclatura~.
en.notar:
From Latin ~notāre~ (“to mark, jot down, observe”), from ~nota~ (“mark, sign, written note, letter or character”). The deeper origin of ~nota~ is debated: it is often linked to ~nōscere~ (“to come to know”), from earlier ~gnōscere~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know”) — a ~nota~ being a means of recognition — but the connection is not certain and is best offered with caution. Cognate with Italian ~notare~, French ~noter~ and Portuguese ~notar~, and with English ~note~ and ~notice~.

In Rome ~nota~ covered the mark that identifies a thing, the shorthand signs of the clerk, and the musical note. Spanish ~notar~ kept the perceptual core — “to notice, observe, mark” — while the noun ~nota~ split into everyday senses: a written note, a grade at school, a musical note. The family is large and useful: ~notable~ (“notable”), ~notario~ (a “notary,” literally one who takes notes), ~anotar~ (“to jot down”) and ~notorio~ (“well-known”).
en.obligar:
From Latin ~obligāre~ (“to bind, to tie up, to bind by oath or duty”), a compound of ~ob-~ (“to, toward, against”) and ~ligāre~ (“to bind, to tie”). ~ligāre~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~leyǵ-~ (“to bind”). The verb runs straight through Romance — Italian ~obbligare~, French ~obliger~, Portuguese ~obrigar~ — and through Latin loans it links to English ~oblige~, ~obligate~, ~ligament~, and ~ally~.

The idea is physical bondage made moral: to ~obligar~ is to “bind toward” a duty, to tie someone to an obligation as with a rope. Portuguese kept the image alive in everyday courtesy — ~obrigado~, the ordinary word for “thank you,” means literally “[I am] obliged.” From ~ligāre~ Spanish also draws ~ligar~ (“to tie, to bind”), ~ligamento~, ~liga~ (“league, garter”), ~aliar~ (“to ally”), and ~obligación~. And ~ligāre~ sits at the center of a famous etymological dispute: the origin of ~religión~.
