Lactantius derived it from ~religāre~ (“to bind fast” — religion as the bond between people and gods), while Cicero had derived it instead from ~relegere~ (“to read over again, to go through carefully”). The two accounts have never been settled, and the word's true origin remains genuinely uncertain.
en.observar:
From Latin ~observāre~ (“to watch over, attend to, heed”), formed from ~ob-~ (“towards, in front of”) and ~servāre~ (“to keep, guard, watch over”). ~Servāre~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~serwāō~ and to a Proto-Indo-European root *~ser-~ (“to protect, watch over”), also seen in Avestan ~haraiti~ (“heeds, protects”). Spanish ~observar~ is cognate with Italian ~osservare~, French ~observer~, Portuguese ~observar~ and English ~observe~. Note that ~servāre~ (“to guard”) is kept distinct by scholars from ~servīre~ (“to serve”), which springs instead from ~servus~ (“slave”).

The core image is guarding: to ~observar~ was first to keep something safe by watching it, and from that vigilant watching grew both meanings the verb carries today — to look attentively (to observe a phenomenon) and to comply, to keep (to observe a rule or a holiday). Latin ~servāre~ “to keep” seeded a productive Spanish family: ~conservar~ (“to conserve”), ~reservar~ (“to reserve”), ~preservar~ (“to preserve”) and the nouns ~observación~ and ~observatorio~. Each still turns on the idea of holding something in careful view — whether a law kept, a resource saved, or a star watched through the night.
en.obtener:
Spanish ~obtener~ comes from Latin ~obtinēre~ (“to hold onto, hold fast, possess”), formed from the prefix ~ob-~ (here “toward, against”) and ~tenēre~ (“to hold”). Because Spanish inherited ~tenēre~ as the everyday verb ~tener~, the compound was reshaped on that model rather than evolving purely by sound law. ~tenēre~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”), which also lies, distantly, behind English ~thin~. Romance cognates include French ~obtenir~, Italian ~ottenere~ and Portuguese ~obter~.

The sense moved naturally from physically holding something to gaining and securing it — what you obtain is what you get a grip on. The root *~ten-~ (a hand stretched to hold) is one of the most productive in Spanish, giving the whole ~tener~ family: ~contener~ (“to contain”), ~mantener~ (“to maintain”), ~retener~ (“to retain”) and ~detener~ (“to stop, detain”), plus ~teniente~ (“lieutenant,” a place-holder) and the adjective ~tenaz~ (“tenacious”).
en.ocupar:
From Latin ~occupāre~ (“to seize, take possession of, occupy”), a compound of ~ob-~ (“over, towards”) and ~capere~ (“to take, seize, grasp”); within the compound ~capere~'s vowel weakened to the ~-cupāre~ seen here. The Proto-Indo-European root is *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp, seize”). Spanish ~ocupar~ is cognate with Italian ~occupare~, French ~occuper~, Portuguese ~ocupar~ and English ~occupy~; through *~keh₂p-~ it also belongs with English ~capture~ and ~captive~ and the wider Latin ~capere~ family.

To ~ocupar~ was first to lay hold of something — a town, a post, a stretch of land — and from that grasping came the milder senses of filling a space and taking up time, so that a chair, a job, or an afternoon can all be “occupied.” A memorable surprise lurks in the family tree: by the standard account English ~have~ is not related to Latin ~habēre~ at all, but to ~capere~, both from *~keh₂p-~ — the two verbs merely look alike. From ~capere~ Spanish inherited ~caber~ (“to fit”), ~captar~, ~capturar~, ~cazar~ (“to hunt”) and, through its compounds, ~recibir~, ~concebir~ and ~ocupación~.
en.ocurrir:
From Latin ~occurrere~ (“to run to meet, to present itself”), an assimilated compound of ~ob-~ (“toward, to meet”) and ~currere~ (“to run”). ~currere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~korzō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱers-~ (“to run”). The root surfaces in English ~car~ (through Latin ~carrus~) and, by a disputed account, in English ~horse~; the verb itself continues as Italian ~occorrere~ and Portuguese ~ocorrer~.

The picture is vivid: something “runs up to meet” you, and so it “happens” or “occurs.” Spanish keeps that liveliness in the reflexive ~ocurrírsele~ algo a alguien — an idea literally runs up to a person's mind, that is, “it occurs to them.” The event sense and the mental sense have coexisted since Latin. The running-root spread widely in Spanish: ~correr~, ~corriente~, ~carrera~, ~recorrer~, ~concurrir~, ~discurrir~, ~socorrer~, and the school word ~currículo~ (from ~currículum~, “a course, a running”).
en.ofrecer:
From Old Spanish ~ofrecer~ (also ~ofrir~), from a Vulgar Latin inchoative *~offerēscere~ reshaping Latin ~offerre~ (“to present, offer”), a compound of ~ob-~ (“toward, before”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, bear”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰer-~ (“to bear, carry”). Cognate with Italian ~offrire~, French ~offrir~, and Portuguese ~oferecer~, and — through ~ferre~ and its root — with English ~bear~ and the Latin borrowings ~offer~ and ~transfer~.

The extra syllable in ~ofrecer~ comes from the Latin inchoative suffix ~-ēscere~, which marked the beginning of an action and pulled the verb into the large Spanish ~-ecer~ class alongside ~parecer~, ~crecer~, and ~conocer~. Semantically the word kept ~offerre~'s literal image of “carrying something before” another — to present a gift, a price, resistance, or oneself. Its religious weight survives in ~ofrenda~ (“offering, oblation”) and the participle-noun ~oferta~ (“offer, bargain”), while the shared root ~ferre~ radiates through ~conferir~, ~preferir~, ~referir~, and ~transferir~, and ~ofrecer~ itself yields ~ofrecimiento~ (“offer, offering”).
en.olvidar:
From Vulgar Latin ~oblītāre~, a verb built on the participial stem of Latin ~oblīvīscī~ (“to forget”). The origin of ~oblīvīscī~ is uncertain; by one proposed account it is ~ob-~ plus the root of ~lēvis~ (“smooth”), which would make its literal sense something like “to smooth away” or “erase from the mind” — but this is speculation, not settled fact. Old Spanish had ~oblidar~ (used by Berceo) and ~olbidar~; the modern form is ~olvidar~. Cognate with French ~oublier~ and Catalan ~oblidar~.

Whatever its deepest root, the Latin verb clearly meant losing something from memory, and Spanish kept exactly that. From the same ~oblīvīscī~ English inherited ~oblivion~ and ~oblivious~, the state and the disposition of forgetting. Within Spanish the root yielded the noun ~olvido~ (“forgetting, oblivion”), the adjective ~olvidadizo~ (“forgetful”), and the prized ~inolvidable~ (“unforgettable”).
en.operar:
From Latin ~operārī~ (“to work, labor, be busy”), a deponent verb built on ~opus~ (genitive ~operis~, “work, labor, a work”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃ep-~ (“to work, produce, to have abundance”). The same noun ~opus~ gave the plural ~opera~, which Spanish and English both borrowed as ~ópera~ / ~opera~ (musical “works”). Cognate Romance forms include Italian ~operare~, French ~opérer~ and Portuguese ~operar~; through the PIE root ~opus~ is kin to Latin ~ops~ (“wealth, resources”), whence Latin ~opulentus~ and Spanish ~opulento~, and to Sanskrit ~ápas~ (“work”).

Latin ~operārī~ meant simply to do work, and Spanish ~operar~ fans out from there: to operate a machine, to bring about an effect (~operar un cambio~), a bank or company that ~opera~ in a market, and — in medicine — to perform surgery, ~operar a un paciente~. That surgical sense, shared with English ~operate~, treats the surgeon's intervention as skilled labor upon the body. The hereditary, popular descendant of ~opera~ is Spanish ~obra~ (“work, deed, building site”), with its verb ~obrar~ (“to act, to work”); learned relatives include ~operación~, ~operario~ (“laborer”), ~opereta~, ~cooperar~ (“to work together”) and ~maniobra~ (“maneuver,” literally hand-work).
en.oponer:
From Latin ~oppōnere~ (“to set against, place before, oppose”), a compound of ~ob-~ (“against, facing”) and ~pōnere~ (“to put, place”). ~pōnere~ is itself, by surface analysis, ~po-~ (“off, away”) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, leave”), and passes through Old Latin ~posnō~ to Proto-Italic; its ~po-~ element goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂epó~ (“off, away”), the same particle behind English ~of~ and ~off~. From ~oppōnere~ descend Italian ~opporre~, Portuguese ~opor~, and French ~opposer~, while the whole ~pōnere~ clan gave the international -pose words: componer, exponer, depositar, proponer.

In Latin the participle was ~oppositus~, and the ~pōnere~/~positus~ split runs right through Spanish: the verb keeps the ~pon-~ stem (~oponer~, ~poner~, ~componer~, ~exponer~) while the nominal forms take ~posición~, ~oposición~, ~opuesto~. To oppose is literally to “place one thing over against another,” a spatial metaphor that hardened into the modern sense of resistance and rivalry. Cousins in the same family are legion: ~puesto~, ~posar~, ~apostar~, ~depósito~, ~propósito~, and the everyday ~oposición~ that names Spain’s competitive civil-service exams.
en.optar:
From Latin ~optāre~ (“to choose, to wish, to desire”), a verb whose deeper origin is uncertain. It appears to continue a Proto-Italic frequentative *~opetāō~ (from *~opeō~), otherwise preserved only in Umbrian ~upetu~, and no secure Proto-Indo-European root has been established for it. Alongside Spanish stand Italian ~optare~ and Portuguese ~optar~, together with the learned family that ~optāre~ generated within Latin itself.

Latin ~optāre~ carried both “to choose” and “to wish,” and Spanish ~optar~ keeps mainly the first — to opt for one path among several. The related noun ~optiō~ (“a choosing, a free choice”) gave Spanish ~opción~, while the compound ~adoptāre~ (“to choose to oneself”) gave ~adoptar~ — literally to choose a child into one’s family. Other members are the grammatical ~optativo~ (the “wishing” mood) and ~cooptar~ (to choose someone onto a body by the votes of its own members). Because the root itself is so obscure, here is a family whose branches are far clearer than its trunk.
en.ordenar:
From Latin ~ōrdināre~ (“to arrange, set in order, appoint”), a verb built on ~ōrdō~ (genitive ~ōrdinis~, “row, rank, order”), of uncertain deeper origin but perhaps connected with ~ōrdīrī~ (“to lay the warp, begin weaving”). Cognate with Italian ~ordinare~, French ~ordonner~, and Portuguese ~ordenar~; English took the same word through ~ordain~ and ~order~.

~ōrdō~ first named a concrete row — one traditional account traces it to the ordered threads of the warp on a loom — and from “row, rank” came “arrangement” and “command” (an order both organizes and instructs). Spanish ~ordenar~ carries all these: to put in order, to give an order, and to ordain a priest. The same ~ōrdō~ gave ~orden~ (“order”), ~ordenador~ (“computer,” in Spain), ~coordinar~, ~subordinar~, and ~ordinario~; through Latin ~ōrnāre~, a syncopated form of ~ōrdināre~, come ~adornar~ and ~ornamento~.
en.organizar:
From Medieval Latin ~organizāre~ (“to furnish with organs, to arrange into a working whole”), from Latin ~organum~ (“instrument, tool, organ”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~órganon~ (ὄργανον, “tool, instrument”). ~órganon~ derives from ~érgon~ (“work, deed”) and the Proto-Indo-European *~werǵ-~ (“to do, to work”). That root is shared, remarkably, with English ~work~ and German ~Werk~. Spanish took ~organizar~ through learned channels. Cognate with Italian ~organizzare~ and French ~organiser~.

The chain of sense is elegant: an ~órganon~ was a tool for doing work, then a bodily “instrument” (an organ), and a body is many organs cooperating — so to ~organizar~ is to make separate parts function together like the organs of a living whole. The word lived in Spanish first in that biological and musical sense (the ~órgano~, the church instrument of many pipes) before it broadened to committees and revolutions. From the same *~werǵ-~ come ~órgano~, ~organismo~, ~orgía~ (Greek rites, literally “workings”), ~cirugía~ (“hand-work”), and ~energía~.
en.orientar:
From ~oriente~ (“the East”), from Latin ~oriēns~ (“rising”), the present participle of ~orīrī~ (“to rise, to come forth”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃er-~ (“to rise, to move, to stir”). The East is simply where the sun rises. It is cognate, through that root, with Latin ~orīgō~ (“origin, source”) and Ancient Greek ~ὄρνυμι~ (“to rouse, to set in motion”); English ~origin~ and ~orient~ are Latin-borrowed kin.

To ~orientar~ meant first, quite literally, to align something toward the East — a habit visible in medieval churches built to face the sunrise and in old maps drawn with the East, ~oriente~, at the top; only later did it soften into “to guide, to position.” Its opposite, ~desorientar~ (“to disorient”), is the loss of that bearing. From the same rising-root come ~origen~, ~originar~, ~orto~ (“sunrise, the rising of a star”), and even ~aborto~ (“miscarriage”), from Latin ~aborīrī~ — to “rise away,” to fail to come forth.
en.otorgar:
From Vulgar Latin *~auctōricāre~ (“to authorize, vouch for, endorse”), from Latin ~auctor~ (“author, originator, one who vouches”), from ~augēre~ (“to increase, augment”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ewg-~ (“to increase, grow”). The road to Spanish ran through monophthongization of ~au~, syncope, and the voicing of the inner consonant, turning *~auctōricāre~ into ~otorgar~. It is cognate with Old French ~otreier~ (Modern French ~octroyer~, “to grant”) and Occitan ~autrejar~; through ~augēre~ it is kin to English ~author~, ~augment~, and ~auction~, and to the Germanic ~wax~ (“to grow”).

An ~auctor~ was one who backs or guarantees, so *~auctōricāre~ meant to give one's backing — and Spanish ~otorgar~ still means to grant, bestow, or consent, keeping a legal flavor (one ~otorgar~ a will or a power of attorney). The patrimonial ~otorgar~ has a learned twin, ~autorizar~ (from Medieval Latin ~auctorizāre~), and shares the family with ~auge~, ~aumentar~, ~augusto~, and ~autoridad~ — all growing from the idea of increase.
en.oír:
From Latin ~audīre~ (“to hear”), from Proto-Italic *~awizdiō~, generally analyzed as a compound of a Proto-Indo-European element *~h₂ewis-~ (“clearly, manifestly”) and the verbal root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to render”) — literally “to render clear to the senses.” It is cognate with Ancient Greek ~αἰσθάνομαι~ (“to perceive”) and Sanskrit ~āvís~ (“manifestly”), and its Romance siblings include Italian ~udire~ and Portuguese ~ouvir~.

The intervocalic Latin d fell away as the word passed into Old Spanish, reducing four syllables to the terse modern ~oír~; the same erosion shaped French ~ouïr~, once the ordinary verb “to hear” and now archaic. A vivid relative is ~obedecer~ (“to obey”), from Latin ~oboedīre~ — ~ob-~ (“toward”) plus ~audīre~ — literally “to lend one's ear toward” someone. From the same Latin verb Spanish also draws ~audición~, ~auditorio~, ~audible~, ~oyente~, and the borrowing ~audio~.
en.pagar:
Spanish ~pagar~ comes from Late Latin ~pācāre~ (“to pacify, appease, satisfy”), a verb on ~pāx~ (“peace”). ~pāx~ goes back, through Proto-Italic *~pāks~, to Proto-Indo-European *~peh₂ḱ-~ (“to fasten, join”) — peace conceived as the binding-together of parties — a root shared with Latin ~pangere~ (“to fix, fasten”) and ~pacīscī~ (“to make a pact”). Its Romance reflexes include French ~payer~, Portuguese ~pagar~, Italian ~pagare~, and Catalan ~pagar~; English ~pay~ was borrowed from Old French ~paiier~.

The meaning traveled a very human road: to ~pācāre~ a creditor was to “appease” him, and appeasing a creditor means handing over money — so “pacify” slid into “pay.” The old sense still peeks through: someone ~pagado de sí mismo~ is “pleased with himself,” satisfied rather than paid. From ~pāx~ Spanish gathered ~paz~ (“peace”), ~pago~ (“payment”), ~pagador~, ~pacífico~, ~pacto~, and ~apaciguar~ (“to appease”). Most striking is ~apagar~ (“to switch off, extinguish”), from Vulgar Latin *~appācāre~: to quiet a flame is, quite literally, to make peace with it.
en.parar:
From Latin ~parāre~ (“to prepare, make ready”), from Proto-Italic *~parō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to grant, provide”). Cognate with Italian ~parare~, Portuguese ~parar~, and French ~parer~ (“to adorn, parry”); from the same Latin verb English drew ~prepare~ and ~apparatus~.

The Latin verb meant “to prepare, arrange,” and in Ibero-Romance it drifted from readying something toward halting and coming to rest — perhaps by way of “to set in position, hold in place.” The sources record the shift but do not fully explain it, so the intermediate step is best offered as a plausible bridge rather than a settled fact. That is why modern Spanish uses the verb for stopping a bus, warding off a blow, and ending up somewhere. The noun ~paro~ carries this to its conclusion — a work stoppage, unemployment, even a cardiac arrest — and ~parada~ names a bus stop or a military parade. From the same Latin verb Spanish also built ~preparar~, ~reparar~, ~amparar~ (“to shelter”), and the noun ~aparato~ (“apparatus, device”).
en.parecer:
From Old Spanish ~pareçer~, from Vulgar Latin *~parēscere~, an inchoative formed on Latin ~pārēre~ (“to appear, become visible, show oneself”). The inchoative suffix ~-ēscere~ marked a coming-into-view, which the ~-ecer~ ending of Spanish still carries. Cognate with Italian ~parere~, French ~paraître~, Portuguese ~parecer~, and Catalan ~parèixer~; through Latin ~appārēre~ English is kin by way of ~appear~ and ~apparent~.

Latin ~pārēre~ meant “to come into sight”; the inchoative *~parēscere~ stressed the moment of appearing, and from “to appear” Spanish ~parecer~ slid naturally into “to seem” — for what appears is not always what is. Reflexive ~parecerse~ took the further step to “to resemble,” and the noun use in ~el parecer~ means an “opinion,” literally how a thing appears to someone. The prefixed ~aparecer~ (“to appear”) and ~desaparecer~ (“to disappear”) stayed closer to the root sense, while ~comparecer~ (“to appear in court”) narrowed it to legal presence. From the same base come ~aparición~, ~apariencia~, ~parecido~, and ~aparente~.
en.parir:
From Latin ~parere~ (also ~parĕre~, “to give birth, to bring forth, to produce”), from Proto-Italic *~parjō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to bring forth, to grant, to allot”). The root shows up in Ancient Greek ~époron~ (“I gave, granted”), Sanskrit ~pṛṇā́ti~ (“grants, bestows”), and — through the Latin agent noun ~parēns~ — in English ~parent~. Sisters of ~parere~ are Italian ~parire~ and Portuguese ~parir~.

The Latin verb meant productive bringing-forth of every kind, but Spanish narrowed ~parir~ almost entirely to animal and human birth, giving it a blunt, earthy register beside the polite ~dar a luz~ (“to give to the light”). A vivid relative hides in ~víbora~ (“viper”): Latin ~vīpera~ was understood as ~vīvus~ + ~parere~, “the one that bears its young alive” — an ancient (if not strictly accurate) belief about the snake. Other kin include ~parto~ (“childbirth”), ~parturienta~, ~posparto~, and the -parous words ~vivíparo~ and ~ovíparo~. Note that ~parere~ (“give birth”) is a different verb from ~parāre~ (“prepare”), which fathered ~preparar~ and ~reparar~.
en.participar:
From Latin ~participāre~ (“to share, to partake”), from the adjective ~particeps~ (“sharing, partaking”), a compound of ~pars~ (“part”) and ~capere~ (“to take, to seize”) — literally “taking a part.” ~capere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp”). Cognate with French ~participer~, Italian ~partecipare~, and English ~participate~ and ~participle~.

The image behind the word is delightfully literal: to participate is to take your portion of something shared. Latin ~particeps~ was originally an everyday adjective for anyone who had a share in an affair. From ~pars~ Spanish drew a large family — ~parte~, ~partícipe~, ~participio~ (the grammatical “participle,” which likewise “shares” properties of verb and adjective), and ~partido~ (“party, match”). The other half, ~capere~, is even more prolific, giving ~caber~ (“to fit”), ~captar~, and even ~cazar~ (“to hunt,” i.e., to catch). To take part, in short, is to seize your slice.
en.partir:
Spanish ~partir~ descends from Latin ~partīre~ (also deponent ~partīrī~, “to divide, to share out”), a verb built on the noun ~pars~ (stem ~partis~, “a part, a share”). The deeper prehistory of ~pars~ is debated: it is usually linked with Latin ~pār~ (“equal”), ~portiō~ (“portion”) and ~parāre~ (“to make ready”), but the Proto-Indo-European root behind them is disputed and no single reconstruction is secure. Romance cognates are plentiful — French ~partir~, Italian ~partire~, Portuguese ~partir~ — and English ~part~ was borrowed from the same Latin stock.

~partir~ still means both “to split” and “to share,” but it also took on the sense “to depart” — to part from company, to set out (~partir de viaje~, “to leave on a trip”); French carried that branch all the way, so its ~partir~ means simply “to leave.” The noun ~pars~ underlies a broad Spanish family: ~parte~ (“part”), ~partido~ (“party; match”), ~partícula~ (“particle”), ~repartir~ (“to distribute”), ~compartir~ (“to share”) and the musical ~partitura~ (“score”).
en.pasar:
From Late Latin ~passāre~, a frequentative of Latin ~passus~ (“a step, a pace”), originally the past participle of ~pandere~ (“to spread out, to stretch”), from Proto-Indo-European *~peth₂-~ (“to spread”). Cognate with Italian ~passare~, French ~passer~, and Portuguese ~passar~; English ~pass~ entered through Old French rather than directly from Latin.

The image at the root is bodily: a ~passus~ was the stretch of the legs in a single stride, and by extension the Roman unit of distance measured by that stride. From “to take a step” the verb widened to “to move past, to cross, to go through,” and then to the whole sweep of senses Spanish now gives it — to happen (« ¿qué pasa? »), to spend time, to pass an exam, to hand something over. The same family seeded ~paso~ (“step”), ~pasaje~ (“passage, fare”), ~pasaporte~ (literally a warrant to ~pasar~ a port or gate), ~paseo~ (“a stroll”), and the ubiquitous ~pasado~ (“the past; passed”).
en.pedir:
From Latin ~petere~ (“to make for, to seek, to ask, to aim at, even to attack”), from Proto-Indo-European *~peth₂-~ (“to fly, to rush”). The root’s flight-sense shows plainly in its cognates: Greek ~pétomai~ (“I fly”) and ~píptō~ (“I fall”), Sanskrit ~pátati~ (“flies, falls”), and — through Germanic — English ~feather~, literally “the flying thing.” In Romance, Portuguese ~pedir~ is the direct sibling; Italian and French chose other verbs for “to ask.”

The semantic heart is motion toward a target: ~petere~ first meant to rush at or make for something, which is why the one verb could mean both “to attack” and “to request” — to ask is to launch yourself at what you want. Spanish wore the sound down to the humble ~pedir~, but the vigorous original survives in a crowd of learned relatives: ~petición~ (“petition, request”), ~competir~ (“to compete,” to seek alongside), ~apetito~ (“appetite,” a seeking-toward), ~ímpetu~ (“impetus, a rushing upon”), ~repetir~ (“to seek again”), and ~perpetuo~ (“continually rushing onward”). English shares the set through ~petition~, ~compete~, ~appetite~, and ~impetus~.
en.pensar:
From Old Spanish ~pensar~, from Latin ~pēnsāre~ (“to weigh, ponder”), the frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to hang”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to pull, stretch”). Cognate with Italian ~pensare~, French ~penser~, and Portuguese ~pensar~, and — through the same stem — with English ~pensive~, ~ponder~, and ~pension~; Spanish keeps a doublet in ~pesar~ (“to weigh; to grieve”).

The heart of this word is a metaphor so old it feels literal: to think is to weigh one thing against another. Latin ~pēnsāre~ meant to weigh out repeatedly, hence to ponder, to balance one option against the next — and Spanish ~pensar~ still does exactly that. The same ~pēnsāre~ took a different turn in French ~panser~ (“to dress a wound, tend a horse”), from the sense “to attend to,” a nice reminder of how far one root can wander. From it Spanish drew ~pensamiento~ (“thought”), ~pensador~ (“thinker”), ~pensativo~ (“pensive”), and ~pensión~ (“pension”), while the popular doublet ~pesar~ gave the noun ~peso~ (“weight; the currency”).
en.percibir:
From Latin ~percipere~ (“to seize, take in, perceive”), a compound of ~per-~ (“thoroughly”) and ~capere~ (“to take, grasp”), from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp”). It is cognate with Italian ~percepire~, French ~percevoir~ and Portuguese ~perceber~, and — through the same ~capere~ — with English ~capture~ and ~capable~.

Latin ~percipere~ meant literally “to take hold of thoroughly,” and that physical grasping was extended to the mind: to seize something with the senses or the intellect is to perceive it. Spanish kept both threads — one perceives a sound and also perceives (collects) a salary, ~percibir~ un sueldo. The same root *~keh₂p-~ seeded a large family in Spanish, among them ~recibir~, ~concebir~, ~capaz~, ~captar~ and ~caber~.
en.perder:
From Latin ~perdere~ (“to lose, to ruin, to squander”), a compound of the prefix ~per-~ (here “thoroughly, to destruction”) and an element ~-dere~. That second element is traditionally identified with ~dare~ (“to give,” from Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~), which would make ~perdere~ a “giving away through and through”; but many etymologists now trace the ~-dere~ of such compounds instead to PIE *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to place”), and the point remains debated. Either way the Romance descent is uniform: Italian ~perdere~, French ~perdre~, Portuguese ~perder~, and Romanian ~pierde~.

Whatever the deep root, the Latin sense was strong — not mild misplacement but thorough undoing: ~perdere~ could mean to destroy, to bring to ruin, as well as to lose. Spanish softened it to everyday “losing,” yet the darker charge survives in ~perdición~ (“perdition, ruin”) and in phrases like ~echar a perder~ (“to spoil, to wreck”). If the older ~dare~ analysis is right, to lose is to “give something away completely,” an oddly generous image for misfortune; if the *~dʰeh₁-~ analysis is right, it is rather to “put something clean out of reach.” From the verb Spanish keeps ~pérdida~ (“loss”), ~perdido~ (“lost”), and ~perdición~.
en.permanecer:
From Latin ~permanēre~ (“to remain, to hold out to the end”), from ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”) + ~manēre~ (“to stay, to remain”); Spanish reshaped it with the inchoative suffix ~-ecer~. ~manēre~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to stay, to remain, to abide”). Cognate with Italian ~permanere~ and Portuguese ~permanecer~, and — through ~manēre~ — with English ~permanent~, ~remain~ (from Latin ~remanēre~), and ~mansion~; French ~permanent~ shares the same source.

The prefix ~per-~ adds thoroughness — to remain not just briefly but all the way through — so ~permanecer~ is a more emphatic “to stay” than plain quedarse. The bare root ~manēre~ meant simply “to stay,” and its participle ~mansiō~ (“a staying, a lodging, a stopping-place on a journey”) traveled far: it became French ~maison~ (“house”) and English ~mansion~. Spanish drew a rich crop from the same root: ~permanente~ (“permanent”), ~mansión~ (“mansion”), ~remanente~ (“remainder”), ~inmanente~ (“immanent”), and even ~menaje~ (“household goods”), which reached Spanish through Old French ~ménage~ from Vulgar Latin *~mansionaticum~ — the belongings of a household.
en.permitir:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~permittere~ (“to let through, give up, allow”), from ~per-~ (“through”) plus ~mittere~ (“to send, let go, release”); ~mittere~ is of uncertain further origin, with no secure Proto-Indo-European etymology. Cognate with Italian ~permettere~, French ~permettre~, and Portuguese ~permitir~, and — through the same Latin verb — with English ~permit~. The base ~mittere~ underlies a huge Romance and English family.

In Latin ~mittere~ first meant “to send,” and ~permittere~ literally “to send through” — to let something pass — from which grew the idea of granting passage, yielding, and finally “allowing.” Because Spanish took ~permitir~ from written Latin rather than through gradual sound-change, it kept the Latin shape almost intact, unlike its inherited cousin ~meter~ (“to put in”), which descends from the very same ~mittere~ by the popular route. That double inheritance — learned and popular — makes ~mittere~ one of the most productive Latin verbs in Spanish: ~permiso~, ~mensaje~ and ~mensajero~ (from ~missus~), ~misión~, ~remitir~, ~admitir~, ~cometer~, ~prometer~, ~someter~, and ~transmitir~ all spring from it.
en.pertenecer:
From Latin ~pertinēre~ (“to reach to, concern, belong”), reshaped in Hispano-Romance with the inchoative suffix ~-ecer~ (from Latin ~-ēscere~), probably through a Vulgar Latin *~pertinēscere~. ~pertinēre~ is ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”) plus ~tenēre~ (“to hold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Cognate with Portuguese ~pertencer~; and, through ~tenēre~, with French ~appartenir~ and English ~pertinent~.

The image behind ~pertinēre~ is of a holding that “reaches all the way through” to something — hence “to concern” and then “to belong.” Latin favored the plain verb; Spanish and Portuguese preferred the inchoative dress in ~-ecer~, the same suffix that turns nouns and adjectives into “becoming” verbs (compare ~florecer~ and ~envejecer~). From ~tenēre~ Spanish inherited a large clan: ~tener~ itself, ~contener~, ~retener~, ~mantener~, ~sostener~ and the adjective ~pertinente~, all sharing the root idea of holding and, further back, of stretching taut.
en.pesar:
From Latin ~pēnsāre~ (“to weigh carefully”), the frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to hang, to weigh, to pay”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)pen-~ (“to draw, stretch, spin”). Cognate with French ~peser~, Italian ~pesare~, and Portuguese ~pesar~, and — through the same root — with English ~pension~ and ~pendant~, both of which recall the old link between weighing and paying.

Roman merchants weighed coins to check their value, and ~pēnsāre~ carried that sense of careful assessment. Spanish inherited the verb twice: the popular line gave ~pesar~ (“to weigh”), while a more learned development gave ~pensar~ (“to think”) — literally, to weigh ideas in the mind. The two are doublets, one physical and one mental. ~pesar~ also came to name sorrow (~a pesar de~, “in spite of”; the noun ~pesar~, “grief”), as though sadness were a weight pressing down. The same family yielded ~peso~ (“weight,” and the currency), ~pesado~ (“heavy”), ~compensar~, and ~dispensar~.
en.pintar:
From Vulgar Latin *~pinctāre~, a verb built on ~pictus~, the past participle of Latin ~pingere~ (“to paint, to embroider, to tattoo”). ~pingere~ shows a nasal-infix present of Proto-Indo-European *~peyḱ-~ (“to mark, to color, to paint”), whence Ancient Greek ~poikílos~ (“many-colored, dappled”), Proto-Germanic *~faihaz~ (“spotted”), and Sanskrit ~piṅkté~ (“paints, tinges”). Romance kept the nasal ~n~ of the present stem: beside Spanish ~pintar~ stands Portuguese ~pintar~, while French ~peindre~ and Italian ~dipingere~ come more directly from ~pingere~.

Latin ~pingere~ meant marking a surface with color of any kind — painting a wall, embroidering cloth, even tattooing skin. Spanish ~pintar~ generalized to “to paint” and, figuratively, to how things “look” (~tener buena pinta~, to have a good appearance). From the participle ~pictus~ and its Vulgar-Latin reflexes come ~pintura~, ~pintor~, ~pinta~, and ~pinto~ (“spotted,” a horse-coat term English borrowed straight from Spanish). The learned branch kept the original ~c~: ~pigmento~ (from ~pigmentum~) and ~pictórico~, plus English “picture” and “pigment.” One root, two textures — the earthy ~pintar~ and the bookish ~pigmento~.
en.plantear:
From ~planta~ (“sole of the foot; plant; ground plan”), from Latin ~planta~, itself of disputed deeper origin: one account traces it to Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₂-~ (“flat”), another to *~pleh₂k-~ (“to strike”); the sources do not settle the question. ~Plantear~ is built on ~plantar~ (“to plant, to set firmly”), from Latin ~plantāre~. Cognates of ~planta~ include Italian ~pianta~, French ~plante~ and English ~plant~, all Latin borrowings or inheritances.

The chain of sense is vivid but the endpoint is figurative: from the ~planta~ (“sole”) one gets ~plantar~ (“to set on the ground, to plant”), then ~plantear~ for laying out the ground plan of a building — and finally the modern abstract sense, “to set out, to pose” a problem, a question, a hypothesis. When you ~planteas~ a doubt, you are, etymologically, staking it out on the ground like a foundation. Kin words include ~planta~, ~plantar~, ~plantación~, ~plantilla~, ~implantar~ and ~trasplantar~. (The very deep origin of ~planta~ remains, as noted, unsettled.)
en.poder:
Spanish ~poder~ descends from a Vulgar Latin verb *~potēre~, a regularized reshaping of Classical Latin ~posse~ (“to be able”). ~posse~ was itself a contraction of ~potis~ (“able, powerful”) plus ~esse~ (“to be”) — “to be able” quite literally “to be capable.” The Proto-Indo-European root is *~poti-~ (“powerful, master”). The reshaped infinitive spread across Romance: Italian ~potere~, French ~pouvoir~, and Portuguese ~poder~.

Like several verbs of ability, ~poder~ doubles as a noun — ~el poder~, “power” itself, the thing one has the capacity to wield. The root's sense of capability and dominance fans out across the vocabulary: ~poderoso~ (“powerful”), ~poderío~ (“might”), ~potente~ and ~potencia~ (“potent,” “power”), ~posible~ (“possible,” what one is able to do), and ~potestad~ (“authority”). Even the English ~potent~ and ~possible~ belong to the same family, borrowed from the same Latin stock.
en.poner:
From Latin ~pōnere~ (“to put, to place, to set down”), earlier *~posinere~, analyzed as the prefix ~po-~ (“away, off”) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, to leave”) — so to “put” was first to “set aside, to let stand.” From Proto-Italic *~posinō~. Its Romance offspring include Portuguese ~pôr~, Italian ~porre~, and French ~pondre~, which narrowed touchingly to mean “to lay eggs.” English holds the root through the learned forms ~position~, ~component~, ~deposit~, and ~compound~.

Because a bird “puts” its eggs in the nest, French preserved the most literal descendant of all; Spanish keeps that sense too in ~poner un huevo~ (“to lay an egg”), alongside every other kind of placing. ~poner~ is also famously irregular — its past participle is ~puesto~, its preterite ~puse~ — and it swarms with prefixes: ~componer~ (“to compose”), ~disponer~ (“to arrange”), ~proponer~ (“to propose”), ~suponer~ (“to suppose”), and ~exponer~ (“to expose”). From the participle ~puesto~ come the nouns ~posición~, ~postura~, and ~puesto~ (“post, stall, position”).
en.poseer:
From Latin ~possidēre~ (“to have and hold, own, be master of”), most likely a compound of ~potis~ (“able, powerful, master,” from Proto-Indo-European *~poti-~ “powerful; lord”) and ~sedēre~ (“to sit,” from *~sed-~ “to sit”). Cognate with French ~posséder~, Italian ~possedere~, and — as a borrowing — English ~possess~.

The metaphor is vivid and legal: to ~possidēre~ was to sit as master over a thing, and the verb began in Roman law as a term for occupying land. Spanish ~poseer~ kept that sense of holding and owning. From the ~potis~ half the language also drew ~poder~ (“power; to be able”), while the ~sedēre~ half seeded ~sede~ (“seat, headquarters”). Everyday relatives include ~posesión~ (“possession”) and ~poseedor~ (“possessor, holder”).
en.practicar:
From Late and Medieval Latin ~practicāre~ (“to do, perform, practice”), from Late Latin ~practicus~ (“practical, active”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~πρακτικός~ (~praktikós~, “fit for action, effective”), from ~πράσσω~ (~prássō~, “to do, act, achieve,” earlier “to pass through, traverse”). Spanish probably received the verb by way of Old French ~pratiquer~. Kindred Romance forms include Italian ~praticare~ and Portuguese ~praticar~, and the borrowed English ~practice~ and ~practical~ belong to the same Greek stock.

The related Greek noun ~πρᾶξις~ (~prâxis~, “action, deed”) captures the core idea: practice is knowledge put into action, as opposed to bare theory — a contrast Spanish keeps in the pair ~teoría~ / ~práctica~. The verb ranges from “to practice, rehearse” to “to carry out”: ~practicar una operación~ is to perform an operation, ~practicar un agujero~ to make a hole. From the same stock Spanish has ~práctica~ (“practice”), ~práctico~ (“practical,” and as a noun a harbor pilot), ~pragmático~ and ~praxis~. That last word, unchanged from the Greek, keeps the ancient sense of a deed actually done.
en.precisar:
From the adjective ~preciso~ (“precise”) plus ~-ar~. ~Preciso~ comes from Latin ~praecīsus~ (“cut off, shortened, clipped”), the past participle of ~praecīdere~ (“to cut off in front”), from ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) and ~caedere~ (“to cut, to strike”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kh₂eyd-~ (“to strike, to hew”). It is cognate with French ~préciser~ and, through ~caedere~, with English ~precise~, ~concise~, ~decide~ and even ~scissors~.

Something ~preciso~ is, at root, something cut short — trimmed of all excess — so precision is a kind of cutting away, and to ~precisar~ a thing is to pare it to its exact outline, to state it with nothing superfluous. Spanish then took a second, striking step: because what is cut to the essential is what one cannot do without, ~preciso~ also came to mean “necessary,” and ~precisar~ acquired the everyday sense “to need.” The cutting root ~caedere~ runs through many relatives: ~conciso~ (“cut short”), ~decidir~ (to “cut off” deliberation and choose), ~incisión~, ~inciso~ and the grim ~homicidio~.
en.preferir:
From Latin ~praeferre~ (“to carry before, set before, prefer”), from ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, bear”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, bear”). Cognate with French ~préférer~, Italian ~preferire~ and English ~prefer~; and, through the very old verb ~ferre~, with English ~bear~ and German ~gebären~.

To ~preferir~ is, etymologically, to “carry one thing in front of” the rest — to hold it forward as the better choice, a vivid spatial metaphor frozen inside the word. Latin ~ferre~ was one of the great suppletive verbs, borrowing its perfect from ~tulī~ and its participle from ~lātus~, and it seeded a huge Spanish family through its compounds: ~ofrecer~, ~conferir~, ~diferir~, ~referir~, ~transferir~ and ~sufrir~, plus nouns like ~oferta~ and ~referencia~. The root *~bʰer-~ is among the most widespread in Indo-European, surviving in English ~bear~ and ~birth~.
en.preguntar:
Spanish ~preguntar~ comes from a Vulgar Latin *~praecontāre~ (or *~praecunctāre~), a reshaping of Classical Latin ~percontārī~ (“to question, inquire”). ~percontārī~ was built from ~per-~ (“through”) and, by the traditional account, ~contus~ (“a long pole,” borrowed from Greek ~kontós~): it was originally a sailors’ word meaning to sound the depth of water with a pole — and, by an old and vivid metaphor, to probe or sound out a person with questions. In Vulgar Latin the prefix ~per-~ was refashioned as ~prae-~ (~pre-~), perhaps under the influence of ~cunctārī~ (“to hesitate, delay”). Portuguese ~perguntar~ keeps the original ~per-~; Spanish generalized ~pre-~.

The pole is the memorable image, but it should be flagged: the derivation of ~percontārī~ from ~contus~ (“pole”) is the traditional explanation and is plausible, yet not beyond dispute, so the seafaring picture is best offered as the received story rather than proven fact. What is certain is that the sense narrowed cleanly to “to ask,” and that Spanish generalized the ~pre-~ form across the board. From it come the noun ~pregunta~ (“question”), ~preguntón~ (“inquisitive; a busybody”), and the reflexive ~preguntarse~ (“to wonder, ask oneself”). A useful pair to keep straight: ~preguntar~ is “to ask a question,” while ~pedir~ (from Latin ~petere~) is “to ask for, request” — Spanish, unlike English, never lets one verb do both jobs.
en.preocupar:
From Latin ~praeoccupāre~ (“to seize beforehand, take possession of in advance”), a compound of ~prae-~ (“before”) and ~occupāre~ (“to seize, occupy”), itself ~ob-~ (“toward, over”) plus a verb built on ~capere~ (“to take, seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kap-~ (“to grasp”). Cognate with Italian ~preoccupare~ and French ~préoccuper~; English took the same root through ~occupy~ and ~capture~.

The mental sense is a metaphor of premature seizure: to ~preocupar~ is literally to “occupy beforehand,” as a worry takes hold of the mind before the feared thing arrives. Latin ~praeoccupāre~ was concrete — to seize a hill or a town ahead of the enemy — but Spanish specialized the reflexive ~preocuparse~ for the anxiety that grabs one first. From ~capere~ comes a huge family: ~ocupar~, ~capturar~, ~capaz~, ~recibir~, ~concebir~, and ~caber~ itself, all turning on the idea of taking hold.
en.preparar:
From Latin ~praeparāre~ (“to make ready beforehand”), from ~prae-~ (“before”) + ~parāre~ (“to make ready, provide”), from Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to provide, grant”). Cognate with Italian ~preparare~, French ~préparer~, Portuguese ~preparar~ and English ~prepare~; through the root, with Latin ~parere~ (“to give birth, bring forth”) and Sanskrit ~pṛṇā́ti~ (“to grant, bestow”).

The simple verb ~parāre~ meant “to make ready,” and its offspring fanned out across Spanish: ~parar~ (“to stop”), ~preparación~, ~preparativo~, ~aparato~ (“apparatus”), ~reparar~, ~separar~ and ~amparar~ (“to shelter”). Through the closely related ~parere~ (“to bear young”) come ~parir~ and ~parto~ (“childbirth”). The root’s basic idea is provision: to prepare is to have things furnished in advance, ready to hand.
en.presentar:
From Latin ~praesentāre~ (“to place before, show, offer”), the verb of ~praesēns~ (“present, at hand”), the present participle of ~praeesse~ (“to be before, be at hand”), from ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) plus ~esse~ (“to be”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁es-~ (“to be”). Cognate with Italian ~presentare~, French ~présenter~, Portuguese ~apresentar~, and English ~present~ and ~represent~.

The core image is spatial: ~prae-~ “before” plus ~esse~ “to be,” so ~praesēns~ described whatever “is before you,” present in place and in time. From ~praesentāre~, “to set before someone,” Spanish ~presentar~ branched into introducing a person, showing a document, staging a show, and lodging a complaint — every sense a variation on putting something in front of an audience. The adjective and noun ~presente~ carries both meanings the Latin fused: the present moment and a present, a gift “placed before” the receiver. From the same ~prae-~ + ~esse~ come ~presencia~, ~presentación~, ~presentador~, and ~presentimiento~ (“foreboding,” a feeling that “is there beforehand”).
en.prestar:
From Latin ~praestāre~ (“to stand before, to excel, to furnish, to provide”), a compound of ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) and ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”) — the very root of ~estar~. Cognates include Italian ~prestare~, French ~prêter~ and Portuguese ~prestar~, all inheriting the same “furnish” sense.

The path from “standing before” to “lending” runs through the sense “to make available, to furnish”: what you ~prestas~ you place at another’s disposal. Latin ~praestāre~ already meant “to guarantee, to supply,” and Romance narrowed that to lending. Spanish preserves both threads — you can ~prestar~ money (lend) but also ~prestar~ attention or a service (furnish). From it come ~préstamo~ (“loan”), ~prestación~ (“benefit, service”), ~prestamista~ (“lender”) and ~empréstito~ (“public loan”). Note that ~prestigio~, despite the look, belongs to a different Latin word.
en.pretender:
From Latin ~praetendere~ (“to stretch forth, hold out before, put forward as a reason”), a compound of ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) and ~tendere~ (“to stretch, extend”). ~tendere~ rests on Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch, extend”), a root that also thinned things out: from its extension *~tenh₂u-~ (“stretched thin”) come Latin ~tenuis~ (“thin”) and English ~thin~. Through the same root ~pretender~ is cognate with Greek ~teínō~ (“I stretch”) and with English ~tend~, ~tension~, and ~tent~ (a stretched cloth). Italian ~pretendere~ and French ~prétendre~ are its direct Romance kin.

To ~praetendere~ was to stretch something out in front of you — a curtain, a pretext, a claim — and that spatial gesture became the abstract one of putting a claim forward. Here English and Spanish part ways, a classic false friend: English “to pretend” slid toward feigning, while Spanish ~pretender~ kept the Roman sense of asserting a claim, and so means “to aspire to, to intend,” and even “to court” (a ~pretendiente~ is a suitor). The stretched root runs through ~tender~ (“to stretch out, tend”), ~extender~, ~atender~ (“to attend,” to stretch one’s mind toward), ~tensión~, and the noun ~pretensión~ (“pretension, aim”). What one ~pretende~ is, quite literally, a goal held out at arm’s length ahead of oneself.
en.prever:
A transparent compound of ~pre-~ (“before, in advance”) and ~ver~ (“to see”), modeled on Latin ~praevidēre~ (“to foresee”), which joins ~prae-~ (“before”) to ~vidēre~ (“to see”). ~vidēre~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, and hence to know”), one of the most productive roots in the family. Through it ~prever~ is cognate with Greek ~idéa~ (“form, idea,” from ‘what is seen’), with English ~vision~ and ~view~, and — on the ‘know’ side of the root — with English ~wit~ and German ~wissen~ (“to know”). Italian ~prevedere~ and French ~prévoir~ are its Romance twins.

Latin ~vidēre~ meant both to see with the eyes and to see with the mind, and the prefixed ~praevidēre~ leaned on the second: to see a thing before it arrives. Spanish keeps ~prever~ for exactly that mental foresight. The richest surprise in this family is ~prudente~: ~prudencia~ and ~prudente~ are worn-down contractions of Latin ~prōvidēns~ / ~prōvidentia~ (“foreseeing, foresight”) — the prudent person is, etymologically, the one who sees ahead. Close relatives include ~providencia~ (“providence,” divine foresight), ~previsión~ (“foresight, forecast”), and the everyday ~ver~, ~vista~ (“sight”), and ~visión~. To ~prever~ is simply to do in advance what the eye and the mind do all the time.
en.privar:
From Latin ~prīvāre~ (“to deprive, to strip of, to free from”), a verb built on the adjective ~prīvus~ (“single, one's own, set apart”). ~prīvus~ traces to Proto-Italic *~preiwos~ and is generally linked to the Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“forward, in front”), by a semantic shift from “standing in front” to “standing apart, being separate.” The Romance descendants are learned rather than inherited: Italian ~privare~, French ~priver~, Portuguese ~privar~. English ~private~ and ~deprive~ belong to the same Latin family.

~prīvus~ first meant “single, individual” — one thing set apart from the common stock — so ~prīvāre~ was to set apart, and thus to take away, to deprive. The same “set apart for oneself” idea runs the other way in ~prīvātus~, what is withdrawn from public life into the private sphere; a Roman ~prīvātus~ was a citizen holding no public office. From ~prīvus~ Spanish gathered ~privado~ (“private”), ~privación~, ~privilegio~ (“a law for one person,” ~prīvus~ + ~lex~), and the adjective ~privativo~. Curiously, ~privar~ also came to mean “to be in favor” or, colloquially, “to be all the rage.”
en.probar:
From Latin ~probāre~ (“to test, prove, approve”), a verb from the adjective ~probus~ (“good, upright, honest”). ~Probus~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~pro-bʰuH-~, roughly “being in front, growing well,” from *~pro-~ (“forward”) and *~bʰuH-~ (“to be, grow”) — the same *~bʰuH-~ that gave Latin ~fuī~ (“I was”) and English ~be~. Cognate with Italian ~provare~, French ~prouver~, and English ~prove~ and ~probe~.

The one Latin verb ~probāre~ fanned out into several ideas — to test, to demonstrate, to approve, to sample — and Spanish ~probar~ still carries all of them: the same ~probar~ covers testing a theory, tasting a dish, and trying on a shirt. English split the load across ~prove~, ~probe~, and ~approve~. From ~probus~ and ~probāre~ Spanish also holds ~prueba~ (“proof, test”), ~probable~, ~aprobar~ (“to approve, pass”), ~comprobar~ (“to verify”), and the lab ~probeta~ (“test tube”).
en.proceder:
From Latin ~prōcēdere~ (“to go forward, advance”), from ~prō-~ (“forward”) and ~cēdere~ (“to go, move, yield”). ~cēdere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~kesd-o-~ and, by the usual account, to Proto-Indo-European *~ked-~ (“to go, yield”), though its deeper origin is debated. Cognate with French ~procéder~, Italian ~procedere~ and English ~proceed~.

The Latin verb meant physically “to march forward,” and Spanish keeps both the literal “to advance, go on” and the derived senses “to originate from” (« procede de… ») and “to behave” (« un proceder honesto »). ~cēdere~ was extraordinarily productive in composition, and Spanish inherited a whole regiment of its compounds: ~ceder~, ~acceder~, ~conceder~, ~exceder~, ~preceder~, ~suceder~ and ~retroceder~, plus the nouns ~proceso~ and ~procedimiento~. Because the underlying root simply meant “to go, give ground,” each prefix merely says in which direction: forward (~pro-~), back (~retro-~), toward (~ad-~), or out beyond (~ex-~).
en.producir:
Spanish ~producir~ descends from Latin ~prōdūcere~ (“to lead forth, bring forth, produce”), a compound of the prefix ~prō-~ (“forward”) and the verb ~dūcere~ (“to lead, draw”). ~dūcere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ (“to lead, draw”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~tow~ and German ~ziehen~ (“to pull”); the Latin verb itself, inherited across Romance, gave Italian ~produrre~ and French ~produire~, and — borrowed — English ~produce~.

Latin ~prōdūcere~ literally meant to lead something forward into view, and from that concrete image the abstract senses of causing, generating and manufacturing developed. The same ~dūcere~ seeded a large Spanish family in ~-ducir~: ~conducir~ (“to drive, conduct”), ~traducir~ (“to translate,” literally to lead across) and ~reducir~ (“to reduce, lead back”), alongside the nouns ~ducto~ and ~duque~ (“the one who leads”). Its participle ~producto~ gave the everyday noun for a “product.”
en.prohibir:
From Latin ~prohibēre~ (“to hold back, hinder, forbid”), a compound of the prefix ~pro-~ (“forward, in front, away”) and ~habēre~ (“to hold, to have”). ~habēre~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~gʰeh₁bʰ-~ (“to grab, to take”), though this descent is disputed: *~bʰ~ is a seldom-attested PIE consonant whose very status is contested, and ~habēre~ — long thought to be akin to English ~give~ — is now doubted to be. Despite the resemblance it is not related to English ~have~, which is instead cognate with Latin ~capere~ (“to seize”). Through ~prohibēre~ Spanish is joined by Italian ~proibire~, Portuguese ~proibir~, and French ~prohiber~.

The image is spatial: to ~prohibēre~ is to hold a thing away from someone, and from “holding off” grew the senses of barring, forbidding, and outlawing. The same ~habēre~ seeded a large Spanish family — the auxiliary ~haber~, plus ~hábil~ (“skilled,” one who “has” a knack), ~hábito~, ~habitar~ (“to dwell,” to keep having a place), ~exhibir~, and ~inhibir~. English took the derived noun directly as “prohibition,” and the United States’ era of banned alcohol is still called Prohibition — a fitting name, since the word’s core was always about holding people back from something.
en.promover:
From Latin ~promovēre~ (“to move forward, push ahead”), a compound of ~pro-~ (“forward”) and ~movēre~ (“to move”), and so, at bottom, from Proto-Indo-European *~mewh₁-~ (“to move, push”). It is cognate with Italian ~promuovere~, French ~promouvoir~ and Portuguese ~promover~; English ~promote~ belongs here too, entering through the Latin participle ~prōmōtus~ rather than the infinitive.

The Latin sense “to move something forward” branched in two directions that Spanish still keeps side by side: to advance a person in rank or office, and to further a cause or set an undertaking in motion — one can ~promover~ an employee or ~promover~ a reform. The participle ~prōmōtus~ yielded ~promoción~ (both “promotion” and an academic “graduating class”) and ~promotor~. All of it shares the movable heart of ~mover~, and so stands beside ~motor~, ~movimiento~ and ~emoción~.
en.proponer:
From Latin ~prōpōnere~ (“to set forth, put forward”), from ~prō-~ (“forward”) and ~pōnere~ (“to put, place”). By the standard analysis ~pōnere~ is itself ~po-~ + ~sinere~ (“to let, set down”), from Proto-Italic *~pozinō~, with the prefix going back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂epó~ (“off, away”) — though this decomposition is a reconstruction, not an attested split. Italian inherits the compound directly as ~proporre~, Portuguese as ~propor~. French ~proposer~ and English ~propose~, however, belong to the ~poser~ family (from Late Latin ~pausāre~, “to pause, rest”), which merged in sense with the ~pōnere~ compounds — a famous etymological tangle.

The core sense is spatial: ~prōpōnere~ is to put a thing forward, to set it before others — before the eyes as an offer, before the mind as a proposition. Latin's participle ~prōpositum~ gave Spanish ~propósito~ (“purpose, what one sets before oneself as a goal”) and ~proposición~, while the deverbal noun is ~propuesta~ (“a proposal”). Few Latin stems were as fertile as ~pōnere~: from it Spanish built ~poner~ and a whole rank of compounds — ~componer~, ~disponer~, ~oponer~, ~suponer~ — each “placing” in its own direction.
en.proporcionar:
From ~proporción~ (“proportion”), from Latin ~proportiō~, itself from the phrase ~pro portiōne~ (“according to each one’s share”), in which ~portiō~ (“share, portion”) is related to ~pars~ (“part”). Cognate with English ~proportion~ and Italian ~proporzione~.

The verb’s modern sense — “to provide, supply” — grew out of a numerical one. To ~proporcionar~ first meant to apportion, to give each part its due measure; from “to furnish in the right proportion” it faded to simply “to furnish, provide.” The mathematical overtones dropped away, leaving an everyday word for supplying whatever is needed. Relatives include ~porción~ (“portion”), ~proporción~ (“proportion”), ~proporcional~ (“proportional”), and, further back through ~portiō~ and ~pars~, the family of ~parte~ (“part”).
en.proteger:
From Latin ~protegere~ (“to cover in front, shield”), from ~pro-~ (“in front, before”) plus ~tegere~ (“to cover”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)teg-~ (“to cover”). Cognate with French ~protéger~ and Italian ~proteggere~, and — through the participle ~protectus~ — with English ~protect~. The same root surfaces in Greek ~stégos~ (“roof”) and English ~thatch~.

Latin built a small set of opposites on ~tegere~: ~protegere~ “covers in front” to defend, while ~detegere~ “uncovers,” the source of ~detectar~ and English ~detect~. Spanish ~proteger~ kept the defensive sense throughout. From *~(s)teg-~ Spanish also inherited the humble roofing words ~techo~ (“ceiling, roof”), ~tejado~ (“tiled roof”), and ~teja~ (“roof tile”), along with the learned ~tegumento~ and ~protección~.
en.provocar:
From Latin ~prōvocāre~ (“to call forth, to challenge, to summon”), a compound of ~prō-~ (“forth, forward”) and ~vocāre~ (“to call”), a verb built on ~vōx~ (“voice”). ~vōx~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~wekʷ-~ (“to speak, to utter”). The Romance line is unbroken — Italian ~provocare~, French ~provoquer~, Portuguese ~provocar~ — and through Latin the family reaches English ~provoke~, ~voice~, ~vocal~, and ~invoke~.

The literal force is “to call out toward” — to summon someone forward, and so to dare or challenge them. In Roman law the noun ~prōvocātiō~ named a citizen's right of appeal, the ~prōvocātiō ad populum~, a call from a magistrate's sentence “out to the people.” From that courtroom sense of calling-forth, ~provocar~ broadened to today's “to provoke, to incite, to bring about.” The ~vocāre~ family is a large one in Spanish: ~voz~ (“voice”), ~vocal~, ~convocar~ (“to convene”), ~evocar~ (“to evoke”), ~invocar~ (“to invoke”), ~revocar~ (“to revoke”), and ~vocación~ (“a calling”) — the last preserving the oldest metaphor of all, a life's work to which one is, quite literally, called.
en.publicar:
From Latin ~publicāre~ (“to make public, publish”), from ~pūblicus~ (“public, of the people”), an alteration of Old Latin ~poplicus~, from ~populus~ (“the people,” itself of unknown origin). The shift of ~poplicus~ to ~pūblicus~ — the ū and the b — is usually credited to the pull of ~pūbēs~ (“adult population”), though whether this is true blending or mere association is debated. It is cognate with Italian ~pubblicare~, Portuguese ~publicar~ and French ~publier~, and — through that French — with English ~publish~.

Latin ~publicāre~ meant to make something common property, even “to confiscate for the state,” and more broadly “to make known.” Only with the printing press did “make known” specialize into “issue a book,” the sense Spanish ~publicar~ now carries first. From the same ~populus~ Spanish drew a broad family: ~público~ (“public”), ~publicidad~ (“advertising, publicity”), ~popular~, ~pueblo~ (“people, town”) and, from ~rēs pūblica~ (“the public thing”), ~república~.
en.quedar:
From Latin ~quiētāre~ (“to calm, quiet, bring to rest”), the verb of ~quiētus~ (“at rest, calm, quiet”), the past participle of ~quiēscere~ (“to rest”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kʷyeh₁-~ (“to rest, be at peace”). Cognate with Italian ~quietare~ and Old Portuguese ~quedar~; through ~quiētus~ Spanish is kin to English ~quiet~, ~quit~, ~coy~ (via French ~coi~), and the noun ~quietus~, and — through the same root — to English ~while~.

The semantic heart of ~quedar~ is stillness: to ~quedar~ somewhere is, at root, to “come to rest” there, and from “grow calm” the verb widened into “remain, stay, be left over,” and reflexively ~quedarse~ (“to stay put”). Spanish also turned it into everyday idiom — ~quedar en~ (“to agree on”), ~quedar bien~ (“to make a good impression”), and ~quedar con~ (“to arrange to meet”) — senses far from the original hush. The same root left the adjective ~quieto~ (“still”), the nouns ~quietud~ and ~inquietud~ (“restlessness, unease”), and the verb ~aquietar~ (“to soothe”); the archaic adverb ~quedo~ (“softly, quietly”) preserves the ancestor most faithfully.
en.querer:
From Latin ~quaerere~ (“to seek, to ask for, to strive after”), inherited through Old Spanish ~querer~. The verb’s deeper ancestry is uncertain: by one proposal it reflects Proto-Indo-European *~kʷeh₂-~ (“to acquire”), with cognates such as Ancient Greek ~pépamai~ (“to acquire”); other scholars connect it instead to a root meaning “to seek, to ask,” and the question remains unsettled. Its Romance kin include Portuguese ~querer~ and Old French ~quérir~.

Where Latin ~quaerere~ meant to search or to petition, Spanish let the sense drift inward — from “to seek” to “to want,” and at last to “to love,” which is why ~te quiero~ — literally “I want you” — is the everyday way to say “I love you.” The learned branch of the family kept the older, more forensic flavor: ~cuestión~ (“question, matter”), ~encuesta~ (“survey”), ~pesquisa~ (“inquiry”), ~requerir~, ~adquirir~, ~inquirir~, ~conquistar~, and ~querella~ (“legal complaint”) all descend from ~quaerere~. English shares the harvest through ~query~, ~quest~, ~question~, ~require~, and ~conquer~.
en.quitar:
Spanish ~quitar~ comes from late Latin ~quiētāre~ (“to make quiet, to release”), a verb built on ~quiētus~ (“at rest, calm”), the past participle of ~quiēscere~ (“to rest, be still”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kʷyeh₁-~ (“to rest”). It is cognate with English ~quit~ and ~quiet~, French ~quitter~, and Portuguese ~quitar~, all of which trace back to the same notion of releasing or coming to rest.

The oldest sense was legal: to ~quitar~ someone was to discharge them from a debt or an accusation — to leave them in peace. From “to release from an obligation” the meaning drifted to “to free from a burden,” then to the plain modern “to take away, remove.” Corominas notes this semilearned path from the tribunal to everyday speech. The same root of rest gave Spanish ~quieto~ (“still”), ~quietud~ (“stillness”), ~inquieto~ (“restless”), and ~aquietar~ (“to calm”), as well as the noun ~quite~ used in bullfighting for the maneuver that draws the bull away.
en.realizar:
A comparatively young verb: Spanish ~realizar~ was formed from the adjective ~real~ (“real, actual”) with the suffix ~-izar~, on the model of Medieval Latin ~reālizāre~ and French ~réaliser~. ~real~ goes back to Late Latin ~reālis~ (“relating to things”), from Latin ~rēs~ (“thing, matter, affair”), from Proto-Indo-European *~reh₁ís~ (“wealth, goods”), akin to Sanskrit ~rayí~ (“property, riches”). English ~real~ and ~realize~ share the same source.

So the verb’s hidden sense is “to make into a thing” — to turn what was only planned or imagined into something that exists. That gives Spanish two everyday meanings that English splits apart: ~realizar~ is both “to carry out, to accomplish” (« realizar un proyecto ») and, more recently and under English influence, “to realize, to become aware.” From the same ~rēs~ descend ~real~, ~realidad~ (“reality”), ~realismo~, the legal ~res~ still used in Latin tags, and — through ~rēs pūblica~ (“the public thing”) — the word ~república~.
en.rechazar:
From ~re-~ (“back”) plus the Vulgar Latin verb *~captiāre~ (“to chase, try to seize”), a frequentative of Latin ~captāre~ (“to grasp at”), itself from ~capere~ (“to take, seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp”). That same *~captiāre~ gave Spanish ~cazar~ (“to hunt”) and French ~chasser~, so ~rechazar~ is, at root, “to chase back.”

The Vulgar Latin verb had a remarkable double life up north: through Central Old French ~chacier~ it entered English as ~chase~, while through the Norman-Picard form ~cachier~ it entered the very same language a second time as ~catch~ — two English words that are, etymologically, one. Spanish meanwhile pushed the sense from “chase away” to “drive back” to “repel, refuse,” giving ~rechazar~ its ideas of a repelled attack, a declined offer, a spurned suitor. Its relatives stay close to the grasping hand: ~cazar~, ~cazador~, ~capturar~, ~captar~ and ~cachar~ — all reaching out to seize.
en.recibir:
From Old Spanish ~recebir~, from Latin ~recipere~ (“to take back, receive, accept”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~capere~ (“to take, seize”). This ~capere~ traces to Proto-Italic *~kapjō~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~kap-~ (“to grasp, seize”), the same root that gave, through Germanic, English ~have~ and ~heave~. Cognate with Portuguese ~receber~, Italian ~ricevere~ and French ~recevoir~; English ~receive~ descends from the same Latin verb by way of Old French.

Latin ~recipere~ literally meant to take something back to oneself, and from that grew the senses of accepting, admitting and welcoming that Spanish ~recibir~ still carries. Its past participle ~recepta~ (“things received”) gave ~receta~, which in Spanish names both a cooking recipe and a doctor’s prescription — each a little list of things to be taken. The root ~capere~ seeded a broad family: ~recepción~, ~recibo~, ~captura~, ~cautivo~, ~capaz~, ~concebir~ and ~percibir~ all turn on the idea of taking hold.
en.reclamar:
From Latin ~reclāmāre~ (“to cry out against, to protest”), from ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~clāmāre~ (“to shout, to cry out, to call”). ~clāmāre~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~kelh₁-~ (“to shout, to call”). Spanish ~reclamar~ is a semi-learned inheritance that stayed close to the Latin form. It is cognate with Italian ~reclamare~, French ~réclamer~, Portuguese ~reclamar~, and English ~reclaim~ and ~claim~, and — through the root — with English ~clamor~ and Latin ~clārus~ (“clear, bright”), the sound-source of clarity itself.

The prefix ~re-~ adds a sense of “back” or “in response,” so reclamar is literally to shout back — to call out in protest or to call a thing back to oneself. Spanish keeps both threads: to ~reclamar~ is to demand or claim what is owed (a right, a debt, lost luggage), and in some regions simply to complain. The *~kelh₁-~ root was noisy across Indo-European, and its Latin descendants gave Spanish a whole vocabulary of calling and clarity: ~clamar~, ~clamor~, ~reclamo~, ~aclamar~, ~exclamar~, ~proclamar~, ~llamar~ (from ~clāmāre~ itself, by popular descent), and — via ~clārus~ — ~claro~ and ~declarar~.
en.recoger:
From ~re-~ (here intensive) plus ~coger~ (“to grasp, catch”), which descends from Latin ~colligere~ (“to gather together”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~legere~ (“to gather, pick, choose”). The verb traces to Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather”). It is cognate with Italian ~cogliere~, French ~cueillir~ and Portuguese ~colher~, and — through the same root — with English ~collect~ and ~legend~.

Latin ~legere~ carried a telling double life: from “to pick out” it moved to “to read” (to pick out letters one by one), the sense that survives in ~leer~. ~Recoger~ kept the gathering branch — to pick up what is scattered, to take in, and, of a harvest, to reap. Its reflexive ~recogerse~ softened into “to withdraw, retire for the night.” The same root fanned out across learned Spanish in ~colección~, ~colegio~, ~elegir~, ~lección~ and ~legión~ (a body of soldiers “gathered” under arms), beside the popular ~coger~, ~acoger~ and ~escoger~.
en.recomendar:
From Latin ~recommendāre~, from ~re-~ (intensive here) plus ~commendāre~ (“to entrust, commit to someone's care”), which is ~com-~ (“with, together”) plus ~mandāre~ (“to entrust, order”). ~Mandāre~ in turn joins ~manus~ (“hand”) and ~dare~ (“to give”) — literally “to give into the hand.” Cognate with Italian ~raccomandare~, French ~recommander~, and English ~recommend~.

The chain of meaning runs from placing something in another's trusted hands to speaking in its favor: to ~recomendar~ a book is to commend it to a friend, to hand it to their good judgment. The ~manus~ plus ~dare~ core also gave ~mandar~ (“to send, command”), and from the wider family Spanish has ~mandato~, ~encomendar~ (“to entrust”), ~comanda~, ~demanda~, and ~recomendación~. The English doublet ~commend~ and ~recommend~ carries the same “entrusting” sense.
en.reconocer:
Spanish ~reconocer~ descends from Latin ~recognōscere~ (“to recall, recognize”), a compound of ~re-~ (“again”) and ~cognōscere~ (“to become acquainted with, learn”), itself ~con-~ (an intensifying “thoroughly”) plus ~gnōscere~ (“to come to know”). Through Proto-Italic *~gnōskō~ the verb reaches Proto-Indo-European *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know, recognize”). That root is among the most widely attested in the family, cognate with English ~know~, Ancient Greek ~γιγνώσκω~ (gignṓskō, “to know”), and Latin ~nōtus~ (“known”). French ~reconnaître~ and Italian ~riconoscere~ are its Romance siblings.

The compound is transparent: to ~reconocer~ is quite literally to “know again,” the ~re-~ marking a second, confirming encounter with what one already knew. From that core Spanish stretched the verb across many fields — acknowledging a debt, scouting ground (~reconocer el terreno~), a doctor’s checkup (~reconocimiento médico~). The same PIE root seeded a wide family: the plain ~conocer~ (“to know”), ~conocimiento~ (“knowledge”), ~noción~, ~noticia~ (“news”), and ~noble~, alongside the negated ~ignorar~ (“to not know”) and ~incógnito~. By way of Greek the root also yielded ~diagnóstico~. Few etymologies link a Spanish everyday word to English ~know~ so plainly across five millennia.
en.recordar:
Spanish ~recordar~ comes from Latin ~recordārī~ (“to remember, to call to mind”), from the prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~cor~ (stem ~cordis~, “heart”) — so to remember was, literally, to bring something back through the heart. ~cor~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~ḱerd-~ (“heart”), the native cognate of English ~heart~ and German ~Herz~. English ~record~ is the very same Latin verb, borrowed through French — a doublet of ~recordar~.

The etymology encodes an old idea: the ancients seated memory and thought not in the brain but in the heart, so recalling was a movement of the heart. That is why “to record” and “to remember” share one word. From ~cor~ Spanish inherited ~corazón~ (“heart”) and built a wide family: ~acordar~ (“to agree; to remind”), the noun ~recuerdo~ (“a memory, a souvenir”), ~cordial~ (“heartfelt”), ~concordia~ (“concord, a harmony of hearts”) and its opposite ~discordia~ (“discord”).
en.recorrer:
From Latin ~recurrere~ (“to run back, to run again”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~currere~ (“to run”), from Proto-Italic *~korzō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱers-~ (“to run”). It is cognate with Italian ~ricorrere~, French ~recourir~ and Portuguese ~recorrer~, and — through the same root — with English ~current~, ~course~ and ~car~.

In Latin ~recurrere~ meant literally to run back; Spanish kept the motion but loosened it into coverage of ground, so that today one ~recorre~ a city, a route or a text — travelling or ranging over the whole of it rather than running anywhere. The spatial sweep is now central: a wire may ~recorrer~ a wall from end to end. The same PIE root *~ḱers-~ underlies a wide Spanish family, including ~correr~, ~corredor~, ~corriente~, ~carrera~, ~recorrido~ and ~socorrer~ (literally “to run to help”).
en.recuperar:
From Latin ~recuperāre~ (“to regain, get back”), built on ~re-~ (“back, again”). The internal make-up is not fully transparent, but the verb is clearly related to ~recipere~ (“to receive, take back”) and, more deeply, to ~capere~ (“to take, seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kap-~ (“to grasp”). Cognate with French ~récupérer~ and, by a different route, English ~recover~.

Spanish holds a matched pair from this one Latin verb: the learned ~recuperar~, borrowed straight from ~recuperāre~, and the inherited ~recobrar~ (“to recover”), worn down through centuries of ordinary speech. English ~recover~ belongs to the same family, having reached it through Old French ~recovrer~. In use the learned verb leans formal and technical — to recover data, health, an investment — while the inherited one keeps a more literary air. The noun ~recuperación~ (“recovery”) rounds out the set, alongside French ~récupérer~.
en.recurrir:
From Latin ~recurrere~ (“to run back, hurry back”), from ~re-~ (“back, again”) + ~currere~ (“to run”), from Proto-Italic *~korzō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱers-~ (“to run”). Cognate with Italian ~ricorrere~ and Portuguese ~recorrer~; through ~currere~ it is kin to English ~current~, ~course~ and ~occur~, and to the ~car~ that rolled in from Gaulish ~carros~.

Latin ~recurrere~ literally sent you “running back,” and Spanish ~recurrir~ still carries that motion figuratively: to resort to a means, or, in law, to appeal — to “run back” to a higher court. The same root *~ḱers-~ underlies a busy Spanish family: ~correr~, ~corriente~, ~carrera~, ~recurso~ and ~socorro~, literally “a running to the rescue.”
en.reducir:
Spanish ~reducir~ comes from Latin ~redūcere~ (“to lead back, bring back”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~dūcere~ (“to lead, draw, guide”). ~dūcere~ reflects Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ (“to lead, draw”), a root remarkably productive in both branches: in Germanic it gave English ~tow~ and ~tug~, plus the borrowed ~duke~ (via Latin ~dux~, “leader”), and German ~ziehen~ (“to pull”) and ~Zug~ (“train, pull”). Latin ~dūcere~ alone spun off ~condūcere~, ~prōdūcere~, ~indūcere~ and dozens more. Italian ~ridurre~, French ~réduire~, and Portuguese ~reduzir~ are the Romance siblings of ~reducir~.

The core sense was spatial — to ~redūcere~ was to lead something back to where it came from. From “bring back” Latin developed “bring to a state or condition,” and that is the sense Spanish generalized: to reduce is to bring a thing back or down to something smaller, simpler, or more basic. Hence ~reducir~ spans lowering a price, boiling down a sauce (~reducir una salsa~), subduing an enemy (~reducir al enemigo~), and setting a broken bone (~reducir una fractura~ — literally leading it back into place). From the same ~dūcere~ root Spanish holds ~conducir~, ~producir~, ~educar~, ~duque~, ~ducha~ (“shower,” via Italian ~doccia~), and ~acueducto~.
en.referir:
Directly from Latin ~referre~ (“to carry back, to bring back word, to report”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, to bear”). ~ferre~ traces to Proto-Italic *~ferō~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, to bear”), the same immensely productive root that gives Ancient Greek ~phérō~, Sanskrit ~bhárati~, and English ~bear~. The verb lives on in Italian ~riferire~, French ~référer~, and Portuguese ~referir~.

The core image is concrete — to carry something back to a source or a listener — which is why ~referir~ spans “to recount,” “to report,” and, reflexively as ~referirse~, “to allude to.” A fossil of Roman grammar rides along in ~referéndum~: it is a gerundive, literally “matters that must be carried back” to the people for a vote. English borrowed the same stem for ~referee~ and ~reference~. Within Spanish the compound sits beside its siblings ~conferir~, ~inferir~, ~proferir~, and ~transferir~, and beside the noun family ~referencia~ and ~relación~.
en.reflejar:
From Latin ~reflexus~ (“bent back, reflected”), the past participle of ~reflectere~ (“to bend back”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back”) and ~flectere~ (“to bend”), a verb of uncertain deeper origin. Spanish did not inherit its verb straight from ~reflectere~; instead Romance rebuilt it on the noun ~reflejo~, itself descended from ~reflexus~, and from that noun derived ~reflejar~. It is cognate with English ~reflect~ and ~reflex~, with Italian ~riflettere~, French ~réfléchir~, and Portuguese ~reflectir~.

The Latin verb described a physical bending-back — of a road, an arm, and above all of light — and that optical sense still dominates: a mirror ~refleja~ an image. From there grew the figure of thought, so that a face may reflect an emotion or a novel reflect its age. The same root fed a large learned family in Spanish, including ~reflexión~, ~reflexivo~, ~reflector~ and the doublet verb ~reflectar~; and beyond the ~re-~ prefix, ~flectere~ itself gave ~flexible~ and ~flexión~.
en.registrar:
From ~registro~ (“register, record”), borrowed from Medieval Latin ~registrum~, an alteration of Late Latin ~regesta~ (“a list, things recorded”) — the neuter plural of ~regestus~, past participle of ~regerere~ (“to carry back, record, enter”). That verb is ~re-~ (“back”) plus ~gerere~ (“to carry, bear, conduct”), from Proto-Italic *~gezō~. The word travelled across Europe: English ~register~, French ~registre~, Italian ~registro~, all from the same medieval Latin source.

The literal notion was that of “carrying things back” into a record — entering them where they can be retrieved — and Spanish ~registrar~ still spans the whole range: to record, to enter in a register, and (perhaps surprisingly) to search or frisk, as customs officers ~registran~ luggage. From ~gerere~, “to carry, manage,” Spanish inherited a rich crop: ~gesto~ (“gesture,” a thing carried out), ~gestión~, ~gerente~, ~digerir~, ~sugerir~ and ~congerie~.
en.regresar:
From Latin ~regressus~, the past participle of ~regredī~ (“to go back, return”), from ~re-~ (“back”) plus ~gradī~ (“to step, walk”), itself from ~gradus~ (“step, pace, degree”). The ultimate source is Proto-Indo-European *~gʰredʰ-~ (“to walk, go”). Spanish built ~regresar~ on the participial stem rather than inheriting the old verb directly. The base ~gradī~ is also the well of Italian and Portuguese ~gradual~, French ~degré~ (“degree”), and — through Latin compounds — the English borrowings ~progress~, ~congress~, ~aggression~ and ~degree~, all of them literally about stepping forward, together, or against.

In Latin ~regredī~ was a plain verb of motion — to step back the way one came. Spanish ~regresar~ keeps that concrete core (“to return, come back”), and in much of Latin America it is the ordinary word for going home, alongside ~volver~. The same participial pattern gave the noun ~regreso~ (“return”) and the adjective ~regresivo~ (“regressive”). The ~gradī~ family is enormous in Spanish: ~grado~ (“degree, grade”), ~gradual~, ~grada~ (“tier, step”), ~progreso~, ~ingresar~ (“to enter, deposit”), ~egresar~ (“to graduate,” American Spanish), ~agredir~ (“to attack,” literally to step toward) and ~transgredir~ (“to transgress,” to step across). Every one hides a footstep inside it.
en.regular:
From Late Latin ~rēgulāre~ (“to control by rule”), from Latin ~rēgula~ (“a straight stick, a ruler, hence a rule”), from ~regere~ (“to keep straight, to direct, to rule”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, to direct, to make right”). This is one of the great PIE roots: cognate with English ~right~ and ~rule~, German ~recht~ (“right”), and — through the Latin ~rēx~ (“king”) — with Spanish ~rey~.

The ~rēgula~ was first a carpenter's straightedge — the physical bar against which things were made true — and ~regular~ still carries that image of bringing something into measure. A homely cousin is ~arreglar~ (“to fix, arrange, tidy”), from Vulgar Latin ~adregulāre~ — literally to bring back to the rule. From the same directing-root Spanish holds ~regla~ (“rule, ruler”), ~regir~ (“to govern”), ~régimen~, ~dirigir~ (“to direct”), and ~corregir~ (“to correct,” to straighten alongside).
en.relacionar:
A modern denominal verb: Spanish ~relación~ (“relation”) plus the verb-forming ~-ar~. ~relación~ comes from Latin ~relātiōnem~ (accusative of ~relātiō~, “a carrying back, a report”), built on ~relātus~, the participle of ~referre~ (“to carry back, to report”), from ~re-~ (“back”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, to bear”). ~ferre~ rests on Proto-Italic *~ferō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, to bear”) — one of the most widespread of all roots, cognate with Ancient Greek ~phérō~, Sanskrit ~bhárati~, and English ~bear~. Portuguese matches it as ~relacionar~.

Notably, where English took ~relate~ straight from the Latin participle, Spanish assembled ~relacionar~ later and from the noun, so it literally means “to put into relation.” A quirk of ~ferre~ is that its own past participle ~lātus~ is suppletive, borrowed from an unrelated root — which is why the “-lation” words look nothing like “fer-.” The vast *~bʰer-~ family in Spanish includes ~referir~, ~preferir~, ~transferir~, ~conferir~, ~diferir~, and — through ~offerre~ and ~sufferre~ — ~ofrecer~ and ~sufrir~.
en.repetir:
From Latin ~repetere~ (“to seek again, to fetch back, to demand anew”), a compound of ~re-~ (“again, back”) and ~petere~ (“to seek, aim at, make for, attack”). ~petere~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~peth₂-~ (“to fly, to fall”) — the notion of darting toward something. It is cognate with Ancient Greek ~pétomai~ (“I fly”) and Sanskrit ~pátati~ (“flies, falls”); through Latin it gave Italian ~ripetere~, French ~répéter~, and English ~repeat~.

In Latin ~petere~ carried the double charge of “to head for” and “to go at,” which is why it could mean both to request and to assault; ~repetere~ added “again,” giving “to fetch back” and then plain “to do over.” Spanish ~repetir~ inherited the “do again” sense, and colloquially even means to take a second helping of food. The flying root sprays through the vocabulary: ~repetición~ (“repetition”), ~petición~ (“request”), ~apetito~ (“appetite,” a reaching toward), ~competir~ (“to compete,” to seek together), ~ímpetu~ (“impetus”), and ~perpetuo~ (“perpetual”).
