Even the ~-peto~ hidden in ~apetecer~ still carries that ancient sense of flying toward what one wants.
en.representar:
From Latin ~repraesentāre~ (“to make present, to bring before one, to display”), from ~re-~ + ~praesentāre~ (“to present”), from the adjective ~praesens~ (“present, at hand”). ~praesens~ is itself ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) plus a participle of ~esse~ (“to be”) — literally, “being before” one's eyes. Spanish took the learned ~representar~ from Latin, alongside the noun ~representación~. Cognate with Italian ~rappresentare~, French ~représenter~, Portuguese ~representar~, and, through Old French, English ~represent~.

The core image is theatrical and literal at once: to ~representar~ is to make something ~praesens~ — present again, brought back before the eyes — whether a lawyer standing in for a client, an actor embodying a role, or a sign standing for a thing. Latin ~repraesentāre~ also meant “to pay on the spot, in cash,” the immediacy of ready money. From ~praesens~ and ~esse~ Spanish gathered ~presente~, ~presencia~, ~representante~, and ~ausente~ (“absent,” from ~ab-~ + the same participle), the mirror image of being there.
en.requerir:
From Latin ~requīrere~ (“to seek again, to ask for, to need”), from ~re-~ (“again, back”) + ~quaerere~ (“to seek, to ask”). The Old Spanish form was ~requerir~, remodeled on the many ~-quirere~ compounds. The origin of ~quaerere~ itself is uncertain: it is usually traced to Proto-Italic *~kʷaizō~ and a Proto-Indo-European *~kʷeh₂-~ (“to acquire”), though older proposals connected it instead to roots meaning “to seek” or “to see.” Cognate compounds gave English ~require~, ~acquire~, and ~inquire~, and the base survives in Spanish ~querer~ and French ~quérir~.

~quaerere~ meant “to seek,” and its ~re-~ intensified that into “to seek insistently, to demand” — the sense modern ~requerir~ keeps when a law or a task “requires” something of us. The plain verb took a startling turn on Spanish soil: it became ~querer~, “to want, to love,” so the Latin idea of seeking softened into Spanish desiring. From the same family come ~cuestión~ (“question”), ~pesquisa~ (“inquiry”), ~encuesta~ (“survey”), ~adquirir~, and ~conquistar~.
en.resolver:
From Latin ~resolvere~ (“to loosen, untie, dissolve, break up”), a compound of ~re-~ (“un-, back”) and ~solvere~ (“to loosen, release, dissolve”). ~solvere~ itself is contracted from *~se-luere~ — ~se-~ (“apart”) plus the verb ~luere~ (“to loosen, release”) — going back to Proto-Indo-European *~leu-~ (“to loosen, divide, cut apart”). The same root gave Greek ~lýein~ (“to loosen, untie”), the source of the ~-lysis~ in analysis, and, through Germanic, English ~loose~ and ~lose~; the learned Latin branch gave English ~solve~. Beside the learned ~resolver~, Spanish also kept a fully popular descendant of ~solvere~: the everyday ~soltar~ (“to let go, release”).

The metaphor beneath ~resolver~ is physical: to un-loosen a knot. From untying a literal tangle the verb moved to dissolving a substance, then to clearing up a difficulty and finally to reaching a firm decision — the modern senses “to solve,” “to resolve,” and “to decide.” Spanish spread the ~solvere~ family widely: ~solución~ (“solution,” originally a loosening or dissolving), ~disolver~ (“to dissolve”), ~absolver~ (“to absolve,” to loosen someone from guilt), ~resolución~, and the popular ~soltar~ with its past participle ~suelto~ (“loose, free”). A ~resolución~ and a knot ~suelto~ are, etymologically, the same act: something once bound has been let go.
en.respetar:
From Latin ~respectare~ (“to look back at, to regard”), a frequentative of ~respicere~ (“to look back, to consider”), from ~re-~ (“back”) and ~specere~ (“to look at”), from Proto-Indo-European *~spek-~ (“to observe”). Spanish ~respetar~ is a semi-learned form; the fully learned doublet ~respectar~ (“to concern, to regard”) survives mainly in the phrase ~respecto a~. It is cognate with English ~respect~, Italian ~rispettare~ and Portuguese ~respeitar~.

The literal core is to look again, to turn one’s gaze back toward something worth a second look — and from that repeated regard grew the moral sense of holding a person or thing in esteem. The two Spanish doublets split the labor: ~respetar~ took the ethical meaning, ~respectar~ the neutral “to concern.” The same root *~spek-~ is enormously productive, giving ~espectáculo~, ~aspecto~, ~inspeccionar~, ~espejo~ (from ~speculum~) and even ~espía~.
en.responder:
From Latin ~respondēre~ (“to answer; to promise in return”), from ~re-~ (“back”) and ~spondēre~ (“to pledge, promise solemnly”), from Proto-Italic *~spondeō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~spend-~ (“to make an offering, perform a rite”). Cognates fill Romance — Italian ~rispondere~, French ~répondre~, Portuguese ~responder~ — and reach English ~respond~; Ancient Greek ~σπένδω~ (“to pour a libation”) shares the root, as, through the participle, does English ~spouse~.

The buried image is ritual: ~spondēre~ was to make a solemn pledge, first sworn over a libation poured to the gods — exactly the sense of Greek ~σπένδω~ — so to respond is to pledge back, to meet a promise with a promise. From the participle ~sponsus~/~sponsa~ (“the betrothed, the promised one”) Spanish drew ~esposo~ and ~esposa~ (“husband, wife”). Strikingly, ~esposas~ also means “handcuffs,” the binding ones — the same notion of being bound by a pledge. Kin include ~respuesta~, ~responsable~, and ~corresponder~.
en.resultar:
From Latin ~resultāre~ (“to spring back, to rebound”), the frequentative of ~resilīre~ (“to leap back”), from ~re-~ (“back”) plus ~salīre~ (“to leap, to jump”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sel-~ (“to jump”). Cognate with French ~résulter~, Italian ~risultare~, and English ~result~ and ~resilient~ — the latter still carrying the sense of springing back.

The metaphor is athletic: a result is what leaps out or rebounds from a set of circumstances, the way a ball bounces off a wall. Classical Latin ~resultāre~ could even mean “to echo,” sound rebounding from a surface. From the same ~salīre~ Spanish inherited a whole leaping family: ~saltar~ (“to jump”), ~salir~ (“to go out,” originally to leap forth), ~resaltar~ (“to stand out”), ~asaltar~ (“to assault,” to leap upon), and ~sobresalir~ (“to excel,” to leap above). Every outcome, etymologically, is a little rebound.
en.retirar:
From ~re-~ (“back, again”) + ~tirar~ (“to pull, throw”), reinforced by French ~retirer~, from which English ~retire~ also descends. The base ~tirar~ is common to the western Romance languages — Italian ~tirare~, French ~tirer~, Portuguese ~tirar~ — yet its ultimate origin is one of the most stubborn puzzles in Romance etymology. Corominas calls it deeply obscure and declines to settle it: no Latin etymon accounts for the whole family cleanly. Among the proposals he weighs are a Germanic ~teran~ (“to tear, rend”), championed by Diez, and a formation in Roman military slang from an Iranian word for “arrow” (~tir~), used by the Parthian archers who harried the legions. Both remain speculative.

In Spanish the prefixed ~retirar~ layered the notion of “back” onto “pull,” yielding “to pull back, withdraw” — a hand, a troop, an offer, or oneself into solitude. From that grew the reflexive ~retirarse~ (“to withdraw, go to bed, retire from work”) and the nouns ~retiro~ (“retreat, seclusion, retirement pension”) and ~retirada~ (“a military retreat”). The same restless base ~tirar~ radiated across the language into ~tiro~ (“a shot”), ~tirón~ (“a yank”), ~tirador~ (“shooter; handle”), and ~estirar~ (“to stretch”). It is a fitting irony that a verb all about pulling things definitively into place should have an origin no etymologist has ever managed to pin down.
en.reunir:
From the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and ~unir~ (“to unite”), itself from Latin ~ūnīre~ (“to make one, join together”), from ~ūnus~ (“one”), from Proto-Indo-European *~óynos~ (“one, single”). Cognate with French ~réunir~ and Italian ~riunire~; through ~ūnus~ it is kin to English ~unite~ and, from the same root, the humble ~one~.

The composition is transparent: to ~reunir~ is literally to “one again” — to make separate things one once more, hence to gather or bring together. The Latin ~ūnus~ was extraordinarily productive, and Spanish reaps the harvest: ~unión~ (“union”), ~unidad~ (“unity”), ~uno~ (“one”), ~único~ (“only, unique”), and even ~universo~ (“universe”), from ~ūniversus~, literally “turned into one.” The reflexive ~reunirse~ (“to meet, get together”) and the noun ~reunión~ (“meeting”) are the verb’s everyday faces.
en.revelar:
From Latin ~revēlāre~ (“to unveil, uncover”), a compound of ~re-~ (here “un-, reversal”) and ~vēlāre~ (“to veil, cover”), from ~vēlum~ (“a veil, cloth, sail”). The deep root of ~vēlum~ is disputed: it goes back to a Proto-Italic *~wekslom~, which some derive from Proto-Indo-European *~weg-~ (“to weave”) — making it kin to English ~wick~ (“candle wick”) — while others trace it instead to *~weǵʰ-~ (“to convey, ride”), i.e. “that which drives (a ship),” a hypothesis that would tie it to Proto-Slavic ~veslo~ (“oar”). The sources do not settle the question, so the veil-versus-sail ancestry is best left open. Spanish inherited the word learnedly; its Romance siblings include French ~révéler~ and Italian ~rivelare~, and, from the same ~vēlum~, French ~voile~ and English ~veil~.

Semantically ~revelar~ is transparent: to pull the ~vēlum~ off something so it can be seen — hence “to reveal, disclose.” Religion supplied its loftiest use: divine ~revelación~ is truth unveiled, and the last book of the New Testament, the Apocalypse, is literally an “un-covering.” Spanish then handed the verb a strikingly modern job: in photography, ~revelar~ is “to develop” film — to coax the latent, hidden image out from behind its chemical veil into the light. Two cautions for learners. First, ~revelar~ (“reveal”) is a near-homophone of ~rebelar~ (“to rebel”), spelled with a b and wholly unrelated. Second, its own family is easy to see: ~velo~ (“veil”), ~velar~ (“to veil; to keep vigil”), ~desvelar~ (“to unveil; to keep awake”), and ~revelación~.
en.revisar:
A learned formation from Latin ~revīsus~, participle of ~revīsere~ (“to look back at, to visit again”), or equally analyzable as Spanish ~re-~ (“again”) + ~visar~. Either way it rests on Latin ~vidēre~ (“to see”), through its frequentative ~vīsere~ / ~vīsāre~. ~vidēre~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”). Cognate with French ~réviser~ and English ~revise~, and — through ~vidēre~ — with English ~vision~, ~view~, and ~evident~.

The prefix ~re-~ carries the whole meaning: to ~revisar~ is to “see again” — to look a second time in order to check, correct, or update. Spanish uses it for everything from proofreading a text to a mechanic servicing a car to a doctor giving a check-up. The PIE root *~weyd-~ was famously double-sided, meaning both “to see” and, in the perfect, “to have seen” hence “to know” — the same pairing that links Latin ~vidēre~ (“to see”) to Greek ~oîda~ (“I know”) and English ~wit~ and ~wise~. From ~vidēre~ Spanish drew ~ver~ (“to see”), ~vista~ (“sight, view”), ~visión~, ~revista~ (“magazine,” something looked over again and again), ~aviso~, and ~evidente~.
en.rodear:
A Spanish formation from the noun ~rueda~ (“wheel”) plus the verbal suffix ~-ear~, so at root “to wheel around” something. ~rueda~ itself comes from Latin ~rota~ (“wheel”), from Proto-Indo-European *~Hroth₂o-~ (“wheel”), a derivative of *~ret-~ (“to run, to roll”). The word is widespread: cognate with German ~Rad~ (“wheel”) and Sanskrit ~rátha~ (“chariot”), while Latin ~rotundus~ yielded Spanish ~redondo~ (“round”) and English ~rotate~.

To ~rodear~ is to trace a circle about a thing — to surround, or to take the long way round. The noun ~rodeo~ names exactly that “going around”: a roundabout route, an evasion, or the cattle roundup in which riders circle the herd — the sense English borrowed wholesale as ~rodeo~. The wheel-root spun off a wide Spanish family besides: ~rodar~ (“to roll”), ~rotar~, ~rodillo~ (“roller”), and ~rótula~ (“kneecap”).
en.romper:
Spanish ~romper~ descends directly from Latin ~rumpere~ (“to break, burst”), inherited through Vulgar Latin with regular loss of the nasal before the plosive. The Latin verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~Hrewp-~ (“to break”), its present formed with a nasal infix. It is cognate with Italian ~rompere~, French ~rompre~, and Portuguese ~romper~, and — through the same root — with Sanskrit ~lumpáti~ (“breaks”) and, more distantly, with the English words below.

Latin ~rumpere~ was extraordinarily productive in prefixed compounds, and English borrowed the lot from its participle ~ruptus~: ~rupture~, ~erupt~, ~corrupt~, ~interrupt~, ~abrupt~, and ~disrupt~. Spanish kept a parallel learned family beside the everyday ~romper~: ~ruptura~ (“rupture”), ~corromper~ (“to corrupt”), ~interrumpir~ (“to interrupt”), and ~irrumpir~ (“to burst in”). A pleasant survival is ~rompeolas~ (“breakwater”), literally “it breaks waves,” preserving the raw physical force of the original verb.
en.saber:
From Vulgar Latin *~sapēre~, a reshaping of Latin ~sapere~ (“to taste; to have good sense, to be wise”), from Proto-Italic *~sapjō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~seh₁p-~ (“to taste, to perceive”). The verb runs straight across Romance as Italian ~sapere~, French ~savoir~, and Portuguese ~saber~; English carries the same root in the borrowings ~sapient~, ~savor~, ~insipid~ (“without taste”), and ~sage~ (“wise”).

The metaphor inside the word is that of the palate: to know is to have tasted, to have discernment — the tongue standing in for the mind. Latin already ran both senses side by side, and Spanish kept the double life, since ~saber~ still means both “to know” and “to taste” (« esta sopa sabe a ajo », “this soup tastes of garlic”). From the same root grew ~sabio~ (“wise; a sage”), ~sabor~ (“flavor”), ~sabroso~ (“tasty”), ~sabiduría~ (“wisdom”), and the adjective ~sabihondo~ (“know-it-all”). Spanish neatly distinguishes ~saber~ (to know a fact) from ~conocer~ (to be acquainted with).
en.sacar:
Modern Spanish ~sacar~ descends from Old Spanish ~sacar~, but its ultimate origin is genuinely disputed. By the account Corominas favors, it comes from Gothic ~sakan~ (“to quarrel, dispute, accuse at law”), a Germanic legal term: to ~sacar~ would first have meant to obtain something by winning a lawsuit, and only later to extract or take out in general. A competing account instead links it to Medieval Latin ~saccāre~ and to ~saccus~ (“sack”) — from Greek ~sákkos~, itself a Semitic loan — imagining the act of pulling goods out of a bag. The earliest Castilian traces are Latinized forms like ~saccāre~ in tenth-century documents. Portuguese ~sacar~ (“to draw out; to draw a weapon or withdraw money”) matches the Spanish form closely, and the two languages share the ambiguity of the source.

Because the origin is unsettled, the vivid legal image — winning by litigation — should be taken as a hypothesis, not a fact. What is clear is the semantic breadth Spanish gave the verb: to take out, extract, withdraw, obtain, and figuratively to deduce (~sacar en claro~) or to snap a photo (~sacar una foto~). From it Spanish built ~sacacorchos~ (“corkscrew”), ~sacapuntas~ (“pencil sharpener”), the noun ~saca~ (“large sack; withdrawal”), and the compound ~entresacar~ (“to pick out, thin out”). The related ~sonsacar~ (“to draw information out of someone, to wheedle”) preserves almost perfectly the notion of extracting something someone would rather keep — whichever of the two etymologies proves right.
en.salir:
From Latin ~salīre~ (“to jump, leap, spring”), from Proto-Italic *~saljō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~sel-~ (“to spring, jump”). The same root gave Ancient Greek ~hállomai~ (“to leap”) and, most likely, Sanskrit ~sárati~ (“flows, runs”). Through Latin and French, ~salīre~ furnished English ~salient~ and ~sally~, while its frequentative ~saltāre~ (“to leap repeatedly, dance”) gave Spanish ~saltar~ and Italian ~saltare~.

The leap became a departure. In Vulgar Latin ~salīre~ drifted from “to jump” toward “to jump out, spring forth,” and Old Spanish ~salir~ settled into the everyday “to go out, leave, exit” it has today — a spring of water still ~sale~ from the ground, keeping the old image alive. Its relatives cluster around leaping and springing: ~salto~ (“a jump”), ~saltar~, ~sobresalir~ (“to stand out,” literally to “leap above”), ~salida~ (“exit, departure”) and ~asaltar~ (“to assault,” to leap upon). English ~assault~ and ~somersault~ leap from the very same Latin verb.
en.saltar:
From Latin ~saltāre~ (“to dance, leap”), the frequentative of ~salīre~ (“to jump, spring”), from Proto-Italic *~saliō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~sel-~ (“to jump”). Cognate with Italian ~saltare~, French ~sauter~ and Portuguese ~saltar~, and — through ~salīre~ — with English ~salient~, ~sally~ and the ~-sault~ of ~assault~ and ~somersault~.

Because ~saltāre~ was the “leap again and again” of a dancer, Latin used it for dancing as well as jumping; Spanish took the leaping sense and let the noun ~baile~ carry dancing. A ~somersault~ hides the etymology neatly: it is “a leap over,” from ~suprā~ (“over”) + ~saltus~ (“a jump”). From the same root Spanish gathers ~salto~, ~saltamontes~ (literally “leap-hills”), ~sobresaltar~ and ~resaltar~.
en.salvar:
From Late Latin ~salvāre~ (“to save, make safe”), a verb built on Latin ~salvus~ (“safe, whole, unharmed”), from Proto-Indo-European *~solh₂-~ (“whole, every”). Cognate with Italian ~salvare~, French ~sauver~, and Portuguese ~salvar~. English ~save~ and ~safe~ both descend, through Old French, from ~salvus~, as does ~salvage~; and through the same PIE root the Latin adjective is cognate with Ancient Greek ~hólos~ (“whole”), source of the ~holo-~ in “holograph.”

The root idea is wholeness: to save is to keep something entire and unharmed. Latin ~salvus~ gave the greeting ~salvē~ (“be well, hail”), and the interjection survives in Spanish ~salve~. Christianity gave ~salvar~ its theological weight — ~salvación~ (“salvation”), ~Salvador~ (“Savior”) — beside the everyday senses of rescuing and the computing sense of saving a file. The family is wide: ~salvo~ (“safe; except”), ~a salvo~ (“in safety”), ~salvavidas~ (“lifeguard, life preserver”), ~salvoconducto~ (“safe-conduct”), and ~salvaguardar~ (“to safeguard”). The noun ~salud~ (“health”), from the related ~salūs~, springs from the same idea of being whole and sound.
en.satisfacer:
From Latin ~satisfacere~ (“to do enough, satisfy”), a compound of ~satis~ (“enough”) and ~facere~ (“to do, make”). ~satis~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~seh₂-~ (“to satiate, be full”) and ~facere~ to *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place, do”). Cognate with Italian ~soddisfare~, French ~satisfaire~, and Portuguese ~satisfazer~; English took ~satisfy~ through Old French. Surprisingly, English ~sad~ belongs to the same *~seh₂-~ family — its original sense was “sated, full” — while ~facere~ shares its root with English ~do~.

The compound is transparent: to satisfy a debt, a creditor, or a hunger is to do (~facere~) enough (~satis~) to meet it. Roman law used ~satisfacere~ for discharging an obligation, and that legal weight survives in the modern range of ~satisfacer~ — to satisfy a person, a requirement, or a curiosity. Like ~hacer~, it conjugates irregularly (~satisfago~, ~satisfizo~, ~satisfaré~). Its family includes ~satisfacción~, ~satisfactorio~, and the past participle ~satisfecho~ (“satisfied, content”). From ~satis~ alone Spanish also drew ~saciar~ (“to sate”) and ~saturar~ (“to saturate”), and the archaic ~asaz~ (“enough”), from ~ad~ ~satis~.
en.seguir:
From Vulgar Latin *~sequēre~, a reshaping of the Latin deponent ~sequī~ (“to follow”), from Proto-Italic *~sekʷōr~, from Proto-Indo-European *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”). The root is deep and wide: cognate with Sanskrit ~sácate~, Ancient Greek ~hépomai~ (“I follow”), and, in the Romance line, Italian ~seguire~, French ~suivre~, and Portuguese ~seguir~. English draws on the same root through Latin borrowings like ~sequence~, ~sequel~, ~second~, and ~pursue~.

Beyond plain “to follow,” Spanish ~seguir~ took on “to continue, to keep on” — « sigo esperando », “I’m still waiting” — so the verb tracks both a person and an action through time. The prefixed compounds are especially productive: ~conseguir~ (“to obtain,” literally to follow through to the end), ~perseguir~ (“to pursue, to persecute”), ~proseguir~ (“to carry on”), and ~subsiguiente~ (“subsequent”). From the same PIE root, through other Latin stems, Spanish also inherited ~secuencia~, ~consecuencia~, ~séquito~ (“retinue”), and ~ejecutar~ (“to execute”).
en.seleccionar:
From the noun ~selección~ (“selection”), a learned borrowing of Latin ~sēlēctiō~ (“a picking out, choice”), the action noun of ~sēligere~ (“to pick out, select”). ~sēligere~ is itself a compound of ~sē-~ (“apart, aside”) and ~legere~ (“to gather, collect,” later “to read”). ~legere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, collect”). The root’s most famous cognate is Ancient Greek ~légō~ (“I gather; I say”) and its offspring ~lógos~ (“word, reason”). The verb ~seleccionar~ itself is a modern denominal — Spanish built it from ~selección~ rather than inheriting it whole — paralleled by Italian ~selezionare~, French ~sélectionner~ and Portuguese ~selecionar~.

The heart of the word is ~legere~’s gathering: to select is to gather items apart from the rest, picking out the chosen few. That gathering-and-choosing sense radiates widely. From ~legere~ Spanish holds ~leer~ (“to read,” gathering letters with the eye), ~elegir~ (“to choose”), ~colegir~ (“to infer, gather”), ~colección~ (“collection”), ~elección~ (“election”), ~lector~ (“reader”) and ~legible~ (“legible”). The same root, through Latin ~intellegere~ (“to discern, gather between”) and ~dīligere~ (“to single out, esteem”), gave ~inteligente~ and ~diligente~. And through Greek ~lógos~ it seeded the whole family of ~-logía~ sciences. To ~seleccionar~ a team, then, is to do in the stadium what a reader does on the page: gather the best and set them apart.
en.sentar:
From Vulgar Latin *~sedentāre~, a verb built on ~sedēns~ (genitive ~sedentis~), the present participle of Latin ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sed-~ (“to sit”). That root is one of the most widespread in the family: it gave English ~sit~ and ~seat~ (via Old English ~sittan~), German ~sitzen~, and the Latin ~sedēre~ that also partly underlies Spanish ~ser~. Portuguese ~sentar~ and Italian ~sedere~ are Romance kin.

Spanish turned the participle into a fresh verb: *~sedentāre~ meant “to cause to be sitting,” which is exactly what ~sentar~ does — you ~sientas~ a guest at the table. The same “sit” root produced a large and varied family: ~sede~ (“seat, see”), ~sesión~ (“a sitting”), ~sedimento~ (what settles), ~sedentario~, ~asentar~, ~presidir~ (“to sit in front of”) and ~residir~. Even ~silla~ (“chair”) descends, through ~sella~, from this root.
en.sentir:
From Latin ~sentīre~ (“to feel, perceive, be of an opinion”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sent-~, reconstructed with the sense “to head for, go, find one’s way.” It is cognate with Italian ~sentire~, Portuguese ~sentir~ and French ~sentir~, and — through the same Latin verb — with English ~sense~, ~sentiment~ and ~scent~; through Germanic the root also gives English ~send~ and German ~Sinn~ (“sense, mind”) and ~senden~ (“to send”).

The semantic leap from “to go” to “to feel” is striking: to perceive was, on this reconstruction, to “find one’s way” mentally toward a thing — to discern it. Latin ~sentīre~ already spanned bodily sensation, emotion and judgment, a breadth Spanish ~sentir~ keeps (“to feel” and “to be sorry”). From the same stem come ~sentido~ (“sense, meaning”), ~sentimiento~ (“feeling”), ~sensación~ (via ~sēnsus~), ~consentir~ (“to consent”), ~presentir~ (“to have a foreboding”) and ~sensato~ (“sensible”).
en.separar:
Spanish ~separar~ comes from Latin ~sēparāre~ (“to pull apart, divide”), a compound of ~sē-~ (“apart, aside”) and ~parāre~ (“to make ready, prepare”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to produce, procure”). Cognates include Italian ~separare~, French ~séparer~, and Portuguese ~separar~; and from ~parāre~ alone come Spanish ~parar~ and ~preparar~ and English ~prepare~.

The image behind ~sēparāre~ is homely: to “make ready apart,” to arrange things each on its own side. From Latin, French produced a second, popularized descendant, ~sevrer~ (“to wean”), and English borrowed its Frenchified doublet ~sever~ (“to cut off”), so ~separate~ and ~sever~ are ultimately the same word wearing different clothes. English ~several~ (“distinct,” then “more than one”) belongs to the family too. Spanish descendants cluster thickly: ~separación~ (“separation”), ~inseparable~ (“inseparable”), ~separata~ (“offprint”), and the noun ~separo~ used in Mexico for a holding cell.
en.ser:
Spanish ~ser~ descends, in its commonest forms, from Latin ~esse~ (“to be”), which reaches back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₁es-~ (“to be”). That root also gave Italian ~essere~, French ~être~, and the English verb itself — ~is~ and ~am~ — as well as German ~ist~. From the Latin present ~esse~ Spanish keeps ~soy~, ~es~, and ~son~; but the paradigm is famously stitched together, and several of its everyday forms descend not from ~esse~ at all.

The present indicative (~soy~, ~eres~, ~es~, ~somos~, ~sois~, ~son~) and the imperfect (~era~, from Latin ~eram~) continue ~esse~ — though ~eres~ is a curiosity, descending from the Latin future ~eris~ (“you will be”), pressed into a present to keep it distinct from ~es~. A second donor, ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), from *~sed-~, supplied the infinitive ~ser~ itself (through Old Spanish ~seer~), the future and conditional (~seré~, ~sería~), the present subjunctive (~sea~), and the imperative (~sé~) — so the very name of the verb means, etymologically, “to sit.” A third donor, the Latin perfect ~fuī~, from *~bʰuH-~ (“to become, grow”), gave the preterite (~fui~, ~fuiste~, ~fue~) — forms shared identically with ~ir~ (“to go”), so that ~fui~ means both “I was” and “I went,” context alone deciding.

From the ~esse~ / *~h₁es-~ side comes a wide family of learned words: ~ente~, ~esencia~, ~presente~, ~ausente~, and ~interés~. From ~sedēre~ (“to sit”) comes another cluster built on the idea of sitting or settling: ~sede~ (“seat, see”), ~sentar~, ~sesión~, and ~residir~. The suppletion that looks so chaotic in the paradigm is, in the vocabulary, two tidy word-families braided into one verb.
en.servir:
From Latin ~servīre~ (“to be a slave, to serve”), derived from ~servus~ (“slave, servant”). There the trail grows faint: the origin of ~servus~ is uncertain. It is usually traced to Proto-Italic *~serwos~ and compared with Umbrian ~seritu~, and it has sometimes been proposed as an Etruscan borrowing, but no account is secure, so the deeper root is best left open. The verb passed intact into Italian ~servire~, French ~servir~, and Portuguese ~servir~.

In Rome ~servīre~ meant literally to live in bondage; as that social reality faded, the word softened into today's neutral senses of waiting on someone, serving food, and — in ~servir~ para algo — simply being useful. A caution for the curious: Latin ~servāre~ (“to keep, to guard”), the source of ~conservar~ and ~observar~, springs from a different root and is not a relative, despite the resemblance. The genuine family of ~servus~ includes ~siervo~, ~servicio~, ~servil~, ~servidumbre~, and ~servidor~; its present participle ~servientem~ gave both Spanish ~sirviente~ and, by a long detour through French, English ~sergeant~.
en.señalar:
A denominative from ~señal~ (“sign, mark, signal”), which comes from Late Latin ~signālis~ (“of a sign”), from Latin ~signum~ (“mark, sign, military standard”). The root of ~signum~ is genuinely disputed: one account derives it from Proto-Indo-European *~sek-~ (“to cut”), making a sign “something cut or carved”; another from *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow,” as in Latin ~sequī~), making it “the standard the troops follow.” The forms are cognate with Italian ~segnalare~, French ~signaler~ and English ~signal~ and ~sign~.

From ~signālis~ Spanish built the noun ~señal~ and then the verb ~señalar~, “to mark” and hence “to point out, indicate.” Because the deeper origin is unsettled, the vivid “a sign is something carved” reading should be offered only as one contested hypothesis, not as fact. The same ~signum~ radiates through Spanish: ~seña~ (“gesture, sign”), ~signo~, ~diseñar~ (“to design,” via Italian) and, most surprisingly, ~enseñar~ (“to teach”), from Latin ~īnsignāre~, literally “to mark in, imprint.”
en.significar:
Spanish ~significar~ was borrowed from Latin ~significāre~ (“to make a sign, to indicate”), a transparent compound of ~signum~ (“sign, mark, token”) and ~-ficāre~, the combining form of ~facere~ (“to make, do,” from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~, “to put, place”). So the word means, literally, “to make a sign.” The deeper root of ~signum~ itself is disputed: it is traced to Proto-Italic *~seknom~ and thence either to Proto-Indo-European *~sek-~ (“to cut”) or to *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”), and the sources do not settle between them. It is cognate with Italian ~significare~, French ~signifier~ and English ~signify~.

If ~signum~ began as a “cut” mark or a “follow” token, both readings suit a sign — a notch scored into a surface, or the trail one follows. From “to make a sign” the verb moved naturally to “to be a sign of,” that is “to mean”; a word ~significa~ something the way a symptom signifies a disease. The ~signum~ family is one of the richest in Spanish. Popular descent gave ~seña~ (“sign”), ~señal~ (“signal”) and ~señalar~ (“to point out”); learned borrowing gave ~signo~, ~significado~ (“meaning”), ~insignia~, and — through ~dēsignāre~ — ~diseñar~ (“to design”). All of them are still, at heart, about setting down a mark that stands for something else.
en.situar:
From Late Latin ~situāre~ (“to place, locate, set in position”), formed on Latin ~situs~ (“site, position, situation”), which is the past participle of the verb ~sinere~ (“to let, allow; to set down, lay”). De Vaan traces ~sinere~ to a Proto-Indo-European root *~tḱey-~ (“to settle, build”), the same root behind Sanskrit ~kṣéti~ (“he dwells”). Because ~situs~ passed into the Romance languages and into learned Latin borrowings alike, its offspring are widespread: English ~site~ and ~situate~, French ~site~, Italian ~sito~, and Portuguese ~sítio~ all stand beside Spanish ~sitio~.

The chain hides a quiet irony: ~sinere~ meant “to let be, leave alone,” so a ~situs~ was first a place where something had simply been left — and one old sense of Latin ~situs~ was precisely the “neglect, mold, decay” that settles on a thing left untouched. Medieval clerks turned the noun back into the verb ~situāre~, “to give a thing its place,” and Spanish inherited it as ~situar~. From the same noun Spanish keeps ~sitio~ (“place; also a military siege,” a spot one occupies and holds) and ~situación~ (“situation”), while the reflexive ~situarse~ means to find or position oneself. What began as land left to itself became the vocabulary of putting things deliberately in their place.
en.soler:
Spanish ~soler~ was inherited through Old Spanish ~soler~ from Latin ~solēre~ (“to be accustomed, to be wont”). Its deeper origin is disputed. One tradition (Walde-Hoffmann, Pokorny) reconstructs Proto-Italic *~sweðēō~ and a Proto-Indo-European *~swé-dʰh₁-~, literally “to set as one's own,” from *~swé~ (“self”) plus *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place”); on this account ~solēre~ would be close kin to ~sodālis~ (“companion”) and ~suēscō~ (“to grow accustomed”). De Vaan rejects that derivation on sound grounds — a following ~ē~ should have blocked the shift *~swe-~ > ~so-~ — and looks instead toward *~sel-~ / ~solum~ (“ground, base”). The safe statement is that ~solēre~ is old and its ultimate root unsettled. It is cognate with Italian ~solere~ and Catalan ~soler~, and with the now-archaic Portuguese ~soer~.

In Spanish ~soler~ became a pure habit-marker, an auxiliary that adds “usually” to whatever verb follows: ~suele~ llover (“it usually rains”), ~solíamos~ caminar (“we used to walk”). Fittingly for a verb about the customary, it is itself defective, living almost entirely in the present and the imperfect — one rarely meets it in the future or the preterite, because a one-off habit is a contradiction. The “custom” sense is preserved beautifully in a common relative: ~insólito~ (“unusual, extraordinary”), from Latin ~insolitus~, literally “un-accustomed” — what does not usually happen. Beside it stand the rarer ~sólito~ (“customary”) and ~desueto~ / ~desuetud~ (“disused, desuetude”). Thus a single Latin verb of habit gave Spanish both its everyday word for “to usually do” and its bookish word for what breaks all habit.
en.solicitar:
Spanish ~solicitar~ comes from Latin ~sollicitāre~ (“to disturb, stir up, agitate”), a verb built on the adjective ~sollicitus~ (“thoroughly moved, anxious, worried”). That adjective is transparent: ~sollus~ (“whole, entire”) plus ~citus~ (“set in motion, roused”), the past participle of ~ciēre~ (“to move, stir”). ~sollus~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~solh₂-~ (“whole”), the root behind Greek ~hólos~ (“whole,” as in ~holo-~) and Latin ~salvus~ (“safe”); ~ciēre~ reflects *~keyh₁-~ (“to set in motion”). English borrowed the family directly: ~solicit~, ~solicitous~, and ~solicitude~ all sit beside the Spanish verb.

The literal Latin sense was physical agitation — to shake something thoroughly, to trouble it entirely. From “to disturb, importune” the meaning softened into “to entreat, petition,” and Spanish ~solicitar~ now spans a polite request (~solicitar una beca~, “to apply for a scholarship”), a formal application, and the still-charged ~solicitar a alguien~ (“to court or proposition someone”), where the old sense of stirring another person up survives. The past participle gave ~solícito~ (“attentive, obliging”) and the noun ~solicitud~ (“request; application; solicitude”). Through the same root *~solh₂-~ Spanish also holds ~sólido~, ~salvo~, ~salud~, and ~católico~ (from Greek ~katholikós~, “universal, on the whole”).
en.someter:
From Latin ~submittere~ (“to place under, lower, let down; to subject”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~mittere~ (“to send, let go”). It is thus a close sibling of ~committere~ above, built on the same ~mittere~, which traces through Proto-Italic *~meitō~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange”), an extension of *~mey-~ (“to change”). Spanish ~someter~ is the inherited reflex; alongside it the language kept learned forms from the participle ~submissus~. Romance cognates include French ~soumettre~ and Italian ~sottomettere~ / ~sommettere~, and English ~submit~ comes from the same ~submittere~.

The literal picture is spatial: to “send under” is to bring beneath one’s power — hence ~someter~ “to subdue, subject, put down (a revolt),” and reflexively ~someterse~ “to submit, yield, give in.” The verb keeps a useful ambiguity English splits between “subdue” (imposing from above) and “submit” (yielding from below), the difference lying only in who does the sending-under. From the participle ~submissus~ came the learned pair ~sumiso~ (“submissive, meek”) and ~sumisión~ (“submission, obedience”), which sit beside ~sometimiento~ (“subjection”) built on the verb. It is a nice symmetry of Latin word-building that ~sub-~ + ~mittere~ (“send under”) and ~com-~ + ~mittere~ (“send together”) should have travelled into Spanish as the near-rhyming ~someter~ and ~cometer~, two prefixes turning one humble verb of “sending” to opposite ends.
en.sonar:
~sonar~ descends from Latin ~sonāre~ (“to make a sound, resound”), a verb from the noun ~sonus~ (“sound, noise”). ~sonus~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~swonos~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~swenh₂-~ (“to sound, resound”). The most charming cognate is English ~swan~: from Proto-Germanic *~swanaz~, literally “the sounding one, the singing bird.” Sanskrit ~svan~ (“to sound”) and Russian ~zvon~ (“chime, ring”) belong to the same family, and English ~sound~ itself is a borrowing of ~sonus~ through Old French.

Spanish kept the plain sense — bells, instruments, and phones all ~sonar~ — plus idiomatic branches: a name that ~suena~ is one that “rings a bell,” and ~sonarse~ (“to blow one's nose”) trades on the noise. From ~sonus~ and ~sonāre~ spring a large family: ~sonido~ (“sound”), ~sonoro~, ~son~ (“tune,” as in the Cuban dance), ~sonata~ (via Italian), ~resonar~, ~consonante~, and ~sonajero~ (“baby's rattle”).
en.sorprender:
Spanish ~sorprender~ came in from French ~surprendre~ (“to overtake, catch unawares”), a compound of ~sur-~ (“over, upon,” from Latin ~super~) and ~prendre~ (“to take”). ~prendre~ continues Latin ~prehendere~ (“to seize, grasp, catch”), itself ~prae-~ (“before”) plus a verbal element ~-hendere~. That ~-hendere~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵʰend-~ (“to seize, take”), whose scattered kin include Greek ~khandánein~ (“to hold, contain”), Old Norse ~geta~ (“to get, obtain”), and, through Germanic, English ~get~ itself. Because Spanish reshaped the French word on the pattern of its own inherited ~prender~ (“to seize, catch; to catch fire”), the family is doubly present in the language — one branch borrowed, one branch inherited.

The metaphor is vivid and physical: to surprise someone is to “take” them from “over” or “above,” catching them before they can react — the same military image that lets ~sorprender~ mean “to take by surprise, ambush.” From the astonishment sense grew the noun ~sorpresa~ (“a surprise”) and the adjective ~sorprendente~ (“surprising, astonishing”). The inherited ~prender~ side of the family is one of the richest in Spanish: ~prisión~ (“prison”) and ~preso~/~presa~ (“prisoner; prey”) for the “seizing,” ~aprender~ (“to learn,” to “grasp” knowledge), ~comprender~ (“to understand,” to grasp fully), ~emprender~ (“to undertake”), and ~prenda~ (“a garment; a pledge”). English ~prehensile~ and ~comprehend~ preserve the fuller Latin ~-hendere~ that French and Spanish wore away.
en.sostener:
From Latin ~sustinēre~ (“to hold up, support, endure”), from ~sus-~ (a form of ~sub-~, “under, up from under”) plus ~tenēre~ (“to hold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Cognate with Italian ~sostenere~, French ~soutenir~, and — through Old French — English ~sustain~.

The image is physical: to hold a thing up from below, and from there to support, maintain, and endure. Spanish ~sostener~ still spans all of these — the same ~sostener~ holds a weight, an argument, or a conversation. The ~tenēre~ core, from *~ten-~ “to stretch,” is one of the most fertile in Spanish, giving ~tener~ (“to have”), ~mantener~ (“to maintain”), ~contener~ (“to contain”), ~detener~ (“to stop”), the noun ~sostén~ (“support”), and — from the “stretched” sense — ~tenso~ and ~tenaz~.
en.subir:
From Latin ~subīre~ (“to go under; to come up, approach; to undergo”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“under, up from below”) and ~īre~ (“to go”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”). The Romance descendants split in meaning: Portuguese ~subir~ climbs like Spanish, while Italian ~subire~ means “to undergo, to suffer,” keeping the older “come under” sense.

The paradox is that a verb built on ~sub-~ (“under”) means “to go up.” The bridge is the idea of coming up from underneath, approaching from below — Latin ~subīre~ could mean both “to go under” and “to steal up on.” Spanish generalized the upward reading, so today one ~sube~ a staircase or a price. The same ~sub-~-plus-~īre~ formation gave ~súbito~ (“sudden” — literally “having come up unawares”), and ~īre~ itself seeded ~éxito~ (“success,” a “going out”), ~tránsito~ and ~ambiente~.
en.suceder:
From Latin ~succēdere~ (“to go under, come up from below, follow after, take the place of”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“under, up from below”) and ~cēdere~ (“to go, move, withdraw, yield”). ~cēdere~ comes through Proto-Italic *~kesd-o-~ (“to go away, withdraw”) from a Proto-Indo-European root *~ked-~ (“to go, yield”). Through it ~suceder~ is cognate with a whole rank of English verbs built on ~cēdere~ — ~cede~, ~concede~, ~proceed~, ~recede~, and ~succeed~ itself — and with ~cease~, from the related ~cessāre~. Italian ~succedere~ and French ~succéder~ are its Romance doubles.

The literal picture is of one thing moving up into the place another has vacated — which is why ~succēdere~ meant at once “to follow after” and “to take over from.” Spanish kept the ‘follow/inherit’ thread in ~sucesor~ (“successor”) and ~sucesión~, but its most common modern sense drifted further: because what follows in time is what next occurs, ~suceder~ came to mean simply “to happen.” Hence the noun ~suceso~ — not a ‘success’ (that false friend trips English speakers) but an “event, occurrence.” The same ~cēdere~ root threads through ~ceder~ (“to yield”), ~exceder~ (“to exceed”), ~proceder~ (“to proceed”), and ~acceder~ (“to accede”). To ask ¿qué ~sucede~? is to ask what is coming up next from below.
en.sufrir:
From Old Spanish ~sofrir~, from Vulgar Latin *~sufferīre~ (a re-conjugated form), from Latin ~sufferre~ (“to bear up under, endure”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, bear”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, bear”). Romance kept the compound: French ~souffrir~, Italian ~soffrire~, Portuguese ~sofrer~; English borrowed ~suffer~ through Anglo-Norman, while the same root *~bʰer-~ gives inherited English ~bear~.

The image is bodily: ~sufferre~ joins ~sub-~ (“under”) to ~ferre~ (“carry”), so to suffer is to bear a load from beneath, to hold up under weight; the sense drifted from “endure, tolerate” to “undergo pain,” though Spanish ~sufrir~ still keeps the older “put up with.” ~ferre~ was one of Latin's great verb-forges, yielding Spanish ~referir~, ~transferir~, ~preferir~, and even ~ofrecer~ (from ~offerre~), plus the adjective ~fértil~ (“bearing, fruitful”). Through *~bʰer-~ it is a cousin of English ~bear~.
en.sugerir:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~suggerere~ (“to bring up from below, to supply, to prompt”), from ~sub-~ (“under, up from under”) plus ~gerere~ (“to carry, to bear, to conduct”). The deeper origin of ~gerere~ is uncertain; De Vaan tentatively links it to the root of ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”), but the reconstruction is disputed. Spanish took the verb from written Latin, so it is cognate with the equally learned Italian ~suggerire~, French ~suggérer~ and Portuguese ~sugerir~, and — through ~gerere~ — with English ~suggest~, ~gesture~ and ~digest~.

Picture a servant carrying supplies up from a cellar: ~suggerere~ first meant to furnish or supply from below, and only then to put a thought quietly into another's mind — to ~sugerir~ is, etymologically, to slip an idea up under someone's notice. That undertone of prompting survives in the theatre, where the ~suggeritore~ (Italian for the offstage prompter) whispers forgotten lines. The Latin root ~gerere~, “to carry on, to manage,” proved enormously fertile in Spanish: from it and its participle ~gestus~ come ~gesto~, ~gestión~, ~gestionar~, ~sugestión~, ~digerir~, ~registro~ and ~gerente~, a whole vocabulary of bearing, doing and managing.
en.sumar:
Spanish ~sumar~ (“to add, sum up”) was borrowed from Medieval Latin ~summāre~ (“to add up”), from Latin ~summa~ (“sum, total, the whole”), the feminine of the adjective ~summus~ (“highest, topmost”), a superlative connected with ~super~ (“above”) and, ultimately, Proto-Indo-European *~upér~ / *~upo~ (“over, up from under”). It is cognate with Italian ~sommare~, French ~sommer~ and Portuguese ~somar~, and — through Latin borrowings — with English ~sum~, ~summit~ and ~summary~.

Why should “the highest” mean “a total”? By the usual account, the connection is a habit of Roman reckoning: numbers were added in a column and the result written at the top, so the ~summa~ — the “topmost” line — was the whole added up. Whether the Romans really summed from the bottom is not certain, but the metaphor of the total as the “high point” is old and vivid; a ~summa~ was also the crowning “sum” of a subject, as in the medieval ~Summa~ of theology. From ~summus~ Spanish keeps ~sumo~ (“utmost,” as in ~sumo sacerdote~, “high priest”) and ~sumamente~ (“extremely”), while from the verb come ~suma~ (“sum, addition”), ~sumando~ (“addend”) and ~sumario~ (“summary”).
en.superar:
From Latin ~superāre~ (“to rise above, overcome, surpass”), a verb built on ~super~ (“above, over”), from Proto-Indo-European *~upér~ (“over, above”). The same root surfaces in Greek ~hupér~, Sanskrit ~upári~, and — through Germanic — English ~over~. Spanish took ~superar~ as a learned borrowing straight from Latin, keeping ~super~ intact where popular speech wore it down: the fully inherited descendant of the same word is the everyday preposition ~sobre~ (“on, above”), and from Vulgar Latin *~superānus~ came ~soberano~ (“sovereign”). Italian ~superare~ and Portuguese ~superar~ are its direct cousins.

Latin ~superāre~ already meant both to physically top something and to get the better of a rival, and modern Spanish keeps both threads: one ~supera~ an obstacle, a record, or an opponent. From ~super~ the language drew a wide learned family — ~superior~, ~superficie~ (“surface,” literally the face on top), and the vice-name ~soberbia~ (“pride,” from Latin ~superbia~, the fault of setting oneself above others). The living prefix ~super-~ that turns any word into a heightened version of itself is that same Latin element, still doing what it did in Rome.
en.suponer:
Spanish ~suponer~ comes from Latin ~suppōnere~ (“to place under, to substitute”), from ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~pōnere~ (“to put, to place”). ~pōnere~ itself is a contraction of an older ~po-~ (“off, away”) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, to leave”), so “to place” was originally “to set down and leave.” Because Spanish inherited ~pōnere~ as the everyday ~poner~, the compound was reshaped on it. Cognate Romance verbs include French ~supposer~ and Italian ~supporre~.

From “to place under” came the mental sense: to suppose is to lay a proposition down as a foundation to reason from — quite literally to place it beneath an argument. The Latin verb's past participle ~positus~ gave Spanish ~puesto~ (“placed; a post, position”) and spread through a large prefixed family built on ~poner~: ~componer~ (“to compose”), ~proponer~ (“to propose”), ~disponer~ (“to arrange”), ~exponer~ (“to expose”) and ~imponer~ (“to impose”), plus the nouns ~posición~ (“position”) and ~apuesta~ (“a bet,” something put down).
en.surgir:
From Latin ~surgere~ (“to rise, spring up”), a worn-down form of ~surrigere~, itself ~subrigere~, from ~sub-~ (“up from below”) and ~regere~ (“to keep straight, guide”); the ultimate root is Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, direct”). It is cognate with Italian ~sorgere~ and Portuguese ~surgir~, and — through the same root — with English ~surge~ and ~source~, the latter from a French reflex of the same Latin verb.

In Spanish the word arrived first as a sailor's term. According to Corominas, ~surgir~ meant “to ride at anchor, put into harbour” — from the Latin picture of a ship “standing upright,” at rest in port (~navis surgit in portu~), much as ~estar~ (“to stand”) came to mean “to be somewhere.” Only later did the nautical sense broaden into today's “to arise, emerge, well up.” The verb left ~resurgir~ and ~insurgente~ in the language, while its Latin root ~regere~ seeded a large family — ~regir~, ~región~, ~dirigir~, ~corregir~ and ~recto~.
en.tener:
Spanish ~tener~ comes from Latin ~tenēre~ (“to hold, keep, grasp”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”) — holding conceived as keeping something taut in the hand. Its Romance cousins keep the shape: Italian ~tenere~, French ~tenir~, and Portuguese ~ter~. Through the same root, Latin also formed ~tendere~ (“to stretch”) and ~tenuis~ (“thin”), and the root even surfaces in the English ~thin~.

In Latin ~tenēre~ meant simply to hold; Spanish then handed it a much bigger job. As ~haber~ retreated into an auxiliary, ~tener~ stepped in as the ordinary verb of possession — the everyday “I have” of ~tengo hambre~ (“I hold hunger”) and ~tener casa~. The idea of holding fast runs through its descendants: ~contener~ (“to contain”), ~obtener~ (“to obtain”), ~mantener~ (“to maintain”), and the adjective ~tenaz~ (“tenacious”), along with ~teniente~ (“lieutenant,” literally one who holds a place).
en.terminar:
From Latin ~termināre~ (“to bound, to limit”), from ~terminus~ (“boundary, limit, end-marker”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ter-~ (“peg, boundary marker”), seen in the extended form *~ter-men-~. Cognate with Ancient Greek ~térma~ (“goal”) and ~térmōn~ (“border”), and with English ~term~ and ~terminal~.

For the Romans a ~terminus~ was a very concrete thing: a boundary stone set between fields. It was sacred enough to have its own god, ~Terminus~, the deity of boundary markers, honored each February at a festival called the ~Terminalia~. To ~terminar~ something, then, is etymologically to set its limit — to mark where it ends. From the same root Spanish built ~término~ (“term, end”), ~terminal~, ~determinar~ (“to bound thoroughly, to decide”), and ~exterminar~ (“to drive beyond the boundary, to destroy”).
en.tirar:
From Old Spanish ~tirar~, from Vulgar Latin *~tīrāre~, of genuinely uncertain origin — one of the murkiest cases in all of Romance etymology. It is cognate with Italian ~tirare~, French ~tirer~, and Portuguese ~tirar~, all built on the core sense “to pull, to draw.” The verb is old and pan-Romance, yet no one has traced it securely back to classical Latin, and lexicographers have often set it aside as insoluble. Two accounts compete. By one, the word descends from a Germanic source; by the other, favored by Corominas, it arose in Latin military slang from the Parthian word for “arrow” — reconstructed as roughly ~tir~, as in the Iranian dialects — the Parthians being Rome's great archer-enemies on the eastern frontier. Both remain proposals, and the honest verdict is that the origin is disputed.

In Spanish, ~tirar~ spread across a remarkable range of meanings — “to throw,” “to pull,” “to shoot,” “to pull down,” “to print” a run of copies, even “to last” — a semantic breadth that itself hints at an original sense of forceful drawing or launching. If Corominas is right that the arrow lies at its root, the modern sense “to throw” would faintly preserve the flight of a Parthian shaft; but because that etymology is only proposed, this is a suggestive story rather than a proven one. Whatever its source, the verb became one of the most productive in the language, yielding ~tiro~ (“shot”), ~tirada~ (“print run; stretch”), ~tirador~ (“shooter; handle”), ~estirar~ (“to stretch”), and ~retirar~ (“to withdraw”).
en.tocar:
Spanish ~tocar~ descends from Vulgar Latin *~toccāre~ (also *~tuccāre~), “to knock, strike, rap,” whose ultimate origin is uncertain — the sources call it “of Germanic or onomatopoeic origin” and do not decide between the two. The likeliest account is imitative: *~tocc~ as a spoken echo of a sharp tap or knock, the same sound-symbolism that shaped a whole Romance family. It is cognate with Italian ~toccare~, French ~toucher~ and Portuguese ~tocar~, and — borrowed from Old French ~tochier~ — with English ~touch~. There is no secure Indo-European root to reach for here; if the word is onomatopoeic, it never had one.

The development is a small drama of the senses. From “to knock” the verb spread to “to touch” in general, and then — because you strike or pluck an instrument to make it sound — to “to play” music: in Spanish one and the same ~tocar~ covers touching a surface and playing the guitar, and to ~tocar~ a bell is to ring it. Idiom pushed it further still, into “to fall to one's lot” (~me toca a mí~, “it's my turn”). The family it heads is homely and wide: ~toque~ (“a touch; a ringing”), ~tocador~ (“dressing table; player”), ~tocadiscos~ (“record player”), ~tocante~ (“concerning”) and the phrase ~tocar fondo~ (“to hit rock bottom”).
en.tomar:
The origin of ~tomar~ is genuinely uncertain — es.Wiktionary and the DLE label it « de origen incierto ». It appears very early in Spanish (already in the medieval Poema de mio Cid) and has a close counterpart in Portuguese ~tomar~, but no agreed Latin ancestor. Two hypotheses compete. Corominas proposed an aphaeresis from Latin ~autumāre~ (“to assert a claim, affirm”), the initial ~au-~ having worn away, though the meaning fits awkwardly. Another account, associated with Walsh, derives it instead from an alteration of ~domāre~ (“to tame, subdue”), noting that early ~tomar~ worked much like ~apropiar~ (“to appropriate, take possession”). The matter remains debated, and any single story should be taken as a proposal, not settled fact.

Whatever its source, ~tomar~ established itself as one of the most versatile verbs in Spanish, spreading from “to seize, take hold of” into a vast web of senses: to take a road, take a decision, take medicine, and — famously in Spain and much of Latin America — to drink (~tomar algo~, “to have a drink”). This last is a native extension of “take into the body,” not a separate root. Reflexive ~tomarse~ intensifies it (~tomarse un café~, ~tomarse su tiempo~). Because its etymology is unsettled, ~tomar~ has left a smaller word-family than the great Latin verbs, but it did yield the nouns ~toma~ (“a taking; a dose; a film take”) and ~tomadura~, and the compound ~tomavistas~ (“a movie camera,” literally a “view-taker”). Its very obscurity is a reminder that even the commonest words can guard a hidden past.
en.trabajar:
From Old Spanish ~trabajar~ (“to toil, torment”), most often traced to a Vulgar Latin *~tripaliāre~ (“to torture”), from Late Latin ~tripalium~, a frame of three stakes (~tri-~ + ~pālus~, “stake”) used to restrain or torment. Cognate with French ~travailler~, Portuguese ~trabalhar~, Catalan ~treballar~, and Italian ~travagliare~, and with the noun French ~travail~ that gave English ~travail~ and, remarkably, ~travel~.

The oft-repeated tale is vivid — a word for “work” born from an engine of torture — but it should be told with the hedge the sources give it: while the DLE and Corominas do derive ~trabajar~ from ~tripalium~, the exact form of the Vulgar Latin verb and the precise semantic path from “torture” to “labor” remain debated, and some scholars are skeptical of the whole chain. What is clear is the drift attested in the Old Spanish records: from “to torment, suffer,” through “to strive, exert oneself,” to the neutral modern “to work.” English ~travel~ preserves the older bite, journeying once being an ordeal. The verb gave Spanish ~trabajo~ (“work”), ~trabajador~ (“worker”), and ~trabajoso~ (“laborious, arduous”).
en.traer:
From Old Spanish ~traer~ (also ~traher~), from Latin ~trahere~ (“to draw, to drag, to pull”). ~trahere~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root *~tragʰ-~ (“to draw, to drag”). Its Romance reflexes are striking: Italian ~trarre~, Portuguese ~trazer~, and French ~traire~, which — from the sense of “drawing out” — narrowed all the way down to “to milk” a cow. Through Latin loans, ~trahere~ also underlies English ~tract~, ~tractor~, ~trace~, and ~train~.

The core Latin sense was physical: to pull, to haul, to drag toward oneself. Spanish ~traer~ kept exactly that pull — to bring is to draw a thing toward the speaker — and built out an unusually neat family of prefixed verbs, each a different direction of pulling: ~atraer~ (“to attract”), ~contraer~ (“to contract, to draw together”), ~distraer~ (“to distract, to draw away”), ~extraer~ (“to extract”), ~retraer~ (“to retract”), and ~sustraer~ (“to subtract, to withdraw”). The frequentative ~tractāre~ (“to handle, to drag about repeatedly”) gave ~tratar~ (“to treat, to deal with”) and ~tratado~ (“treatise, treaty”), while the participle ~tractus~ left ~retrato~ (“portrait” — a face “drawn” from life) and ~tracción~. Nearly every “draw” in Spanish pulls back to ~trahere~.
en.transformar:
From Latin ~transformare~ (“to change in shape”), a compound of ~trans-~ (“across, over”) and ~formare~ (“to form, to shape”), from the noun ~forma~ (“form, shape, figure”), a word of disputed origin. Spanish took it as a learned borrowing. It is cognate with English ~transform~, Italian ~trasformare~, French ~transformer~ and Portuguese ~transformar~, all continuing the same classical compound.

The literal sense is to carry a form across into another, and Latin poets already used it for metamorphosis, the bodily changes of myth. Spanish keeps both the physical sense — matter that ~transforma~ into energy — and the figurative, an experience that transforms a person. The base ~forma~ is unusually productive: from it and its relatives come ~formar~, ~formación~, ~fórmula~, ~formal~, ~deformar~ and ~reformar~, a whole vocabulary of shaping.
en.transmitir:
From Latin ~transmittere~ (“to send across, to convey”), a compound of ~trans-~ (“across, beyond”) and ~mittere~ (“to send, to let go”). ~mittere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~meitō~; its deeper origin is uncertain, but it is often traced to Proto-Indo-European *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, to remove”), an extension of the root *~mey-~ (“to change”). Spanish took ~transmitir~ as a learned borrowing rather than by unbroken popular descent. It is cognate with Italian ~trasmettere~, French ~transmettre~, Portuguese ~transmitir~, and English ~transmit~, all resting on the same Latin verb.

The literal image in ~transmittere~ is of sending something over or beyond a boundary — across a river, a frontier, a distance — and Spanish ~transmitir~ still carries it: one transmits a disease, a signal, an inheritance, a piece of news, passing it from one point or generation to the next. The rise of radio and television gave the verb its now-dominant broadcasting sense. Because ~mittere~ was extraordinarily prolific in Latin compounds, it seeded a large Spanish family sharing the notion of sending or letting go: ~admitir~, ~emitir~, ~permitir~, ~remitir~, ~someter~, ~mensaje~, and ~misión~.
en.trasladar:
From Latin ~trānslātāre~, a frequentative built on ~trānslātus~ (“carried across”), which served as the suppletive past participle of ~trānsferre~ (“to carry over, transfer”). The compound is ~trāns-~ (“across, beyond”) plus ~lātus~, an old participle meaning “borne, carried” that belonged not to ~ferō~ but to the unrelated verb ~tollō~ (“to lift, raise”); ~lātus~ goes back to *~tlātos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~telh₂-~ (“to bear, carry, endure”). Through that root ~lātus~ is cognate with English ~tolerate~ and ~extol~, and the family shows up in Portuguese ~trasladar~ and Italian ~traslatare~.

The image beneath ~trasladar~ is purely physical — to lift something and carry it across — and Spanish keeps that literal weight: one ~traslada~ an office, a prisoner, a body, or a holiday to another date. Because ~trānslātus~ also meant “carried over” in a figurative sense, the same Latin stem gave ~traslado~ (“transfer, removal”) and ~traslación~ / ~translación~ (the Earth's orbital motion, and also figurative or metaphorical language — a meaning literally “carried across”). English ~translate~ is the very same word: where Spanish carried bodies from place to place, English carried meaning between tongues.
en.tratar:
From Latin ~tractāre~ (“to drag about, handle, manage, deal with”), the frequentative of ~trahere~ (“to draw, drag, pull”), which is perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰregʰ-~ (“to draw, pull”), though ~trahere~’s deeper origin is uncertain. Cognate with Italian ~trattare~, French ~traiter~, and Portuguese ~tratar~; through the same Latin verb English acquired ~treat~, ~treaty~, and ~tract~, and through ~trahere~’s participle ~tractus~, English ~trace~, ~trait~, and ~portray~.

A frequentative names repeated or intensive action, so ~tractāre~ was “to keep dragging or handling,” and from physical handling grew the ideas of managing an affair, dealing with people, and discussing a subject — the whole spread of Spanish ~tratar~. To ~tratar a alguien~ is to treat someone (well or badly); ~tratar de~ means both “to try to” and “to be about”; and ~tratarse de~ means “to be a question of.” The inherited verb ~traer~ (“to bring”) descends from the very same ~trahere~ by the popular route, a doublet of learned ~tratar~. From this root also flow ~trato~, ~tratado~, ~tratamiento~, ~retrato~, ~contrato~, ~atraer~, and ~tracción~.
en.ubicar:
From Latin ~ubi~ (“where”), through a Late/Medieval Latin verb *~ubicāre~ and the noun ~ubicātiō~ (“a locating, position”). ~ubi~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European interrogative-relative stem *~kʷo-~ (as in ~quis~, “who”) and is parallel to Latin ~ibi~ (“there”). Unlike most Spanish verbs, ~ubicar~ was not inherited from spoken Latin but built on a Latin adverb — a learned coinage, long especially current in American Spanish.

To ubicar is, literally, to answer the question “where?” — to fix a thing’s place. From the same ~ubi~, plus the enclitic ~-que~, Latin formed ~ubīque~ (“everywhere”), which gave Spanish ~ubicuo~ (“ubiquitous”) and ~ubicuidad~; ~ubicuidad~ began life as a theological term for God’s presence everywhere. English ~ubiquitous~ descends from the same ~ubīque~, and everyday ~ubicación~ shares the verb’s root. The homely adverb “where” thus underlies a small, learned family.
en.unir:
From Latin ~ūnīre~ (“to unite, join into one”), derived from ~ūnus~ (“one”). ~ūnus~ comes from Old Latin ~oinos~, from Proto-Italic *~oinos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~óynos~ (“one, single”). The same root gave English ~one~, ~an~ and ~only~, German ~ein~, and Greek ~oínē~ (the “one” on a die). Among cognate Romance forms are Italian ~unire~, Portuguese ~unir~ and French ~unir~; English ~unite~ is a learned borrowing of the same Latin verb.

The Latin verb was built straightforwardly from the numeral: to ~unir~ is to make things ~ūnus~, one. Because the notion of oneness is so basic, its descendants spread everywhere in Spanish — ~uno~, ~unión~, ~unidad~, ~único~, ~universo~ (literally “turned into one”), ~reunir~ and ~unánime~ (“of one mind”). Even the humble ~onza~ and English ~ounce~ trace back to ~ūnus~ through ~uncia~, a “single” twelfth part. Few roots pack so much of a language’s vocabulary into one small word for “one.”
en.usar:
From Vulgar Latin ~ūsāre~, a frequentative built on ~ūsus~, the past participle of Latin ~ūtī~ (“to use, employ, make use of”). The deeper origin of ~ūtī~ is uncertain: it has been tentatively linked to Proto-Indo-European *~h₃eyt-~ (“to take along, fetch”), but the connection is disputed and far from secure. Cognate Romance descendants include Italian ~usare~, Portuguese ~usar~ and French ~user~; English ~use~ came through Old French ~user~ from the same Vulgar Latin verb.

Latin already used ~ūtī~ very broadly — to employ, enjoy, or associate with something — and the frequentative ~ūsāre~ simply meant to do so habitually, which is why Spanish ~usar~ covers everyday “using” of every kind. The participial stem ~ūsus~ is the productive one in Spanish: ~uso~, ~usar~, ~usado~, ~usuario~, ~usual~ and ~abusar~ (“to misuse”) all grow from it, as do the learned ~útil~ (“useful”) and ~utilizar~ from the related adjective ~ūtilis~. Even English ~utensil~ shares that adjective — a thing fit to be used.
en.utilizar:
A relatively modern formation, from the adjective ~útil~ (“useful”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-izar~, and closely paralleling French ~utiliser~ (whence it likely took its impulse in the nineteenth century). ~útil~ descends from Latin ~ūtilis~ (“useful, serviceable”), from ~ūtī~ (“to use, make use of”), a verb of uncertain origin with no secure Proto-Indo-European etymology. Cognate through Latin with Italian ~utilizzare~, Portuguese ~utilizar~, and English ~utilize~ and ~utility~.

The chain is short but instructive: from ~ūtī~ “to use” Latin built the adjective ~ūtilis~ “usable,” Spanish inherited it as ~útil~, and only later did the language forge a verb from the adjective with ~-izar~, giving a slightly bookish ~utilizar~ beside the older, plainer ~usar~ (from Latin ~ūsāre~, itself a frequentative of ~ūtī~ through its participle ~ūsus~). The two coexist, ~utilizar~ often carrying a shade of “to put to use, make instrumental use of.” From the same ~ūtī~ come ~útil~, ~utilidad~, ~inútil~, ~utensilio~, ~uso~, ~usar~, and ~usual~, and the borrowed ~utilitario~ (“utilitarian”).
en.valer:
From Latin ~valēre~ (“to be strong, be healthy, be worth”), from Proto-Indo-European *~welh₁-~ (“to be strong, to rule”). It is cognate with Italian ~valere~, French ~valoir~, and Portuguese ~valer~; through the same root it is kin to the Latin-derived English ~value~, ~valid~, and ~prevail~, and to the Germanic ~wield~, which kept the “rule, be powerful” side of the root.

In Latin ~valēre~ ran from “to be physically strong” to “to be well” to “to be worth,” and Spanish ~valer~ inherited the whole span. The imperative ~valē~ (“be well!”) served the Romans as a parting word, and its descendant survives in the colloquial Spanish ~vale~ — an all-purpose “OK, agreed” heard across Spain. The root seeded a broad family: ~valor~ (“worth, courage”), ~válido~, ~valiente~ and ~valentía~, ~equivaler~, ~evaluar~, and ~prevalecer~. Even the proper name ~Valerio~ traces back to this same idea of strength and worth.
en.valorar:
From ~valor~ (“worth, value”), from Late Latin ~valor~, a noun built on Latin ~valēre~ (“to be strong, to be worth”). ~valēre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~walēō~ and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂welh₁-~ (“to rule, to be strong”). Cognate with Italian ~valere~ and Portuguese ~valer~, and — through the same root — with English ~value~ and ~valiant~ and the given name ~Valerie~.

The root's core idea is strength, and Spanish kept both branches of it: to be worth something and to be physically able. ~valer~ still means “to be worth,” while the derived ~valorar~ specialized as “to appraise, to assign a value” and, more recently, “to esteem, to appreciate.” A person of ~valor~ shows courage — strength of character — while an object of ~valor~ has monetary worth; the two senses share one Latin heart. The same root seeded a broad family of Spanish words: ~valiente~ (“brave”), ~válido~ (“valid”), ~valía~ (“worth”), ~equivaler~ (“to be equivalent”), ~prevalecer~ (“to prevail”), and ~convalecer~ (“to convalesce,” literally to grow strong again). Even the everyday interjection ~¡vale!~ (“okay!”) is the same verb, meaning literally “it is worth, it holds.”
en.variar:
From Latin ~variāre~ (“to diversify, change, make various”), from the adjective ~varius~ (“variegated, spotted, of different kinds”). The origin of ~varius~ is unknown. De Vaan records a tentative link to a Proto-Italic *~wasios~ shared with ~vafer~ (“crafty, sly”), and separately weighs — and rejects as unconvincing — a derivation from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁weh₂-~ said to lie behind ~vārus~ (“bent, bow-legged”), ~vānus~ (“empty”), and ~vāstus~ (“vast”). No proposal has cognates outside Italic to anchor it, so the deep root is genuinely open. What is clear is the near end of the chain: Spanish ~variar~, French ~varier~, Italian ~variare~, and English ~vary~ all rest transparently on ~variāre~.

The oldest sense of ~varius~ was visual — “mottled, many-colored, dappled,” a coat or a marble of mixed hues — and from “displaying different colors” the notion generalized to “differing, changing,” which is what ~variar~ carries today: to vary, change, or differ. The Spanish family is large and plain: ~variedad~ (“variety”), ~varios~ (“several, various”), ~variable~, ~variación~, ~variante~, and ~invariable~. English shares the whole learned set — ~variety~, ~various~, ~variation~ — and the medical ~varicose~, from Latin ~varix~ (“a dilated vein”), is often linked to this same cluster, though that connection, like the root itself, is not firmly established. A word for endless change turns out to have an endlessly uncertain past.
en.vencer:
From Latin ~vincere~ (“to conquer, defeat”), from Proto-Italic *~winkō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~weyk-~ (“to fight, conquer, overpower”). Cognate with Italian ~vincere~, French ~vaincre~ and Portuguese ~vencer~, and — through Latin — with English ~victor~, ~convince~, ~evince~ and ~invincible~. The Old Irish ~fichid~ (“fights”) springs from the same root.

Latin ~vincere~ ranged from winning battles to winning arguments, and Spanish ~vencer~ kept both, adding a quieter sense: a debt or deadline ~vence~ when it “falls due,” as if time had overcome it. From the same root come ~victoria~, ~vencedor~, ~invencible~, ~convencer~ and ~vencimiento~. A ~convicto~ is, etymologically, one thoroughly ~vencido~ in court.
en.vender:
From Latin ~vēndere~, a fusion of the phrase ~vēnum dare~ (“to give for sale”), from ~vēnum~ (“sale, that which is for sale”) plus ~dare~ (“to give”). ~vēnum~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~wes-~ (“to buy, sell”), and ~dare~ to *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Romance kept the compound intact: Italian ~vendere~, French ~vendre~, Portuguese ~vender~.

Latin welded a two-word phrase — “give for sale” — into a single verb, whose passive twin ~vēneō~ meant “to be sold,” literally “to go to sale.” What ~vender~ carries is a deep commercial vocabulary: the ~vēnum~ element (“price, sale”) is cognate with Ancient Greek ~ὦνος~ (“price”) and Sanskrit ~vasná~ (“price”), showing how old the idea of a fixed price is. From it Spanish keeps ~venta~ (“sale”), ~vendedor~, and ~venal~ (“that can be bought, corruptible”), while ~dare~ seeds another vast family, beginning with ~dar~ (“to give”).
en.venir:
From Latin ~venīre~ (“to come”), from Proto-Italic *~gʷeniō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to come, go, step”). This is one of the great Indo-European roots: it gave English ~come~ (through Germanic), Ancient Greek ~baínō~ (“to walk, step”) and Sanskrit ~gácchati~ (“goes”). Cognate Romance verbs include Italian ~venire~, Portuguese ~vir~ and French ~venir~; English ~venue~ is Old French ~venue~, literally “a coming.”

The Latin sense “to come” passed intact into Spanish ~venir~, and the verb’s prefixed compounds became a workshop of vocabulary in both Latin and Spanish. From ~venīre~ Spanish draws ~venida~ (“arrival”), ~porvenir~ (“future,” literally “what is to come”), ~convenir~ (“to suit, agree” — to “come together”), ~intervenir~, ~prevenir~ (“to prevent,” to “come before”) and ~aventura~ (“adventure,” from ~adventūra~, “things about to come”). Through Latin the same root reaches English ~advent~, ~convene~, ~invent~ and ~revenue~ — a striking spread from one small word for “to come.”
en.ver:
Spanish ~ver~ comes, through Old Spanish ~veer~, from Latin ~vidēre~ (“to see”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~weyd-~, which meant both “to see” and “to know” — for the ancients, to have seen a thing was to know it. That double sense survives in the Germanic cousins: English ~wit~ and ~wise~, and German ~wissen~ (“to know”), all from the same root, as is Greek ~idéa~ (“form, idea”). The Romance reflexes stayed on the “see” side: French ~voir~, Italian ~vedere~.

Latin ~vidēre~ kept mainly the visual sense, and Spanish inherited it whole, down to the irregular participle ~visto~ (“seen”). The root spreads through a family of looking and seeming: ~vista~ (“sight, view”), ~visión~ (“vision”), ~evidente~ (“evident,” what is plainly seen), ~prever~ (“to foresee”), ~revisar~ (“to review”), and ~aviso~ (“notice, warning”). Modern ~vídeo~ — Latin for “I see” — joins the same ancient family, the newest branch on a very old root of seeing.
en.vestir:
From Latin ~vestīre~ (“to clothe, to dress”), a verb from ~vestis~ (“garment, clothing”). ~vestis~ descends from Proto-Italic *~westis~ and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~wéstis~, from the root *~wes-~ (“to clothe, to wear”). Spanish ~vestir~ continues the Latin verb by regular popular descent. It is cognate with Italian ~vestire~, French ~vêtir~, and Portuguese ~vestir~, and — through the same PIE root — with English ~wear~ and with Gothic ~wasti~ (“garment”).

The root *~wes-~ is among the oldest clothing words in Indo-European, surfacing in Sanskrit ~vaste~ (“he puts on”) and Ancient Greek ~esthḗs~ (“clothing”). Latin ~vestīre~ meant simply to put clothes on someone or something, and Spanish ~vestir~ keeps that sense plainly — one dresses a child, and figuratively a landscape may be “dressed” in green. A memorable derivative is ~investir~ (~investidura~, “investiture”): to invest someone with office is, etymologically, to clothe them in the robes of authority, and English “invest” drew its financial sense from that same image of putting resources into new garb. Other relatives include ~vestido~ (“dress”), ~vestuario~ (“wardrobe”), ~revestir~ (“to coat”), and ~travestir~ (“to cross-dress”).
en.viajar:
From ~viaje~ (“journey, trip”), a noun Spanish borrowed from Old Occitan and Catalan ~viatge~, from Latin ~viāticum~ — originally the “provisions or money for a journey,” a neuter use of the adjective ~viāticus~, from ~via~ (“way, road”). The verb ~viajar~ was then built on ~viaje~ with the ordinary ending ~-ar~. The deeper origin of ~via~ is debated: it goes back to Proto-Italic *~wiā~, and has often been tied to the Proto-Indo-European root *~weyh₁-~ (“to pursue, go after”), though this connection is rejected by some scholars. Latin ~viāticum~ also gave Portuguese ~viagem~, Italian ~viaggio~, and French ~voyage~.

The semantic path runs from a thing to a journey: ~viāticum~ named the supplies a traveler carried, then the trip itself, and finally ~viajar~ came to mean simply “to travel.” A striking turn happened in Church Latin, where ~viāticum~ was applied to the Eucharist given to the dying — provisions for the last journey of all — a sense English keeps in the word ~viaticum~. From the same ~via~ Spanish inherited ~vía~ (“track, way”), ~enviar~ (“to send,” from ~inviāre~, “to put on the road”), ~desviar~ (“to divert”), ~extraviar~ (“to lose, mislay”), and ~trivial~ (from ~trivium~, the “meeting of three roads,” hence commonplace).
en.vincular:
From Latin ~vinculāre~ (“to bind, fetter”), from ~vinculum~ (“a bond, cord, chain”), itself ~vincīre~ (“to bind”) plus the instrumental suffix ~-ulum~. The verb ~vincīre~ goes back through Proto-Italic to a Proto-Indo-European root of winding and binding, reconstructed as *~weyk-~ (“to bend, wind”), which appears in Latin in a nasal-infixed shape (as if *~wi-n-k-~). Care is needed here: this ~vincīre~ (“to bind”) is a different verb from the near-identical ~vincere~ (“to conquer”), and the two should not be run together. Romance kept the “bind” family as a learned borrowing — Italian ~vincolare~, and the Spanish pair below — rather than as an inherited word worn down by centuries of speech.

Because it entered Spanish through the written, legal, and scholarly register rather than everyday talk, ~vincular~ kept the clean shape of its Latin source and much of its literal force: to bind one thing to another. In older law a ~vínculo~ was the entail that tied an estate permanently to a family line, and to this day ~vincular~ means to link, connect, or make binding — legally, emotionally, or logically. Its negative ~desvincular~ (“to disconnect, sever ties”) is now everywhere in talk of data and relationships. The parent noun ~vinculum~ even survives untranslated in English as a technical term — the overline drawn across grouped symbols in mathematics, and a band of connective tissue in anatomy. The living Spanish family stays small and transparent: ~vínculo~, ~vincular~, ~desvincular~, ~vinculación~ (“linkage, bond”).
en.visitar:
From Latin ~vīsitāre~ (“to go to see often, visit”), a frequentative of ~vīsere~ (“to go to see, behold”), which was itself built on the past-participle stem of ~vidēre~ (“to see”). The chain reaches back to Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”). Spanish ~visitar~ is cognate with Italian ~visitare~, French ~visiter~, Portuguese ~visitar~ and English ~visit~; through the deep root *~weyd-~ it is also kin to English ~wit~ and ~wise~, to the borrowed ~video~, and to Greek ~idéā~.

The frequentative is the whole story: ~vidēre~ is simply “to see,” ~vīsere~ is “to set out to see,” and ~vīsitāre~ piles the iterative on top — “to go and see, again and again.” That habitual, repeated going is exactly what a visit still is. In Latin the verb also meant to go and inspect, and from there came the sense of an official ~visita~ and the medical or pastoral house-call. From the same root *~weyd-~ Spanish inherited a rich seeing-and-knowing family: ~ver~ (“to see”), ~vista~ (“sight”), ~visión~, ~visible~, ~visitante~ and the borrowed ~vídeo~.
en.vivir:
From Latin ~vīvere~ (“to live”), from Proto-Italic *~gʷīwō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷeyh₃-~ (“to live”). The root is deeply Indo-European: it gave Old English ~cwic~ (“alive”), source of modern English ~quick~ (which once meant “living,” as in “the quick and the dead”), and Ancient Greek ~bíos~ (“life”). Cognate Romance verbs include Italian ~vivere~, Portuguese ~viver~ and French ~vivre~; English ~vivid~ and ~revive~ borrow the Latin verb directly.

Latin ~vīvere~ meant simply “to be alive,” and Spanish ~vivir~ inherited both that and the richer “to dwell, to spend one’s life.” Its family is full of life in every sense: ~vida~ (“life,” from ~vīta~), ~vivo~ (“alive, lively”), ~vívido~, ~vitalidad~, ~convivir~ (“to live together”), ~sobrevivir~ (“to survive,” to “over-live”) and ~víveres~ (“provisions,” the things that keep one living). Through the Greek cognate ~bíos~ the same idea underlies ~biología~, so that a Spanish speaker’s ~vida~ and a biologist’s ~bio-~ meet in one Indo-European root.
en.volver:
From Latin ~volvere~ (“to roll, turn, revolve”), from Proto-Italic *~welwō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~welH-~ (“to turn, wind, roll”). The same root turns up in Greek ~helíssō~ (“to roll, wind”) and ~hélix~, in Old English ~wealwian~ (source of English ~wallow~), and — by way of French — in English ~vault~. Among Romance kin are Italian ~volgere~ and Portuguese ~volver~; the learned English ~revolve~ borrows the Latin compound directly.

Latin ~volvere~ described a rolling or turning motion, and Spanish ~volver~ kept the “turn” while adding the everyday sense “to return,” as if one turned back the way one came. The idea of turning runs through its family: ~volver~ a hacer algo is to “turn” to doing it again, a ~vuelta~ is a turn or lap, ~revolver~ is to stir (and gave English the ~revolver~, whose cylinder turns), and ~volcar~ (“to overturn”) descends through a Vulgar Latin *~volvicāre~. Further out sit ~volumen~ (originally a rolled scroll), ~revolución~ and ~envolver~ (“to wrap, en-roll”).
en.votar:
From Latin ~vōtum~ (“a vow, solemn promise, offering to the gods”), the neuter past participle of ~vovēre~ (“to vow, pledge”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁wegʷʰ-~ (“to vow, promise solemnly”). The root surfaces in Ancient Greek ~εὔχομαι~ (“I pray, I vow”) and Sanskrit ~vāghát~ (“one who makes an offering”). English took the noun as the borrowings ~vote~ and, by way of French, ~vow~.

A vote began as a prayer: ~vōtum~ was what you promised a god in exchange for a favor, then an earnest wish, and only later a formal expression of will in an assembly — the political sense the verb now carries. The most charming descendant hides the sacred origin entirely: the Latin plural ~vōta~ (“the vows”) passed through Old Spanish into ~boda~ (“wedding”), so a Spanish wedding is, etymologically, a bundle of vows.
